title: 3  Anatomy of a Multirotor: Frames, Motors, and Propulsion
text:
3.6 Motors
Almost every flying multirotor uses a brushless outrunner. The stationary inner stator carries three sets of copper windings on a laminated iron core; the rotating outer bell carries permanent magnets. Energizing the windings in sequence pulls the magnets around, and because the windings are the stationary part, they can be cooled and driven without any sliding contact. Brushed motors are cheaper and simpler and survive only on toys, because brushes wear, arc, and cap efficiency well below what the same mass of brushless machine achieves.
The commutation sequence is the ESC’s job, and it requires knowing where the rotor is. Some motors report position with Hall-effect sensors; most drone motors omit them and infer position from the back-EMF waveform on the undriven phase, which is why a sensorless drone motor stutters at startup — there is no back-EMF until it is already turning.

3.6.1 Reading a motor designation
A label such as 2812 900KV encodes three numbers. The first two digits, 28, are the stator diameter in millimetres. The next two, 12, are the stator height. Together they specify the volume of the magnetic circuit and therefore the continuous torque available before the copper overheats: a 2812 has substantially more iron and copper than the 2207 typical of a 5-inch racing aircraft, and vastly more than the 0802 of an indoor micro. The third number, 900KV, is the speed constant.






Figure 3.3: What a motor designation labels. The size digits measure the stationary stator — a 2812 has a 28 mm stator diameter and a 12 mm lamination-stack height — while the permanent magnets ride on the rotating outer bell, separated from the stator by the air gap, and the shaft turns with the bell on two bearings. The KV figure describes the winding wound onto that stator, not any dimension of it.



Figure 3.3 locates all three numbers on the machine itself: the first two describe the stationary stack of iron and copper, and the third describes the winding wound onto it.
KV is not a power rating and it is not a quality rating. It is a winding property: the number of turns per phase determines how much back-EMF the machine generates per unit of rotational speed, and KV is the reciprocal of that constant expressed in convenient units. Rewinding a given stator with fewer turns of thicker wire raises KV and lowers torque per amp in exact proportion. Two motors with the same stator and different KV values contain the same iron and produce very nearly the same power; they simply divide it differently between speed and torque.
That reciprocal relationship is quantitative. If \(K_V\) is given in RPM per volt, the torque constant in SI units is
\[K_t = \frac{60}{2\pi K_V}\ \ \left[\frac{\text{N}\cdot\text{m}}{\text{A}}\right],\]
which for the 900KV motor is \(K_t = 60/(2\pi \cdot 900) = 0.0106\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m/A}\). A 450KV motor built on the same stator would deliver 0.0212 N·m/A — twice the torque per amp, at half the speed per volt.


3.6.2 Worked example: 900KV on a 6S pack
Take the 2812 900KV motor and a six-cell lithium-polymer battery, and follow the calculation all the way through.
Step 1 — battery voltage. A 6S pack is six cells in series. Nominal cell voltage is 3.7 V, so the pack is quoted at \(6 \times 3.7 = 22.2\ \text{V}\). Fully charged it sits at \(6 \times 4.2 = 25.2\ \text{V}\), and at the practical discharge floor of 3.5 V per cell it delivers \(6 \times 3.5 = 21.0\ \text{V}\). “6S” therefore names a voltage range of about 21 to 25 V, and the nominal figure is a convention for comparison, not a measurement.
Step 2 — no-load speed. By definition, KV is the shaft speed per volt of back-EMF with nothing on the shaft:
\[
\begin{aligned}
N_0 &= K_V \cdot V = 900\ \frac{\text{RPM}}{\text{V}} \times 22.2\ \text{V} \\
    &= 19{,}980\ \text{RPM} \approx 20{,}000\ \text{RPM}.
\end{aligned}
\]
On a freshly charged pack the same motor spins at \(900 \times 25.2 = 22{,}680\) RPM, and on a nearly exhausted one at \(900 \times 21.0 = 18{,}900\) RPM. A 20 % speed variation across a single flight is built into the chemistry, and it is one reason flight controllers close a loop on measured attitude rather than commanding motor speeds open-loop.
Step 3 — what happens under load. The no-load figure is never reached in flight, for two separate reasons that are often conflated. The first is the motor’s own resistance. In steady state the applied terminal voltage splits between back-EMF and the resistive drop, \(V = E + IR\), and the shaft speed tracks the back-EMF alone, \(N = K_V E = K_V(V - IR)\). Suppose the propeller loads this motor to 12 A and the effective winding resistance is \(R = 0.08\ \Omega\). Then the drop is \(IR = 0.96\) V, the back-EMF is \(E = 22.2 - 0.96 = 21.24\) V, and
\[N = 900 \times 21.24 = 19{,}116\ \text{RPM},\]
about 4 % below no-load. Shaft power is the back-EMF power, \(P_{\text{shaft}} = EI = 21.24 \times 12 = 255\ \text{W}\), against an electrical input of \(VI = 22.2 \times 12 = 266\ \text{W}\); the missing \(I^2R = 144 \times 0.08 = 11.5\ \text{W}\) is heat in the copper. This first-order model omits iron and windage losses, so its implied efficiency is optimistic — measured peak efficiency for a motor of this class is nearer 80–85 % — but the structure is right, and it shows that resistive droop alone is a small effect.
The second and much larger reason is throttle. The ESC does not apply the full pack voltage except at maximum throttle; at partial throttle it applies a reduced effective voltage, and the motor settles wherever the torque it produces equals the torque the propeller absorbs. That equilibrium is the intersection of two curves — a motor curve, torque falling linearly with speed, and a propeller curve, absorbed torque rising as roughly the square of speed. A 10-inch propeller in hover, computed in the next section, holds a motor near 5,400 RPM, nowhere near any no-load figure. The no-load speed is a ceiling, useful for checking that a motor and battery are compatible at all, not a prediction of flight behaviour.
Step 4 — sanity-check the propeller against that speed. Nearly 20,000 RPM is \(\omega = 19{,}980 \times 2\pi/60 = 2092\ \text{rad/s}\). On a 5-inch propeller (radius 0.0635 m) the blade tip travels at \(2092 \times 0.0635 = 133\ \text{m/s}\), Mach 0.39 at sea level — fast, noisy, and acceptable. Put a 10-inch propeller (radius 0.127 m) on the same motor and the tip speed becomes \(2092 \times 0.127 = 266\ \text{m/s}\), Mach 0.78, where compressibility destroys the blade section’s lift-to-drag ratio and the noise becomes intolerable. The motor would never actually reach that speed, because the torque a 10-inch propeller absorbs at high RPM far exceeds what this winding can supply, so in practice it would stall the motor thermally instead. This is the whole content of the familiar rule that high KV pairs with small propellers and low KV with large ones: KV must be chosen so that the speed the battery can drive is the speed the propeller wants.
The design consequence runs in the other direction too. Suppose a 10-inch propeller must turn at a hover speed of 5,400 RPM on a 4S pack (14.8 V nominal). A motor of \(5{,}400/14.8 \approx 365\) KV would reach that speed only at full throttle, leaving no authority to climb or to reject a gust. Hover should instead sit near 40 to 50 % of the available throttle range, which means choosing a KV roughly twice as high — 730 to 900 KV, exactly the familiar rating for this propeller class. An 880KV motor confirms the arithmetic: at 5,400 RPM its back-EMF is \(5{,}400/880 = 6.1\) V, so the ESC is applying about 41 % of the pack voltage and the remaining 59 % is headroom. Move the same aircraft to a 6S pack and the equivalent motor is a \(900 \times 14.8/22.2 = 600\) KV unit, which draws two-thirds the current for the same mechanical power. Since copper loss goes as \(I^2R\), that is a \((2/3)^2 = 0.44\) factor — a 56 % reduction in resistive heating — which is precisely why larger and more serious aircraft run higher pack voltages. Voltage is free; current is expensive, in copper, in connector mass, and in ESC silicon.

title: 3  Anatomy of a Multirotor: Frames, Motors, and Propulsion
text:
3.7 Propellers
The propeller is a rotating wing, and its two headline numbers are diameter and pitch, both quoted in inches. A designation such as 10 × 4.5 means a 254 mm diameter and a 4.5-inch geometric pitch; a three-number form such as 5 × 5 × 3 adds the blade count, here three blades. Figure 3.4 lays the three numbers out on the geometry itself.






Figure 3.4: What a propeller designation labels. Diameter is the tip-to-tip span of the swept disc; pitch is the axial distance the blade’s helical path would advance in one revolution through a solid medium, with no slip; and a third number, when present, gives the blade count.



Diameter determines how much air the disc can act on, and by the momentum result above it is the dominant efficiency lever. Pitch is the theoretical axial advance per revolution — the distance the propeller would screw forward through a solid — and it sets the blade’s built-in angle of attack and thus the airspeed at which the blade stops working. Multiply pitch by rotational speed and the result is pitch speed, a hard theoretical ceiling on forward flight:
\[v_{\text{pitch}} = \text{pitch} \times N.\]
A 4.5-inch (0.1143 m) pitch at 9,000 RPM (150 rev/s) gives \(0.1143 \times 150 = 17.1\ \text{m/s}\), about 62 km/h; real aircraft achieve 60 to 70 % of pitch speed, because the blade needs a positive angle of attack to make thrust at all and reaches zero thrust before the theoretical limit. The dimensionless form of the same statement is the advance ratio \(J = v/(nD)\), which for that propeller at 15 m/s is \(J = 15/(150 \times 0.254) = 0.39\), uncomfortably close to the pitch-to-diameter ratio \(4.5/10 = 0.45\) at which thrust vanishes.
Blade count is the third lever. More blades add thrust in a given diameter but at worse efficiency, because each blade flies in its predecessor’s wake. Racing aircraft, which are propeller-diameter-limited by their frames and care about response rather than endurance, use three or more blades; endurance aircraft use two.
For quantitative work, thrust and shaft power come from empirically measured non-dimensional coefficients:
\[T = C_T \rho n^2 D^4, \qquad P = C_P \rho n^3 D^5,\]
with \(n\) in revolutions per second and \(D\) in metres. Both coefficients are specific to a propeller and rise strongly with pitch-to-diameter ratio: a 10 × 4.5 survey propeller (\(P/D = 0.45\)) has \(C_T\) near 0.10, while an aggressive 5 × 5 racing tri-blade (\(P/D = 1.0\)) may be two to three times higher. They are measured on a thrust stand, not derived, and manufacturers publish them alongside thrust tables — which is why component selection for a real aircraft is a table-lookup exercise anchored by the scaling laws rather than a pure calculation.
Those scaling laws are nonetheless the ones to internalize. At fixed RPM, thrust scales as \(D^4\) and power as \(D^5\); at fixed thrust, induced power scales as \(D^{-1}\). Doubling propeller diameter therefore halves the power needed to hover — the single most effective efficiency change available to a designer, and the reason every endurance-driven design pushes propellers to the largest size the frame, the regulations, and the transport case will allow.

section: 3.8 Putting It Together: Sizing a Research Quadcopter
text:
3.8 Putting It Together: Sizing a Research Quadcopter
The components only make sense together, so consider the platform the running example actually flies: a 500 mm-wheelbase quadcopter of the Holybro X500 V2 class, carrying a Pixhawk 6C flight controller, a companion computer, and a depth camera. That configuration is examined as a system in the Systems Architecture chapter in Part V; here the question is narrower — do the numbers work?
Mission requirements. Hover-capable, because the mission is to loiter over and pursue a target on the ground rather than to cover a corridor; 12 to 15 minutes of usable flight time; roughly 500 g of autonomy payload; and a total mass low enough to stay far below the 25 kg regulatory threshold that the Commercial Drone Landscape chapter identified as the dividing line for small uncrewed aircraft.
Configuration. Hover rules out a fixed wing despite the roughly fourfold endurance advantage computed at the start of this chapter. The redundancy argument for six rotors does not apply over an unpopulated test area, and the added mass, wiring, and cost would degrade every other figure. A quadcopter it is — chosen deliberately, over the hexacopter and fixed-wing alternatives, because maneuverability and simplicity are what the mission needs.
Mass budget. Frame, motors, ESCs, and wiring come to roughly 1.2 kg for a platform of this class; a 4S 5200 mAh lithium-polymer pack adds about 0.5 kg; autonomy payload adds 0.5 kg. Take the aircraft first without payload, at \(m = 1.7\) kg, and add the payload afterwards to see what it costs.
Propeller and disc loading. The frame accommodates 10-inch propellers with 100 mm of tip clearance, as computed earlier, so \(D = 0.254\) m and the disc area per rotor is \(A = \pi (0.127)^2 = 0.0507\ \text{m}^2\). Hover thrust per rotor is
\[T = \frac{mg}{4} = \frac{(1.7)(9.81)}{4} = 4.17\ \text{N},\]
a disc loading of \(4.17/0.0507 = 82\ \text{N/m}^2\), which is typical for this class. The figure matters because induced velocity, and therefore the power spent, grows as its square root: a rotor lifting the same weight over ten times the disc area would move the air an order of magnitude more gently and spend \(1/\sqrt{10} = 0.32\) — about a third — of the power. Small multirotors have poor endurance because they are forced by their own size into high disc loading.
Ideal hover power. From momentum theory, with \(\rho = 1.225\ \text{kg/m}^3\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_i &= \sqrt{\frac{4.17}{2(1.225)(0.0507)}} = \sqrt{33.6} = 5.80\ \text{m/s}, \\
P_{\text{ideal}} &= (4.17)(5.80) = 24.2\ \text{W}
\end{aligned}
\]
per rotor, or 96.7 W for the aircraft. That is the aerodynamic floor: no propeller of this diameter, however well designed, can hover this mass for less, because the number counts only the kinetic energy left in the wake and ignores every real loss.
Real shaft power. Invert the thrust coefficient to find the rotational speed the hover thrust demands. With \(C_T = 0.10\) and \(D^4 = 4.16 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^4\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
n &= \sqrt{\frac{T}{C_T \rho D^4}} = \sqrt{\frac{4.17}{(0.10)(1.225)(4.16\times10^{-3})}} \\
  &= \sqrt{8180} = 90.4\ \text{rev/s} = 5{,}425\ \text{RPM},
\end{aligned}
\]
which is the 90 Hz excitation frequency quoted in the frame-vibration discussion above. Shaft power at that speed, with \(C_P = 0.05\) and \(D^5 = 1.057\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^5\), is
\[P = (0.05)(1.225)(90.4)^3(1.057\times10^{-3}) = 47.9\ \text{W}\]
per rotor, 192 W for the aircraft. The implied figure of merit is \(24.2/47.9 = 0.51\), squarely in the expected range for a small propeller and a useful check that the coefficients and the momentum estimate are mutually consistent.
Electrical power and endurance. Motor and ESC efficiency together are about 80 % at this operating point, giving \(192/0.80 = 240\ \text{W}\) of electrical draw, plus roughly 12 W for the flight controller, receiver, telemetry radio, and companion computer — call it 252 W. A 4S 5200 mAh pack stores \(14.8 \times 5.2 = 77\ \text{Wh}\), of which about 80 % should be used if the cells are to survive many cycles, so 61.6 Wh is available. Hover endurance is
\[t = \frac{61.6\ \text{Wh}}{252\ \text{W}} = 0.244\ \text{h} = 14.7\ \text{min}.\]
That figure matches published flight times for platforms of this class, which is the point of doing the calculation: a first-principles estimate that lands within a minute or two of the manufacturer’s number confirms that the model captures what matters, and can therefore be trusted when the configuration changes.
The payload penalty. Now add the 500 g autonomy payload, taking the aircraft to 2.2 kg. Shaft power scales as \(m^{3/2}\) at fixed disc area, so
\[P' = 192 \times \left(\frac{2.2}{1.7}\right)^{3/2} = 192 \times 1.47 = 282\ \text{W},\]
electrical draw becomes \(282/0.80 + 12 = 365\ \text{W}\), and endurance falls to \(61.6/365 = 0.169\ \text{h} = 10.1\ \text{min}\). A 29 % increase in mass costs 31 % of the flight time. This is the payload-versus-endurance curve in one line of arithmetic, and it is why every gram on a research aircraft is contested: the companion computer’s heatsink, the length of the camera cable, and the choice between two connectors all appear eventually as seconds of loiter time.
Motor, ESC, and battery selection. Motors of the 2216-class turning a 10 × 4.5 propeller on 4S are rated at roughly 1.0 kgf of static thrust at about 20 A each, so the four together give about 4.0 kgf against a 2.2 kg loaded aircraft — a thrust-to-weight ratio of 1.8, marginal, and against the 1.7 kg unloaded aircraft a ratio of 2.35, adequate. Hover consumes only \(0.425/1.0 \approx 43\ \%\) of available thrust unloaded, which leaves genuine control authority for gust rejection and aggressive attitude commands; a ratio near 1.8 with payload is the point at which a designer should be looking at either larger motors or a lighter payload before adding anything else. Full-throttle current is about 20 A per motor, so 30 A ESCs give a comfortable margin, and a 4-in-1 ESC board is preferred because it halves the wiring mass and puts all four current paths on one plane with one battery connection. Peak battery draw is \(4 \times 20 = 80\ \text{A}\), which for a 5.2 Ah pack is a discharge rate of \(80/5.2 = 15\ \text{C}\) — well inside the 50 C rating typical of packs in this size, so the battery is chosen for its energy rather than its power.
What the numbers decided. Every choice above traces to the mission statement: hover capability forced a rotorcraft, the endurance requirement forced the largest propeller the frame would carry, propeller diameter and pack voltage jointly forced the motor KV, motor current forced the ESC rating, and the payload mass — the only part of the aircraft that exists for the mission rather than for flight — consumed a third of the endurance. That is mission-driven design in its actual form: not a slogan, but a chain of arithmetic in which each link constrains the next.
Two links in that chain were taken on trust. The arms were assumed stiff enough to hold the rotor discs where the geometry says they are, and the pack was assumed to deliver the energy printed on its label. Neither assumption is aerodynamic — the first belongs to materials and the second to chemistry — and both fail in ways that show up as bad flights rather than as bad numbers. They are where the next chapter begins.






NoteFor More



The momentum-theory model used here is the simplest of a family. Blade-element momentum theory divides the blade into radial elements, applies two-dimensional aerofoil data to each, and integrates, which predicts how thrust and power vary with pitch distribution, blade planform, and Reynolds number rather than taking \(C_T\) and \(C_P\) as measured constants. It is the right tool for asking whether a propeller is well designed rather than merely how a given propeller performs. Readers pursuing endurance optimization should also study the Reynolds-number problem specific to small propellers: at 10-inch scale the blade sections operate near \(\mathrm{Re} \sim 10^5\), where laminar separation bubbles dominate and standard aerofoil data taken at \(\mathrm{Re} \sim 10^6\) substantially overpredicts performance. This is the single largest source of error when scaling published propeller data down to small aircraft.

title: 3  Anatomy of a Multirotor: Frames, Motors, and Propulsion
text:
3.9 Check Your Understanding

A motor is labelled 2207 2400KV and is run on a 4S lithium-polymer pack. What is its no-load speed at nominal voltage, at full charge, and at the discharge floor? What do the digits 2207 tell you that the KV rating does not?







TipShow answer





A 4S pack is 14.8 V nominal, 16.8 V fully charged (\(4 \times 4.2\)), and 14.0 V at a 3.5 V-per-cell floor. No-load speeds are \(2400 \times 14.8 = 35{,}520\) RPM, \(2400 \times 16.8 = 40{,}320\) RPM, and \(2400 \times 14.0 = 33{,}600\) RPM respectively. The digits 2207 give the stator’s physical size — 22 mm diameter, 7 mm height — which sets how much iron and copper carry the magnetic circuit and therefore the continuous torque available before thermal limits bite. KV describes only how the winding trades speed against torque; it says nothing about how much of either the motor can sustain. Two motors can share a KV rating and differ by a factor of three in continuous power.




Explain why a 900KV motor and a 10-inch propeller is a poor pairing, using a quantitative argument rather than the rule of thumb.







TipShow answer





Take the pairing on a 6S pack. No-load speed is \(900 \times 22.2 = 19{,}980\) RPM, or 2092 rad/s. On a 10-inch propeller (radius 0.127 m) the tip speed would be \(2092 \times 0.127 = 266\) m/s, Mach 0.78, where compressibility collapses the blade section’s lift-to-drag ratio. The motor never actually gets there, which is the real failure mode: absorbed propeller power scales as \(n^3 D^5\), so a 10-inch disc demands enormously more torque at any given speed than the winding of a 900KV motor — whose torque constant is only 0.0106 N·m/A — can supply without drawing currents that overheat the copper. The motor settles at a low speed, at high current, at poor efficiency, and gets hot. Correct pairings hold tip speed and absorbed torque in range simultaneously: 900KV suits 5-inch propellers, while a 10-inch propeller wants roughly 800–900KV on 4S or about 600KV on 6S.




A survey quadcopter has a 450 mm wheelbase. What is the largest propeller diameter it can physically swing, and what practical diameter would you actually fit?







TipShow answer





Adjacent motors on a symmetric X frame are separated by \(s = d/\sqrt{2} = 450/1.414 = 318\) mm. Propeller discs intersect once the diameter exceeds that spacing, so 318 mm (12.5 inches) is the absolute geometric limit and would leave the tips touching. In practice one wants tens of millimetres of clearance so that adjacent tip vortices do not interact and so that flexing arms cannot bring discs together in flight: a 9-inch propeller (229 mm) leaves 89 mm of clearance and a 10-inch (254 mm) leaves 64 mm, either of which is sensible; 11 inches (279 mm) leaves 39 mm and is aggressive. Fit 10-inch propellers.




An aircraft of 1.4 kg all-up weight hovers on four 8-inch propellers. Estimate its ideal induced hover power, and state how that figure would change if the same mass were carried on four 10-inch propellers.







TipShow answer





Thrust per rotor is \(T = (1.4)(9.81)/4 = 3.43\) N. An 8-inch propeller has radius 0.1016 m and disc area \(A = \pi(0.1016)^2 = 0.0324\ \text{m}^2\). Then \(v_i = \sqrt{3.43/(2 \times 1.225 \times 0.0324)} = \sqrt{43.2} = 6.57\) m/s and \(P_{\text{ideal}} = 3.43 \times 6.57 = 22.5\) W per rotor, or 90 W total. On 10-inch propellers (\(A = 0.0507\ \text{m}^2\)), induced power scales as \(A^{-1/2}\), so the total falls by a factor of \(\sqrt{0.0324/0.0507} = 0.80\) to about 72 W — a 20 % saving for a 25 % increase in diameter, consistent with \(P \propto 1/D\) at fixed thrust. The saving is only realizable if the frame can accommodate the larger discs and if the motors are re-selected to a lower KV; swapping propellers alone would overload the existing motors.




A hexacopter and a quadcopter each weigh 4 kg all-up and carry 10-inch propellers. State the induced-power advantage of the hexacopter, then explain why hexacopters are nonetheless not chosen for efficiency.







TipShow answer





Total disc area is \(6 \times 0.0507 = 0.304\ \text{m}^2\) against \(4 \times 0.0507 = 0.203\ \text{m}^2\). Induced power for a fixed total thrust scales as the inverse square root of total disc area, so the hexacopter needs \(\sqrt{0.203/0.304} = 0.82\) of the quadcopter’s induced power, an 18 % saving. But two extra motors, ESCs, arms, and wiring runs typically add 15–25 % to empty weight, and hover power scales as \(W^{3/2}\): a 20 % mass increase alone costs \(1.20^{1.5} = 1.31\), a 31 % power penalty that more than erases the aerodynamic gain. Hexacopters are selected for lift capacity and for graceful degradation after a rotor failure — where the remaining five each take \(6/5 = 1.2\) times their previous thrust share, though controllability is retained only by surrendering yaw control — not for efficiency.




The sized aircraft above draws 252 W in hover and achieves 14.7 minutes from a 77 Wh pack at 80 % usable capacity (61.6 Wh). A colleague proposes doubling battery capacity to double flight time. Evaluate the proposal.







TipShow answer





It does not work, because the battery is part of the mass that must be lifted. Doubling to a 4S 10400 mAh pack adds about 0.5 kg, taking all-up weight from 1.7 to 2.2 kg. Shaft power rises by \((2.2/1.7)^{3/2} = 1.47\) to 282 W, so electrical draw becomes \(282/0.80 + 12 = 365\) W. Usable energy doubles to 123 Wh, giving \(123/365 = 0.337\ \text{h} = 20.2\) minutes — a 37 % improvement, not 100 %. Continuing to add cells yields progressively less, and eventually nothing, since each increment of energy arrives attached to an increment of mass that consumes part of it; the optimum for a given airframe and chemistry falls at a battery mass fraction that is typically a third to a half of all-up weight. Real endurance gains come from larger propellers, lighter structure, or a different configuration entirely — which is the argument for a fixed wing when the mission does not require hover.

title: 3  Anatomy of a Multirotor: Frames, Motors, and Propulsion
text:
3.10 Try It
Specify a complete propulsion system for a mission of your own choosing, and defend every number in it.
Begin by writing one sentence stating what the aircraft must do, then convert it into four quantities: payload mass, required endurance, required cruise or loiter speed, and the maximum dimension that fits your transport case. Choose a configuration from those four figures and justify it explicitly against the two alternatives you rejected — if you choose a quadcopter, say what the hexacopter’s redundancy would have bought and why the mission does not need it; if you choose a fixed wing, say what you give up by not being able to hover.
Then size the system in the order the physics dictates. Pick the largest propeller diameter your frame span allows, computing adjacent-motor spacing as wheelbase divided by \(\sqrt{2}\) and leaving real tip clearance. Estimate all-up weight, compute hover thrust per rotor, and use momentum theory to get ideal induced power. Assume a figure of merit between 0.45 and 0.55 to convert that to shaft power, then a combined motor-and-ESC efficiency of about 0.8 to get electrical draw, and add an avionics allowance. Choose a pack voltage — justify 4S against 6S using the \(I^2R\) argument — and size its capacity for your endurance target, remembering that only about 80 % is usable. Select KV so that the propeller’s hover speed sits comfortably below no-load speed at your pack voltage, size the ESCs from full-throttle current with margin, and check thrust-to-weight against the 2:1 minimum.
Finally, run the sensitivity that separates a design from a wish. Add 200 g to your payload and recompute endurance using the \(m^{3/2}\) scaling. If the loss is tolerable, your design has margin; if it is not, identify which single change — a larger propeller, a lighter frame material, a different configuration — recovers the most flight time per gram or per dollar. That question, not the initial specification, is where real design begins.

title: 4  Materials and Power: Structural Choices and LiPo Battery Management
text:
4.1 Learning Objectives
Two components of a drone are consumed by the act of flying it. The airframe is consumed in crashes — every development program breaks arms, cracks plates, and strips mounts, and the rate at which it does so is a design parameter, not an embarrassment. The battery is consumed by chemistry — every charge cycle, every deep discharge, and every week spent sitting on a shelf at the wrong state of charge takes an irreversible bite out of its capacity. Both consumables are routinely mismanaged for the same reason: the practical rules (“carbon fiber is stiff but shatters,” “store LiPos at half charge”) circulate widely, while the physics that generates the rules does not, so the rules get applied mechanically and fail exactly at the edge cases the physics would have caught.
This chapter supplies the physics behind both sets of rules. The first half takes the material comparison sketched at the end of the Anatomy of a Multirotor chapter — plastic, aluminium, carbon fiber, arranged in a suspiciously tidy table of trade-offs — and develops it quantitatively: what specific stiffness and specific strength actually are, why a laminate fails differently from a printed part, and how to decide, with arithmetic rather than folklore, when a frame component should be carbon and when it should come off a 3D printer. The second half opens up the lithium-polymer cell itself: what sets its voltage, what is physically happening inside a cell stored full or stored empty, and why the storage-charge window of 3.80 to 3.85 V per cell is not a superstition but a chemically motivated optimum with margin you can compute.

text:
Compare carbon-fiber composite and 3D-printed thermoplastics (PLA, ABS, nylon) as airframe materials using specific stiffness and specific strength, and compute the mass penalty of matching a carbon part’s bending stiffness in printed plastic.
Describe the dominant failure mode of each material class — brittle fracture and delamination for carbon laminate, layer separation for printed parts — and derive the print-orientation and design rules that follow.
Explain, at the level of electrode potentials and side reactions, why a LiPo cell degrades when stored fully charged (electrolyte oxidation, gas generation, swelling) and why it is destroyed by over-discharge (copper current-collector dissolution and subsequent internal shorting).
Specify a correct storage-charge range in volts per cell and state of charge, and justify it quantitatively from calendar-ageing data and self-discharge arithmetic.
Use internal resistance as a battery health metric: measure it from voltage sag under a known load, and compute the heating and usable-voltage consequences of its growth as a pack ages.

title: 4  Materials and Power: Structural Choices and LiPo Battery Management
text:
4.2 Key Vocabulary

Strength-to-weight ratio (specific strength) — a material’s failure stress divided by its density, in kJ/kg when stress is in MPa and density in g/cm³. It ranks materials for structures whose mass budget, not whose volume, is the binding constraint — which is every airborne structure.
Specific stiffness — elastic modulus divided by density, in MJ/kg. For aircraft structure it usually matters more than specific strength, because frames fail their mission by flexing (vibration, resonance, sensor corruption) long before they fail by breaking.
Layer separation (delamination) — the characteristic failure mode of fused-filament 3D-printed parts, in which the part splits along the weld planes between deposited layers. Interlayer welds are diffusion bonds formed in the seconds before the plastic cools, and typically reach only 30–70 % of the bulk material’s strength.
LiPo (Lithium Polymer battery) — a lithium-ion cell built as a laminated foil pouch with a gel-polymer electrolyte, rather than as a rigid metal cylinder. The pouch format saves case mass and permits very high discharge currents, at the price of no mechanical protection: a LiPo that generates internal gas visibly swells.
Cell voltage — the potential difference between a cell’s cathode and anode, itself a function of state of charge: 4.20 V fully charged, 3.7 V nominal, roughly 3.5 V at the practical in-flight floor, and 3.0 V at the damage threshold below which over-discharge chemistry begins.
State of charge (SoC) — the fraction of a cell’s rated capacity currently stored, inferred in practice from resting voltage via the cell’s discharge curve.
Storage charge — the state of charge at which a LiPo should be kept when not in use for more than a few days: roughly 50–60 % of capacity, corresponding to about 3.80–3.85 V per cell.
Internal resistance — the effective series resistance of a cell, typically a few milliohms when new. It sets the voltage sag under load and the internal heating rate, rises irreversibly as the cell ages, and is the single most useful measurable indicator of pack health.
C rating — a battery’s rated continuous discharge current expressed as a multiple of its capacity: a 5.2 Ah pack rated 50C may deliver \(50 \times 5.2 = 260\) A continuously. Physically it is a claim about internal resistance and heat rejection, not a separate property.
Thermal runaway — the self-accelerating failure of a lithium cell in which internal heating drives exothermic decomposition reactions that generate more heat, culminating in venting or fire. It is the hazard that dictates fireproof charging and storage containers.

text:
4.3 The Materials Problem

4.3.1 What the frame is being asked to do
The Anatomy of a Multirotor chapter established the frame’s three jobs — carry the rotor loads into the vehicle’s mass, hold the propeller discs in fixed relative geometry, and keep the airframe’s structural resonances away from the propellers’ 90 Hz and 180 Hz excitation bands so the inertial sensors report vehicle motion rather than frame flex. All three jobs are stiffness jobs before they are strength jobs. A frame that is strong enough not to break but too compliant to hold its geometry produces oscillating attitude estimates, hot motors, and unexplained short flights; a frame that is stiff enough rarely turns out to be the one that breaks in normal flight. Breakage happens in crashes, which is a separate design case with its own logic.
That framing dictates the two figures of merit. For a component whose mass is contested — and on an aircraft every gram is contested, at the exchange rate the payload-endurance calculation in the previous chapter established — materials are compared per kilogram, not per cubic centimetre. Specific stiffness \(E/\rho\) governs the flying structure; specific strength \(\sigma/\rho\) governs crash survival and highly loaded fittings.

Across the layers, printed strength falls to 30–70 % of these figures — a point developed below, because it is the single most important fact about printed structure.






Figure 4.1: The materials table drawn to scale. Left: specific stiffness, which governs the flying structure. Right: specific strength, which governs crash survival and fittings. On both axes the gap between carbon laminate and the printed thermoplastics is an order of magnitude, while aluminium sits close to quasi-isotropic carbon — the composite pulls decisively ahead only when its fibers are oriented along the load.



Two readings of the table matter, and Figure 4.1 draws both of them to scale. First, the gap between carbon and the printed thermoplastics is not an increment but an order of magnitude: even the pessimistic quasi-isotropic laminate carries ten times the specific stiffness of PLA. Second, aluminium sits close to quasi-isotropic carbon in specific stiffness — the composite’s decisive advantage appears only when the layup is oriented to put fibers along the load, which is exactly what a frame arm (a cantilever in bending, fibers along its length) allows. This is why carbon dominates drone frames rather than aluminium: not because aluminium is bad, but because a tube or plate loaded in a known direction lets the designer spend the fibers where the stress is.


4.3.2 What the stiffness gap costs in practice
The gap can be converted into mass. Suppose a frame arm must reach a given bending stiffness \(EI\) — the product that sets both its deflection under thrust and its resonant frequency. For a solid rectangular section of fixed width, \(I \propto t^3\), so matching a carbon plate’s \(EI\) in PLA requires a thickness ratio of
\[\frac{t_{\text{PLA}}}{t_{\text{CF}}} = \left(\frac{E_{\text{CF}}}{E_{\text{PLA}}}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\frac{50}{3.5}\right)^{1/3} = 2.4,\]
and the mass ratio is that thickness ratio times the density ratio: \(2.4 \times (1.24/1.6) = 1.9\). An equally stiff printed arm is roughly twice the mass — and since hover power scales as mass to the three-halves, the aircraft pays for that in flight time forever. Alternatively, print the arm at the same geometry and accept the stiffness loss: a cantilever’s first resonant frequency scales as \(\sqrt{E/\rho}\) at fixed geometry, so the printed arm’s first mode falls by a factor of \(\sqrt{31/2.8} \approx 3.3\) — typically from comfortably above the blade-passing excitation to squarely inside the band the propellers excite. Neither option is free; that is why flying primary structure is carbon on essentially every serious airframe.


4.3.3 How each material fails
Carbon laminate fails by fracture and delamination, without warning. A carbon-epoxy laminate is elastic to failure: it reaches perhaps 1–1.5 % strain and then breaks, releasing all the stored energy at once. There is no yield, no bend, no visible warning. In a crash this means an arm either survives intact or snaps — the material cannot absorb impact energy by deforming plastically the way a metal or a tough polymer does. Carbon also fails unpleasantly: fracture surfaces are sharp, splinters are genuinely hazardous to handle, and cutting or sanding carbon releases conductive dust that should be kept out of lungs and electronics alike. Damage short of fracture is more insidious. An impact can delaminate the plies — separate the layers internally — leaving a part that looks intact, measures the right dimensions, and has lost a large fraction of its stiffness and strength. A tap test (delaminated regions sound dull rather than ringing) or flex comparison against a known-good part is part of any competent post-crash inspection.
One more property matters on a flying robot: carbon fiber conducts electricity. A carbon plate behaves as a lossy ground plane, and the Anatomy chapter’s warning about antennas follows directly — GNSS, radio-control, and telemetry antennas mounted flush against carbon are detuned and shadowed, which is why receivers ride on standoffs and antenna tubes on real airframes. The conductivity also means a frayed carbon edge can short an exposed pad, and that carbon dust inside an electronics bay is a slow-motion electrical fault.
Printed parts fail by layer separation, and orientation is destiny. A fused-filament part is a stack of extruded beads welded to their neighbours by heat and time. Within a layer, the plastic approaches its bulk strength; between layers, the weld is a partial diffusion bond formed in the few seconds before the interface cools below the glass transition, and it typically reaches only 30–70 % of bulk strength. A printed part is therefore an anisotropic laminate with its weak planes set by whichever orientation it was printed in — and unlike a carbon layup, where the designer orients fibers along the load, a careless print orients the weak planes wherever the slicer found convenient. The design rule is mechanical common sense once the mechanism is visible: orient the part so that tensile and bending stresses lie within the layer planes, never across them, and treat any load path that must cross layers as operating at roughly half strength. Fillet every corner, because layer lines plus a sharp corner is a crack-starter kit.






Figure 4.2: Three failure modes. A carbon laminate is elastic until it fractures — or delaminates internally after an impact while still looking intact. Aluminium yields: the bend is the warning, and the plastic deformation absorbs energy. A fused-filament part splits along its interlayer weld planes, which reach only 30–70 % of bulk strength.



Figure 4.2 puts the three behaviours side by side: the laminate that snaps or delaminates without warning, the metal that bends visibly before it breaks, and the printed part whose weakest planes sit wherever the slicer put them.
The three common filaments then differentiate on toughness and temperature. PLA prints easily and stiffly but is brittle and, critically, has a glass-transition temperature near 60 °C — a black PLA part on a dashboard, in a parked car, or in direct summer sun will warp under no load at all, which disqualifies it from anything structural that lives outdoors. ABS trades printability for a glass transition near 105 °C and much better toughness. Nylon is the least stiff of the three but extraordinarily tough — elongation at break over 100 % — which makes it the choice for parts that must survive impact by deforming: landing-gear feet, camera mounts, propeller guards. Carbon-filled nylon splits the difference, roughly doubling stiffness while keeping useful toughness, and has become the default serious filament for printed drone fittings.


4.3.4 Choosing: a cost model instead of a slogan
The source material frames the decision as premium-durable versus cheap-replaceable, and the frame is right; it just needs numbers attached. For any crash-exposed component, compare the expected cost per incident, not the purchase price. A carbon arm might cost $15 and survive, say, nine out of ten hard landings; a printed arm costs $0.50 in filament and three hours of unattended printer time and might survive half of them. The printed arm is cheaper per crash if the program can tolerate the downtime and the arm’s mass and stiffness penalties — which, per the arithmetic above, flying structure cannot, but brackets, mounts, and guards can. Hence the hybrid rule that every experienced builder converges on and that this book’s build lab applies directly:

Flying primary structure — arms, centre plates: carbon laminate. Stiffness is the mission.
Fittings and crash structure — camera mounts, companion-computer trays, landing gear, antenna masts, sensor housings: printed, in ABS or (carbon-)nylon, oriented with the load in the layer plane. Iteration speed is the mission; a bracket that took three hours to print and gets redesigned twice a week is a feature of the development process, not a compromise.
Threaded and precision interfaces — motor mounts on larger craft, standoffs: aluminium, because machinability and thread strength in a small volume beat both alternatives.

Prototyping deserves the last word: a printed version of a carbon part, flown gently, answers fit and packaging questions in a day for pennies, and the carbon part is then cut once, correctly. The materials are not rivals; they are stages of the same workflow.

title: 4  Materials and Power: Structural Choices and LiPo Battery Management
section: 4.4 The Power Problem: Living with Lithium Polymer
text:
4.4 The Power Problem: Living with Lithium Polymer

4.4.1 What a LiPo cell is
Every pack discussed in this book is a series string of lithium-polymer cells — the “S rating” of the previous chapter. Each cell is a flat laminated-foil pouch containing a layered sandwich: a cathode of lithium metal oxide (lithium cobalt oxide, LiCoO₂, or a nickel-manganese-cobalt blend) coated on aluminium foil; an anode of graphite coated on copper foil; a microporous polymer separator between them; and an organic carbonate electrolyte, gelled into a polymer matrix — the “polymer” in the name. Charging pumps lithium ions out of the metal-oxide lattice, across the separator, and into the graphite, where they intercalate between carbon planes; discharge runs the shuttle in reverse and drives the external circuit. Nothing is consumed in the ideal cycle — the same lithium inventory shuttles back and forth — and everything that permanently degrades the cell is a side reaction that steals lithium, electrolyte, or electrode material from that inventory.
The pouch construction is why LiPo dominates drones. Without a steel can, the cell reaches pack-level specific energy around 150–200 Wh/kg (the previous chapter’s 0.5 kg, 77 Wh pack sits at 154 Wh/kg, a useful cross-check) and, more importantly, very low internal resistance per unit mass, which is what high-discharge flight loads demand. The same construction is why a degrading LiPo visibly swells: there is no rigid case to hide the gas.


4.4.2 Voltage and state of charge
A cell’s voltage is the difference between its two electrode potentials, each set by how much lithium the electrode currently holds. The resting voltage therefore maps to state of charge — the curve of Figure 4.3: 4.20 V at 100 %, a long shallow plateau through the middle of the discharge — roughly 3.85 V near 55–60 %, 3.7 V around a quarter — and then a steep knee below about 3.5 V, where the remaining few percent drain away with the voltage falling fast. Three consequences of that curve shape run through all battery practice. First, voltage is a usable fuel gauge only because the mapping is repeatable — but only at rest; under load the reading is depressed by internal resistance, which is why in-flight voltage alarms are set conservatively. Second, the flatness of the plateau means most of the flight happens within a couple of tenths of a volt, so the 20 % speed variation per cell voltage computed in the previous chapter is concentrated at the ends of the flight. Third, the steep knee is why the practical floor is ~3.5 V per cell: below it there is almost no energy left to collect, and the damage threshold at 3.0 V is minutes away at flight loads.






Figure 4.3: The resting-voltage fuel gauge. The mapping from state of charge to resting cell voltage, with the thresholds the chapter’s battery rules use: 4.20 V full, the long shallow plateau through the middle, 3.7 V near one-quarter charge, the knee at roughly 3.5 V, the 3.0 V damage threshold — and the 3.80–3.85 V storage window at 50–60 % state of charge sitting between the two failure regimes.





4.4.3 Why storing a cell full degrades it
At full charge the cell is at its maximum chemical stress in both directions at once. The cathode is maximally delithiated — at a cell voltage of 4.20 V it sits near 4.3 V versus lithium, right at the oxidative stability limit of the carbonate electrolyte — and the graphite anode is maximally lithiated, sitting within a tenth of a volt of lithium metal itself and hungry to reduce anything that touches it. Both interfaces therefore run continuous parasitic side reactions: the electrolyte slowly oxidizes at the cathode surface and is slowly reduced into ever-thickening interphase layers at the anode. These reactions consume electrolyte and cyclable lithium (permanent capacity loss), thicken the interface films (rising internal resistance), and — the visible symptom — generate gaseous products, chiefly CO₂ and CO, which inflate the pouch. A “puffed” LiPo is the exhaust of its own electrolyte decomposition, and the puffing is doubly harmful: beyond marking lost capacity, the gas layer physically separates electrode from separator, lengthening the ionic path and raising resistance further.
Both reaction families are thermally activated and accelerate with state of charge, which is why the damage is a strong function of how full and how warm the cell sits. Typical published calendar-ageing measurements make the point numerically: a cell stored fully charged at room temperature loses on the order of 20 % of its capacity in a year, against roughly 4 % for the same cell stored near half charge — and both figures roughly double for each 10–15 °C of storage temperature. A charged pack left in a hot car combines the worst of both axes. The practical rule — charge shortly before flying, not days ahead — is this chemistry read backwards.


4.4.4 Why storing a cell empty destroys it
The empty end fails by a different and nastier mechanism. A cell landed at the ~3.5 V floor holds only a few percent of its capacity, and self-discharge does not stop at zero percent: the same parasitic reactions keep nibbling, and with the discharge curve’s knee already passed, the voltage now falls quickly and keeps falling. Below about 3.0 V per cell the cell enters territory its chemistry cannot tolerate. As the graphite gives up its last lithium, the anode’s potential climbs — and once it climbs to roughly 3.1 V versus lithium, the copper foil the anode is coated on becomes electrochemically unstable and begins to dissolve into the electrolyte as copper ions. This is not a metaphor: the current collector itself corrodes away.
The damage is twofold and irreversible. Capacity is lost outright, because the interphase layers and dissolution products consume lithium inventory that can never be recovered. Worse, a copper-contaminated cell is dangerous to recharge: charging drives the dissolved copper ions to plate back out as metallic copper wherever the field concentrates — including as filaments through the separator’s pores — creating internal micro-shorts. A micro-shorted cell self-discharges rapidly, heats internally, and is a thermal-runaway candidate sitting on a bench. This is why the correct disposition for a pack found deeply over-discharged after storage is disposal, not a “recovery charge,” whatever the charger’s recovery mode offers: the 3.0 V threshold is not where the battery stops working, it is where recharging it stops being safe. The familiar story of a pack that “stopped functioning after long-term storage” is this mechanism playing out in a drawer: a pack put away nearly empty drifts under 3.0 V within weeks, and every week below the threshold dissolves more copper.


4.4.5 The storage-charge window, justified
The two failure modes bracket an optimum. Full storage maximizes parasitic reaction rates; empty storage courts the copper cliff. The window in between — roughly 50–60 % state of charge, a resting voltage of about 3.80–3.85 V per cell (15.2–15.4 V for a 4S pack, 22.8–23.1 V for 6S; the shaded band in Figure 4.3) — is chosen to sit well down from the oxidative stress of the full cathode while banking a large energy margin above the damage threshold. The margin is worth computing, because it is the part of the rule people doubt. Take the book’s 5200 mAh pack, stored at 3.85 V per cell, about 55 % SoC — 2860 mAh in the bank. LiPo self-discharge runs on the order of 1–2 % of rated capacity per month, 52–104 mAh. Merely reaching the 20 % mark — still entirely healthy — means losing the difference between the 2860 mAh on hand and 20 % of capacity (1040 mAh), i.e. 1820 mAh, which takes \(1820/104 \approx 17\) months even at the pessimistic rate; reaching genuine danger takes years. Now run the same arithmetic for a pack tossed in the drawer as it came back from its last flight, resting near 3.5 V with perhaps 5 % — 260 mAh — remaining: at 52–104 mAh per month it is fully empty within a few months and dropping through 3.0 V soon after. The storage rule is not fussiness; it is the difference between a shelf life measured in years and one measured in weeks. Every mainstream hobby charger has a storage mode that charges or discharges the pack to this window automatically; ending a flying day by putting every pack into storage mode is the single highest-value battery habit there is.
Where the pack sits matters too, because the failure it guards against is thermal. Cool storage slows every parasitic reaction (the same Arrhenius factor working in your favour); dry storage protects the pouch laminate and connectors; and a fire-resistant container — a LiPo bag or steel ammunition box, vented rather than sealed, because containment must not become a pressure vessel — bounds the consequences if a damaged cell does run away. A cell in thermal runaway is its own oxidizer and cannot be starved like an ordinary fire; the container’s job is to keep one pack’s failure from propagating to the shelf above it.


4.4.6 Internal resistance: the health gauge
Everything that ages a cell — interphase growth, electrolyte loss, gas separation, copper contamination — shows up in one measurable number: internal resistance. It is measured from Ohm’s law with the pack as its own instrument: read the resting voltage, apply a known load, read the sag. A healthy modern 5 Ah pouch cell measures a handful of milliohms; call it 5 mΩ. Consider what happens as that triples to 15 mΩ — a typical end-of-life figure — on the aircraft sized in the previous chapter, whose four motors draw 80 A at full throttle.
At 80 A, the healthy cell sags \(80 \times 0.005 = 0.40\) V and dissipates \(80^2 \times 0.005 = 32\) W of internal heat; across a 4S pack, 1.6 V and 128 W. Ugly but sustainable for the seconds a full-throttle climb lasts. The aged cell sags \(80 \times 0.015 = 1.2\) V — from a 3.7 V plateau down to 2.5 V under load, deep past any voltage alarm — and dissipates 96 W per cell, 384 W per pack — against roughly 800 W actually delivered to the motors (\(4 \times 2.5\ \text{V} \times 80\ \text{A}\)), so nearly a third of the chemical power the pack produces is now cooking the pack itself. The symptoms pilots report — the pack that “sags,” triggers failsafes on punch-outs, comes back warm, and shows fine resting voltage — are all this one parameter. In hover the same aircraft draws about 17 A (\(252\ \text{W} / 14.8\ \text{V}\)), where even the aged pack sags only 0.26 V per cell, which is why a dying pack flies gentle missions convincingly and fails exactly when full performance is demanded. The C rating now reads as what it always was: a manufacturer’s claim that internal resistance is low enough to sustain a stated current — \(50\text{C} \times 5.2\ \text{Ah} = 260\) A for the book’s pack against an 80 A worst case — and the reason that rating erodes with age is that the resistance underneath it grows.
A battery log — pack serial, cycle count, per-cell internal resistance at each charge, post-flight resting voltages — costs a minute per flight and converts battery management from anecdote to data. Retirement criteria then stop being arguments: a pack leaves service when internal resistance has roughly tripled from new, when any cell puffs visibly or holds a resting voltage persistently out of balance with its siblings, or after any excursion below 3.0 V per cell, regardless of how it seems to perform afterwards.
Structure and chemistry between them settle what the aircraft can carry and how long it can stay up. They say nothing about what it knows while it is up there — and a frame stiff enough to keep its resonances clear of the rotors was, in the argument above, valuable mainly because of what it does for a sensor. Those sensors are the subject of the next chapter.






NoteFor More



Two variations on the chemistry appear in drone work. LiHV cells shift the charge cutoff from 4.20 to 4.35 V per cell, buying roughly 10 % more energy per gram at the direct cost of intensified high-voltage electrolyte oxidation — the calendar-ageing penalty of this chapter’s “stored full” section, purchased deliberately, cycle after cycle. They suit racing, where packs live hard and die young, and are a poor trade for endurance platforms. In the opposite direction, endurance-oriented builds increasingly use cylindrical Li-ion cells (18650/21700 format), which reach ~250 Wh/kg at cell level — well above pouch LiPo — but with internal resistance too high for aggressive discharge: a fine trade at a survey platform’s steady 2–3C hover draw, a disqualifying one for anything that needs punch. The selection logic is this chapter’s internal-resistance arithmetic with different inputs, which is the point: chemistry choices, like material choices, are the same trade study with the same handful of numbers.

title: 4  Materials and Power: Structural Choices and LiPo Battery Management
text:
4.5 Check Your Understanding

A colleague proposes 3D-printing replacement frame arms in PLA at the same dimensions as the carbon originals, arguing that PLA is “strong enough” since the arms rarely break in flight. Using \(E_{\text{CF}} = 50\) GPa, \(E_{\text{PLA}} = 3.5\) GPa, evaluate the proposal on the correct figure of merit.







TipShow answer





Strength is the wrong figure of merit — arms are sized by stiffness, for geometry-holding and for keeping structural resonances above the propellers’ excitation. At identical geometry, a cantilever’s first resonant frequency scales as \(\sqrt{E/\rho}\): with \(E/\rho\) of 31 MJ/kg for quasi-isotropic carbon against 2.8 MJ/kg for PLA, the printed arm’s first mode drops by a factor of \(\sqrt{31/2.8} \approx 3.3\), likely landing inside the 90–180 Hz band the propellers excite, corrupting the IMU and destabilizing the attitude loop. Matching the carbon arm’s bending stiffness instead requires \((50/3.5)^{1/3} = 2.4\) times the thickness, and \(2.4 \times (1.24/1.6) \approx 1.9\) times the mass — roughly doubling arm mass on an aircraft whose hover power scales as \(m^{3/2}\). Additionally, PLA’s ~60 °C glass transition disqualifies it outdoors in summer sun. Print the camera bracket; buy the carbon arm.




A 6S pack will not be flown for three weeks. State the storage voltage for the whole pack, the approximate state of charge it represents, and the two failure mechanisms the storage window is positioned between.







TipShow answer





Storage is 3.80–3.85 V per cell, so \(6 \times 3.80\) to \(6 \times 3.85\) = 22.8–23.1 V for the pack, about 50–60 % state of charge. The window sits below the high-SoC regime — where the near-4.3 V (vs. lithium) cathode continuously oxidizes electrolyte, generating gas (puffing), consuming lithium inventory, and raising internal resistance — and far above the low-SoC cliff, where self-discharge drags the cell below 3.0 V and the anode potential rises high enough (~3.1 V vs. lithium) to dissolve the copper current collector. Three weeks at full charge is survivable but pointlessly costly; three weeks starting from a nearly empty pack could cross the 3.0 V threshold. Storage mode covers both.




Explain why a LiPo cell found at 2.6 V after winter storage should be disposed of rather than recharged, even if a charger’s “recovery mode” will accept it.







TipShow answer





Below about 3.0 V, the delithiated graphite anode’s potential climbs to the point (~3.1 V vs. lithium) where the copper foil it is coated on becomes electrochemically unstable and dissolves into the electrolyte as copper ions. Recharging then drives those ions to redeposit as metallic copper, including as filaments through the separator’s pores, creating internal micro-shorts. The cell may accept charge and read a normal voltage, but it will self-discharge abnormally, heat internally, and carries an elevated risk of thermal runaway during charge — precisely when it is on a bench, indoors, possibly unattended. The capacity lost to the excursion is also unrecoverable. Recovery mode can restore the voltage; it cannot un-dissolve the copper.




A cell rests at 3.75 V; under a 30 A load it reads 3.45 V. Compute its internal resistance and its internal heating at that load. The same cell measured 5 mΩ when new — what does the comparison tell you, and what would you check next?







TipShow answer





\(R = \Delta V / I = (3.75 - 3.45)/30 = 0.30/30 = 10\ \text{m}\Omega\); heating is \(I^2R = 900 \times 0.010 = 9\) W in this one cell at 30 A. Resistance has doubled from new — meaningful ageing, though short of the tripled-from-new retirement criterion. Next: measure every cell in the pack, not just one, because degradation is rarely uniform — a single outlier cell dominates pack sag and is the first to hit the under-load voltage floor; check per-cell resting voltages for balance drift and the pouch for the onset of swelling; and project the trend from the pack’s log. A pack at 2× resistance still flies, but it should be demoted from performance flights and watched.




A printed nylon landing-gear leg survives crashes that snap its carbon predecessor, yet this chapter assigns arms to carbon and only fittings to printing. Reconcile the two facts.







TipShow answer





The two parts have different jobs. An arm’s job is stiffness in normal flight — holding rotor geometry and keeping resonances above the excitation band — and there carbon’s order-of-magnitude specific-stiffness advantage is decisive; the arm is not supposed to absorb crash energy, and carbon could not do so anyway, being elastic to fracture at ~1 % strain. A landing leg’s job is the opposite: it exists precisely to absorb impact energy, which favours a tough material with large plastic strain — nylon’s elongation beyond 100 % lets it deform and recover or fail cheaply — and its stiffness barely matters. The general rule: match the material’s failure behaviour to the component’s role. Stiff and brittle for structure that must not flex; tough and compliant for structure that must survive abuse; and print the latter with load in the layer plane so layer separation is not the governing failure.




Using the calendar-ageing figures in this chapter, estimate the capacity remaining after one year for two identical packs: one stored fully charged on a sunny windowsill (averaging ~35 °C), one at storage charge in a cool basement (~15 °C). Assume ~20 %/year loss at 100 % SoC and ~4 %/year at storage charge, both at 25 °C, with rates doubling per 10–15 °C.







TipShow answer





The windowsill pack is stored full and roughly 10 °C above the reference, so its ~20 %/year loss roughly doubles to ~40 %: about 60 % of capacity remains, and the pack has likely also puffed and gained resistance — effectively ruined for flight loads. The basement pack is at storage charge and ~10 °C below reference, halving its ~4 %/year to ~2 %: about 98 % remains. The two habits differ by a factor of about twenty in annual degradation, which is the quantitative content of “storage charge, cool, dry.” (Both estimates are order-of-magnitude — the point is the ratio, not the decimals; self-discharge over the year is comfortably covered by the storage-charge margin computed in the chapter.)

text:
4.6 Try It
Part 1 — a materials decision, defended with numbers. Pick one crash-exposed component of a drone you have access to (or the book’s 500 mm-class platform): an arm, a camera mount, a leg, an antenna mast. Decide what its actual job is — stiffness, strength, or energy absorption — and choose a material with the table in this chapter, showing the specific-stiffness or specific-strength arithmetic. If you choose a printed part, state the print orientation and justify it from the load path and the layer-separation mechanism; estimate the cost and time per replacement against the carbon alternative, and state the crash rate at which each option wins. If a printer is available, print the part in two orientations — load in-plane and load across layers — and break both by hand: the difference you feel is the 30–70 % interlayer knockdown made tangible.
Part 2 — a battery standard operating procedure. Write a one-page battery SOP for a small drone program, and make every rule in it traceable to a mechanism from this chapter. It should specify: the storage window in volts per cell and why (both failure modes, with the self-discharge arithmetic for your pack’s actual capacity); when packs are charged relative to flights; the container and location for storage and charging; per-flight log fields (cycle count, per-cell internal resistance, post-flight resting voltages); and numeric retirement criteria (resistance multiple from new, balance drift, puffing, any sub-3.0 V excursion). Then take a real pack, measure its per-cell internal resistance from voltage sag under a known load, and start the log with an entry. A rule you can defend with a mechanism will survive contact with a busy flight line; a rule that is only a rule will not.

title: 5  Sensing the World: IMUs, Magnetometers, and Barometers
text:
5.1 Learning Objectives
The last two chapters followed energy through the aircraft: out of the pack, through the structure, and into the air. The Anatomy of a Multirotor chapter identified a second chain running alongside it — sensors \(\rightarrow\) flight controller \(\rightarrow\) ESC, closing an attitude loop at several hundred hertz — that carries information rather than power, and that chain begins with a word which has so far gone unexamined. Sensors. Everything the aircraft will ever know about its own orientation, rotation, heading, and height originates in a few grams of micromachined silicon soldered to the flight controller: an inertial measurement unit, a magnetometer, and a barometer. None of these devices measures what the autopilot actually wants. The accelerometer measures the deflection of a microscopic spring; the gyroscope measures energy leaking between two vibration modes; the magnetometer measures a field that the drone’s own power wiring pollutes; the barometer measures a pressure that the propellers themselves disturb. The quantity the control loops need — a smooth, drift-free estimate of the vehicle’s attitude and altitude — exists nowhere on the aircraft as a direct reading. It has to be constructed, at hundreds of times per second, from several noisy, biased, mutually disagreeing measurements.
This chapter follows the data from physics to estimate in three stages. First, what the sensors physically are: how a MEMS accelerometer and gyroscope convert motion into capacitance, why that transduction chain works as well as it does, and where its error sources live. Second, how the measurements get aboard: the two serial buses, I2C and SPI, that carry nearly every sensor stream in embedded robotics, and the bandwidth arithmetic that decides which sensor goes on which bus. Third, how disagreement becomes trust: the complementary filter, derived from the observation that the gyroscope and the accelerometer fail in exactly opposite ways, and the extended Kalman filter that production autopilots run in its place. The treatment is deliberately quantitative, because every rule of thumb in this domain — “gyros drift,” “don’t trust the accelerometer in a turn,” “put the IMU on SPI” — is an arithmetic conclusion wearing a slogan’s clothing.

Explain what a MEMS accelerometer and a MEMS gyroscope physically measure — proof-mass displacement against a flexure spring, and Coriolis coupling between two vibration modes — and why each output is an inference from Newton’s laws rather than a direct reading of motion.
Catalogue the principal IMU error sources (bias, bias instability, white noise specified as noise density, temperature drift, and vibration rectification), and compute the attitude error that results from integrating a given gyroscope bias over time.
Derive the complementary filter from the complementary failure modes of the gyroscope and accelerometer, implement it in a few lines of code, and choose its gain from a desired correction time constant.
Compare I2C and SPI as sensor buses — wire count, addressing, clock rate, duplex, and DMA compatibility — and use bandwidth arithmetic to justify the topology commonly found on flight controllers: IMU on SPI, magnetometer and barometer on I2C.
Convert a barometric pressure reading to altitude with the standard-atmosphere formula, estimate the sensor’s resolution in metres, and explain why propeller wash corrupts barometric altitude on a multirotor and what mitigations are used in practice.

title: 5  Sensing the World: IMUs, Magnetometers, and Barometers
text:
5.2 Key Vocabulary

MEMS (Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems) — the fabrication technology of etching microscopic mechanical structures — springs, masses, membranes — into silicon alongside the electronics that read them, which is what makes gram-scale, milliwatt-scale inertial sensors possible at consumer prices.
IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) — the packaged combination of a three-axis accelerometer and a three-axis gyroscope (sometimes with a magnetometer added, making nine axes), sampled together and timestamped as the primary input to attitude estimation.
Accelerometer — a sensor that measures specific force: the deflection of a spring-suspended proof mass relative to its housing. At rest it reads 1 g upward (the support force), in free fall it reads zero, and in unaccelerated hover its output vector points away from the Earth — which is precisely what makes it a usable gravity reference.
Gyroscope — a sensor that measures angular rate. MEMS gyroscopes drive a proof mass into resonant vibration and detect the Coriolis force that rotation couples into an orthogonal sense axis; the output is degrees per second, which must be integrated to yield an angle.
Magnetometer — a sensor measuring the local magnetic field vector, used to reference the vehicle’s heading (yaw) against the Earth’s field — the one attitude axis that neither the gyroscope nor the accelerometer can stabilize long-term.
Barometer — a pressure sensor built on a micromachined membrane over a sealed reference cavity, used to infer altitude from the roughly 12 Pa of pressure lost per metre of climb near sea level.
I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit, often written I²C) — a two-wire, shared, addressed serial bus: many devices on one data line and one clock line, each selected by a 7-bit address. Wiring-cheap and convenient at modest data rates (100 kbit/s standard, 400 kbit/s fast mode).
SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface) — a four-wire, full-duplex serial bus with a dedicated chip-select line per device and clock rates commonly in the tens of megahertz, the usual choice where a single sensor must be read fast and often.
Sensor fusion — the algorithmic combination of multiple imperfect sensors into one estimate better than any of them alone, by exploiting the fact that different sensors fail in different ways at different timescales.
Complementary filter — the simplest useful fusion algorithm for attitude: a weighted blend \(\hat\theta = \alpha(\hat\theta + \omega\,\Delta t) + (1-\alpha)\,\theta_{\text{accel}}\) that trusts the gyroscope at short timescales and lets the accelerometer’s absolute gravity reference slowly remove the gyroscope’s accumulated drift.
Noise density — a sensor’s white-noise floor normalized per unit bandwidth (e.g. µg/√Hz or °/s/√Hz); multiplied by the square root of the measurement bandwidth it predicts the RMS noise of the delivered signal, which is why low-pass filtering buys noise reduction at the price of latency.

title: 5  Sensing the World: IMUs, Magnetometers, and Barometers
section: 5.3 What the Flight Controller Must Know
text:
5.3 What the Flight Controller Must Know
The attitude control loops developed in Part II consume two quantities: the vehicle’s orientation (roll, pitch, yaw) and its angular rates, at update intervals of a few milliseconds. Altitude hold adds a third: height and vertical velocity. The sensor suite maps onto those needs with a deliberate redundancy — every quantity is observable through at least two different physical channels, and no single channel is good enough alone:

The gyroscope delivers angular rate directly, at kilohertz rates, with low noise — but an angle obtained by integrating rate inherits every error in the rate signal, accumulated without bound.
The accelerometer delivers the direction of gravity whenever the vehicle is not accelerating — an absolute, drift-free reference for roll and pitch — but it is noisy, and it is corrupted the moment the vehicle maneuvers, because it cannot distinguish gravity from the vehicle’s own acceleration.
The magnetometer delivers heading against the Earth’s magnetic field — the only absolute reference for yaw, since gravity is silent about rotation around the vertical — but the field it measures is weak (tens of microtesla) and easily polluted by the tens of amperes flowing through the drone’s own power wiring, which is why flight controllers commonly place the magnetometer on the GPS mast, as far from the battery leads as the airframe allows.
The barometer delivers altitude through pressure — absolute over minutes, but noisy over seconds and disturbed by the propellers’ own airflow.

The pattern to hold onto: each sensor is trustworthy at a timescale where another fails. That asymmetry is not a nuisance; it is the entire basis of sensor fusion, and the rest of the chapter builds toward exploiting it.

title: 5  Sensing the World: IMUs, Magnetometers, and Barometers
section: 5.4 The MEMS Accelerometer: A Spring Scale in Silicon
text:
5.4 The MEMS Accelerometer: A Spring Scale in Silicon
Mechanically, a MEMS accelerometer is a mass on a spring, etched into a silicon die. A proof mass of tens to hundreds of micrograms is suspended over the substrate by thin silicon flexures — meandering “serpentine” beams anchored to the fixed frame, compliant along the sensing axis and stiff across it. When the package accelerates, the proof mass, by Newton’s first law, initially stays put, so it displaces relative to the housing, stretching one flexure and compressing the other. The system is the classic mass-spring-damper:
\[m\ddot{x} + c\dot{x} + kx = ma,\]
where \(x\) is proof-mass displacement relative to the housing, \(a\) the applied acceleration, \(k\) the flexure stiffness, and \(c\) the damping — largely squeeze-film damping of the gas sealed in the package. Once transients settle, the steady-state displacement is
\[x \approx \frac{m}{k}\,a:\]
the structure converts acceleration into displacement at a fixed, known exchange rate set by geometry. Everything after this is readout. The dominant readout scheme in consumer and robotics-grade parts is capacitive: comb-shaped fingers attached to the proof mass interleave with fixed fingers anchored to the substrate, forming a differential capacitor pair. When the mass deflects, one air gap narrows and the other widens, so \(C_1\) rises as \(C_2\) falls; an on-die ASIC measures \(\Delta C = C_1 - C_2\), which is proportional to \(x\) and therefore to \(a\), then digitizes it and serves it over I2C or SPI. A three-axis part repeats the structure (or arranges electrodes to resolve three axes) on one die.






Figure 5.1: Simplified structure of a single-axis MEMS capacitive accelerometer, viewed from above. The proof mass is suspended by flexure springs anchored to the substrate; acceleration along the sense axis displaces the mass, narrowing one capacitive gap and widening the other, and the differential capacitance change is proportional to the applied acceleration.



Two consequences of this construction shape everything downstream. First, the accelerometer does not measure coordinate acceleration; it measures specific force — the net non-gravitational force per unit mass acting on the housing. A sensor at rest on a bench reads 1 g pointing up, because the bench pushes up on it; the same sensor in free fall reads zero, because mass and housing fall together and the spring relaxes. This is not a defect. It is exactly what makes the accelerometer a gravity reference: in unaccelerated flight, its output vector points opposite to gravity, and the roll and pitch angles can be recovered from its components by simple trigonometry. The corollary is equally important: during a hard maneuver, the vehicle’s own acceleration adds to that vector, and the “gravity direction” the accelerometer reports is simply wrong. A fusion algorithm must know when not to listen.
Second, the sensing element is a mechanical resonator with microscopic displacements — capacitance changes of femtofarads riding on picofarads. That makes the device sensitive to exactly the environment a multirotor provides: broadband mechanical vibration at the propeller rotation and blade-passing frequencies (about 90 and 181 Hz for the platform sized in the Anatomy chapter). Vibration does not merely add noise; through small nonlinearities in the transduction it can rectify into a false DC offset — an effect examined below — which is why IMU mounting, discussed in the Materials and Power chapter’s stiffness arguments, is a flight-quality issue and not a packaging afterthought.

title: 5  Sensing the World: IMUs, Magnetometers, and Barometers
section: 5.5 The MEMS Gyroscope: Rotation Through the Coriolis Effect
text:
5.5 The MEMS Gyroscope: Rotation Through the Coriolis Effect
A classical gyroscope stores angular momentum in a spinning rotor; nothing that spins survives miniaturization to silicon, so MEMS gyroscopes use vibration instead. The device — a Coriolis vibratory gyroscope — again suspends a proof mass on flexures, but now drives it electrostatically into sustained resonant oscillation along one axis, the drive mode, like one tine of a tuning fork. When the package rotates at angular rate \(\omega\) about an axis perpendicular to that vibration, each element of the moving mass experiences a Coriolis acceleration
\[\vec{a}_{\text{cor}} = -2\,\vec{\omega} \times \vec{v},\]
where \(\vec{v}\) is the instantaneous drive-mode velocity. That acceleration is perpendicular to both the rotation axis and the drive motion, so it pumps energy into a second, orthogonal sense mode, whose displacement is picked off by capacitive electrodes exactly as in the accelerometer. Because the Coriolis term is linear in \(\omega\), the sense-mode amplitude directly encodes angular rate, and the ASIC delivers a calibrated output in degrees per second.






Figure 5.2: Simplified structure of a MEMS Coriolis vibratory gyroscope, viewed from above. The proof mass is driven into resonant oscillation along the drive axis; when the package rotates about the axis out of the page, the Coriolis acceleration pushes the mass along the orthogonal sense axis, toward one of the fixed sense electrodes, and the resulting differential capacitance change is proportional to the angular rate.



The construction carries its own fine print. The sense signal is proportional to the product of drive velocity and rotation rate, so any wander in drive amplitude appears as a scale-factor error; drive amplitude and flexure stiffness both move with temperature, which is why gyroscope bias and scale factor are specified with temperature coefficients and why the bias you measure at power-on is not the bias you will have ten minutes into a flight, after motor and battery heat have warmed the die. And the structure is, again, a high-Q mechanical resonator living on a vibrating airframe — the same vibration-sensitivity caveat as the accelerometer, sometimes worse, because external vibration near the drive frequency interferes directly with the mechanism.
One more property matters for everything that follows: the gyroscope measures rate, but control and navigation need angle. The only route from one to the other is integration, \(\theta(t) = \theta_0 + \int_0^t \omega\,dt\), and integration is an error amplifier: a constant rate bias \(b\) becomes an angle error \(b\,t\) that grows without limit. The numbers below make that concrete.
