7  From Radio to Root Shell: Companion Computers and the UART Link

title: 7  From Radio to Root Shell: Companion Computers and the UART Link
text:
7.6 The UART, from First Principles
The Sensing the World chapter introduced the two buses that carry sensor data inside the flight controller: I2C and SPI, both synchronous — a shared clock wire tells every participant exactly when each bit is valid. The UART is the third great serial interface of embedded systems, and its defining feature is the letter A: asynchronous. There is no clock wire. A UART link between two devices is, at minimum, three conductors: a transmit line (TX) driven by one device, a receive line (RX) listened to by the other, and a common ground. Each device contains an independent transmitter and receiver, so a full bidirectional link is TX and RX in each direction plus the shared ground — three wires total, since each data line is unidirectional and the ground is common.
Dropping the clock wire is a real engineering trade, and understanding what replaces it explains every UART wiring rule that is usually handed down without justification.
How bits survive without a clock. An idle UART line rests at logic high. To send a byte, the transmitter first pulls the line low for exactly one bit period — the start bit — then shifts out the eight data bits, least significant first, each held for one bit period, and finally returns the line high for at least one bit period — the stop bit. The receiver’s job is timing recovery: it watches the idle line for the falling edge of a start bit, waits half a bit period to land in the middle of the start bit, confirms the line is still low, and then samples the line at one-bit-period intervals thereafter — hitting, if all is well, the center of each data bit. The frame therefore carries its own synchronization: every byte begins with an edge that restarts the receiver’s timing, which is why the scheme is called asynchronous. In the common 8N1 configuration — 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit — each byte costs 10 bit periods on the wire, so the useful data rate is 80 % of the baud rate.
Why the baud rate must match. The receiver times its samples with its own local oscillator, and the transmitter times its bits with its own; the configured baud rate is the agreement that makes those two clocks interchangeable. The tolerance can be computed, and it is instructive to do so. After synchronizing on the start-bit edge, the receiver takes its final sample — the stop bit — 9.5 bit periods later. If the two clocks disagree by a fraction \(\varepsilon\), the sampling point drifts by \(9.5\,\varepsilon\) bit periods by frame’s end, and the frame decodes correctly only if that drift stays inside the half-bit margin:
\[9.5\,\varepsilon < 0.5 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \varepsilon < 5.3\ \%.\]
A total mismatch beyond about 5 % — under 3 % per side, once rise times and jitter consume part of the margin — and the receiver samples the wrong bits: framing errors, or worse, plausible-looking garbage. This is why baud mismatch is the classic serial failure mode, and why its symptom is so distinctive: a terminal full of random characters means the electrical link is fine and the timing agreement is broken. It is also why the parameter must be set identically in two places that never see each other — the flight controller’s serial-port configuration and the companion computer’s port-opening code — and why the number is worth writing down. At this book’s standard rate of 921,600 baud, one bit lasts \(1/921{,}600 \approx 1.09\ \mu\text{s}\), a 10-bit frame carries one byte in about \(10.9\ \mu\text{s}\), and the link moves at most \(921{,}600 \times 0.8 = 737{,}280\) data bits per second — roughly 90 kB/s, comfortable headroom for MAVLink telemetry and command traffic in both directions.
Why TX and RX must cross. Each UART pin has a fixed role: TX is an output, always driven by its own device; RX is an input, always listening. Communication therefore requires each device’s output to feed the other device’s input — the flight controller’s TX wired to the companion computer’s RX, and the companion computer’s TX to the flight controller’s RX. Wire it straight — TX to TX, RX to RX — and the result is two push-pull output drivers fighting each other on one wire (contention, and potential damage) while the two inputs listen to each other’s silence on the other. Nothing about the swap is subtle once the pin roles are stated, yet reversed TX/RX remains the single most common wiring fault in companion-computer integration, partly because different vendors label pins from different points of view. The reliable discipline is to ignore the labels and trace the signal: every wire in a UART link runs from exactly one transmitter to exactly one receiver.
Why grounds are shared. A logic signal is not a voltage; it is a voltage difference, measured between the signal conductor and a reference. The receiver decides “high” or “low” by comparing the RX line against its own ground pin. If the two boards’ grounds are not connected, that comparison is against a floating reference — the two devices’ ground potentials can drift volts apart, and the same physical signal may read as high, low, or noise depending on the moment. The third wire ties the two boards to a common reference so that “3.3 V” means the same thing on both ends. Three wires, then, and each is load-bearing: two directed data lines and the reference that gives their voltages meaning.
Figure 7.2 assembles the rule into a picture.






Figure 7.2: The UART crossover between a flight controller and a companion computer: the flight controller’s TX drives the computer’s RX, the computer’s TX drives the flight controller’s RX, and the two grounds are tied together to establish a common voltage reference.




7.6.1 Wiring the Link: The Pixhawk TELEM2 Port
On Pixhawk-family flight controllers the conventional attachment point for a companion computer is the TELEM2 port, a 6-pin JST-GH connector whose pinout rewards close reading:



Pin
Signal
Voltage




1 (red)
VCC
+5 V


2
TX (out)
3.3 V logic


3
RX (in)
3.3 V logic


4
CTS (in)
3.3 V logic


5
RTS (out)
3.3 V logic


6
GND
GND



Three observations turn the table into practice. First, the signal lines are 3.3 V logic while pin 1 carries +5 V power — and the red wire’s job is to make that distinction impossible to miss. Connecting the 5 V VCC pin to a 3.3 V signal input, one loose crimp away, can destroy a UART on either board; the 5 V pin exists to power small peripherals, not to signal, and in a companion-computer hookup (where the computer has its own supply) it is typically left unconnected. Second, pins 4 and 5 are hardware flow control — RTS/CTS lines by which each side can signal “stop sending, my buffer is full.” They are optional at moderate rates but recommended at 921,600 baud, where a stalled receiver can drop bytes faster than software can notice; if unused, flow control must be disabled in the flight controller’s port configuration, or it will wait forever for a permission signal that never comes. Third, on the companion side the same three signals appear on the board’s GPIO header or a dedicated serial header — on a Jetson, the pins corresponding to the device node /dev/ttyTHS1 — and carry the same 3.3 V constraint. The finished harness is three (or five, with flow control) crimped wires, and per the crossover rule the flight controller’s pin 2 (TX) lands on the computer’s RX pin while the computer’s TX lands on pin 3 (RX).

title: 7  From Radio to Root Shell: Companion Computers and the UART Link
section: 7.7 Verify Before You Code: The Heartbeat Test
text:
7.7 Verify Before You Code: The Heartbeat Test
The temptation after wiring is to start writing mission code; the discipline this book teaches is to first prove the link carries data, because a loose crimp or a wrong baud rate discovered through the lens of a misbehaving Python script wastes hours that a two-minute serial test would have saved. The proof is organized around a property of the protocol that will occupy Part II: every device speaking MAVLink — the standard message protocol between flight controllers, ground stations, and companion computers — broadcasts a heartbeat message at roughly 1 Hz, announcing its system ID, type, and flight mode. A heartbeat arriving on the companion computer is therefore end-to-end evidence: the wiring is right, the grounds are common, the baud rates agree, and the flight controller’s firmware is routing MAVLink to that port. The verification sequence is four steps:

Identify the serial port. Find the companion computer’s device node for the UART that was physically wired — on a Jetson, typically /dev/ttyTHS1; on a Raspberry Pi, /dev/serial0.
Configure the flight-controller port. In the PX4 parameter set, assign a MAVLink instance to TELEM2 and set its baud rate — the flight controller’s half of the timing agreement.
Set port permissions. Linux guards serial devices; add the working user to the dialout group (then log out and back in) rather than reaching for sudo.
Listen for the heartbeat with MAVProxy:

# On the companion computer, attached to the wired UART:
mavproxy.py --master=/dev/ttyTHS1 --baudrate 921600

# A healthy link prints, within a second or two:
#   Heartbeat from system 1
The test doubles as a diagnostic decision tree. Silence — no heartbeat at all — points at the physical layer or configuration: TX/RX not crossed, a missing ground, the wrong device node, or a flight-controller port not yet assigned to MAVLink. Garbage — a stream of malformed bytes or framing errors — is the baud-mismatch signature derived above: the electrons are arriving, the timing agreement is broken. A steady heartbeat is the milestone: the flight controller and the companion computer are peers on a working link, and every subsequent layer — MAVLink commands, the MAVSDK library, the ROS 2 bridge — is software riding on a wire already known to be good. What those layers look like, and how a Python program turns this link into an autonomous takeoff, is where the PX4 and the Autopilot Stack chapter in Part II picks up.
With that heartbeat, the physical platform is complete. The airframe is sized, the power system budgeted, the sensors understood, the regulations mapped, and a programmable computer now sits on the aircraft with a verified channel to the machine that flies it. What is still missing is the view of the whole: how these pieces stand to one another once they are assembled into a single vehicle that flies a mission by itself. That is where Part I ends, and it is the last thing to settle before the work becomes code.

title: 7  From Radio to Root Shell: Companion Computers and the UART Link
text:
7.8 Check Your Understanding

A flight controller already contains a processor. State precisely what the companion computer adds, and give the architectural reason the flight controller cannot simply absorb those functions.







TipShow answer





The companion computer adds general-purpose compute under a full Linux OS: onboard mission planning, computer-vision inference, obstacle avoidance, and network access (SSH, remote monitoring). The flight controller cannot absorb these because it is a real-time microcontroller: its scheduler guarantees millisecond-deterministic attitude control precisely by excluding unpredictable workloads, and it lacks the memory, OS services, and GPU that perception and planning software require. The division of labor is deliberate — hard-real-time stability on one processor, computationally heavy intelligence on the other — with a serial link between them.




A team is building two aircraft: one relays telemetry and executes pre-planned GPS waypoint missions; the other must detect and track objects with an onboard neural network. Recommend a companion computer for each, and justify both recommendations with the deciding criterion.







TipShow answer





The waypoint aircraft should fly a Raspberry Pi: mission scripting and telemetry relay are light CPU workloads, and the Pi wins on cost, mass, power draw (well inside a ~12 W avionics budget), and simplicity. The detection aircraft needs a Jetson (Nano or Orin NX): real-time neural-network inference is a GPU-shaped workload, and a CPU-only Pi drops to single-digit frame rates on modern detectors. The deciding criterion is whether the mission requires onboard GPU inference; every other factor (power, mass, cost, setup effort) argues for the Pi, which is why the Jetson is chosen only when perception forces it.




Explain why a UART link fails if the two ends’ baud rates differ by, say, 10 %, using the receiver’s sampling mechanism — and compute the approximate maximum tolerable total clock mismatch for a 10-bit frame.







TipShow answer





The receiver has no clock wire; it resynchronizes on each start-bit edge and then samples at intervals timed by its own oscillator, aiming for the center of each bit. A fractional rate mismatch \(\varepsilon\) makes the sampling point drift by \(9.5\,\varepsilon\) bit periods by the final (stop) bit of a 10-bit frame; correct decoding requires that drift to stay within half a bit: \(9.5\,\varepsilon < 0.5\), so \(\varepsilon < 5.3\ \%\) total (in practice under ~3 % per side once noise and rise times eat margin). At 10 % mismatch the sample point has drifted a full bit period before the frame ends, so the receiver reads wrong bits — the classic symptom being a stream of garbage characters and framing errors rather than silence.




A student wires flight-controller TX to companion-computer TX and RX to RX, reasoning that “like connects to like.” Describe both electrical consequences of this wiring and state the rule that prevents it.







TipShow answer





TX is always an output and RX always an input. TX-to-TX places two output drivers on the same wire: whenever they drive opposite logic levels, current flows directly between the drivers (bus contention), which at best corrupts the line and at worst damages a transceiver. RX-to-RX places two inputs on one wire with no driver at all, so both receivers listen to a floating line and hear nothing. The rule: every UART wire must run from exactly one transmitter to exactly one receiver — cross TX to RX in both directions, and verify by tracing signal direction rather than trusting pin labels, which vendors write from inconsistent points of view.




The Pixhawk TELEM2 pinout puts +5 V on pin 1 (the red wire) and 3.3 V logic on pins 2-5. Explain the hazard this adjacency creates, and why the 5 V pin is usually left unconnected in a companion-computer harness.







TipShow answer





The hazard is crossing power into a signal line: a mis-crimped or mis-seated connector can present +5 V to a UART input designed for 3.3 V logic, overstressing and potentially destroying the transceiver on either board. The red wire convention exists to keep the power pin visually distinct. It is left unconnected because its purpose is to power small peripherals (e.g., a telemetry radio), and a companion computer has its own independent supply — so the harness needs only the two crossed signal lines, ground, and optionally the RTS/CTS pair; omitting VCC removes the failure mode entirely.




After wiring, mavproxy.py --master=/dev/ttyTHS1 --baudrate 921600 prints nothing at all. A second attempt at a different baud rate prints unreadable garbage. Diagnose both observations.







TipShow answer





Garbage is diagnostic gold: it means the physical layer works — electrons are arriving with edges the receiver can see — but the timing agreement is broken, i.e., the flight controller is transmitting at a different baud rate than the one MAVProxy is now using. Total silence at the (correct) first baud rate therefore most likely means the configuration is wrong somewhere other than wiring — commonly, the flight controller’s TELEM2 port has not been assigned a MAVLink instance at 921,600 baud. (Silence in general implicates the physical layer too — TX/RX not crossed, missing ground, wrong device node — but the garbage observation has already exonerated the wiring.) The fix: set the flight controller’s serial protocol and baud parameters for TELEM2 to match, then rerun the heartbeat test at 921,600.

title: 7  From Radio to Root Shell: Companion Computers and the UART Link
text:
7.9 Try It
Part 1 — decode a UART frame by hand. Draw the voltage-versus-time waveform for the byte 0x4D (ASCII M, binary 01001101) transmitted in 8N1 format at 9,600 baud: idle high, start bit low, eight data bits least-significant-bit first, stop bit high. Label the duration of each bit period in microseconds. Then play receiver: mark the sampling instant for each bit (start-bit edge plus 1.5, 2.5, … bit periods) and confirm the byte decodes. Finally, redo the sampling marks assuming your receiver’s clock runs 4 % fast, and identify the first bit at which the sampling point has left the correct bit cell — then check your answer against the \(9.5\,\varepsilon < 0.5\) margin from the chapter. If you have access to a logic analyzer or an oscilloscope and any UART source (an Arduino’s serial port suffices), capture a real frame and repeat the exercise against the measured waveform.
Part 2 — bring up a real link and break it on purpose. Using any two UART-capable devices available to you — a Pixhawk and a Jetson or Pi is ideal, but two USB-serial adapters looped together, or a Pi and an Arduino, teach the same lessons — wire the three-conductor crossover and run the heartbeat test (or, for non-MAVLink devices, an echo test with a terminal program at both ends). Document the working configuration: device nodes, baud rate, and which physical pin each wire lands on. Then break the link three ways, recording the observed symptom of each: swap TX and RX (expect silence), change one end’s baud rate by a factor of two (expect garbage), and disconnect the ground while keeping both data lines attached (expect anything from intermittent errors to apparent normality — and write two sentences on why this failure is the most dangerous of the three precisely because it can seem to work). Conclude with the diagnostic table you would hand a teammate: symptom in one column, most probable cause and first check in the other.
Related Lab: See Appendix B for the lab assignment that applies this chapter’s concepts.

title: 8  Putting It Together: The Autonomous Drone Stack
text:
8.1 Learning Objectives
Part I has approached the drone six times from six directions, and each approach stopped where the next one began. The Commercial Drone Landscape chapter established what the vehicle is for and why the industry converged on commodity hardware carrying custom software. The Anatomy of a Multirotor chapter sized a specific airframe from a specific mission. The Materials and Power chapter explained what that airframe is made of and what its battery will tolerate. The Sensing the World chapter followed a measurement from a silicon flexure to a fused attitude estimate. The Airspace Law chapter established the legal envelope the finished vehicle must fly inside. And the previous chapter bolted a Linux computer to the airframe and proved, with a MAVLink heartbeat, that the computer and the autopilot can talk.
What has not happened yet is assembly. Six correct components lying on a bench are not an aircraft, and an aircraft is not a system: the interesting properties of an autonomous vehicle — that it can decide, that it can be trusted, that it fails in bounded ways — are properties of the arrangement, not of any part. This chapter makes that arrangement explicit. It lays out the complete vehicle in one labeled figure, names the single control pattern that repeats at every level of it, walks one mission from the pre-flight briefing to the landing, and sketches — at altitude, leaving the detail to Part V — the software architecture that sequences it.
The system in question is the Goose Management System, the running example the Commercial Drone Landscape chapter introduced as the wildlife-management vertical in miniature: an aircraft that searches a protected area, detects geese with onboard computer vision, deters them, evades any bird that contests the airspace, and returns. That chapter answered its own five questions about the mission in a sentence — the payload is a depth camera and a companion computer, the binding constraint is visual line of sight plus wildlife-disturbance permission, the corrupting physics is illumination and background clutter in the detector, the workflow is a search grid transitioning into a pursuit, and the deliverable is the deterrence itself. Those answers can now be spent rather than merely stated, because every noun in them has been developed in the intervening chapters.

title: 8  Putting It Together: The Autonomous Drone Stack
text:
8.2 Key Vocabulary

Sense–think–act loop — the fundamental cycle of any autonomous system: measure the world, compute a decision from the measurement, command actuators that change the world, and measure again. Every layer of an autonomy stack is an instance of it, differing only in rate and in the consequence of missing a deadline.
Autonomy stack — the layered software that converts a remotely piloted vehicle into a self-directed one: state estimation and stabilization at the bottom, perception and guidance in the middle, mission sequencing and safety supervision at the top.
Offboard control — a flight-controller mode in which the autopilot stops taking direction from a human pilot or a preloaded waypoint list and instead follows a continuous stream of position, velocity, or attitude setpoints supplied by an external computer, reverting to a safe behavior if that stream stops.
ROS 2 node (Robot Operating System 2) — an independent operating-system process in the ROS 2 middleware that performs one job and exchanges data with other nodes only through named, typed channels, so that nodes can be developed, tested, restarted, and replaced independently.
Topic — a ROS 2 publish–subscribe channel carrying a continuous stream of messages from one publisher to any number of subscribers, with no acknowledgment; the right mechanism when data is always flowing and only the latest value matters.
Service — a ROS 2 request–response channel in which a caller asks one node to perform a discrete action and waits for its reply; the right mechanism when an action happens once and the caller must know it succeeded before proceeding.
Failsafe monitor — a supervisory process that watches a small set of safety-critical quantities and can override whatever is currently commanding the vehicle. Its defining property is independence: it must not share a failure mode with the logic it supervises.
Mission time budget — the usable flight time remaining after a reserve is set aside, allocated in advance across the phases of a mission, and the quantity against which an autonomous vehicle’s decision to continue or return is actually made.

title: 8  Putting It Together: The Autonomous Drone Stack
text:
8.3 The Vehicle Part I Built
Figure 8.1 shows the assembled aircraft from above, with every component Part I selected in the place it physically occupies.






Figure 8.1: The assembled research quadrotor, viewed from above, with the components developed across Part I in their physical positions: carbon-fibre arms carrying four motor–propeller pairs, a stacked centre section holding the companion computer above the flight controller, the four-in-one electronic speed controller and radios below them, the battery slung underneath through a power module, a forward-facing depth camera at the nose, and the GPS receiver and compass on a mast at the rear.



The figure is worth reading against the arithmetic that produced it. The 500 mm wheelbase puts adjacent motors 354 mm apart, which is what allows 10-inch propellers with 100 mm of tip clearance and forbids anything larger; the Anatomy of a Multirotor chapter derived that geometry and then followed it through to 5,425 RPM in hover, 192 W of shaft power, and 252 W of electrical draw at 1.7 kg empty. The arms are carbon because the Materials and Power chapter’s specific-stiffness argument leaves no alternative for a structure whose resonances must stay clear of the 90 Hz and 181 Hz the propellers inject; the camera bracket and the tray under the companion computer are the printed parts that same argument permits. The two counter-rotating pairs marked in the figure are the whole mechanism of yaw control, and their symmetry is why four rotors is the minimum for full attitude control with fixed-pitch blades.
Three items in the figure exist for the mission rather than for flight, and together they are the 500 g of autonomy payload the sizing calculation carried: the Jetson Nano companion computer, the Intel RealSense D455 depth camera at the nose, and the mounting hardware that holds them. The previous chapter justified the Jetson against the cheaper, lighter Raspberry Pi with one criterion — a goose has to be recognized by a neural network running on the aircraft, and no CPU-only board runs one at a useful frame rate — and it was explicit that the choice is paid for twice, in the mass that shortens every flight and in the watts that overrun the 12 W avionics allowance the power budget assumed. The bill is exact: adding the payload takes all-up weight from 1.7 kg to 2.2 kg, raises hover draw from 252 W to 365 W by the \(m^{3/2}\) scaling, and cuts hover endurance from 14.7 minutes to 10.1 minutes. Every mission decision in this chapter is made inside those ten minutes.
The remaining components are there to make the aircraft legal, recoverable, and observable rather than to make it fly. The GPS receiver and compass ride a mast because the magnetometer measures tens of microtesla and the power wiring beneath it carries tens of amperes. The power module between the battery and the distribution board measures pack voltage and current, which is what turns the Materials and Power chapter’s battery arithmetic from a bench exercise into a quantity the autonomy software can act on in flight. The telemetry radio and the RC receiver are the other two of the three command paths the previous chapter enumerated, and both stay live throughout: the RC link is the safety pilot’s override, which is the Airspace Law chapter’s layered-margin logic implemented in hardware rather than in policy.

section: 8.4 One Loop, Nested at Three Rates
text:
8.4 One Loop, Nested at Three Rates
Underneath the component inventory there is exactly one architectural idea, and Figure 8.2 is all of it. An autonomous system measures the world, decides what the measurement implies for its goal, acts to change the world, and measures again. Everything else is a question of what is being measured, how hard the decision is, and how fast the cycle must close.






Figure 8.2: The sense–think–act cycle: measurements feed a decision, the decision drives an action, and the action changes what the next measurement will see.



On this aircraft the loop runs at three rates simultaneously, nested one inside another, and the hardware in Figure 8.1 is partitioned along exactly those nesting lines.
The attitude loop, on the flight controller, at kilohertz. The Pixhawk reads its inertial measurement unit over a dedicated SPI bus — the Sensing the World chapter did the bandwidth arithmetic showing why the fast, lonely sensor gets its own bus while the slow, sociable barometer and magnetometer share I2C — runs the extended Kalman filter that fuses gyroscope, accelerometer, magnetometer, barometer, and GPS into an attitude and position estimate, and resolves the error between commanded and actual attitude into four motor commands. This loop cannot be late. A quadrotor holds no attitude on its own; a stall of a tenth of a second is the end of the flight. That is precisely why it runs on a microcontroller whose scheduler is designed to exclude anything unpredictable, and why nothing else is allowed onto that processor.
The perception loop, on the companion computer, at camera rate. Frames arrive from the depth camera at tens of hertz, a neural network decides whether a goose is present, and a target position is published for anything that cares. Missing a frame here costs nothing but a frame; the vehicle is still flying, still stable, still where it was. The deadline is soft, the computation is enormous, and the hardware is chosen accordingly.
The mission loop, on the companion computer, at roughly one hertz. Given everything sensed so far, should the vehicle keep searching, close on a target, execute the deterrence maneuver, evade, or go home? A decision deferred by a second at this level is a decision deferred by a second; nothing falls out of the sky.
The seam between the two computers is the three-wire UART the previous chapter wired and verified, and it is worth being precise about what that seam can and cannot carry, because the bandwidth decides the architecture. At 921,600 baud in the standard 8N1 framing, the link moves about 90 kB/s. A stream of position setpoints — a few dozen bytes at a few tens of hertz — occupies a fraction of a percent of that, so commanding the vehicle across the seam is comfortable. Moving imagery across it is not: a 640 × 480 colour frame is 921,600 raw bytes, and thirty of them per second is roughly 27 MB/s, some three hundred times the link’s capacity. Even aggressively compressed to a few megabits per second, video would still exceed it, and the telemetry radio to the ground is slower again by orders of magnitude. This is the quantitative version of the argument the Commercial Drone Landscape chapter made about cheap onboard compute: perception must run where the pixels already are. The camera talks to the companion computer over USB, the companion computer talks to the flight controller over three wires, and the only things that cross those three wires are decisions.

title: 8  Putting It Together: The Autonomous Drone Stack
text:
8.5 The Mission, End to End
With the platform and the loop in place, one flight can be told properly. Each phase below names the Part I result that binds it — the constraint that decides whether the phase is possible at all.

8.5.1 Before the battery is connected
Nothing has been built yet that removes the human obligations of the Airspace Law chapter. A research flight is non-recreational by definition and therefore a Part 107 operation: a certificated remote pilot in command is present, the aircraft is registered and its actual weight recorded, and the flight is logged. The crew confirms airspace status, checks current NOTAMs and Temporary Flight Restrictions through a briefing source, and captures the evidence. PAVE and I’M SAFE are run and answered out loud. Wildlife-disturbance permission — the second half of the running example’s binding constraint, and the half that has nothing to do with aviation — is in hand. The RC transmitter is on and its override tested before anything is armed.
None of this is preamble to the engineering. It is the reason the vehicle in Figure 8.1 is shaped as it is: an aircraft that must stay within visual line of sight is an aircraft whose search area is bounded by what a person can see, and an aircraft under a 400-foot (122 m) ceiling is one whose sensor must resolve a bird from a few tens of metres rather than from any altitude that would be convenient.


8.5.2 Launch and handoff
The vehicle is armed and takes off under the flight controller’s own control, with the safety pilot on the sticks. The barometer records pad pressure at arming as its reference, which is why altitude is reported relative to the launch point and not against a weather-dependent sea-level datum; the same paragraph of the Sensing the World chapter warned that the propellers’ own wash, intensified by ground effect, makes barometric altitude least trustworthy exactly during takeoff and landing, which is why the climb is flown on the fused estimate rather than on pressure alone.
At a safe altitude the flight controller is switched to offboard mode and the companion computer begins publishing setpoints. This is the handoff the whole of Part I has been building toward: from this instant the decisions come from a process rather than from a person. Offboard mode carries its own protection — if the setpoint stream stops for more than a fraction of a second, the autopilot does not coast, it falls back to a safe behavior — and that protection is the first of several places where the system’s safety does not depend on the autonomy software being correct.


8.5.3 Search
The vehicle flies a search pattern over the protected area. Two Part I results set its shape. Altitude is fixed from below by the pixels-on-target requirement the Commercial Drone Landscape chapter identified for every wildlife survey — a bird must span enough pixels for the detector to classify it, which is the ground-sample-distance relation read backwards — and from above by the 122 m regulatory ceiling and by the range at which the depth camera still returns useful depth. In practice the search leg is flown a few tens of metres above ground: high enough to see a useful swath, low enough to resolve a goose, and nowhere near the legal limit. The pattern’s own geometry, and the question of what an efficient search looks like when the target moves, belong to Part IV.
The second result is the clock, and it is the tighter of the two. The platform’s 10.1 minutes is a hover figure computed for a new pack in still air; forward flight and maneuvering cost more, and wind costs more again, so it is an optimistic ceiling rather than a plan. Holding back a 25 % reserve leaves about 7.6 minutes of mission, which has to be allocated before takeoff rather than discovered in flight:








Phase
Allocation
What sets it




Climb and transit to the search area
1.0 min
Distance from the launch point, bounded by visual line of sight


Search leg
3.5 min
Area to be covered at the chosen altitude and speed


Approach and deterrence
2.0 min
Time to close on a detection and complete the maneuver


Return and land
1.0 min
Transit back plus a controlled descent


Reserve (held, not spent)
2.6 min
Wind, a second detection, a diverted landing



Seven and a half allocated minutes against a ten-minute battery is not a generous budget, and reading it honestly changes the design: the search pattern must be sized to the time available, not the time available discovered after the pattern is chosen. This is the payload–endurance exchange rate of the Anatomy of a Multirotor chapter arriving as a mission constraint. Every gram the autonomy hardware added was paid for here.


8.5.4 Detection
The detector, running on the Jetson, publishes a target position when a goose appears in frame. The depth camera earns its mass at this moment: a monocular camera reports a bearing to a detected object and leaves its range ambiguous, while a depth camera returns range directly, so the target can be placed in the vehicle’s own coordinates without maneuvering to triangulate. How the network is trained, compressed, and run inside the Jetson’s power envelope is the subject of Part III; what matters here is that the estimate is produced onboard, at frame rate, and that everything downstream consumes it as a stream rather than requesting it.


8.5.5 Deterrence
Once a target is localized, authority over the vehicle’s motion transfers from the search behavior to the deterrence behavior, which closes on the bird and executes the maneuver that moves the flock along. Two constraints bound it. The first is the wildlife-disturbance framing of the Commercial Drone Landscape chapter: the same disturbance that makes deterrence effective is a documented stressor on the animals, which is why the permission exists and why the maneuver is designed to be the least disturbance that works — an engineering requirement, not a courtesy. The second is separation. The vehicle must not contact a bird, and the reason is quantitative: the Anatomy of a Multirotor chapter showed that a quadrotor which loses one of four rotors cannot produce net thrust with zero net moment and simply falls, where a hexacopter would degrade. A quadrotor has no graceful failure to fall back on, so separation distance is monitored continuously and enforced by something other than the behavior that is trying to close the distance.


8.5.6 Evasion
If a goose contests the airspace and closes on the aircraft, the vehicle breaks away — and what it can do is set by thrust margin. Loaded to 2.2 kg against roughly 4.0 kgf of static thrust, the aircraft’s thrust-to-weight ratio is about 1.8, so hover consumes 55 % of available thrust and the surplus available for acceleration is
\[a_{\max} = (\mathrm{TWR} - 1)\,g = (1.8 - 1)(9.81) = 7.8\ \text{m/s}^2.\]
A 5 m evasive climb therefore takes at least \(t = \sqrt{2h/a} = \sqrt{2(5)/7.8} = 1.1\ \text{s}\), arriving at about 8.8 m/s — and that is an optimistic bound, ignoring the time the rotors need to spool up and the drag of a fast vertical climb. The number is worth carrying because it tells the behavior designer what is physically purchasable: an evasion that must complete in half a second is not available on this airframe at this weight, and the remedy is a lighter payload or a larger aircraft, not a cleverer state machine.
The maneuver also costs the pack its worst moment. Full throttle draws roughly 80 A, a 15 C discharge for the 5.2 Ah pack, and at that current the Materials and Power chapter’s internal-resistance arithmetic becomes operationally visible: a healthy 5 mΩ cell sags 0.40 V, while an aged 15 mΩ cell sags 1.2 V, dropping from the 3.7 V plateau to about 2.5 V under load — well past any naive low-voltage alarm, on a pack that looked entirely healthy in hover at 17 A. A dying pack flies gentle missions convincingly and fails exactly when the vehicle needs to evade.


8.5.7 Return, land, and the failsafe that watches all of it
The mission ends deliberately: the vehicle returns to the launch point and lands, or triggers return-to-launch early. The decision to end early belongs to the failsafe monitor, and the threshold it uses is a direct consequence of the paragraph above. Triggering on measured pack voltage under load is unsound, because sag under load is a function of the pack’s age as much as its charge, and the aged pack’s 1.2 V of sag would fire the alarm in a climb and clear it in a hover. The defensible trigger is consumed capacity, integrated from the current the power module reports, checked against a resting-voltage floor referenced to the 3.5 V-per-cell practical limit — with the reserve in the budget table above as the quantity actually being protected. The monitor watches separation distance on the same footing, and it can override whichever behavior is flying the aircraft.
On landing, the barometer becomes untrustworthy again in ground effect, the RC pilot is ready to take the vehicle back, and the flight log becomes the input to the diagnostics of Part V. The pack goes into storage charge, at 3.80–3.85 V per cell, before the crew leaves the field.

title: 8  Putting It Together: The Autonomous Drone Stack
text:
8.6 The Software Above the Wire
The autonomy stack on the companion computer is not one program. It is a set of independent ROS 2 nodes — separate operating-system processes, each with one responsibility — communicating only through named channels. The modularity is a deliberate engineering decision with two payoffs: nodes can be developed, tested, and replaced independently, and a crash in one does not take down the others. The second payoff is the one that matters for safety.
ROS 2 offers two communication mechanisms, and the choice between them is not stylistic. Services are request–response: one node asks another to perform a discrete action — arm the vehicle, enter offboard mode, trigger return-to-launch — and waits for an acknowledgment before proceeding. Topics are publish–subscribe: a node publishes a stream of messages — target position, distance remaining, battery state — and any number of nodes subscribe, with no acknowledgment exchanged. The rule of thumb follows from what each contract guarantees. Use a service when the action happens once and the caller must know it succeeded; use a topic when data is always flowing and only the latest value matters. Arming is the archetypal service: a mission that advances without confirming that the vehicle actually armed is a mission that has lost track of reality. Target position is the archetypal topic: it changes every frame, several nodes need it, and a stale value is worse than no value.
Mapped onto those two mechanisms, the running example’s stack resolves into four functional groups: a mission sequencer that holds the state machine and announces which behavior currently has authority; a vehicle interface that translates high-level requests into autopilot commands over the link verified in the previous chapter; the motion behaviors — search navigation, deterrence, evasion — that generate setpoints when they hold authority; and the Failsafe node, which subscribes to battery state and separation distance and can override any of the others. The Failsafe node is the reason the modularity is worth its overhead. If the safety checks lived inside the mission sequencer, then a hung state transition or an unhandled exception in the sequencer would disable the checks at the exact moment the system was misbehaving. As a separate process it shares no failure mode with the logic it supervises, and — as the Sensing the World chapter noted from the other end of the pipeline — it consumes the flight controller’s fused state estimate rather than raw sensor readings, trusting the estimator to have already fought the battles that chapter described.
That sketch is deliberately shallow. The node-by-node architecture, the message types on each channel, the state machine’s transitions, and what happens when two nodes claim authority at once are the subject of the Systems Architecture chapter in Part V, which returns to this same system with the whole book behind it. The purpose here is only to make the shape legible: independent processes, streams for data, calls for decisions, and a supervisor outside the thing it supervises.

title: 8  Putting It Together: The Autonomous Drone Stack
section: 8.7 What Part I Settled, and What Comes Next
text:
8.7 What Part I Settled, and What Comes Next
The previous chapter framed the change this Part has been working toward in one line: with a radio transmitter, the drone is a vehicle you drive; with a companion computer, it is a platform you program. Part I has now delivered that platform completely. The airframe is sized and its geometry fixed. The materials are chosen and the battery’s chemistry understood well enough to specify how it is charged, stored, and retired. The sensors are characterized down to their bias and noise, and their fusion into a usable state estimate is no longer a mystery. The regulatory envelope is mapped, and the human procedures that keep an operation inside it are specified. A general-purpose Linux computer sits on the aircraft with a verified channel to the machine that flies it.
That is the entire physical contribution. Every remaining question in this book is a question about software running on that computer, and the Parts divide along the loop of Figure 8.2. Part II takes the innermost cycle and makes it quantitative — feedback control, the PX4 autopilot and the MAVLink protocol that carries commands across the wire, the MAVSDK and ROS 2 interfaces through which a program commands flight, and the geofences and failsafes that re-express the Airspace Law chapter’s rules as parameters the firmware enforces rather than habits a pilot maintains. Part III takes the perception cycle: how images become tensors, how a network is trained and then compressed to run inside the Jetson’s power and memory budget, and how inference latency bounds the behaviors the vehicle can support. Part IV takes the outermost cycle: search and coverage patterns, path planning, the behavior architectures that sequence discrete actions, and coordination among several aircraft. Part V puts them back together and asks the harder questions — integration, field diagnosis from telemetry logs, and the ethics of an aircraft that decides for itself.
The hardware is finished; from here the work is code. The vehicle in Figure 8.1 will not change again. What changes is how much of its behavior a program, rather than a person, is responsible for.

title: 8  Putting It Together: The Autonomous Drone Stack
text:
8.8 Check Your Understanding

The loaded aircraft achieves 10.1 minutes of hover endurance. A colleague proposes planning a mission that uses 9 minutes of it, arguing that a one-minute reserve is enough since the vehicle lands where it took off. Evaluate the proposal, and state what the 10.1-minute figure does and does not include.







TipShow answer





The 10.1 minutes is a hover figure for a new pack in still air, computed from 61.6 Wh of usable energy against 365 W of hover draw. It excludes the extra power of forward flight and maneuvering, excludes wind, and assumes a pack whose internal resistance has not risen with age — all of which push actual endurance down, never up. A one-minute reserve is therefore not a reserve at all: it is smaller than the error in the estimate it is protecting against. The 25 % reserve used in the budget table (about 2.6 minutes) covers the modelling error, an unplanned second detection, and a diverted landing. The general principle is that a reserve protects against the uncertainty in the number it is subtracted from, so a figure known only to within 20 % cannot be planned to within 10 %.




Explain, with arithmetic, why the neural network that detects geese must run on the companion computer rather than on a ground station receiving the video stream.







TipShow answer





Because the imagery cannot leave the aircraft fast enough. A 640 × 480 colour frame is \(640 \times 480 \times 3 = 921{,}600\) bytes; at 30 frames per second that is roughly 27 MB/s. The wired UART between the companion computer and the flight controller carries about 90 kB/s at 921,600 baud — some three hundred times less — and the telemetry radio to the ground is slower again by orders of magnitude. Even heavily compressed to a few megabits per second, the stream would still exceed the serial link and would be fragile over a range-limited radio. The bandwidth asymmetry decides the architecture: pixels stay where they are produced, and only decisions — target positions, setpoints, mode changes, a few dozen bytes at a time — cross the wire. This is also why the mission does not require a ground link to proceed.




The aircraft weighs 2.2 kg loaded and has about 4.0 kgf of static thrust. Compute the maximum vertical acceleration available for an evasive climb and the time to gain 4 m of altitude. Then state what would change if 300 g of additional payload were fitted.







TipShow answer





Thrust-to-weight is \(4.0/2.2 = 1.8\), so the surplus acceleration is \((1.8-1)(9.81) = 7.8\ \text{m/s}^2\) and a 4 m climb takes at least \(t = \sqrt{2(4)/7.8} = 1.01\ \text{s}\) — optimistic, since it ignores rotor spool-up and drag. Adding 300 g takes the aircraft to 2.5 kg. Thrust-to-weight falls to \(4.0/2.5 = 1.6\), surplus acceleration to \((0.6)(9.81) = 5.9\ \text{m/s}^2\), and the same climb now takes \(\sqrt{8/5.9} = 1.17\ \text{s}\) — 16 % slower. Endurance suffers at the same time: shaft power scales as \(m^{3/2}\), so \(192 \times (2.5/1.7)^{3/2} = 343\) W of shaft power gives \(343/0.8 + 12 = 440\) W of electrical draw and \(61.6/440 = 0.140\) h, about 8.4 minutes, down from 10.1. Two independent constraints degrade together, which is the recurring shape of the payload argument.




A team proposes triggering return-to-launch whenever measured pack voltage drops below 3.5 V per cell. Explain why this is unsound on this aircraft, and describe a defensible alternative.







TipShow answer





Measured voltage under load is depressed by internal resistance, and internal resistance rises with age. A healthy 5 mΩ cell sags 0.40 V at the 80 A of a full-throttle maneuver; an aged 15 mΩ cell sags 1.2 V, taking it from the 3.7 V plateau to about 2.5 V under exactly the load the vehicle experiences during an evasion. The threshold would therefore fire spuriously during every aggressive maneuver on an aged pack and clear again in hover, and would fire at genuinely different states of charge depending on the pack’s age — the trigger would be measuring the wrong thing. The defensible alternative integrates current from the power module to track consumed capacity against the pack’s known usable energy, protects the planned reserve rather than a voltage number, and uses a resting per-cell voltage floor as a cross-check rather than as the primary trigger.




The vehicle arms through a service call but receives its target position on a topic. Justify each choice, and predict the failure mode if the two mechanisms were swapped.







TipShow answer





Arming is a discrete action whose success must be known before anything else proceeds, which is exactly the request–response contract of a service: the caller blocks until the vehicle confirms it is armed. Target position is a continuously changing quantity with several consumers, where only the newest value has any use — the publish–subscribe contract of a topic, which delivers to every subscriber without the publisher knowing who they are. Swapped, an “arm” topic would give the mission sequencer no confirmation, so it would advance to takeoff on the assumption that a message it published had been acted on; and a “target position” service would force each consumer to poll independently, delivering different, stale values to different nodes between requests, and coupling the detector’s rate to its callers’ request patterns.




The Failsafe node runs as a separate process rather than as a check inside the mission sequencer, and it consumes the flight controller’s fused state estimate rather than raw sensor data. Give the reason for each design decision.







TipShow answer





Separation of process is about failure independence. If the safety checks lived inside the mission sequencer, any defect that hung or crashed the sequencer — a logic bug, an unhandled exception, a deadlocked transition — would silence the safety checks at precisely the moment the system was misbehaving, which is when they are needed. As an independent process, the monitor shares no failure mode with the logic it supervises and can still force a hover, a return-to-launch, or an abort. Consuming the fused estimate rather than raw sensor data is about not duplicating a solved problem: the flight controller’s extended Kalman filter already tracks sensor biases, weights each measurement by its current uncertainty, and rejects outliers. A safety monitor that read raw accelerometers would have to re-solve estimation badly, and a monitor that reasons from a worse estimate than the vehicle is flying on is not a safeguard.

title: 9  Closed-Loop Control: PID Theory for Multirotors
text:
9.1 Learning Objectives
Part I closed with a finished vehicle and a promise: the hardware will not change again, and everything from here forward is software running on the two computers it carries. This chapter starts where that promise pointed — at the innermost of the three nested loops the previous chapter identified, the one running on the flight controller at kilohertz rates, the one whose deadline cannot be missed. The Putting It Together chapter could say only that the flight controller “resolves the error between commanded and actual attitude into four motor commands.” This chapter is about how. The mechanism is feedback control, its workhorse is the proportional–integral–derivative (PID) controller, and by the end the sentence in quotes will have become an equation, a worked numeric design, a dozen lines of code, and a set of symptoms you can diagnose from the way an aircraft misbehaves.
The material earns its place at the front of Part II for a blunt reason: nothing above it works if it doesn’t. Every mission script, every offboard setpoint, every clever behavior the rest of this book builds ends its life as a request handed to these loops, and the request is granted only as well as the loops are tuned. A vehicle whose rate controller oscillates cannot hold a camera steady enough for the perception of Part III; one whose altitude controller carries a steady-state error will fly its search grid at the wrong height. Control is the floor everything else stands on.

title: 9  Closed-Loop Control: PID Theory for Multirotors
text:
Explain why a multirotor is unflyable without feedback: the plant is underactuated, its hover is an unstable equilibrium, and it is continuously disturbed.
Derive the PID control law \(u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int_0^t e(\tau)\,d\tau + K_d \frac{de(t)}{dt}\) from the three questions a controller can ask of its error signal, and state each term’s physical effect on a multirotor’s response.
Design a PD altitude-hold controller for a vehicle of known mass by choosing a natural frequency and damping ratio, and verify the design against the aircraft’s thrust margin.
Identify overshoot, oscillation, sluggishness, and steady-state error as tuning symptoms, attribute each to a specific gain, and state the standard remedy.
Convert the continuous PID law into the sampled-data form that actually runs on a flight controller, including integrator clamping and derivative filtering, and explain why each modification exists.
Explain why multirotor flight control uses a cascade of loops — position, velocity, attitude, angular rate — rather than one PID, and why the innermost rate loop is tuned first.

9  Closed-Loop Control: PID Theory for Multirotors

title: 9  Closed-Loop Control: PID Theory for Multirotors
text:
9.2 Key Vocabulary

Setpoint — the reference value \(r(t)\) a control loop is asked to achieve: a commanded altitude, attitude, or angular rate. In a cascaded controller, each loop’s output is the next inner loop’s setpoint.
Plant — the physical system a controller acts on. Here, the quadrotor’s rigid-body dynamics: four motor thrusts in, translational and rotational motion out.
Proportional gain (\(K_p\)) — the weight on the present error. It acts like a spring stiffness: the command it produces is proportional to how far the vehicle currently is from the setpoint.
Integral gain (\(K_i\)) — the weight on the accumulated error. It builds up a corrective command as long as any error persists, which is what removes steady offsets caused by unmodeled forces such as a payload shift or a weak motor.
Derivative gain (\(K_d\)) — the weight on the error’s rate of change. It acts like a damper, opposing rapid motion toward or away from the setpoint, which is what suppresses overshoot.
Steady-state error — the offset that remains after the transient response has died out. A proportional-only controller facing a constant disturbance always leaves one, because it needs a nonzero error to produce a nonzero command.
Overshoot — the amount by which the response passes beyond the setpoint before settling back, a symptom of too little damping relative to stiffness.
Cascaded control loop — an architecture in which a slow outer controller does not command the actuators directly but instead generates the setpoint for a faster inner controller, repeated over as many layers as the plant’s time scales demand.
Integrator windup — the failure mode in which the integral term keeps accumulating while the actuators are saturated and cannot act on it, then discharges as a large overshoot once the vehicle finally catches up; prevented by clamping the integrator.

title: 9  Closed-Loop Control: PID Theory for Multirotors
section: 9.3 Why a Multirotor Cannot Fly Open Loop
text:
9.3 Why a Multirotor Cannot Fly Open Loop
An open-loop controller computes its command from the request alone: to climb one metre, add some thrust for some duration, and hope. For a few plants — a stepper motor, a toaster — hoping works, because the plant is stable and the disturbances are small. A multirotor fails every part of that description, for three reasons the vehicle of Part I makes concrete.
First, the plant is underactuated. The aircraft has six degrees of freedom — position \(x, y, z\) and attitude roll \(\phi\), pitch \(\theta\), yaw \(\psi\) — but only four independent inputs, the four motor thrusts. It cannot accelerate sideways while staying level; as the Anatomy of a Multirotor chapter established, translation is bought with tilt, and yaw is bought with the drag-torque imbalance between the two counter-rotating propeller pairs. Rotation and translation are permanently coupled, so any position command is really an attitude command in disguise.
Second, hover is an unstable equilibrium. All four thrusts summing exactly to weight, with the thrust vector exactly vertical, is a balance point — but nothing restores it. Tilt the aircraft a degree and the thrust vector tilts with it, producing a sideways acceleration that grows the disturbance rather than fighting it. A fixed-wing aircraft can be built with passive aerodynamic stability; a multirotor has none. The often-quoted consequence from the previous chapter — that a stall of a tenth of a second in the attitude loop is the end of the flight — is just this instability stated as a deadline.
Third, the plant is continuously disturbed. Wind gusts apply torques; the battery sags, changing thrust per unit command as the flight proceeds; motors and propellers are never perfectly matched; a payload sits a centimetre off the centre of gravity. None of these appear in any feedforward calculation, and all of them push the state away from wherever it was commanded to be.
The remedy is to stop computing commands from the request and start computing them from the error. A closed-loop controller continuously compares the setpoint \(r(t)\) against the measured (in practice, estimated) output \(y(t)\) and forms
\[e(t) = r(t) - y(t),\]
the tracking error, which is the only signal the controller ever consumes. Figure 9.1 shows the structure. The loop answers three questions, over and over, at whatever rate the plant demands: where am I, where should I be, and what command shrinks the difference?






Figure 9.1: The closed control loop: the setpoint and the estimated state meet at a summing junction, and only their difference reaches the controller. Disturbances enter the plant uninvited; feedback is what makes them survivable.



Two details in the figure deserve emphasis because they recur all book long. The feedback path runs through sensors and an estimator, not through the world directly: as the Sensing the World chapter showed, the controller acts on EKF2’s fused estimate \(\hat{y}(t)\), with all the bias-tracking and outlier rejection that implies, and a controller is only ever as honest as the estimate it is fed. And the sign convention matters: with \(e = r - y\), a vehicle rolled to \(+8^\circ\) against a commanded \(0^\circ\) produces \(e_\phi = -8^\circ\), and the controller output — a negative roll torque — is what rotates it back toward level. Every loop in this chapter, and every loop in the PX4 firmware, is built around exactly this signal.

title: 9  Closed-Loop Control: PID Theory for Multirotors
text:
9.4 The PID Control Law
Given the error signal, what command should the controller produce? The PID answer is that there are exactly three useful questions to ask of \(e(t)\) — what is it now, what has it been, and where is it going — and that the command should be a weighted sum of the three answers:
\[u(t) = K_p\, e(t) \;+\; K_i \int_0^t e(\tau)\, d\tau \;+\; K_d\, \frac{de(t)}{dt}.\]
The three gains \(K_p\), \(K_i\), \(K_d\) are the entire design space, and each maps onto a distinct physical behavior of the aircraft.
The proportional term is stiffness. It responds to the present error, immediately and in proportion: a large tilt produces a large corrective torque, a small tilt a small one. A vehicle with low \(K_p\) feels soft and sluggish, leaning downwind like a reed and returning lazily. Raise \(K_p\) and it stiffens — corrections come faster and harder. Raise it too far and the vehicle overshoots the setpoint, corrects back, overshoots again, and oscillates: the command is always proportional to an error that the vehicle’s inertia has already carried it past.
The integral term is memory. A proportional controller has a structural blind spot: it can only produce a command while there is an error, so any constant disturbance settles into a standoff — a permanent offset at which the proportional command exactly balances the disturbance and nothing changes. Suppose one motor is a few percent weak, or the battery of the running example sits a centimetre aft of the vehicle’s centreline. The aircraft hovers with a small persistent tilt, and \(K_p\) alone will hold that tilt forever. The integral term accumulates the error over time, growing its contribution until the bias is cancelled and the error is actually zero. Its cost is sluggishness of a particular kind: too much \(K_i\) produces slow, wallowing oscillation, and — as the next sections make precise — an integrator that accumulates while the motors are saturated causes the overshoot called windup.
The derivative term is damping. It responds not to the error but to its trend. If the vehicle is rotating rapidly toward the setpoint, the derivative term begins braking before the setpoint is reached, exactly as a damper resists velocity regardless of position. This is what converts an oscillatory response into a crisply settling one. Its cost is noise sensitivity: differentiation amplifies exactly the high-frequency content — gyro noise, propeller vibration at the blade-passage frequencies the Materials and Power chapter computed — that the rest of the system works to suppress. Too much \(K_d\) shows up as a hot, twitchy vehicle whose motors buzz in response to vibration the pilot cannot even see.
The three terms are not independent knobs so much as three forces in negotiation — stiffness pulling toward the setpoint, damping resisting the speed of the pull, memory removing whatever offset the other two leave behind. Tuning is the act of setting the terms of that negotiation, and it becomes concrete the moment real numbers are attached.

title: 9  Closed-Loop Control: PID Theory for Multirotors
text:
9.5 A Worked Design: Altitude Hold
Take the running example’s aircraft as Part I left it: all-up mass \(m = 2.2\) kg, maximum static thrust about \(4.0\) kgf \(= 39.2\) N, hover thrust \(mg = 2.2 \times 9.81 = 21.6\) N, leaving a climb margin of about \(17.7\) N above hover. The task is the simplest loop on the vehicle: hold a commanded altitude \(z_d\).
Near hover, write total thrust as hover thrust plus a correction, \(T = mg + \Delta T\). Newton’s second law for the vertical axis, neglecting drag at the low vertical speeds of altitude hold, is
\[m\ddot{z} = T - mg = \Delta T.\]
Let the controller be PD for now — proportional and derivative, with the integral term’s role examined afterward — commanding
\[\Delta T = K_p\, e - K_d\, \dot{z}, \qquad e = z_d - z.\]
(Using \(-\dot z\) rather than \(\dot e\) is the standard derivative-on-measurement form; for a constant setpoint they are identical, and for a setpoint that jumps it avoids differentiating the jump.) Substituting into the dynamics and using \(\ddot z = -\ddot e\), \(\dot z = -\dot e\) for constant \(z_d\) gives a second-order linear system in the error:
\[
\begin{aligned}
m\ddot{e} + K_d\, \dot{e} + K_p\, e &= 0,\\
\text{i.e.}\quad \ddot{e} + \frac{K_d}{m}\,\dot{e} + \frac{K_p}{m}\, e &= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Comparing against the canonical form \(\ddot e + 2\zeta\omega_n \dot e + \omega_n^2 e = 0\) identifies the two quantities a designer actually chooses: the natural frequency \(\omega_n = \sqrt{K_p/m}\), which sets how fast the loop responds, and the damping ratio \(\zeta = K_d / (2 m \omega_n)\), which sets how the response settles. This is the central trick of classical design — pick the behavior, then read off the gains:
\[
\begin{aligned}
K_p &= m\,\omega_n^2,\\
K_d &= 2\,\zeta\,\omega_n\, m.
\end{aligned}
\]
Choose a response with a time constant under a second and essentially no overshoot: \(\omega_n = 2.0\) rad/s and \(\zeta = 0.9\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
K_p &= m\,\omega_n^2 = 2.2 \times (2.0)^2 = 8.8\ \text{N/m},\\
K_d &= 2\,\zeta\,\omega_n\, m = 2 (0.9)(2.0)(2.2) = 7.92\ \text{N}\cdot\text{s/m}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Two checks make this a design rather than an arithmetic exercise. Overshoot: for a second-order system the peak overshoot is \(M_p = \exp\!\left(-\pi\zeta/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}\right)\), and at \(\zeta = 0.9\) that is \(\exp(-2.827/0.436) \approx 0.0015\) — about 0.15 %, invisible in flight. Saturation: a 1 m altitude error commands \(8.8\) N of extra thrust against the \(17.7\) N available, comfortable; a 2 m error commands \(17.6\) N and sits at the very edge of the climb margin. Larger steps saturate the motors, and the linear analysis above stops describing the vehicle — a fact that will matter shortly.
Now break the design deliberately, because the failure modes are the point. Figure 9.2 shows all three responses to the same 1.0 m climb command.
Too much proportional gain. Multiply \(K_p\) by ten, to 88 N/m, leaving \(K_d\) alone. The closed-loop parameters follow from the same two formulas, run backward:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\omega_n &= \sqrt{K_p/m} = \sqrt{88/2.2} = \sqrt{40} = 6.32\ \text{rad/s},\\
\zeta &= \frac{K_d}{2 m \omega_n} = \frac{7.92}{2(2.2)(6.32)} = 0.285,\\
M_p &= \exp\!\left(\frac{-\pi (0.285)}{\sqrt{1-0.285^2}}\right) = \exp(-0.93) \approx 0.39.
\end{aligned}
\]
The response is fast — and rings, overshooting the setpoint by 39 % and oscillating through several diminishing cycles. This is the universal signature of excessive gain, and the standard remedy is exactly what the algebra says it is: reduce \(K_p\), or restore the balance by adding derivative damping until \(\zeta\) is back near critical. Worse, the linear prediction is optimistic here: a 1 m error now commands 88 N of correction against 17.7 N of authority, so the motors saturate hard and the real response is uglier than the formula admits. On an attitude loop the same mistake is more than ugly — a 39 % overshoot in roll near the ground, or near the 122 m ceiling the Airspace Law chapter established, is an incident.
No integral term. Suppose the vehicle carries 200 g the controller’s model does not know about — mud on the airframe, a heavier battery, the payload creep every field program experiences. The feedforward hover term \(mg\) is now short by \(0.2 \times 9.81 = 1.96\) N, a constant downward disturbance. The PD loop settles where proportional command balances deficit: \(K_p e_{ss} = 1.96\) N, so
\[e_{ss} = \frac{1.96}{8.8} = 0.22\ \text{m}.\]
The aircraft flies its entire mission 22 cm below every altitude it is asked for — stable, smooth, and wrong. This is steady-state error, and no amount of \(K_p\) or \(K_d\) tuning removes it; raising \(K_p\) only shrinks it at the price of the ringing computed above. The integral term is the cure. With an integral gain \(K_i = 2\) N/(m·s), the integrator accumulates at \(K_i e \approx 0.45\) N/s while the error stands at 0.22 m, so it would need roughly \(1.96/0.45 \approx 4.4\) s to supply the missing force — in practice somewhat longer, since the error shrinks as the integrator does its work. The response is a slow, deliberate closing of the last centimetres: memory, doing exactly its job, on exactly the time scale its small gain implies.






Figure 9.2: Three tunings of the same altitude loop answering the same 1.0 m climb command: the worked design settles cleanly; ten times the proportional gain overshoots 39 % and rings; removing the integral term while carrying 200 g of unmodeled mass leaves a permanent 0.22 m steady-state error.



One design, three behaviors, and every one of them legible in the shape of the response — that legibility is why log plots of setpoint against estimate are the primary diagnostic tool for control problems, a thread Part V’s diagnostics material picks up in earnest.

title: 9  Closed-Loop Control: PID Theory for Multirotors
text:
9.6 From Calculus to Code
The law derived above is continuous mathematics; what a flight controller runs is a loop over samples. At each tick \(k\), separated by the sampling period \(\Delta t\), the derivative becomes a difference, the integral becomes a running sum, and the controller becomes a handful of lines executed on the order of a thousand times per second:
def pid_step(setpoint, measurement, dt, state):
    error = setpoint - measurement

    # P: the present error
    p_term = KP * error

    # I: accumulate, but clamp -- see "windup" below
    state.integral = clamp(state.integral + KI * error * dt,
                           -I_LIMIT, +I_LIMIT)

    # D: differentiate the *filtered* measurement, not the raw error
    d_term = -KD * state.deriv_filter.update(measurement, dt)

    return p_term + state.integral + d_term
The differences between this and the textbook equation are not blemishes; they are the accumulated flight experience of every autopilot project, and three of them matter enough to name.
Saturation and integrator windup. Motors have a floor and a ceiling. When the loop commands more than the hardware can deliver — the 3 m step that wants 26 N of the 17.7 N available — the command clips, but a naive integrator keeps accumulating the error the clipped command failed to remove. By the time the vehicle finally reaches the setpoint, the integrator holds a large stale total that must be un-accumulated, and it discharges as a long overshoot on the far side. The fix in the code above is the clamp: bound the integrator so it can never hold more authority than a modest fraction of the actuator range. Production controllers go further (freezing integration while saturated, or back-calculating), but the clamp is the load-bearing idea.
Derivative filtering. Differencing adjacent samples of a noisy signal divides the noise by \(\Delta t\), and at kilohertz rates \(\Delta t\) is small — raw differentiation of a vibrating airframe’s gyro signal produces a derivative term that is mostly amplified vibration, fed straight to the motors as heat and twitch. Every practical implementation low-pass filters the signal before (or while) differentiating it. This is also where the mechanical world reaches into the control law: the propeller balance and frame stiffness the Materials and Power chapter argued for are, among other things, what makes a useful \(K_d\) possible at all.
Derivative on measurement. The code differentiates the measurement rather than the error. When a setpoint changes stepwise — a new altitude command arrives — the error jumps discontinuously, and differentiating it produces a one-sample spike of enormous magnitude (a “derivative kick”) that bangs the actuators for no physical reason. The measurement itself never jumps; differentiating it yields the same damping with no kick. It is a one-line change that every flight stack makes.

section: 9.7 Why One Loop Is Not Enough
text:
9.7 Why One Loop Is Not Enough
Nothing so far explains the architecture the previous chapter promised — so consider trying to fly with a single PID from position error straight to motor commands. The loop must then handle, all at once, dynamics living on wildly different time scales: position responds over seconds, attitude over tenths of a second, angular rate over hundredths. One set of three gains cannot serve all three regimes — tuned tight enough to stabilize the fast rotational dynamics it will be violently aggressive about position errors; tuned gentle enough for position it will be far too slow to catch a tilt. And the coupling runs deeper: because the vehicle is underactuated, a position error does not even correspond to any particular motor command — it corresponds to a desired tilt, which corresponds to a desired rotation, which finally corresponds to a torque.
The architecture that resolves both problems is the cascade, shown in Figure 9.3: a chain of loops, each consuming the setpoint the loop outside it produced and producing the setpoint for the loop inside it, each running faster than the one outside it. This is the structure PX4 implements for multirotors, and its stages map exactly onto the chain of physical implications above.






Figure 9.3: The cascaded control stack as PX4 structures it: position and velocity loops at roughly 50 Hz generate a thrust vector, an attitude loop at roughly 250 Hz converts thrust direction into body-rate setpoints, the rate PID at roughly 1 kHz converts rate error into torque, and control allocation converts torque and thrust into four motor commands — with every loop closing against the same EKF2 state estimate.



Read the chain left to right as a sequence of translations, each answering one question. The position controller — a plain proportional loop, no I or D — answers where should I be? by converting position error into a velocity setpoint. The velocity controller, a full PID, answers how fast should I move? — and its output is worth pausing on, because it is not a motor command but a thrust vector: a magnitude (how hard to push) and a direction (which way), which is precisely the “translation is bought with tilt” coupling made explicit. The attitude controller answers which way should thrust point? by comparing desired against estimated orientation — as quaternions, not Euler angles, to stay free of singularities — and emitting body-rate setpoints through a proportional law. The rate controller answers how fast should I rotate? and is the innermost loop of the entire vehicle: three independent PIDs, one per body axis, converting rate error into a torque demand at approximately the gyro rate, on the order of a kilohertz. Finally, control allocation solves the geometry problem the Anatomy of a Multirotor chapter set up — given a desired total thrust and three desired torques, choose four motor thrusts, using the motor positions and spin directions, that realize them within limits.
The cascade works because of time-scale separation: each loop runs several times faster than the loop outside it, so from the outer loop’s viewpoint the inner loop is essentially a solved problem — command a body rate, and it simply happens. The discipline this imposes runs both ways. Inner loops must actually be fast and well-tuned, which is why the rate loop is tuned first and best: every flight mode, from full manual to full autonomy, passes through it, and a defect there surfaces everywhere. And outer loops must not ask for motion faster than the inner loops can deliver, which is the control-theoretic root of a rule the previous chapter stated operationally — the mission layer requests, the flight controller disposes.
The cascade is also why the running example’s software never touches a motor. When Part II’s later chapters script the Goose Management System’s search grid, its companion computer will publish position and velocity setpoints into the left end of this chain, and when a detected goose demands the evasive climb whose 7.8 m/s² ceiling the previous chapter computed, that maneuver too will be delivered as setpoints and honored by these same four loops. Where do the gains themselves live? In PX4 they are ordinary named parameters — MC_ROLLRATE_P, MC_PITCHRATE_D, MPC_Z_VEL_P_ACC, and their kin — stored on the flight controller and adjustable without recompiling firmware; the PX4 and the Autopilot Stack chapter maps that parameter system, and the loops above are what its numbers feed.
One trace ties the whole architecture together. A wind gust over the protected area rolls the aircraft: the gyro reports a roll rate that the rate setpoint never asked for; the rate PID sees the error, and its proportional term commands an opposing torque within a millisecond or two while its derivative term brakes the buildup; the allocator converts the torque into four slightly changed motor commands; the airframe rotates back. If the gust is sustained rather than momentary, the attitude loop’s error persists, the position loop watches the vehicle drift downwind, and each outer layer leans its setpoints upwind until the drift stops — the integral terms quietly absorbing whatever steady lean the gust demands. Nothing above the rate loop needed to know the gust happened quickly, and nothing below the position loop needed to know the mission cared. That division of labor, running hundreds of times per second in silence, is what “the flight controller stabilizes the vehicle” actually means.
