section: 9.8 Tuning: Reading the Gains from Flight Behavior
text:
9.8 Tuning: Reading the Gains from Flight Behavior
Gains are not abstract. Each mistuning has a physical signature, and a practiced eye diagnoses a vehicle from thirty seconds of hover the way a mechanic diagnoses an engine from idle. The table collects the symptoms developed through this chapter.








Gain
Too low
Too high




\(K_p\)
Sluggish, soft response; poor tracking; leans with disturbances
Oscillation and twitching; overshoot; high motor activity


\(K_i\)
Steady drift; persistent offset never removed
Slow wallowing oscillation; overshoot after saturation (windup)


\(K_d\)
Overshoot and ringing; poor damping
Noise amplification; hot motors; vibration sensitivity



The workflow that turns the table into a safe procedure has a fixed order, and each step exists because of something quantitative from earlier chapters. Mechanics first: balanced propellers, a rigid frame, a sane centre of gravity, correct motor order and spin direction — no gain can compensate for a vibration source feeding the derivative term or a mixer commanding the wrong motor. Then sensors: a calibrated IMU and acceptable vibration metrics, because every loop closes against the estimate. Then start conservative, from published defaults for a similar airframe class. Then tune from the inside out: rate loop first, then attitude, then velocity and position — because every outer loop’s correctness assumes the loops inside it already track well, an assumption the cascade’s whole architecture rests on. Then read the logs, comparing setpoint against estimate for each loop and watching for saturation. Bench tests happen with propellers removed; aggressive tuning happens nowhere near people. The natural place to practice all of this without bending an aircraft is simulation, where the same PX4 code runs against a modeled plant — the subject of this chapter’s related lab.
It is fair to ask why, in an era of model-predictive and learning-based control, a law from the age of steam governs every small multirotor flying. The honest answer is engineering economics: PID is computationally almost free, which matters at a kilohertz on a microcontroller; it is transparent, so a log tells you which term misbehaved; it requires no model of the plant beyond what tuning extracts; and the cascade structure lets a stack of simple loops manage a nonlinear vehicle that no single simple loop could. Its limits are real — performance degrades away from hover, saturation can exceed its authority, and gains tuned for one payload are wrong for another — but within the envelope a multirotor actually flies, it has proven very hard to beat at the price.






NoteFor More



The natural next steps beyond PID each relax one of its simplifications. The linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) derives all gains at once from a linearized model by minimizing a stated cost, replacing per-loop hand-tuning with a principled trade between error and effort. Model-predictive control (MPC) re-solves a short constrained optimization every cycle, which lets it respect actuator limits inside the law rather than clamping after the fact — increasingly practical on companion-computer-class hardware for aggressive trajectories. Adaptive and learning-based controllers re-estimate the plant in flight, attacking the payload-changes-the-gains problem directly. Each buys capability with computation and with opacity, which is why the innermost loop of certified and hobby aircraft alike remains, for now, the law of this chapter.

title: 9  Closed-Loop Control: PID Theory for Multirotors
text:
9.9 Check Your Understanding

The empty research airframe from Part I has a mass of 1.7 kg. Using the same design targets as the worked example (\(\omega_n = 2.0\) rad/s, \(\zeta = 0.9\)), compute the altitude-hold gains \(K_p\) and \(K_d\) — and explain why the gains tuned for the 2.2 kg loaded vehicle are wrong for the empty one.







TipShow answer





\(K_p = m\omega_n^2 = 1.7 \times 4 = 6.8\) N/m and \(K_d = 2\zeta\omega_n m = 2(0.9)(2.0)(1.7) = 6.12\) N·s/m. The gains scale with mass because the plant does: the same thrust correction accelerates a lighter vehicle harder. Flying the empty airframe on the loaded vehicle’s gains (\(K_p = 8.8\), \(K_d = 7.92\)) raises \(\omega_n\) to \(\sqrt{8.8/1.7} = 2.28\) rad/s — a stiffer, faster response than designed, though with \(\zeta = 7.92/(2 \times 1.7 \times 2.28) = 1.02\) it stays well damped. The general lesson is the last row of the chapter: gains encode a model of the plant, and changing the payload silently changes the plant.




A proportional-only altitude controller with \(K_p = 8.8\) N/m faces a steady 3.0 N downdraft. Compute the steady-state error, state which PID term removes it, and name the failure mode that term introduces if the vehicle spends time at full throttle.







TipShow answer





At equilibrium the proportional command balances the disturbance: \(K_p e_{ss} = 3.0\) N, so \(e_{ss} = 3.0/8.8 = 0.34\) m below setpoint. The integral term removes it, accumulating command as long as any error persists until the disturbance is fully cancelled at zero error. The introduced risk is integrator windup: if the motors saturate — a long full-throttle climb, or a disturbance larger than the thrust margin — the integrator keeps accumulating error it cannot act on, then discharges as a large overshoot once authority returns. The remedy is to clamp the integrator (or freeze it during saturation).




A colleague tunes the altitude loop to \(\zeta = 0.5\) to get a faster rise. Compute the resulting overshoot, and explain why that tuning is acceptable for a climb from 30 m to 40 m over open water but unacceptable for a climb commanded to the 122 m regulatory ceiling.







TipShow answer





\(M_p = \exp(-\pi\zeta/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}) = \exp(-\pi(0.5)/\sqrt{0.75}) = \exp(-1.814) \approx 0.163\), so about 16 % overshoot. Overshoot scales with step size: a 10 m climb overshoots by about 1.6 m, harmless with 80 m of sky above. But commanded to the ceiling, the same controller passes 1.6 m per 10 m of step beyond it — the vehicle physically busts the limit before settling back, even though the setpoint itself was legal. Either the damping must be restored toward critical, or the mission layer must leave altitude margin at least equal to the worst-case overshoot — the layered-margin logic of the Airspace Law chapter, now derived from a control parameter.




Three vehicles misbehave in hover: (a) one twitches rapidly, motors audibly busy, oscillating several times per second; (b) one slowly wanders off altitude and never comes back; (c) one holds attitude but its motors run hot and it reacts violently to the slightest airframe vibration. Diagnose the gain problem in each.







TipShow answer






Excessive \(K_p\) (or insufficient damping relative to it) in a fast loop, classically the rate loop: the fast oscillation is the stiffness/inertia cycle of the chapter’s \(K_p \times 10\) example. Remedy: reduce \(K_p\) or add \(K_d\). (b) Insufficient (or absent) \(K_i\): a steady disturbance — payload offset, weak motor, drift — is being balanced by a permanent error the proportional term cannot remove. (c) Excessive \(K_d\): the derivative term is amplifying high-frequency vibration and gyro noise into motor commands — heat and twitch with no visible attitude error. Remedy: reduce \(K_d\), strengthen derivative filtering, and fix the mechanical vibration source first.





Explain why PX4 controls a multirotor with a cascade of four loops rather than one PID from position error to motor commands, and why the tuning workflow insists the rate loop be tuned first.







TipShow answer





Two reasons. Time scales: position dynamics evolve over seconds while rotational dynamics evolve over hundredths of a second, and no single set of gains can be simultaneously gentle enough for one and fast enough for the other. Underactuation: a position error does not map to any motor command directly — it maps to a desired velocity, which maps to a desired thrust vector (tilt), which maps to desired body rates, which finally map to torque; the cascade makes each translation an explicit loop. Each outer loop treats the inner loop as a solved problem, so the assumption only holds if inner loops genuinely track well — which is why the rate loop, the innermost, is tuned first: every flight mode passes through it, and a rate-loop defect surfaces in all of them.




The digital controller differentiates the filtered measurement rather than the raw error. Give both reasons, and explain what each failure would look like in flight if the implementation did neither.







TipShow answer





Filtering: differencing adjacent samples amplifies high-frequency noise by roughly \(1/\Delta t\), so an unfiltered derivative of a vibrating airframe’s gyro signal is mostly amplified vibration — in flight, hot motors, audible twitching, and sensitivity to propeller imbalance. Measurement instead of error: when the setpoint steps, the error jumps discontinuously, and its derivative is a one-sample spike (“derivative kick”) that slams the actuators at the moment of every new command — in flight, a thump or lurch each time a new altitude or attitude setpoint arrives. The measurement is continuous even when the setpoint is not, so differentiating it gives the same damping with no kick.

9.10 Try It
Part 1 — build the altitude loop and break it. Write a short Python simulation of the worked example: state \((z, \dot z)\), mass 2.2 kg, Euler integration at \(\Delta t = 0.004\) s (250 Hz), thrust command clamped to the real vehicle’s range (\(-21.6\) N to \(+17.7\) N of correction about hover). Implement the digital PID exactly as the chapter’s code sketch has it — clamped integrator, derivative on measurement. First reproduce Figure 9.2’s three curves: the worked design, the \(K_p \times 10\) ringing, and the 200 g steady-state error (add \(-1.96\) N of constant disturbance with \(K_i = 0\), then watch \(K_i = 2\) remove it). Then command a 3 m step with the integrator clamp removed and watch windup happen: the command saturates at 17.7 N, the integrator accumulates through the whole climb, and the vehicle sails past the setpoint. Restore the clamp and measure how much overshoot it saved.
Part 2 — predict, then verify. Before touching a simulator, write down predictions in the symptom language of the tuning table: what should doubling \(K_d\) alone do to the worked design’s response? Halving \(K_p\)? Setting \(\zeta = 0.3\) by computing the required \(K_d\)? Run each in your Part 1 script and check yourself. Prediction-before-experiment is exactly the habit the related lab exercises against a full PX4 software-in-the-loop vehicle, where the same gains live in real firmware parameters.

title: 10  PX4 and the Autopilot Stack: MAVLink, MAVSDK, and ROS 2
text:
10.1 Learning Objectives
The previous chapter ended inside the flight controller, with the cascade’s gains living as named parameters — MC_ROLLRATE_P and its kin — in a piece of software it kept calling “the PX4 firmware” without ever justifying the choice. And the Companion Computers chapter of Part I ended at the other side of the wire, with a MAVLink heartbeat arriving over three verified conductors and a promise that Part II would show how a Python program turns that link into an autonomous takeoff. This chapter keeps both promises at once, because they are the same promise: it maps the software stack that stands between a mission script and the four motor commands, layer by layer, and makes the three decisions every autonomy project has to make before writing its first line of flight code. Which autopilot firmware runs the loops — PX4 or ArduPilot, a choice that turns out to hinge on law as much as engineering? Which programming layer does the mission code use to command it — MAVSDK, a library that makes a drone feel like an object with methods, or ROS 2, a middleware that makes it one participant in a graph of cooperating processes? And where does the code fly first — because the correct answer is nowhere, until the identical firmware has flown the identical mission in simulation.
The stakes of the chapter are inherited directly from the one before. The cascade of PID loops is superb at what it does and completely indifferent to why: it will track a setpoint into the ground as faithfully as into a perfect hover. Everything that makes the running example a system rather than a stabilizer — the search, the detection, the deterrence — enters the flight controller from outside, as messages on the wire Part I installed. This chapter is about the grammar of those messages and the software that speaks it.

title: 10  PX4 and the Autopilot Stack: MAVLink, MAVSDK, and ROS 2
text:
Compare PX4 and ArduPilot as autopilot firmware, and explain concretely what the BSD 3-clause and GPL v3 licenses each oblige a team to do when it modifies the firmware and distributes vehicles containing it — and why neither license reaches mission code on the companion computer.
Describe MAVLink’s role as the common protocol among flight controller, ground station, and companion computer, and distinguish its two idioms: streamed telemetry and acknowledged commands.
Write and explain a minimal MAVSDK mission — connect, verify, arm, take off, land — and identify the class of project for which MAVSDK is the right programming layer.
Explain how ROS 2 talks to PX4 without MAVLink, through uORB topics exposed across the Micro XRCE-DDS bridge, and why the mission-side architecture becomes a timer-driven node rather than a linear script.
State Offboard mode’s two hard rules — stream setpoints before entering, keep streaming above about 2 Hz to stay — and justify them as a dead-man’s switch protecting the vehicle from its own companion computer.
Explain why “simulate, then fly” is standard practice: PX4 SITL runs the identical firmware against a modeled plant, so the mission code that survives Gazebo is byte-for-byte the code that flies.

title: 10  PX4 and the Autopilot Stack: MAVLink, MAVSDK, and ROS 2
text:
10.2 Key Vocabulary

PX4 — an open-source autopilot firmware, licensed BSD 3-clause, that implements the estimator, the cascaded control loops, the flight modes, and the failsafe logic on Pixhawk-class flight controllers; the firmware this book’s platform runs.
ArduPilot — the other major open-source autopilot firmware, licensed GPL v3, older and more extensively documented than PX4, with a faster-moving but historically rockier release cadence.
MAVLink (Micro Air Vehicle Link) — the lightweight binary message protocol spoken among flight controllers, ground stations, and companion computers: framed packets carrying typed payloads, addressed by system and component ID, over any serial or network transport.
QGroundControl — the cross-platform ground-control station developed alongside PX4: mission upload, live telemetry, parameter editing, sensor calibration, and firmware flashing through one MAVLink-speaking interface.
Mission Planner — ArduPilot’s companion ground-control station, Windows-first and denser, exposing more of the firmware’s features at the cost of a steeper interface.
MAVSDK — a library (with Python, C++, and other language bindings) that wraps MAVLink in high-level calls — arm(), takeoff(), land() — so a single linear program can command a vehicle without composing protocol messages by hand.
ROS 2 (Robot Operating System 2) — the middleware, introduced with the running example’s architecture at the close of Part I, in which independent nodes exchange typed messages over named topics and services; here, the scalable alternative to MAVSDK for mission software.
uORB — PX4’s internal publish–subscribe message bus, over which the firmware’s own modules (estimator, controllers, commander) exchange data; the DDS bridge exposes these same topics to ROS 2 rather than translating them.
Micro XRCE-DDS — the bridge protocol between PX4 and ROS 2: a lightweight client inside the firmware serializes uORB topics across the UART to an agent process on the companion computer, which republishes them as ordinary ROS 2 topics.
Offboard mode — the PX4 flight mode in which the autopilot follows position, velocity, or attitude setpoints streamed by an external computer, entered only while a setpoint stream is already flowing and abandoned, in favor of a failsafe behavior, the moment the stream stalls.
SITL (Software-in-the-Loop) — running the unmodified autopilot firmware as a desktop process against a physics simulator such as Gazebo, so that missions, modes, and failsafes can be exercised — and crashed — with no aircraft at risk.

section: 10.3 Choosing the Firmware: PX4 versus ArduPilot
text:
10.3 Choosing the Firmware: PX4 versus ArduPilot
The flight controller Part I selected is a piece of hardware; what the previous chapter analyzed — the estimator, the cascade, the parameters — is firmware running on it, and that firmware is a choice. Two open-source projects dominate the space, and the striking thing about the comparison is what it is not about. Both PX4 and ArduPilot are mature, both fly multirotors, fixed-wings, and stranger vehicles, both implement an EKF-based estimator and a cascaded control architecture of exactly the shape the previous chapter derived, and both are trusted by commercial operators. A team choosing between them on control performance is choosing on noise. The real differences are a software license, a ground station, and a development culture — and the first of these deserves more attention than engineering teams usually give it, because it is the one difference that can bind a company years later. Figure 10.1 lays the comparison out.






Figure 10.1: The PX4 versus ArduPilot decision: identical control theory, different licenses, ground stations, and release cultures — with the licensing consequence drawn out for a team that modifies the firmware and ships vehicles containing it.




10.3.1 What the licenses actually oblige
The source-of-record difference is one line — PX4 is licensed under the BSD 3-clause license, ArduPilot under the GPL v3 — and the line is easy to read past, because both licenses grant the same generous core: anyone may use, study, modify, and redistribute the code, free of charge, forever. The divergence is entirely about what happens to modifications, and it only activates at a specific, well-defined moment: distribution. A team that modifies either firmware and flies it on its own aircraft owes nobody anything, under either license. The obligations attach when copies of the firmware leave the team’s hands — most commonly, when it sells or delivers vehicles with the modified firmware flashed aboard.
At that moment the two licenses part company. The BSD 3-clause license is permissive: it asks that the copyright notice and license text be preserved, and that the project’s name not be used to endorse the derivative — and that is the entire bill. The modification itself may remain a trade secret. A drone manufacturer can develop a proprietary control module inside PX4, ship a thousand vehicles running it, and never show a line of it to anyone; this is precisely why a long roster of commercial autopilot vendors builds on PX4, and why the Dronecode ecosystem around it is structured as an industry consortium. The GPL v3 is copyleft: distributing a binary built from modified ArduPilot obliges the distributor to offer the corresponding source — the modification included — to every recipient, under the same GPL terms, which means every recipient is in turn free to redistribute it to the world. A proprietary firmware advantage built on ArduPilot is therefore, structurally, a contradiction: the act of selling the product is the act of publishing the advantage.
Neither position is “better”; they encode different theories of how a commons should grow. Copyleft ensures improvements flow back — one reason ArduPilot’s feature set and vehicle support are so broad is that two decades of forks were legally obliged to remain open. Permissiveness ensures companies can invest without forfeiting their differentiation — one reason PX4 attracts commercial teams whose autonomy stack is their product. What a team must not do is discover the difference after the fact. The scenario that matters is concrete: a startup builds custom autonomy behavior into the firmware itself — a tighter rate controller, a proprietary failure-detection module — and later takes on customers. On PX4, that intellectual property is theirs to keep. On ArduPilot, their first shipment is a publication event.
One boundary of the obligation matters just as much and is drawn at the bottom of Figure 10.1: the license governs the firmware, not the system around it. Mission code running on the companion computer — a MAVSDK script, the ROS 2 nodes of the running example — is a separate program communicating with the firmware over a serial protocol, not a derivative work of it, and neither license reaches across that link. A team can keep its entire autonomy stack proprietary above a GPL autopilot. The license question bites only those who modify the autopilot itself — which is exactly why the architecture this book builds does all of its innovating on the companion-computer side of the wire.


10.3.2 Tooling and culture
The second difference a team lives with daily is the ground station. QGroundControl grew up alongside PX4: cross-platform, comparatively clean, organized around the workflow of flying — mission upload, live telemetry, parameter editing, sensor calibration, firmware flashing. Mission Planner grew up alongside ArduPilot: Windows-first, denser, and famously feature-rich, exposing more of the firmware’s considerable surface area at the cost of a steeper interface. Both speak MAVLink, and either can talk to either firmware in a pinch, but each is at home with its own. The remaining differences are cultural and worth stating as tendencies rather than laws: ArduPilot, the older project, carries deeper documentation and a longer public record of prior builds to learn from, while PX4 has a reputation for cleaner, more conservative release engineering — patches that arrive less often and break less.
This book’s platform runs PX4, and the reasons can now be stated honestly rather than by fiat. The permissive license matches the book’s premise — a team whose value lives in custom autonomy software. QGroundControl is the tool the coming chapters use for parameter work and mission upload. And one reason outranks the others for what follows: PX4’s first-class ROS 2 integration, which gives the running example’s node graph a direct line into the autopilot that ArduPilot’s MAVLink-translation route does not match. Everything the previous chapter said about the cascade still holds verbatim — PX4’s parameters (MC_ROLLRATE_P, MPC_Z_VEL_P_ACC, and hundreds more) are those loops’ gains, stored on the flight controller, inspected and changed live from QGroundControl without recompiling anything. The firmware is chosen; the question becomes how to talk to it.

title: 10  PX4 and the Autopilot Stack: MAVLink, MAVSDK, and ROS 2
text:
10.4 MAVLink: One Protocol, Three Speakers
The Companion Computers chapter introduced MAVLink operationally — the heartbeat arriving at 1 Hz was the proof the wire worked — and deferred the protocol itself to this chapter. MAVLink is a lightweight binary message protocol designed for exactly the environment Part I built: low-bandwidth serial links shared by devices that must not waste bytes. A MAVLink packet is a typed payload of at most 255 bytes wrapped in roughly a dozen bytes of framing — a start marker, a length, sequence and address fields, a message ID identifying which of the protocol’s several hundred defined message types the payload is, and a checksum computed over both the bytes and the message definition, so that two ends compiled against mismatched dialects reject each other’s traffic rather than misreading it. Every participant carries a system ID (the vehicle is conventionally system 1, a ground station 255) and a component ID (the autopilot, a camera, a gimbal), so one link can multiplex conversations among many parties. At the 921,600-baud link’s roughly 90 kB/s, the arithmetic from Part I holds comfortably: full telemetry and command traffic occupy a small fraction of the wire.
Two idioms cover nearly all of the traffic. Streams are periodic, unacknowledged broadcasts — attitude, position, battery state, and the 1 Hz HEARTBEAT itself — carrying data where only the latest value matters and a lost packet costs nothing, because a fresher one is already on the way. Commands are the opposite contract: a COMMAND_LONG message carries a command ID and up to seven parameters — arm, set mode, return to launch — and the recipient answers with a COMMAND_ACK accepting or rejecting it, because “arm the vehicle” is not a request whose fate a sender can shrug about. The reader will recognize this pair: it is the topics-versus-services distinction the closing chapter of Part I drew for ROS 2, appearing one layer down, in a protocol that predates ROS 2 — the same engineering fork (streamed state versus acknowledged action) recurs at every level of the stack because the underlying question recurs.
Figure 10.2 places the protocol in the geography Part I established. Three speakers address the autopilot, along the three command paths enumerated in the Companion Computers chapter. QGroundControl speaks MAVLink over the telemetry radio: monitoring, mission upload, parameter changes. The companion computer speaks over the wired UART — and here the figure shows a fork this chapter spends its remaining pages on, because mission code has two quite different ways to form its side of the conversation. The RC transmitter speaks neither protocol; it is a straight radio link to the receiver, which is exactly why it survives as the safety pilot’s override when every software layer above it has failed.






Figure 10.2: The autopilot software stack: MAVSDK scripts and QGroundControl speak MAVLink to PX4 — over the UART and the telemetry radio respectively — while ROS 2 bypasses MAVLink entirely, exchanging PX4’s own uORB topics across the Micro XRCE-DDS bridge on the same three wires; the RC transmitter’s stick commands arrive with no protocol stack at all.

section: 10.5 MAVSDK: Flying in a Dozen Lines
text:
10.5 MAVSDK: Flying in a Dozen Lines
Raw MAVLink is a wire format; nobody should hand-assemble packet bytes to fly an aircraft. MAVSDK is the standard library answer: language bindings (Python here; C++, Swift, and others exist) that wrap the protocol in the vocabulary a mission author actually thinks in. The vehicle becomes an object; flying becomes method calls. Here is the entire program that takes the running example’s aircraft off the ground and brings it back — connecting over precisely the serial device and baud rate the Companion Computers chapter wired and verified:
import asyncio
from mavsdk import System

async def run():
    drone = System()
    # The same UART link the heartbeat test proved, wrapped by MAVSDK
    await drone.connect(system_address="serial:///dev/ttyTHS1:921600")

    # The same liveness check as the heartbeat test, far less code
    async for state in drone.core.connection_state():
        if state.is_connected:
            break

    await drone.action.arm()
    await drone.action.takeoff()
    await asyncio.sleep(10)      # hover
    await drone.action.land()

asyncio.run(run())
The program is linear — do this, then this, then this — and Python’s asyncio machinery is what lets a linear story coexist with a fundamentally asynchronous world: each await yields until the underlying MAVLink exchange completes, so await drone.action.arm() does not return until the autopilot has actually acknowledged the arm command, the acknowledged-command idiom of the previous section surfacing as ordinary control flow. The connection_state loop is worth a second look, because it is the heartbeat test of Part I reborn as three lines of code: the program refuses to proceed until MAVLink heartbeats prove the far end is alive. The discipline is identical; only the notation changed. (One implementation note for the curious: the Python binding delegates protocol work to a small native server process it launches automatically — invisible in normal use, but the explanation for the extra process a ps will show.)
What MAVSDK is for follows from what the example shows. For single-vehicle missions — waypoint surveys, scripted photography passes, the take-off-fly-land shape of most first projects — it is close to ideal: minutes from idea to flying code, no infrastructure, no middleware to configure. Its plugins (action, telemetry, mission, offboard) cover the autopilot’s whole public surface. What it is not built for is the thing the running example needs: a system in which perception, navigation, deterrence, and safety monitoring are separate concerns producing and consuming live data streams. A MAVSDK program is one process; as the mission grows, everything — the camera driver, the detector, the state machine, the failsafe checks — must grow inside that one process, and the modularity argument the closing chapter of Part I made (a crash in one function must not take down the safety monitor) has no purchase. The limitation is architectural, not a missing feature, and it is the doorway to ROS 2.

title: 10  PX4 and the Autopilot Stack: MAVLink, MAVSDK, and ROS 2
text:
10.6 ROS 2: The Middleware Path
Part I’s closing chapter already introduced ROS 2’s vocabulary on the way to sketching the running example’s architecture: independent nodes, each one process with one job; topics, named publish–subscribe channels for streaming data; services, request–response channels for acknowledged actions; typed messages on all of them. That sketch stands; this section adds the one piece it deferred — how a graph of ROS 2 nodes actually reaches the autopilot.
The answer is unexpectedly elegant: it doesn’t translate. PX4 is itself, internally, a publish–subscribe system — its modules exchange data over an in-firmware message bus called uORB, with topics for vehicle status, local position, trajectory setpoints, and everything else the firmware knows. Rather than converting uORB traffic to MAVLink and back, PX4 embeds a Micro XRCE-DDS client: a lightweight process in the firmware that serializes selected uORB topics across the UART to an agent running on the companion computer, which republishes them as native ROS 2 topics. From a mission node’s point of view, the autopilot’s internals simply appear in the ROS 2 graph, under a reserved namespace: subscribe to /fmu/out/vehicle_local_position and the EKF2 estimate of the previous chapter streams into your callback; publish to /fmu/in/trajectory_setpoint and the cascade’s outermost loop consumes your setpoint directly. There is no protocol seam for a concept to be lost in — the position estimate a ROS 2 node receives is the same message, in the same type, that PX4’s own position controller reads. Figure 10.3 sets the two programming layers side by side.






Figure 10.3: MAVSDK and ROS 2 compared as programming layers: a linear awaited script speaking MAVLink, against a graph of independent nodes whose setpoints cross the Micro XRCE-DDS bridge into PX4’s own uORB topics — with the strengths and limits of each, and the running example committed to the graph.



The comparison in the figure is a genuine trade, not a ranking. ROS 2 costs more before the first flight: a bridge agent to run, message packages to install, quality-of-service profiles to match, and a programming model — covered below — that is less natural than a script. It pays that cost back the moment the mission stops being one program’s story. Computer-vision output feeding flight decisions, multiple sensors fused on the companion computer, behaviors developed and tested as separate processes, a safety monitor that must not share a failure mode with the logic it supervises — each of these is a topic-and-node shape, and the running example needs all four. That is why the Goose Management System is built on ROS 2 rather than on MAVSDK, exactly as Part I’s closing sketch assumed: its mission sequencing, vehicle interfacing, navigation and deterrence behaviors, and Failsafe node are separate processes wired by the Services-for-actions, Topics-for-streams rule that chapter established. The full graph — every node, channel, and authority-transfer rule — is the business of the Systems Architecture chapter in Part V; this chapter’s job is the layer underneath it: how any one of those nodes commands flight at all.

title: 10  PX4 and the Autopilot Stack: MAVLink, MAVSDK, and ROS 2
text:
10.7 Offboard Mode: A Dead-Man’s Switch
PX4 has many flight modes — manual stabilization, altitude hold, position hold, autonomous mission, return-to-launch — and one of them is the entire reason this book’s architecture works. In Offboard mode, the autopilot follows setpoints streamed by an external computer: position, velocity, or attitude targets, consumed by the cascade of the previous chapter at whatever loop the setpoint type addresses. Offboard is the handoff Part I’s closing chapter described — from this mode onward, a process is flying the aircraft — and PX4 makes it deliberately the hardest mode to stay in, because an external computer is the least trustworthy source of commands the autopilot ever accepts. A pilot’s sticks fail rarely and visibly; a Python process on a companion computer can hang, crash, or deadlock silently at any moment, and the autopilot has no way to inspect its health. So PX4 imposes two hard rules, both enforced by the firmware rather than by convention:

Stream before you enter. PX4 refuses to switch into Offboard mode until setpoints are already arriving. A computer that cannot yet produce a steady stream has no business being handed the aircraft.
Keep streaming to stay in. If the setpoint stream stalls — drops below roughly 2 Hz — PX4 concludes the companion computer has died, exits Offboard on its own authority, and executes a failsafe behavior instead of coasting on the last command it heard.

Both rules are one idea: a dead-man’s switch. The stream itself is the proof of life, and the proof must be continuous. This design converts the scariest failure in the system — autonomy software dying mid-flight — from a catastrophe into a mode change, and it does so without trusting a single line of companion-computer code. It also dictates, completely, the shape of the mission software: any program that flies in Offboard mode must be built around something that publishes a setpoint on a reliable clock, no matter what else the program is doing. A linear script structure fights that requirement; a timer-driven one embodies it.

section: 10.8 A Complete Mission Node: Flying a Square
text:
10.8 A Complete Mission Node: Flying a Square
The shape becomes concrete in a full ROS 2 mission: take off, fly a square, land — the same flight a MAVSDK script would express in fifteen sequential lines, rebuilt around the streaming obligation. The rebuild is worth every line, because this node’s skeleton (setup once, then a 10 Hz callback that consults a few state flags and does exactly one thing per tick) is the skeleton of every Offboard node in the rest of this book, the running example’s included.
The flight plan itself is plain data — a Python list the loop will walk:
# Each waypoint: (x, y, z, hold_seconds, label)
# NED frame, metres, origin where the EKF started.
# z is negative-up: -5.0 means 5 m altitude.
TRAJECTORY = [
    ( 0.0,  0.0, -5.0, 10.0, 'takeoff_climb'),
    ( 0.0,  0.0, -5.0,  5.0, 'takeoff_settle'),
    (10.0,  0.0, -5.0, 12.0, 'corner_1'),
    (10.0, 10.0, -5.0, 12.0, 'corner_2'),
    ( 0.0, 10.0, -5.0, 12.0, 'corner_3'),
    ( 0.0,  0.0, -5.0, 12.0, 'corner_4_return'),
    ( 0.0,  0.0, -5.0,  5.0, 'pre_land_settle'),
]
CMD_NAV_LAND = 21   # raw MAVLink command id for auto-land
Three conventions in ten lines deserve flagging. Coordinates are NED — x north, y east, z down, so altitude is negative, and -5.0 means five metres up; the frame conventions behind that choice get a chapter of their own in Part IV, but the sign discipline starts now, because the single most common simulator “crash” in a first Offboard mission is a positive z commanding five metres underground. The origin is wherever the EKF initialized — the launch point, echoing the barometer-reference discussion of Part I. And each waypoint carries a hold time rather than an arrival test: progression will be purely time-based, the simplest scheme that can work, with its obvious weakness (the vehicle advances on schedule whether or not it arrived) left for the state-machine treatment in the next chapter to repair.
The node’s constructor wires it to PX4’s topics and starts the clock:
class OffboardSquare(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('offboard_square')
        qos = QoSProfile(reliability=BEST_EFFORT,
                         durability=TRANSIENT_LOCAL,
                         history=KEEP_LAST, depth=1)
        self.mode_pub = self.create_publisher(
            OffboardControlMode, '/fmu/in/offboard_control_mode', 10)
        self.sp_pub = self.create_publisher(
            TrajectorySetpoint, '/fmu/in/trajectory_setpoint', 10)
        self.cmd_pub = self.create_publisher(
            VehicleCommand, '/fmu/in/vehicle_command', 10)
        self.create_subscription(
            VehicleLocalPosition, '/fmu/out/vehicle_local_position',
            self.on_pos, qos)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.1, self.loop)   # 10 Hz
The quality-of-service profile is the one genuinely ROS 2-specific trap here. PX4 publishes its topics best-effort — the streaming contract, where a lost message is cheaper than a retransmission — and ROS 2 only connects a publisher and subscriber whose QoS policies are compatible. A subscriber left at the default reliable policy is not degraded; it is silent, receiving nothing, with no error raised. Every integration checklist for this stack includes “match PX4’s QoS” for the same reason every serial checklist in Part I included “match the baud rate”: both are timing-and-contract agreements between parties who cannot see each other’s configuration, and both fail quietly. The 10 Hz timer is the node’s heart, chosen to clear PX4’s roughly-2 Hz Offboard floor with five-fold margin.
The dead-man’s obligation gets its own method, called on every tick that the node wants PX4 to keep trusting it:
def publish_setpoint(self, x, y, z):
    # Heartbeat AND setpoint stream together at >= 2 Hz,
    # or PX4 refuses to enter (or stay in) Offboard mode.
    m = OffboardControlMode()
    m.timestamp = self.now()
    m.position = True                  # commanding by position
    self.mode_pub.publish(m)

    sp = TrajectorySetpoint()
    sp.timestamp = self.now()
    sp.position = [float(x), float(y), float(z)]
    sp.yaw = 0.0
    self.sp_pub.publish(sp)
Two messages ship together: the OffboardControlMode heartbeat, which tells PX4 what kind of setpoint to expect (position = True — the outermost loop of the cascade, exactly where the previous chapter said the mission layer plugs in), and the TrajectorySetpoint itself. The remaining logic is the 10 Hz callback, a handful of flags deciding which one thing this tick does:
def loop(self):
    self.counter += 1

    if self.land_sent:                     # landing: stay silent
        return

    if not self.armed_sent:                # warm-up, then arm
        self.publish_setpoint(0.0, 0.0, -5.0)
        if self.first_pos_tick is None:    # PX4 not talking yet
            return
        if self.counter - self.first_pos_tick < 10:
            return                         # stream for >= 1 s first
        self.send_cmd(VEHICLE_CMD_DO_SET_MODE, 1.0, 6.0)  # Offboard
        self.send_cmd(VEHICLE_CMD_COMPONENT_ARM_DISARM, 1.0)
        self.armed_sent = True
        self.wp_start_tick = self.counter
        return

    if self.wp_index < len(TRAJECTORY):    # fly the square
        x, y, z, hold, label = TRAJECTORY[self.wp_index]
        self.publish_setpoint(x, y, z)     # re-stream active target
        if (self.counter - self.wp_start_tick) * 0.1 >= hold:
            self.wp_index += 1
            self.wp_start_tick = self.counter
        return

    self.send_cmd(CMD_NAV_LAND)            # hand off to PX4's landing
    self.land_sent = True
Read the branches in mission order and each one is a rule from earlier in the chapter made executable. The warm-up branch streams setpoints before attempting anything — rule one — and goes further: it waits for the first VehicleLocalPosition message (proof PX4 is talking at all), then keeps streaming a full second more so the autopilot sees an established stream, and only then sends the mode change and the arm command. Arming earlier simply fails, and the failure is PX4 doing its job. The mode-change parameters (1.0, 6.0) say “custom mode, main mode six” — Offboard, in PX4’s numbering. The flying branch re-publishes the active waypoint every tick — rule two, the stream never pauses just because the target hasn’t changed — and advances on elapsed hold time. And the landing handoff inverts everything: the node sends NAV_LAND once, latches land_sent, and then deliberately falls silent. The silence is not sloppiness; it is the safest line in the program. PX4’s own landing logic — tuned descent rate, ground detection, auto-disarm — is more trustworthy than anything this node could stream, and a node that kept heartbeating could allow the autopilot to be flipped back into Offboard, fighting the landing it just requested. The dead-man’s switch is symmetric: the way software hands back control is to stop proving it wants control.
That is the complete pattern — data, wiring, heartbeat, flags — and it scales. Replace the trajectory list with a search-grid generator and the time-based advance with position-error tests and a detection subscriber, and this node grows up into the running example’s navigation behavior; keep the skeleton and swap the branch logic, and it becomes any Offboard behavior at all.

title: 10  PX4 and the Autopilot Stack: MAVLink, MAVSDK, and ROS 2
text:
10.9 Simulate, Then Fly
Everything above can be typed, and none of it should be trusted. The mission node has a dozen ways to be subtly wrong — a positive z, a QoS mismatch, arming before the stream is warm, heartbeats that continue through the landing — and several of them end with an aircraft on its back. The remedy is the last of this chapter’s three decisions, and the only one with a unanimous answer: PX4 SITL, software-in-the-loop simulation, shown in Figure 10.4.






Figure 10.4: Software-in-the-loop: the identical mission code and identical PX4 firmware run on the bench against Gazebo’s modeled physics and synthetic sensors, and in the field against the real airframe — only the plant is swapped, so a bug caught in simulation is the same bug that would have cost the aircraft.



The load-bearing word in the figure is identical. SITL is not a model of the autopilot; it is the autopilot — the same PX4 source, with the same EKF2, the same cascaded loops, the same mode logic, the same Offboard dead-man’s switch and failsafe behaviors, compiled for a desktop processor instead of the Pixhawk’s microcontroller. What is simulated is only the plant: Gazebo supplies the physics — rigid-body dynamics, propeller thrust, wind if asked — and synthesizes the sensor readings (IMU, GPS, barometer) that the real airframe would produce, closing the same sense–think–act loop Part I drew, entirely in software. The mission node connects to this simulated vehicle exactly as it would to the real one and cannot tell the difference; when the mission finally flies, nothing about the software changes — the plant is swapped under it, and that is all.
That identity is what gives simulation its teaching and its safety value at once. The mistakes listed above are not hypothetical; every one of them is a rite of passage, and in SITL each produces its instructive failure — the underground setpoint, the silent QoS mismatch, PX4 curtly rejecting a premature arm — at a cost of one restart. The economics are stark and settle the practice: a bug caught in Gazebo costs nothing, and the same bug on hardware costs a drone — and Part I priced the drone. Standing the environment up (building PX4 SITL, installing the ROS 2 bridge packages, driving Gazebo’s worlds) and flying real waypoint missions in it is the opening business of the next chapter, and this chapter’s related lab walks the same ground; the habit, though, begins here, because it is a design principle rather than a tool: no Offboard code touches the aircraft until the identical code has flown the identical mission in simulation. The running example honors it throughout — every behavior in the chapters ahead debuts in Gazebo, and the field flights of Part V fly code that simulation has already tried to break.
The stack is now complete from mission to motor. PX4 was chosen with reasons, MAVLink read as a protocol rather than folklore, the two programming layers weighed and the middleware path taken, Offboard mode’s contract turned into a working node, and a place established where all of it can fail safely. What the mission node still lacks is judgment: its square is flown on a timer, blind to whether the vehicle actually reached anything, and its plan cannot respond to the world at all. Giving mission logic that judgment — waypoints with arrival criteria, state machines that branch on events, and the SITL environment to prove them in — is the next chapter’s work.

title: 10  PX4 and the Autopilot Stack: MAVLink, MAVSDK, and ROS 2
text:
10.10 Check Your Understanding

A startup modifies autopilot firmware with a proprietary fault-detection module and sells 200 vehicles with the firmware flashed aboard. State its source-code obligations if the base firmware was PX4, and if it was ArduPilot. Then explain why the startup’s ROS 2 mission stack, running on the companion computer, is unaffected in both cases.







TipShow answer





On PX4 (BSD 3-clause), the obligations are to preserve the copyright notice and license text and not use the project’s name for endorsement; the module itself may remain secret. On ArduPilot (GPL v3), selling the vehicles is distribution, which obliges the startup to offer the corresponding source — the fault-detection module included — to every recipient under the GPL, and recipients may redistribute it further. The ROS 2 stack is unaffected because it is a separate program communicating with the firmware over a serial protocol, not a derivative work of the firmware; neither license’s terms reach across that process boundary. Note also that a team that modifies either firmware but never distributes it — flying only its own aircraft — owes nothing under either license, because the obligations attach at distribution.




PX4 refuses to enter Offboard mode until setpoints are already streaming, and drops out of Offboard if the stream falls below roughly 2 Hz. Explain the single design idea behind both rules, and why the square-mission node goes silent — stops publishing entirely — after sending NAV_LAND.







TipShow answer





Both rules implement a dead-man’s switch: the setpoint stream is the companion computer’s continuous proof of life, and PX4 will neither accept nor retain authority from a computer that cannot maintain it, because a hung or crashed process cannot be detected any other way. Requiring the stream before entry proves the computer is healthy before it is trusted; requiring it continuously converts a mid-flight software death into a mode change and failsafe rather than a coast on stale commands. The silence after NAV_LAND is the same mechanism used in reverse: the safest descent is PX4’s own landing logic, and by stopping its stream the node guarantees it cannot be flipped back into Offboard mid-landing — software relinquishes control by ceasing to prove it wants control.




In the mission’s trajectory list, one waypoint reads (10.0, 10.0, -5.0, 12.0, 'corner_2'). Decode all five fields, state the side length and altitude of the square being flown, and predict what happens on the first flight of a student who writes 5.0 instead of -5.0 for the altitude.







TipShow answer





The fields are x = 10.0 m north of the EKF origin, y = 10.0 m east, z = −5.0 m in the NED (north-east-down) frame — 5 m above the origin, since z points down — held for 12.0 seconds, with a human-readable label. The square is 10 m on a side, flown at 5 m altitude, with the origin at the launch point where the EKF initialized. Writing +5.0 commands a position 5 m below the origin: the vehicle attempts to descend through the ground. In SITL this produces the classic first-mission crash into the floor of the Gazebo world at a cost of one restart — which is precisely the class of sign error the simulate-then-fly rule exists to catch before hardware is involved.




Two projects need mission software: (a) a bridge-inspection drone that flies a pre-planned path and records video, operated by one script on the companion computer; (b) the running example, where a detector’s output must alter flight behavior in real time and a failsafe monitor must survive a crash of the mission logic. Choose the programming layer for each and give the deciding criterion.







TipShow answer





Project (a) fits MAVSDK: a single vehicle flying a linear mission is exactly the one-process, one-story shape a MAVSDK script expresses in a few dozen lines, with no middleware to stand up. Project (b) needs ROS 2: perception feeding flight decisions requires live typed data streams between separate concerns, and a failsafe monitor that must not share a failure mode with the mission logic must be a separate process — both are node-and-topic shapes that a single monolithic script cannot provide. The deciding criterion is architectural: whether the drone is the whole system (MAVSDK) or one participant in a multi-process system exchanging live data (ROS 2). Convenience favors MAVSDK; modularity, and safety by process isolation, force ROS 2.




A student’s mission node runs without errors, but its position callback never fires and PX4 rejects every arm attempt. The bridge agent is running and the heartbeat test from Part I passes. Diagnose the most likely fault, and explain why this failure — like a baud-rate mismatch — produces silence rather than an error message.







TipShow answer





The signature fault is a quality-of-service mismatch: PX4 publishes its /fmu/out/... topics best-effort, and a subscription created with ROS 2’s default reliable policy is incompatible, so the middleware never connects the pair — no messages arrive, and no error is raised, because unmatched QoS is a legal configuration, not a fault. With no VehicleLocalPosition received, the node’s warm-up gate (first_pos_tick is None) never opens properly and its arm attempt comes before PX4 sees a warm stream, so PX4 correctly rejects it. The failure is silent for the same structural reason baud mismatch is: it is a contract disagreement between two parties who cannot inspect each other’s configuration — the wire (or middleware) faithfully does what both sides asked, and what they asked for happens to be nothing. The fix is to subscribe with a PX4-compatible profile (best-effort reliability).




SITL is sometimes described as “testing against a model of the autopilot.” Explain precisely what is and is not modeled in PX4 SITL, and why the distinction determines which classes of bug simulation can catch.







TipShow answer





The autopilot is not modeled — SITL compiles the actual PX4 source, so the estimator, cascaded loops, mode logic, Offboard entry rules, and failsafe behaviors are the real code, bit-for-bit the logic that flies. What is modeled is the plant: Gazebo supplies rigid-body physics, propeller forces, and synthetic IMU, GPS, and barometer readings in place of the real airframe and sensors. Consequently SITL reliably catches every bug that lives in software and its contracts — sign errors in NED coordinates, QoS mismatches, arming before the stream is warm, heartbeats that continue through landing, state-machine logic errors — because the code paths involved are identical to flight. What it cannot fully catch are plant-fidelity issues: real vibration corrupting the IMU, real battery sag, wind beyond the model, sensor noise the synthesis underestimates. Simulation removes the software unknowns so that the first hardware flight risks only the physics.

10.11 Try It
Part 1 — dry-run the mission loop with no ROS 2 installed. The loop() method’s branch logic is plain Python, and its correctness is testable on any machine: write a harness that instantiates the flags (counter, first_pos_tick, armed_sent, wp_index, wp_start_tick, land_sent), stubs publish_setpoint() and send_cmd() to append to a log list instead of publishing, and calls loop() 1,500 times (150 simulated seconds), injecting first_pos_tick = 25 to mimic PX4 first talking at tick 25. From the log, verify every contract in the chapter: no arm or mode command before ten ticks of established stream; a setpoint published on every tick between warm-up and landing with no gaps (count them); waypoints advancing exactly on their hold times; NAV_LAND sent exactly once; and zero publications of any kind afterward. Then break it the instructive way: reorder the branches so the trajectory check comes before the land_sent check, rerun, and find the contract violation in your log. This is the cheapest simulation level of all — below even SITL — and catching a flag bug here costs milliseconds.
Part 2 — rebudget the square as a mission. The trajectory holds each of its seven entries for the listed dwell times. Compute the mission’s minimum duration from the table alone, then re-plan it as a search pattern for the running example: replace the square with a four-leg lawnmower pass over a 40 m × 30 m area at the same 5 m altitude, choosing hold times from leg lengths at a conservative 2 m/s cruise. Check the total against the 3.5-minute search allocation in Part I’s mission time budget — and if it does not fit, decide what to trade (area, speed, or altitude) and defend the choice in two sentences. Then note what the time-based scheme cannot do: if wind slows the vehicle so a leg is unfinished when its hold expires, the plan advances anyway. Write down what signal the node would need to subscribe to, and what test it would apply, to advance on arrival instead — you have just specified the next chapter.

title: 11  Mission Scripting: Waypoints, State Machines, and Software-in-the-Loop
text:
11.1 Learning Objectives
The previous chapter ended with a working mission node and two honest confessions about it. The node flew its square on a timer, advancing to the next corner when a stopwatch expired rather than when the vehicle arrived — a scheme that works exactly until the first gust of wind makes the schedule and the aircraft disagree. And the whole program had, so far, flown nowhere: the chapter closed by declaring the simulate-then-fly rule and deferring the simulator itself. This chapter pays both debts. It stands up the software-in-the-loop environment — PX4, Gazebo, and QGroundControl running together on one desk — and then rebuilds mission logic properly: waypoints as data with a real arrival test instead of a stopwatch, and the mission itself as an explicit state machine instead of a thicket of boolean flags. Along the way it does something the abstract treatment cannot: it opens a real mission file — a QGroundControl .plan, JSON from end to end, whose coordinates trace an actual lawnmower search over a grass field at 39.68° N, 75.75° W — and reads every field, because the day a mission goes wrong, the plan file is the flight’s source code and someone has to be able to read it.
The chapter’s through-line is a single idea wearing three outfits. A waypoint mission is a list; executing it means asking, over and over, “am I there yet, and what do I do next?” — and that question can be answered by the firmware’s own navigator (upload the list, let PX4 fly it), or by mission code streaming setpoints in Offboard mode (the running example’s way), or by a simulator exercising either path with no aircraft at risk. List, arrival test, state machine: everything else is detail.

title: 11  Mission Scripting: Waypoints, State Machines, and Software-in-the-Loop
text:
11.2 Key Vocabulary

Waypoint — a single target position in a mission: latitude, longitude, and altitude, plus per-point details such as hold time and acceptance radius; the atomic unit of a flight plan.
Mission item — one entry in a mission’s ordered list: a MAVLink command identifier, a coordinate frame, and up to seven parameters. Every waypoint is a mission item, but not every mission item is a waypoint — speed changes and camera triggers ride the same list.
Home position — the reference location the autopilot records at arming: the origin of relative altitudes and the destination of Return-to-Launch. It is set where the vehicle actually armed, which is not always where the plan assumed it would.
RTL (Return-to-Launch) — the autonomous recovery behavior that climbs to a safe altitude, flies back to the home position, descends, and lands; both a mission’s normal ending and the standard failsafe response.
Acceptance radius — the distance threshold of the arrival test: a waypoint counts as reached when the estimated position comes within this radius of it, at which point the navigator advances to the next item.
SITL (Software-in-the-Loop) — the practice, introduced in the previous chapter and made operational here, of running the unmodified autopilot firmware as a desktop process against simulated physics, so mission logic can be exercised and crashed for free.
Gazebo — the physics simulator paired with PX4 SITL: it integrates the vehicle’s rigid-body dynamics, models propeller thrust and (optionally) wind, and synthesizes the IMU, GPS, magnetometer, and barometer streams the firmware expects.
QGroundControl (QGC) — the PX4-ecosystem ground control station, already met as a parameter editor; in this chapter it is the mission planning tool — the map on which waypoints are placed and the program that uploads the resulting plan to the vehicle, real or simulated.
Geofence — a boundary polygon (or circle) the vehicle must respect, stored alongside the mission; crossing it triggers a configured failsafe such as RTL. Introduced here as a .plan ingredient; the Geofencing and Fail-Safes chapter treats it fully.
Finite state machine (FSM) — a program structure consisting of a set of discrete states, exactly one active at a time, and transitions between them that fire when guard conditions become true; the standard shape of mission logic.

section: 11.3 The Workbench: Three Processes on One Desk
text:
11.3 The Workbench: Three Processes on One Desk
The previous chapter argued why SITL — the identical firmware, only the plant swapped — and left the how for here. The how turns out to be one command. From a PX4 source checkout:
make px4_sitl gz_x500
builds the firmware for the host machine and launches it, and what appears on the desk is the entire architecture of the previous chapter with every aircraft part replaced by a process. The first process is PX4 itself — the same estimator, cascade, modes, and failsafes, compiled for the laptop, announcing itself with a pxh> shell prompt into which commands like commander takeoff can be typed directly. The second is Gazebo, launched alongside, simulating a quadrotor (the x500 model, a research airframe of the same class as the running example’s) in a rendered world: it consumes the firmware’s motor commands, integrates the physics, and feeds back synthetic IMU, GPS, magnetometer, and barometer streams — the same sensor suite Part I installed, now generated by arithmetic. The third is QGroundControl, started as an ordinary application; it discovers the simulated vehicle automatically, because PX4 SITL broadcasts MAVLink over a local UDP port exactly where QGC expects a vehicle to appear, and within seconds the ground station shows a drone sitting on simulated grass, EKF happy, “Ready to Fly.” The wiring diagram of Part I has become a process diagram: UDP sockets where the UART and telemetry radio were, and nothing else different. ROS 2 nodes join the same way — the Micro XRCE-DDS agent connects to the simulated firmware over UDP rather than a serial device, and every topic of the previous chapter flows as before.
Two habits make the workbench productive rather than merely impressive. First, treat the simulated vehicle as a vehicle: arm it from QGC, watch the EKF initialize, upload missions to it, and let it refuse things — a premature Offboard request fails in SITL for exactly the reason it would fail in the field, and learning to read those refusals on the bench is the cheap version of learning them outdoors. Second, break things on purpose. Command the classic underground setpoint, kill the setpoint stream mid-flight and watch the dead-man’s switch catch it, fly at the geofence and watch the failsafe fire. A simulator that is only ever shown working code teaches nothing; its entire economic argument — a crash costs a restart — is an argument for crashing it often.

title: 11  Mission Scripting: Waypoints, State Machines, and Software-in-the-Loop
section: 11.4 The Mission as Data: Waypoints and Mission Items
text:
11.4 The Mission as Data: Waypoints and Mission Items
With the workbench up, the first thing to fly is the oldest and most robust form of autonomy: the waypoint mission. Its premise is that a useful flight can be specified entirely as data — an ordered list of positions with associated actions — handed to the autopilot, and executed by the firmware’s own navigator with no companion computer involved at all. This is the second of the three command paths from the previous chapter (QGroundControl’s path) doing its real job: the operator draws the mission on QGC’s map, QGC uploads the list over MAVLink, the flight controller stores it, and from that moment the plan lives on the vehicle. Switch to Mission mode and PX4 flies the list — takeoff, each waypoint in order, the closing action — feeding target positions to the same cascaded loops as always. The ground station can disconnect mid-flight and nothing changes, which is precisely the robustness argument for onboard missions: the plan does not depend on any link staying alive.
The unit of the list is the mission item, and its anatomy is MAVLink’s command anatomy from the previous chapter reused: a command identifier, a coordinate frame, and up to seven parameters. Navigation items carry a position — NAV_TAKEOFF (command 22) climbs to a given altitude, NAV_WAYPOINT (command 16) flies to a latitude/longitude/altitude, NAV_LAND (21) and NAV_RETURN_TO_LAUNCH (20) end the flight — while action items carry none: DO_CHANGE_SPEED (178) alters cruise speed from that point in the list onward, camera commands start and stop capture, and the navigator executes them in sequence between position targets. Two reference points anchor the whole structure. The home position is recorded at the moment of arming — not planned, recorded — and serves as both the origin for relative altitudes and the destination for RTL, the return behavior that climbs to a configured safe altitude, flies home, and lands. A mission that ends in an RTL item is a round trip by construction. Figure 11.1 assembles the pieces into the pattern that matters most for the running example: the lawnmower sweep.






Figure 11.1: A simple waypoint mission over a fenced field: takeoff at the home position, a five-waypoint lawnmower sweep flown as north–south legs joined by row steps, an acceptance radius around each waypoint defining arrival, and a Return-to-Launch item closing the loop — all of it inside a geofence polygon the next chapter arms.



The lawnmower (formally boustrophedon — “as the ox plows”) earns a moment of respect before it is flown, because it is not an arbitrary shape. A drone searching an area with a downward-looking sensor sees a swath of finite width; parallel legs spaced at most one swath apart, joined by short row steps, are the minimal-overlap way to guarantee the whole area passes under the sensor. The row pitch in the figure is therefore not an aesthetic choice but a sensor parameter — camera field of view times altitude, derated for required overlap — and the entire pattern can be computed from the field polygon and the sensor footprint rather than clicked out by hand. That computation, and what happens to it when the target moves, is the business of the Path Planning on the Edge chapter in Part IV; here the pattern is drawn manually in QGC, which is exactly how a first search mission should be built.

title: 11  Mission Scripting: Waypoints, State Machines, and Software-in-the-Loop
text:
11.5 Reading a Real Plan File
QGroundControl saves a drawn mission as a .plan file — plain JSON — and reading one repays the effort the way reading a hex dump of a MAVLink packet would not: every field is legible, and every field teaches something. The file examined here is a real one: a lawnmower survey of a grass field in Newark, Delaware, drawn in QGC and flown in simulation, its coordinates clustered around 39.680° N, 75.752° W. Abridged to its skeleton:
{
    "fileType": "Plan",
    "geoFence": {
        "polygons": [{
            "inclusion": true,
            "polygon": [
                [39.68034009, -75.75245036],
                [39.68036725, -75.75206443],
                [39.67992608, -75.75200019],
                [39.67990044, -75.75236953]
            ]
        }]
    },
    "mission": {
        "cruiseSpeed": 15,
        "hoverSpeed": 1.5,
        "firmwareType": 12,
        "vehicleType": 2,
        "globalPlanAltitudeMode": 1,
        "items": [
            { "command": 178, "frame": 2,
              "params": [1, 1.5, -1, 0, 0, 0, 0] },
            { "command": 22, "frame": 3, "Altitude": 5.5,
              "params": [0, 0, 0, null,
                         39.67992584, -75.75214500, 5.5] },
            { "command": 16, "frame": 3, "Altitude": 5.5,
              "params": [0, 0, 0, null,
                         39.67991219, -75.75234666, 5.5] },
            { "comment": "... eleven more NAV_WAYPOINT items ..." },
            { "command": 20, "frame": 2,
              "params": [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0] }
        ],
        "plannedHomePosition": [39.67992611, -75.75214484, 42]
    },
    "rallyPoints": { "points": [] }
}
Top to bottom. The geofence block stores one inclusion polygon — four vertices, each a latitude/longitude pair, defining the region the vehicle must stay inside (an exclusion polygon would mark a region to stay out of). The fence is data here and law later: uploading it arms nothing by itself, but the next chapter will wire it to a failsafe so that crossing the boundary triggers RTL automatically. The mission block opens with context QGC and the firmware both consume: firmwareType: 12 identifies the PX4 dialect (the MAVLink autopilot enumeration from two chapters ago, appearing in a file on disk), vehicleType: 2 a multirotor, and globalPlanAltitudeMode: 1 declares that the plan’s altitudes are relative to home rather than absolute above sea level — the same launch-point-relative convention the barometer discussion of Part I arrived at, now a mission-wide setting. The hoverSpeed of 1.5 m/s is the planning speed for a multirotor; cruiseSpeed is the fixed-wing counterpart, present but idle.
Then the list. The first item, command 178 (DO_CHANGE_SPEED), is an action item: its frame: 2 (MAV_FRAME_MISSION) is the tell that no coordinate is attached, and its parameters read “speed type 1 — ground speed — to 1.5 m/s, throttle unchanged.” A deliberate, camera-friendly walking pace. The full file’s next item (elided above) is command 2500, VIDEO_START_CAPTURE — start recording, another action item, because a survey that isn’t recorded didn’t happen. Command 22 (NAV_TAKEOFF) then climbs to 5.5 m; its frame: 3 is MAV_FRAME_GLOBAL_RELATIVE_ALT — latitude and longitude in degrees, altitude in metres above home — and its last three parameters carry the coordinate itself. Twelve command-16 waypoints follow, every one at exactly 5.5 m relative altitude, and command 20 (NAV_RETURN_TO_LAUNCH) closes the list. Finally plannedHomePosition — the launch point the planner assumed, with its third element, 42, being the field’s ground elevation in metres above sea level. The name is a quiet warning: the real home position is recorded at arming, wherever that actually happens, and every relative altitude and the RTL destination bind to the recorded one. Launch from the wrong corner of the field and the whole mission shifts with you.

11.5.1 The geometry hiding in the sixth decimal place
The coordinates look like noise — a wall of 39.680-something — until they are converted to metres, and the conversion is worth internalizing because it turns every GPS log and plan file into geometry on sight. A degree of latitude is essentially constant at 111.3 km. A degree of longitude shrinks with the cosine of latitude, since meridians converge toward the poles:
\[
\begin{aligned}
1^\circ \text{ latitude} &\approx 111{,}320 \text{ m} \\
1^\circ \text{ longitude at } 39.68^\circ\,\text{N} &\approx 111{,}320 \times \cos 39.68^\circ \approx 85{,}700 \text{ m}
\end{aligned}
\]
A convenient mental unit follows: at this latitude, the fifth decimal place of a coordinate — 0.00001° — is about 1.1 m of latitude or 0.86 m of longitude. The sixth decimal place is a decimetre. Now the file becomes a map. The fence polygon spans 0.00044° of latitude and 0.00045° of longitude:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{fence, north--south} &\approx 0.00044 \times 111{,}320 \approx 49 \text{ m} \\
\text{fence, east--west} &\approx 0.00045 \times 85{,}700 \approx 39 \text{ m}
\end{aligned}
\]
— a field about half a football pitch in size. The first three waypoints share nearly one longitude while their latitude climbs by 0.000417°: a north–south leg of \(0.000417 \times 111{,}320 \approx 46.4\) m, with 7.3 m of westward drift along it (the operator’s hand was not perfectly steady on the map), for a leg length of \(\sqrt{46.4^2 + 7.3^2} \approx 47\) m. Between legs, the longitude steps east by about 0.000075°, a row pitch of roughly 6.5 m. Twelve waypoints resolve into four such legs — a 3½-pass lawnmower over the fenced field, the exact pattern of Figure 11.1 with real numbers attached.
The numbers even audit the mission’s schedule. Summing the track — a 17 m transit from the takeoff point to the first corner, four legs near 47 m, three row steps, and the RTL hop home — gives roughly 230 m of path. At the commanded 1.5 m/s ground speed:
\[
t \approx \frac{230 \text{ m}}{1.5 \text{ m/s}} \approx 153 \text{ s} \approx 2.6 \text{ min},
\]
call it three minutes once the takeoff climb and landing descent are added. Part I’s mission time budget allocated 3.5 minutes to the running example’s search leg; this real, hand-drawn plan fits that allocation with margin, and the fact that a JSON file plus two conversion constants can prove it before anything flies is the entire case for treating missions as data. (The altitude passes its own audit trivially: 5.5 m over a 42 m-elevation field is nowhere near the 122 m ceiling — though note the ceiling is measured above ground, not above sea level, a distinction the relative-altitude mode conveniently respects.)

title: 11  Mission Scripting: Waypoints, State Machines, and Software-in-the-Loop
section: 11.6 Arrival: From Stopwatch to Acceptance Radius
text:
11.6 Arrival: From Stopwatch to Acceptance Radius
The firmware’s navigator, flying that plan in Mission mode, does something the previous chapter’s Offboard node never did: it decides it has reached each waypoint before moving to the next. The test is geometric. Around every waypoint stands an invisible sphere — the acceptance radius, exposed in PX4 as the parameter NAV_ACC_RAD — and the waypoint is complete when the EKF’s position estimate enters it:
\[
\lVert \hat{\mathbf{p}} - \mathbf{p}_{\text{wp}} \rVert < r_{\text{acc}}.
\]
That one inequality is the difference between a schedule and a navigation. The stopwatch scheme advances whether or not the vehicle arrived; the acceptance test advances because it arrived, and automatically absorbs everything that makes flight times unpredictable — headwinds that stretch a leg, the gentle cornering the position controller applies, a conservative speed setting. The radius itself is a genuine tuning choice with failure modes on both sides. Too large, and the vehicle “arrives” early and cuts corners: with a 10 m radius on a lawnmower whose rows are 6.5 m apart, legs blur together and coverage develops holes. Too small, and the test may never pass: the position estimate carries metre-scale GNSS scatter, and asking the vehicle to hit a 30 cm sphere through metre-scale noise produces the signature failure of an aircraft loitering beside a waypoint it cannot satisfy, mission stalled, battery draining. The radius should comfortably exceed the position estimate’s expected error and comfortably undercut the mission’s geometry — for the field above, one to two metres sits well inside both bounds.
The same test is exactly what the Offboard node from the previous chapter was missing, and retrofitting it is two lines: subscribe to /fmu/out/vehicle_local_position (the node already does, for its warm-up gate) and replace the hold-time check with the inequality. But bolting one more condition onto that node’s growing pile of boolean flags — armed_sent, land_sent, first_pos_tick — points at a deeper problem worth solving properly. The flags are a state machine, written in the least maintainable possible notation. Time to write it in the right one.

section: 11.7 Mission Logic as a State Machine
text:
11.7 Mission Logic as a State Machine
A finite state machine is the standard shape of mission logic across robotics, and its appeal is austerity: the program is in exactly one state at any moment; each state has one job; transitions between states fire when their guard conditions — tests on observed data, not on elapsed time — become true. Nothing about the formalism is exotic; its value is what it forbids. A linear script encodes “what happens next” in the program counter, which cannot jump backward when the world misbehaves; a pile of flags encodes the current situation across four booleans whose sixteen combinations include several the author never intended. An FSM makes the situation a single enumerated value, makes every legal situation-change a drawn arrow, and makes everything not drawn illegal by construction. Figure 11.2 draws the mission node’s.






Figure 11.2: The Offboard mission rebuilt as a finite state machine: IDLE, TAKEOFF, NAVIGATE, LAND, and DONE in normal sequence, each transition guarded by a test on estimated state, with the NAVIGATE state looping over the waypoint list via its arrival test, and a failsafe transition that preempts any flying state into RTL.



The machine keeps the previous chapter’s skeleton — a 10 Hz timer, one action per tick, the setpoint stream never pausing while the node holds Offboard authority — and reorganizes everything else. In code, the flags collapse into one enum and the branch pile becomes a dispatch:
class MissionState(Enum):
    IDLE = auto(); TAKEOFF = auto(); NAVIGATE = auto()
    LAND = auto(); DONE = auto(); FAILSAFE = auto()

ACCEPT_RADIUS = 1.5   # m — comfortably above GNSS scatter,
                      # comfortably below the 6.5 m row pitch

def arrived(self, target):
    dx = self.pos.x - target[0]
    dy = self.pos.y - target[1]
    dz = self.pos.z - target[2]
    return (dx*dx + dy*dy + dz*dz) ** 0.5 < ACCEPT_RADIUS

def loop(self):                        # the 10 Hz tick
    if self.failsafe_event():          # 1. safety outranks progress
        self.state = MissionState.FAILSAFE

    match self.state:                  # 2. one state, one job
        case MissionState.IDLE:
            self.publish_setpoint(*WAYPOINTS[0])
            if self.stream_warm() and self.arm_offboard_acked():
                self.state = MissionState.TAKEOFF
        case MissionState.TAKEOFF:
            self.publish_setpoint(0.0, 0.0, -5.0)
            if abs(self.pos.z - (-5.0)) < 0.5:
                self.state = MissionState.NAVIGATE
        case MissionState.NAVIGATE:
            wp = WAYPOINTS[self.i]
            self.publish_setpoint(*wp)
            if self.arrived(wp):
                self.i += 1
                if self.i == len(WAYPOINTS):
                    self.send_cmd(CMD_NAV_LAND)
                    self.state = MissionState.LAND
        case MissionState.LAND:
            if self.landed_and_disarmed():
                self.state = MissionState.DONE
        case MissionState.FAILSAFE:
            pass                       # stream stopped: PX4 flies RTL
Three design decisions carry the weight. First, guards test estimated state, never elapsed time: the TAKEOFF exit asks whether the vehicle is actually at altitude (within half a metre — takeoff tolerates a looser test than the mission’s own acceptance radius, since the only question is “safe to translate?”), and NAVIGATE advances on the acceptance test. Wind can now stretch any phase indefinitely without breaking the logic; the schedule became a consequence of flight instead of a controller of it. Second, the failsafe check runs before the state dispatch, every tick. Whatever the machine is busy doing, one question outranks it, and putting that question first in the tick makes the priority structural rather than aspirational. What events feed failsafe_event() — the geofence breach, the low-battery threshold, the lost link — is the next chapter’s subject; the slot they plug into is built here. Third, the machine inherits the previous chapter’s silence discipline: LAND and FAILSAFE stop streaming setpoints, because both states hand the aircraft back to PX4’s own logic, and a node that stops proving it wants control is a node that cannot accidentally retake it.
The payoff is not this small mission — the flag version flew the square too. The payoff is what the structure absorbs without deforming. Add a DETECT event from a perception node and a PURSUE state, and the lawnmower search becomes the running example’s search-then-deter behavior; add an EVADE state guarded by a proximity test, and the machine expresses the whole reactive repertoire of Part IV — every addition a new box and its arrows, every existing box untouched. The Systems Architecture chapter of Part V will draw the full machine that runs the Goose Management System; the reader will recognize it, because it is this figure with more boxes.
