text:
11.8 Proving It in SITL
Everything in this chapter converges on the workbench, and the closing exercise runs the full circuit in simulation twice — once per command path. First the mission-mode pass: draw the lawnmower in QGC over any convenient field (or load the .plan structure examined above), upload it to the SITL vehicle, arm, and switch to Mission mode. Watch the firmware’s navigator do everything this chapter described — the takeoff climb, the acceptance-radius arrivals visible as the vehicle rounds each waypoint without stopping, the speed change taking effect, the RTL climb-return-land. Then the Offboard pass: run the state-machine node against the same simulated vehicle and watch it fly the same geometry under its own arrival logic. The two passes look almost identical from Gazebo’s camera, and the difference is the point: in the first, the intelligence is in the firmware and the plan is data; in the second, the intelligence is the node and can therefore change its mind mid-flight — which is why the running example, whose mission depends on what the camera sees, is built on the second path even though the first is simpler and more robust for surveys.
Simulation is also where the chapter’s tuning claims should be tortured rather than trusted. Set ACCEPT_RADIUS to 0.2 m and watch the NAVIGATE state stall beside a waypoint while simulated GNSS noise keeps the inequality false — the mission equivalent of an integrator that never settles. Set it to 10 m and watch the lawnmower’s rows smear into a shapeless loop. Kill the node mid-NAVIGATE and watch PX4’s dead-man’s switch drop the vehicle out of Offboard into a failsafe, exactly as promised two chapters running. Each experiment costs a restart; each buys an intuition that would cost an airframe outdoors. One deliberate gap remains, and it is the seam to the next chapter: the geofence polygon has been drawn, uploaded, and ignored — nothing yet happens when the simulated vehicle wanders across it. Arming that boundary, and the battery, link-loss, and RTL failsafes beside it, turns the fence from a line in a JSON file into the thing that brings the aircraft home when everything else has gone wrong — the safety half of mission scripting, and the business of the Geofencing and Fail-Safes chapter.

text:
11.9 Check Your Understanding

A mission item in a .plan file reads: "command": 16, "frame": 3, "params": [0, 0, 0, null, 39.68013, -75.75239, 5.5]. Decode the item: what command is this, what does frame 3 mean, where is the target, and what altitude will the vehicle fly there — relative to what reference?







TipShow answer





Command 16 is NAV_WAYPOINT: fly to a position. Frame 3 is MAV_FRAME_GLOBAL_RELATIVE_ALT: the coordinate is global latitude/longitude in degrees with altitude in metres relative to the home position, not above sea level. The target is 39.68013° N, 75.75239° W, and the vehicle will fly there at 5.5 m above home — where “home” is the position the autopilot recorded at arming, not the plan’s plannedHomePosition. (The first three params are hold time, acceptance radius override, and pass-through radius; zeros mean “use defaults,” and the null is an unused yaw field.)




Two teams fly the same lawnmower survey. Team A uploads the mission and flies it in Mission mode; Team B streams the waypoints from a companion-computer node in Offboard mode. Mid-flight, the telemetry link to the ground station drops for both, and Team B’s node process crashes. What happens to each aircraft, and what does the comparison say about when each command path is the right choice?







TipShow answer





Team A’s aircraft continues the mission unaffected: the plan was uploaded and lives on the flight controller, and the firmware’s navigator needs no link to execute it (the link-loss failsafe may be configured to continue-mission for exactly this case). Team B’s aircraft loses its setpoint stream; within about half a second PX4’s dead-man’s switch detects the stall, exits Offboard, and executes a failsafe such as RTL — a controlled recovery, not a continuation. The comparison is the decision rule: for a fixed, pre-plannable flight (a survey), Mission mode is more robust because the intelligence is in the firmware and the plan is data. Offboard earns its fragility only when the mission must change in response to live data — as the running example’s must — because only mission code can change its mind mid-flight.




Two consecutive waypoints in the worked plan sit at (39.67991219, −75.75234666) and (39.68032916, −75.75243136). Using 111,320 m per degree of latitude and 85,700 m per degree of longitude at this latitude, compute the leg length between them. Then estimate how long the leg takes at the plan’s commanded 1.5 m/s ground speed.







TipShow answer





Latitude difference: \(0.00041697^\circ \times 111{,}320 \approx 46.4\) m north. Longitude difference: \(0.0000847^\circ \times 85{,}700 \approx 7.3\) m west. Leg length \(\sqrt{46.4^2 + 7.3^2} \approx 47\) m. At 1.5 m/s the leg takes about \(47 / 1.5 \approx 31\) s. (The general skill: at mid-northern latitudes, read the fifth decimal place of a coordinate as roughly a metre — 1.1 m of latitude, 0.86 m of longitude — and any plan file or GPS log becomes geometry by inspection.)




A student’s mission node stalls: the vehicle hovers a metre from waypoint 3 indefinitely, mission never advancing, until the battery failsafe finally lands it. Another student’s vehicle “completes” the same lawnmower suspiciously fast, but the recorded coverage has gaps between rows. Diagnose both, and state the two bounds that a well-chosen acceptance radius must respect.







TipShow answer





The first student’s acceptance radius is too small relative to the position estimate’s noise: GNSS scatter of a metre or more keeps \(\lVert \hat{\mathbf{p}} - \mathbf{p}_{\text{wp}} \rVert\) from ever dropping below the threshold, so the arrival guard never fires — the vehicle orbits a test it cannot pass. The second student’s radius is too large relative to the mission’s geometry: the vehicle “arrives” several metres early at each waypoint and cuts the corners, so legs shorten and inter-row coverage opens gaps (with a radius comparable to the row pitch, adjacent legs blur together). The bounds: the radius must comfortably exceed the expected position-estimation error (or arrival never triggers) and comfortably undercut the smallest geometric feature of the mission, such as the row pitch (or the pattern deforms). For metre-scale GNSS noise and a 6.5 m pitch, one to two metres satisfies both.




In the state machine of this chapter, the failsafe check is evaluated before the state dispatch on every tick, rather than as a transition drawn from each individual state’s logic. Give the engineering argument for this ordering, and explain what property of the flag-based implementation from the previous chapter it repairs.







TipShow answer





Evaluating the failsafe first makes safety preemption structural: no matter which state is active — including states added years later by someone who never read the original code — the failsafe question is asked and answered before any state’s own logic runs, so no code path can shadow it. Encoding it per-state would require every current and future state to remember to include the check, converting a guarantee into a convention. The flag implementation had the related defect that the “current situation” was distributed across several booleans whose combinations included unintended ones (e.g., branch-ordering bugs where a landing check could be bypassed); the FSM makes the situation a single enumerated value and makes every legal change of situation an explicit, drawn transition — everything not drawn is impossible by construction.




The plan file contains both a plannedHomePosition and, implicitly, the home position the autopilot will record at arming. A field crew loads the plan but launches from the opposite corner of the field, 40 m from where the plan was drawn. Which parts of the mission shift with the actual launch point, which parts do not, and what is the operational lesson?







TipShow answer





The recorded home position — set at arming — becomes the reference for everything home-relative: the takeoff climb happens wherever the vehicle actually is, all relative altitudes are measured above the actual launch elevation, and RTL returns to the actual launch point, 40 m from where the plan’s author assumed. The waypoints themselves do not shift: they are absolute latitude/longitude coordinates, so the lawnmower is flown over the intended ground regardless of launch point (only the transit to the first waypoint changes). The geofence polygon likewise stays fixed to the earth. The lesson: plannedHomePosition is a planning convenience, not a command — verify before arming that the actual launch point is inside the geofence, that the transit to waypoint one is clear, and that the RTL destination (where the vehicle really sits) is where you want an emergency return to end.

11.10 Try It
Part 1 — fly both command paths on the workbench. Stand up SITL (make px4_sitl gz_x500, plus QGroundControl) and reproduce this chapter’s closing circuit. Draw a lawnmower of at least four waypoints over any field on QGC’s map at 5–10 m altitude, add a takeoff item, a DO_CHANGE_SPEED to 2 m/s, and a closing RTL; save the .plan, then open it in a text editor and find every field this chapter decoded — commands 22, 16, 178, 20, the frames, the altitude mode, the planned home. Upload and fly it in Mission mode, watching arrivals round the corners. Then convert your own waypoints to metres with the two conversion constants, predict the mission duration, and check the prediction against the simulator’s clock. Finally, port the same waypoint list (converted to local NED coordinates about the home point) into the state-machine node and fly it again in Offboard mode. One mission, two intelligences.
Part 2 — break the arrival test, then armor the machine. Extend the dry-run harness from the previous chapter’s Try It to the FSM version: feed the node a scripted position stream (a point moving at 1.5 m/s along the plan plus Gaussian noise of \(\sigma = 1\) m per axis) and verify every transition fires in order. Now lower ACCEPT_RADIUS until the NAVIGATE state stalls, and record the failure threshold — it should land near where the noise magnitude predicts. Restore a sane radius, then add one state of your own: a HOLD state entered from NAVIGATE when a simulated detection flag goes true, which loiters at the current position for five seconds before resuming the list at the same index. Confirm you touched no existing state’s logic to do it — then write two sentences on why the flag-based version of the same change would have been riskier. You have just rehearsed, in miniature, how the running example’s search behavior will absorb Part III’s detector.
Related Lab: See Appendix B for the lab assignment that applies this chapter’s concepts.

title: 12  Geofencing and Fail-Safes: Designing for the Unexpected
text:
12.1 Learning Objectives
The previous chapter ended on a deliberately loose thread. A geofence polygon had been drawn in QGroundControl, stored in the .plan file, decoded vertex by vertex, uploaded to the simulated vehicle — and then ignored. Nothing happened when the aircraft crossed it, because nothing had been told to happen. The fence was data without consequences, and the mission’s state machine carried a matching hole: a failsafe_event() check evaluated first on every tick, wired to nothing. This chapter closes both gaps. It arms the fence, fills the failsafe slot, and more generally takes up the discipline the whole Part has been circling: designing flight software for the flights that go wrong. The happy path — waypoints reached, battery ample, links alive — needs remarkably little engineering once the previous three chapters are absorbed. What separates a demonstration from a system is everything else: the gust that carries the vehicle toward the boundary, the battery that reads 28% with the aircraft 200 metres from home, the mission process that dies mid-flight. None of these is exotic. Each will happen, on a long enough sequence of flights, with probability one — and the entire craft of safety engineering is arranging, in advance, that when it happens the aircraft does something boring.
There is also an older thread to pick up. The Airspace Law chapter closed by observing that every rule it covered — the altitude ceiling, the authorized operating area, the rehearsed emergency procedure — was enforced by human discipline, and promised that this chapter would revisit those same constraints as software: coordinates the autopilot refuses to leave, thresholds compiled into parameters, emergency procedures that execute without waiting for a human to remember them. That promise is the right frame for everything below. A geofence is airspace law translated into a boundary check; a battery failsafe is the fuel-reserve rule translated into a threshold comparison; and the layered-margin doctrine — the organization’s 10-foot ceiling sitting far beneath the FAA’s 400-foot (122 m) one — reappears here, exactly, as mission thresholds sitting far above the firmware’s own floors.

Read the running example’s failsafe_monitor.py and explain its structure — an independent watchdog node with thresholds as parameters, a 1 Hz evaluation tick, and a publish-while-active protocol — and implement the evaluation logic its scaffold leaves open.

title: 12  Geofencing and Fail-Safes: Designing for the Unexpected
text:
12.2 Key Vocabulary

Geofence — a software-defined boundary the vehicle must respect — an inclusion polygon or a radius about home for the horizontal plane, plus an altitude ceiling — checked continuously against the estimated position and wired to an automatic action on breach; introduced as .plan data in the previous chapter, armed here.
Breach action — the configured response to a geofence violation, chosen from a graded menu: log only, warn the operator, hold position, return to launch, land immediately, or terminate flight.
Point-in-polygon test — the geometric core of a polygonal fence check: cast a ray from the test position and count polygon-edge crossings — an odd count means inside, an even count outside.
Failsafe — a pre-programmed automatic response to a detected fault or rule violation — link loss, low battery, boundary breach — designed so that the vehicle’s default behavior under failure is a safe one rather than a continuation of the mission.
Hard failsafe — a failsafe that seizes authority when it fires: the triggering condition changes the flight mode itself (RTL, land, hold), and the mission software’s consent is neither requested nor required.
Soft warning — an advisory response to an approaching limit — a margin fence, a battery caution — that informs the operator or mission logic while leaving authority where it is; the graceful layer that fires before the hard one must.
Hover-in-place — the gentlest hard response: the vehicle stops and holds its current position (PX4’s Hold mode, a commanded loiter), buying time for a human decision without moving through any more of the world.
Battery failsafe — the graded response ladder tied to remaining charge: a warning threshold, a return threshold sized to cover the worst-case trip home, and a land floor below which the only safe destination is straight down.
Watchdog — an independent process that monitors a system it does not control, holding no mission state and sharing no failure mode with the logic it supervises; the running example’s failsafe_monitor node is one.
Override authority — the explicit ordering of who may preempt whom in a multi-node system — safety pilot above firmware, firmware above watchdog, watchdog above mission logic, mission logic above behaviors — with overrides flowing strictly downward.

title: 12  Geofencing and Fail-Safes: Designing for the Unexpected
text:
12.3 Arming the Fence
The previous chapter’s .plan file stored its geofence as four latitude/longitude vertices and an "inclusion": true flag — a region the vehicle must stay inside. Turning that stored polygon into an enforced boundary takes one decision, not more code: telling the autopilot what to do about a breach. PX4 exposes the choice as a parameter — the geofence action — with a graded menu: do nothing but log; warn the operator over telemetry; hold position at the boundary; fly Return-to-Launch; land immediately; or terminate flight, cutting the motors outright. QGroundControl presents the same menu in its safety settings, and uploads the fence geometry alongside the mission over the same MAVLink session. With the polygon uploaded and the action set to RTL, the fence from the previous chapter stops being documentation. The firmware now checks the estimated position against the boundary continuously — and, in modern PX4, checks a short prediction of the trajectory as well, so a vehicle flying fast at the fence is turned back before the line rather than after it. Even with no polygon uploaded at all, two parameters provide a minimal fence — a maximum horizontal distance from home and a maximum altitude — which is exactly the shape the running example’s own watchdog will adopt later in this chapter.
The graded menu deserves a moment, because choosing from it is a genuine design decision with the same structure every failsafe response will have. Warning preserves all authority and all risk: appropriate only when a human is watching and able to act. Hold — hover in place — is the gentlest seizure of authority: the vehicle stops moving through the world, which converts a developing situation into a static one, at the price of hovering indefinitely on a draining battery. Return trades airspace for energy: the vehicle leaves the situation entirely, along a predictable path, at a known cost. Land trades everything for immediacy: minimum time to the ground, wherever the ground happens to be. And termination is the response of last resort — a falling aircraft is the certain cost, paid to bound the harm a flying one might do; it exists for the case where continued powered flight is itself the hazard. The right choice depends on what surrounds the fence: a boundary with open field beyond it can afford RTL; a boundary shared with a crowd line cannot afford anything that keeps flying toward it. For the lawnmower survey of the previous chapter — a fenced grass field, nothing beyond the boundary but more grass — RTL is the standard and correct choice, and it is the choice the simulation exercise at the end of this chapter demonstrates: fly at the fence on purpose, and watch the mission end and the trip home begin.

12.3.1 The boundary check itself
The firmware does this checking for you, and the running example’s watchdog will do it again independently — so it is worth owning the few lines of geometry involved. The horizontal question is: given the estimated position and a polygon of \(m\) vertices, is the point inside? The standard answer is the ray-casting test, drawn in Figure 12.1: cast a ray from the test point in any fixed direction (east, by convention) and count how many polygon edges it crosses. A point inside the polygon must cross the boundary an odd number of times to escape to infinity; a point outside crosses an even number of times (possibly zero). The parity of the count is the answer, for any simple polygon, convex or not.






Figure 12.1: The geofence boundary check: a ray cast east from the estimated position crosses the fence boundary an odd number of times from inside, an even number from outside. A soft-warning fence, shrunk inward from the hard fence, fires an advisory before the hard boundary fires an action, and an independent altitude comparison closes the top of the fenced volume.



In code, working in the local metric coordinates the previous chapter’s conversion produces (east and north in metres about home):
def inside(fence, e, n):
    """Ray-cast point-in-polygon: fence is a list of (east, north)
    vertices; (e, n) is the position under test. Casts a ray east
    and counts edge crossings — odd means inside."""
    crossings_odd = False
    m = len(fence)
    for i in range(m):
        e1, n1 = fence[i]
        e2, n2 = fence[(i + 1) % m]
        if (n1 > n) != (n2 > n):              # edge spans the ray's northing
            e_cross = e1 + (n - n1) * (e2 - e1) / (n2 - n1)
            if e_cross > e:                    # crossing lies east of the point
                crossings_odd = not crossings_odd
    return crossings_odd
Each edge is examined once, so the test is \(O(m)\) — for the four-vertex fence of the previous chapter, four comparisons and at most four multiplications, comfortably nothing at any update rate a position estimate arrives at. Three practical points turn the textbook test into a fence worth trusting. First, the fence is a volume, not a polygon: the horizontal test is paired with an independent altitude comparison against a ceiling, and breach of either is a breach — that ceiling is where the layered-margin doctrine lands in code, set not at the 122 m legal maximum but at the mission’s own working limit, the same way an organization’s 10-foot training ceiling sat far below the FAA’s number. Second, the test runs against an estimate, and the previous chapter’s acceptance-radius lesson applies unchanged: the position carries metre-scale scatter, so a vehicle hovering exactly on the boundary would flicker between inside and outside at the noise rate. The standard repairs are a margin and a debounce — which is the third point: build two fences. A soft fence, shrunk inward from the hard one by a few metres, fires a warning (to the operator, to the mission logic) while everything is still legal; the hard fence fires the action. The gap between them is bought room for the graceful response — the mission node can turn the vehicle around on its own terms inside the margin, and the hard failsafe becomes what its name should always mean: the layer that fires only when the layer above it has already failed.

title: 12  Geofencing and Fail-Safes: Designing for the Unexpected
text:
12.4 A Taxonomy of Fail-Safes
The geofence is one instance of a general pattern, and naming the pattern organizes everything the firmware offers. A failsafe is a trigger bound to a response. The triggers PX4 monitors continuously: loss of the RC link; loss of the data link to the ground station; loss of the Offboard setpoint stream — the dead-man’s switch of two chapters standing, now recognizable as one row of a larger table; low, critical, and emergency battery; geofence breach; and estimator failure, the EKF losing a usable position fix. The responses are the graded menu already met: warn, hold, return, land, terminate. The engineering content is in the binding — which response suits which trigger — and in one distinction that runs through the whole table: a hard failsafe changes the flight mode itself when it fires, seizing authority from whatever was flying the vehicle, while a soft warning informs and leaves authority in place. The previous chapter’s state machine already encoded where hard failsafes live in mission logic: checked first, every tick, outranking every state. What it left open — what fires the check — is precisely this table.
Return-to-Launch, the workhorse hard response, is itself a small mission: climb to a configured return altitude (so the path home clears whatever the vehicle was working beneath), fly to home — the position recorded at arming, with everything the previous chapter said about that — descend, and land. Its predictability is its virtue and its trap. The virtue: everyone on the crew knows, before the flight, exactly what the aircraft will do when something fails, and can stand where that path is not. The trap: RTL flies a straight line home through whatever happens to be in the way, which is why the return altitude is a safety parameter and not a convenience, and why a fence breach at the far side of a field must leave enough battery to fly the whole diagonal back.
That last clause is a calculation, and it sizes the battery failsafe. The running example’s pack stores 77 Wh, and the loaded aircraft draws about 365 W in mission flight — the numbers carried since Part I — so one percent of charge is about 0.77 Wh, or 7.6 seconds of flight. Now price the worst-case trip home for the watchdog’s fence geometry (a 200 m radius about home, a 30 m ceiling — the parameters met in the next section): 200 m of return cruise at 5 m/s is 40 s; the climb to return altitude and a metre-per-second descent from 30 m add roughly another 40–50 s; call the trip 90 seconds, about 12% of the pack. A Return-to-Launch trigger at 30% remaining therefore buys the worst-case trip home twice over — margin for a headwind, a detour, a slow human noticing — and a land floor at 15% marks the honest boundary below which the trip home is no longer affordable at all: under two minutes of flight remain, the cells are approaching the steep knee of the discharge curve where indicated charge falls fastest, and the only destination that is guaranteed reachable is straight down. Figure 12.2 draws the ladder, and its most important feature is what sits beneath the mission thresholds: the firmware’s own defaults — warn near 15%, act near 7%, land near 5% — which protect the aircraft, not the mission. The mission thresholds are set far above them deliberately, and the doctrine is the Airspace Law chapter’s, verbatim: the platform’s floor is where your margins begin, not where they end.






Figure 12.2: The battery failsafe ladder for the running example: mission-level thresholds — Return-to-Launch at 30% remaining, land at 15% — sized against the worst-case 90-second trip home from the fence edge, sitting far above the firmware’s own default floors near 15%, 7%, and 5%.



Two remaining rows of the table complete the taxonomy. Link-loss failsafes answer the question “who is flying this aircraft?” when the answer becomes “nobody”: RC loss and data-link loss each trigger a configurable response after a configurable delay, with RTL the common choice — and the Offboard stream timeout from two chapters ago is the same mechanism applied to a companion computer, with the vital property that the absence of messages is the trigger, so no failed component needs to succeed at announcing its own failure. Estimator failure is the humbling row: every response above assumes the vehicle knows where it is, and RTL toward a hallucinated home position is worse than useless, so a vehicle that loses its position fix falls back to responses that need progressively less state — attitude-stabilized descent, ultimately termination. It is the table’s reminder that failsafes are software running on the same estimates as everything else, which is exactly the argument for the independent monitor the next section builds: not because the firmware’s table is deficient, but because the mission has rules the firmware cannot know.

title: 12  Geofencing and Fail-Safes: Designing for the Unexpected
text:
12.5 The Running Example’s Watchdog: failsafe_monitor.py
Everything so far lives in the firmware, guarding limits any aircraft shares: batteries, links, fences. But the Goose Management System has safety rules PX4 has never heard of — a standoff distance from a living animal, a mission battery budget stricter than the firmware’s, an altitude ceiling set by policy rather than physics — and enforcing mission rules takes mission software. The architecture Part I sketched for the running example includes a dedicated node for exactly this: a Failsafe node that continuously monitors mission safety — battery state and safe separation among its concerns — and, when an unsafe condition is detected, can override the active controller and trigger a protective action: hover, Return-to-Launch, or mission abort. Here is the node, in full — the real code, not a sketch:
"""
Failsafe Monitor

Independent mission specific watchdog

Publishes to /goose/failsafe that triggers various overrides
"""

import math
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from std_msgs.msg import String
from px4_msgs.msg import VehicleLocalPosition, BatteryStatus, VehicleStatus
from goose_ops.px4_defs import (PX4_QOS, T_VEHICLE_LOCAL_POSITION,
                                T_BATTERY, T_VEHICLE_STATUS, T_FAILSAFE)


class FailsafeMonitor(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('failsafe_monitor')
        self.declare_parameter('battery_rtl', 0.30)
        self.declare_parameter('battery_land', 0.15)
        self.declare_parameter('geofence_radius_m', 200.0)
        self.declare_parameter('max_altitude_m', 30.0)
        self.pos = None
        self.batt = None
        self.status = None
        self._last_reason = None
        self.create_subscription(VehicleLocalPosition,
                                 T_VEHICLE_LOCAL_POSITION,
                                 self._on_lpos, PX4_QOS)
        self.create_subscription(BatteryStatus, T_BATTERY,
                                 self._on_batt, PX4_QOS)
        self.create_subscription(VehicleStatus, T_VEHICLE_STATUS,
                                 self._on_status, PX4_QOS)
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(String, T_FAILSAFE, 10)
        self.create_timer(1.0, self._tick)
        self.get_logger().info('failsafe_monitor up')

    def _on_lpos(self, m): self.pos = m
    def _on_batt(self, m): self.batt = m
    def _on_status(self, m): self.status = m

    def _evaluate(self):
        return None

    def _tick(self):
        reason = self._evaluate()

        if reason is not None:
            if reason != self._last_reason:
                self.get_logger().error(f'FAILSAFE: {reason}')
            self.pub.publish(String(data=reason))
        elif self._last_reason is not None:
            self.get_logger().info('failsafe condition cleared')
        self._last_reason = reason


def main():
    rclpy.init()
    rclpy.spin(FailsafeMonitor())


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
Read it as three design decisions, because that is what it is. First, independence. The node is a separate process holding no mission state — it does not know whether the vehicle is searching, engaging, or returning, and does not care. It subscribes to three PX4 telemetry streams (local position, battery status, vehicle status — the same uORB-over-DDS topics the previous chapters established) and publishes one string. A crash in the mission logic cannot take it down; a bug in a behavior node cannot corrupt its view of the battery. This is the modularity argument from Part I’s closing chapter made concrete: the safety monitor must not share a failure mode with the logic it supervises, and the only way to guarantee that is a process boundary. Second, thresholds as parameters, not constants: battery_rtl at 0.30, battery_land at 0.15, a geofence_radius_m of 200 and a max_altitude_m of 30 are declared as ROS 2 parameters, so the field crew can tighten them per site — a smaller field, a lower ceiling — without touching code, exactly the property that made the autopilot’s own parameter system the right home for NAV_ACC_RAD in the previous chapter. (Note the fence shape: a radius about home and a ceiling — a cylinder in the local NED frame where home is the origin, so the whole horizontal check is one hypotenuse. The polygon test earlier in this chapter is what this becomes when the site demands a shape; the cylinder is what it is when 200 m of grass in every direction makes the shape irrelevant.) Third, the publish protocol, which lives in _tick and repays close reading: while a condition holds, the reason string is published every second — a continuous assertion, not a single event, so a subscriber that starts late or drops a message still hears about an active failsafe within a tick; the log gets one FAILSAFE: line when the reason first appears and one cleared line when it goes away, the same latching discipline (_last_reason) that keeps a persistent condition from flooding the log at 1 Hz.
And then the fourth thing, which is not a decision but a seam: _evaluate returns None. The shipped file is the watchdog’s scaffold — subscriptions, parameters, tick, protocol, all the plumbing that makes a monitor trustworthy — with the monitored conditions themselves left as the open socket (note import math, sitting unused at the top of the file, waiting). Everything this chapter has built is the material for filling it:
    def _evaluate(self):
        """Return 'SEVERITY:reason' for the worst active condition, else
        None. Rules are ordered worst-first, so the first match wins."""
        p = self.get_parameter
        if self.batt is not None:
            if self.batt.remaining < p('battery_land').value:
                return 'LAND:battery below land floor'
        if self.pos is not None:
            if math.hypot(self.pos.x, self.pos.y) > p('geofence_radius_m').value:
                return 'RTL:geofence breach'
            if -self.pos.z > p('max_altitude_m').value:
                return 'RTL:altitude above ceiling'
        if self.batt is not None:
            if self.batt.remaining < p('battery_rtl').value:
                return 'RTL:battery below mission threshold'
        return None
The details carry the chapter’s lessons. BatteryStatus.remaining is a fraction of full charge, compared directly against the parameter thresholds of Figure 12.2. The position is PX4’s local NED estimate — north, east, down, metres from home — so altitude is \(-z\), the sign convention that has been earning its keep since the coordinate discussion of Part I, and the horizontal fence check is math.hypot of the two horizontal components against the radius. The ordering is a severity sort: a vehicle that is simultaneously outside the fence and below the land floor must land, not fly home, so LAND conditions are tested before any RTL condition. The reason strings are deliberately static: fold the live battery percentage into the string and it would change on every percent step, defeating the _last_reason latch and turning the one-line log into a stream — the tick’s latching discipline works only if “same condition” means “same string.” And the returned string is not prose — it is a tiny protocol, SEVERITY:reason, whose consumer is the next section’s subject.

section: 12.6 Override Authority: Who May Preempt Whom
text:
12.6 Override Authority: Who May Preempt Whom
A watchdog that publishes a string has detected a problem, not solved one. The failsafe_monitor node deliberately owns no ability to fly the aircraft — it never streams a setpoint, never calls a flight-mode service. Authority to act lives one layer down, in the mission manager: the top-level state machine node (the production version of the previous chapter’s figure, with a FAILSAFE state among its states) subscribes to /goose/failsafe, and on the first message during an active mission (it ignores the topic while idle, done, or already in failsafe) it executes the override in four moves. It sets the shared active-controller token — the topic on which it continuously names which behavior node currently owns the vehicle — to none, which silences the navigation and harassment nodes within a message, because those nodes stream setpoints only while the token names them. It abandons whatever service call was in flight. It enters its own terminal FAILSAFE state, from which no transition leads back to the mission. And it parses the severity prefix and calls the matching flight-controller service — LAND calls land, RTL calls return, HOLD calls hold — which the flight-controller node translates into a PX4 mode command. One subtlety in the parsing is a design lesson in itself: an unrecognized severity does not guess. The manager logs that it is standing down and assumes a PX4 native failsafe is already in control — deference, encoded, to the layer above.
That phrase — the layer above — is the load-bearing structure, and Figure 12.3 draws it in full. Authority in the running example is a strict ladder. At the top, the safety pilot’s RC transmitter: sticks wired to a receiver on the flight controller with no companion software in the path, able to seize control in any mode at any time — the human backstop the Airspace Law chapter’s rules (a licensed remote pilot present, one pilot flying at a time) put in place, now visible as the top rung of a software diagram. Below it, PX4’s native failsafes: the firmware acts by changing flight mode itself and needs no cooperation from anything above the autopilot — the dead-man’s switch fires whether or not the companion computer agrees, which is the point of it. Below the firmware, the watchdog and the mission manager, splitting detection from execution across a process boundary. And at the bottom, the behavior nodes — navigation and harassment — which hold the least authority in the system by construction: they may act only while the token names them, and they are never consulted about losing it. The design rule the ladder encodes: overrides flow strictly downward. The watchdog never streams a setpoint; the behavior nodes never see the failsafe topic; authority is revoked at the token, not negotiated with the node losing it. Every rung can silence every rung below it, and no rung can veto one above.






Figure 12.3: Override authority in the running example, drawn as a ladder: the safety pilot’s transmitter above PX4’s native failsafes, above the independent failsafe-monitor watchdog, above the mission manager that executes overrides by revoking the active-controller token and calling flight-controller services, above the behavior nodes that may act only while the token names them.



Three further details show the ladder working end to end. The mission manager carries hard-failsafe consumers and producers — with an escalation ladder of its own. Its watchdogs — an engagement timeout, a target-lost timer — do not invoke _enter_failsafe directly: they route the vehicle into a resume state that attempts recovery first, handing control back to the firmware’s mission so the search can continue — the soft response, tried before the hard one. Only when that recovery itself fails three times running does the manager escalate, feeding the same _enter_failsafe path with an RTL: reason — so a mission that cannot continue safely ends the same way a breached fence does, through one code path, one log line, one behavior the crew has rehearsed. The operator’s abort service is the same path again — a human on the ground station commands RTL:operator abort through precisely the machinery a low battery would use, which means the emergency everyone practices is also the button anyone can press. And the flight-controller node closes the loop upward: its preflight check refuses to launch while PX4 reports an active failsafe, and its status stream republishes the firmware’s failsafe flag so every layer can see when the rung above has taken over. The full node graph — every topic, every service, every authority transfer, including the perception nodes Part III adds — is the business of the System Architecture chapter in Part V; the reader arriving there will find this ladder unchanged at its core, with more rungs’ worth of detail, not more rungs.
One last symmetry closes the Part. The software ladder’s top rung is a person, and that is not an implementation compromise — it is the design. The Airspace Law chapter’s institutional rules (the licensed pilot present, the single pilot flying, the 10-foot training ceiling under the 122 m legal one) are the human layers of exactly this diagram, enforcing what software cannot: judgment about weather, bystanders, and the thousand conditions no _evaluate enumerates. The software layers, in turn, enforce what humans cannot: a 300-millisecond response at 2 a.m. of attention span, every second, without boredom. Designing for the unexpected is not choosing between the two. It is stacking them, each layer honest about what it can catch, each one armed before the flight on which it is needed — because the flight on which it is needed does not announce itself.

title: 12  Geofencing and Fail-Safes: Designing for the Unexpected
text:
12.7 Check Your Understanding

A fence polygon has vertices, in local metres (east, north): (0, 0), (100, 10), (90, 80), (−10, 70). Using the ray-casting test with a ray cast east, determine whether the point (40, 40) is inside. Which edges does the ray cross?







TipShow answer





The ray from (40, 40) runs east at northing 40. Test each edge for spanning \(n = 40\): edge (0,0)→(100,10) spans northings 0–10, no; edge (100,10)→(90,80) spans 10–80, yes — crossing at \(e = 100 + (40-10)\times(90-100)/(80-10) = 100 - 4.3 \approx 95.7\), which is east of 40, so it counts; edge (90,80)→(−10,70) spans 70–80, no; edge (−10,70)→(0,0) spans 0–70, yes — crossing at \(e = -10 + (40-70)\times(0-(-10))/(0-70) \approx -5.7\), which is west of 40, so it does not count. One eastward crossing — odd — so (40, 40) is inside the fence.




The same mission is protected by a QGC geofence with the breach action set to RTL and by the running example’s failsafe_monitor publishing RTL:geofence on breach. These look redundant. Give two concrete failure scenarios in which exactly one of the two layers catches the problem, and state the general principle.







TipShow answer





Firmware-only catch: the companion computer crashes or hangs entirely — the watchdog node is dead and publishes nothing, but PX4’s fence check runs on the flight controller and fires regardless (as does the Offboard dead-man’s switch). Watchdog-only catch: a mission rule the firmware cannot know — the watchdog’s fence is deliberately tighter than the uploaded one (or the crew set geofence_radius_m down for a small site without re-uploading firmware fence geometry), or a mission-specific condition such as a separation distance fires — the firmware sees a perfectly legal flight while the mission layer correctly aborts. The principle is layered enforcement with independent failure modes: the firmware layer survives companion-computer death; the mission layer encodes rules above the firmware’s floor. Neither substitutes for the other, which is why both are armed.




Using the running example’s numbers — 77 Wh pack, 365 W mission draw, fence radius 200 m, ceiling 30 m, return cruise 5 m/s — a teammate proposes lowering battery_rtl from 0.30 to 0.18 to buy more search time. Evaluate the proposal quantitatively.







TipShow answer





One percent of the pack is \(0.77\ \text{Wh} / 365\ \text{W} \approx 7.6\) s of flight. The worst-case return — 200 m at 5 m/s (40 s) plus climb and a descent from 30 m (roughly 40–50 s) — costs about 90 s, i.e. about 12% of the pack. Triggering RTL at 18% means arriving in the landing phase near \(18 - 12 = 6\%\) — at or below the firmware’s own critical threshold (~7%), inside the steep knee of the discharge curve where indicated charge falls fastest and voltage sag under load is worst, with zero margin for a headwind or a delayed trigger. The 30% setting lands the aircraft near 18% — above the 15% land floor with the worst case already paid. The proposal converts about 90 s of extra search into the elimination of the entire safety margin; reject it, or fund the search time honestly with a larger pack or a tighter fence (a smaller radius shrinks the worst-case return and legitimately lowers the defensible threshold).




In failsafe_monitor.py, the reason string is re-published every tick while the condition holds, but logged only when it changes; and in the mission manager, the first failsafe message latches the FAILSAFE state, which is terminal. Explain what each of the three choices (continuous publish, change-only logging, latched terminal state) protects against.







TipShow answer





Continuous publish protects against lost messages and late joiners: with a best-effort transport and independently restarting nodes, a single event message could be missed forever, but an assertion repeated at 1 Hz reaches any subscriber within a tick — the same “stream as proof” logic as the Offboard heartbeat. Change-only logging protects the log (and the human reading it) from 1 Hz flooding during a persistent condition: one line when the condition appears, one when it clears, is the record an incident review needs. The latched terminal state protects against oscillation and secondary logic re-entering the mission: a battery hovering around the threshold or a fence flicker under GNSS noise would otherwise toggle the system between mission and failsafe repeatedly — once safety has been invoked, the flight is over, and only a human (restarting the mission after landing) resets it.




The mission manager, on receiving LAND:battery below land floor, sets the active-controller token to none before calling the land service. Why does the order matter, and what could happen with the reverse order?







TipShow answer





The behavior nodes stream Offboard setpoints while the token names them. If the manager called the land service first, PX4 would begin the landing — but the still-authorized behavior node would keep streaming setpoints, and an active setpoint stream is precisely the condition for (re-)entering Offboard mode: the mission logic could fight the landing, or flip the vehicle back out of it. Revoking the token first silences every setpoint source (the nodes stop publishing within one message), so when the land command arrives there is no competing claimant to authority. It is the mission-layer version of the previous chapters’ silence discipline: software hands back control by ceasing to prove it wants control — and the manager makes that happen for the nodes, by decree, rather than trusting each to do it itself.




PX4’s own low-battery failsafe would eventually return and land the aircraft with no companion software at all. State two distinct reasons the running example nonetheless sets its mission thresholds (0.30/0.15) far above the firmware defaults (~0.15/0.07/0.05), and connect the pattern to a rule from the Airspace Law chapter.







TipShow answer





First, the firmware defaults protect the aircraft, not the mission’s geometry: they know nothing about the 200 m fence radius or the 30 m ceiling, so they cannot guarantee the worst-case trip home is affordable when they fire — at 7% remaining, the ~12% return trip is already unpayable. The mission thresholds are sized against the mission’s own worst case, with margin. Second, acting early converts an emergency into a routine: an RTL at 30% is a calm, predictable end-of-mission with the crew watching; an emergency landing at 5% happens wherever the vehicle is, on a sagging pack. The pattern is the layered-margin doctrine of the Airspace Law chapter — the organization’s 10-foot ceiling under the FAA’s 400-foot (122 m) limit — recurring in software: the platform’s legal or firmware floor is where an operation’s margins begin, and every responsible layer adds rules matched to its own hazard profile above it.

text:
12.8 Try It
Part 1 — arm the fence and break it on purpose. Reload the previous chapter’s SITL workbench and the lawnmower mission, and this time finish the job: in QGroundControl, draw an inclusion polygon around the field (or reuse the plan’s), set the geofence breach action to Return-to-Launch, and upload. Fly the mission once inside the fence to confirm nothing fires. Then edit one waypoint to sit outside the polygon and fly again: watch the mission proceed until the boundary, the fence trigger, and the RTL climb-return-land sequence — the mission plan, the vehicle’s track, and the moment of the trigger are the demonstration that matters, so record the screen. Repeat with the action set to Hold and note the difference in what you would do next as an operator: the returning aircraft solved its own problem; the hovering one is holding a draining battery and waiting for you. Finally, lower the fence’s altitude ceiling below the mission altitude and confirm the vertical half of the volume triggers exactly like the horizontal half.
Part 2 — fill the watchdog’s seam. Implement _evaluate in the running example’s failsafe_monitor.py (or a copy of its scaffold) with the four parameterized conditions from this chapter — land-floor battery, fence radius, altitude ceiling, RTL-threshold battery, in that severity order — and test it the way the previous chapter tested the state machine: feed it scripted telemetry rather than a live vehicle. Drive remaining down through 0.30 and 0.15 and check the published severities and the single logged line per transition; walk the position out through 200 m and confirm RTL:geofence; hold the battery at exactly 0.299 and watch the 1 Hz re-publish. Then add the two refinements the chapter argued for: a soft layer (publish WARN: at radius minus a margin — and decide, in writing, who should consume it), and a debounce (a condition must hold for \(k\) consecutive ticks before it is published; pick \(k\) by reasoning about GNSS scatter at the fence line versus the cost of a one-second delay). Finish by wiring your monitor to the SITL vehicle from Part 1 and forcing one real trigger — the moment the simulated aircraft turns for home because your code said so is the moment this Part has been building toward.

title: 13  Images as Data: From Pixels to Tensors
text:
13.1 Learning Objectives
Part II ended with a vehicle that can fly a scripted mission and, more importantly, end one safely: a state machine that sequences behaviors, a geofence that bounds them, and a failsafe ladder that outranks them all. But threaded through all of that machinery is a placeholder. The mission state machine of the Mission Scripting chapter was built to absorb a detect event from a perception node — the addition, that chapter promised, that would turn its lawnmower search into the running example’s search-then-deter behavior — yet its own closing exercise could only simulate that event with a hand-set flag; the watchdog of the previous chapter counts safe separation from an animal among its concerns; Part I’s closing chapter promised a target position, published at frame rate, that everything downstream consumes as a stream. Every one of those signals originates in one node that has so far been treated as a black box: the Detector. Part III opens the box.
The reason the box must be opened onboard was settled by arithmetic in Part I: a 640 × 480 colour frame is 921,600 raw bytes, thirty of them a second is roughly 27 MB/s, and no link off the aircraft — not the 90 kB/s UART, not the telemetry radio — carries a fraction of that. Pixels stay where they are produced, so the Jetson must understand them where they are produced. Understanding begins with a question so basic it is easy to skip: when the depth camera delivers a frame over USB, what — exactly — does the companion computer receive? The answer is numbers, a great many of them, in a very particular arrangement, and everything in this Part follows from taking that arrangement seriously. This chapter establishes the representation: how light becomes a grid of quantized samples, why that grid is properly a tensor and what each of its axes encodes, why the grid’s spatial structure is the property a vision model must exploit rather than discard, and how the same input tensor supports three differently shaped answers — a label, a set of boxes, a skeleton of keypoints — of which the running example needs precisely one.

Trace how a camera converts light into a grid of quantized intensity samples, and state what spatial resolution and bit depth each control.
Represent a digital image as a height × width × channels tensor, explain what each axis encodes, and compute the memory footprint of a frame from its shape and data type.
Explain what spatial structure means — why neighbouring pixels are statistically related — and show, with a parameter-count argument, why a representation that flattens the grid into a vector discards exactly the property vision depends on.
Describe what a convolution kernel does to an image tensor, define a feature map, and state why weight sharing makes convolutional processing both small and translation-tolerant.
Distinguish classification, object detection, and pose/keypoint estimation as differently structured outputs computed from the same tensor input, and select the appropriate task for a stated mission requirement.
Carry a camera frame through the standard preprocessing steps — resize, crop, normalize, re-layout — and quantify what input resolution costs in memory and compute, and what reducing it costs in pixels on target.

13  Images as Data: From Pixels to Tensors

title: 13  Images as Data: From Pixels to Tensors
text:
13.2 Key Vocabulary

Pixel (picture element) — one cell of the image grid: a single spatial sample of the scene, holding one intensity value per channel.
Bit depth — the number of bits used to store one intensity sample, which fixes how many distinguishable levels it can take; 8 bits gives the 0–255 range of standard camera output.
Channel — one complete plane of the image grid measuring a single quantity across the whole scene: red, green, and blue planes for a colour camera, a single luminance plane for grayscale or thermal, a range plane for a depth camera.
Tensor — a multidimensional array of numbers indexed along a fixed number of axes; a colour image is a rank-3 tensor of shape height × width × channels, and every intermediate result inside a vision network is a tensor too.
Spatial structure — the property that an image’s meaning lives in the arrangement of its values, not their distribution: neighbouring pixels sample neighbouring patches of the world, so edges, textures, and objects exist only as local patterns across the grid.
Convolution kernel — a small grid of learned weights slid across the image; at each position the kernel is multiplied element-wise with the window beneath it and summed to one output value, so the same few weights examine every neighbourhood in the frame.
Feature map — the output plane a kernel produces: a map, aligned with the image, whose value at each position measures how strongly the kernel’s pattern is present there.
Bounding box — the axis-aligned rectangle a detector reports around an object, typically as a centre, width, and height in pixel coordinates, accompanied by a class label and a confidence score.
Pose (keypoint) estimation — the task of locating named anatomical or structural points — head, joints, extremities — as pixel coordinates, recovering geometry within a detected object rather than just its extent.
Inference — running a trained model forward on a new input to produce an output, as distinct from training; the operation the companion computer performs on every frame, and the only one it performs in flight.

title: 13  Images as Data: From Pixels to Tensors
section: 13.3 From Photons to a Grid of Numbers
text:
13.3 From Photons to a Grid of Numbers
A camera is a sampling instrument, and it samples twice. Behind the lens sits a rectangular array of photosites — light-sensitive wells, a few micrometres across, one per pixel of the final image. During an exposure each photosite accumulates charge in proportion to the light striking it; at readout that charge is measured and converted to a number. The first sampling is spatial: the continuous pattern of light the lens projects is measured only at the discrete grid positions the photosites occupy, so a 640 × 480 mode means the scene has been reduced to 480 rows of 640 samples — 307,200 point measurements of a continuous world. The second sampling is in amplitude: the measured charge, a continuous quantity, is rounded to one of a fixed set of levels set by the converter’s bit depth. Eight bits — the near-universal choice for camera output — gives \(2^8 = 256\) levels, so each sample is an integer from 0 (no light) to 255 (photosite saturated).
A grayscale image is therefore nothing more exotic than a matrix: a 480 × 640 array of small integers, indexable as \(I[v, u]\) with row index \(v\) and column index \(u\). Two conventions attach to that indexing and both matter later. The origin is the top-left corner, with \(v\) increasing downward and \(u\) increasing rightward — a screen-drawing inheritance, and one more coordinate convention to keep straight alongside the NED frame the reader has carried since Part I (image coordinates are their own frame; converting a pixel position into a vehicle-frame direction is camera geometry, taken up when the detection pipeline is built). And the pair is written row first: \(I[v, u]\) is row \(v\), column \(u\) — height before width — which is why image shapes are quoted as 480 × 640 while the same camera mode is marketed as 640 × 480.
Colour requires a third dimension, because a photosite is colour-blind — it counts photons, not wavelengths. A colour camera lays a mosaic of tiny red, green, and blue filters over the photosite array, so each site measures only one colour band, and an interpolation step in the camera (demosaicking) fills in each pixel’s two unmeasured colours from its neighbours. What the camera delivers, after this processing, is three full planes: a red plane, a green plane, and a blue plane, each 480 × 640, together specifying every pixel’s colour as an additive mix. Those planes are the image’s channels, and they are the third axis of the object this chapter is named for.

13  Images as Data: From Pixels to Tensors

title: 13  Images as Data: From Pixels to Tensors
text:
13.4 The Image as a Tensor
The progression is familiar from linear algebra: a single number is a scalar, a line of numbers indexed by one subscript is a vector, a grid indexed by two is a matrix. A tensor, in the machine-learning sense of the word, simply continues the sequence — a multidimensional array indexed by any fixed number of axes. (Mathematicians reserve tensor for objects with specific transformation rules; deep-learning usage keeps only the shape and drops the rest, and this book follows the field.) A colour image is the canonical rank-3 example, with shape written \(H \times W \times C\):

Axis 0, height \(H\) — which row, top to bottom: 480 for the running example’s camera mode.
Axis 1, width \(W\) — which column, left to right: 640.
Axis 2, channels \(C\) — which measured quantity: 3, ordered red, green, blue.

Figure 13.1 draws the whole object: the pixel grid a person would recognize as a picture on the left, and the same numbers arranged as three indexed planes on the right, with one sample pinned down as \(I[v, u, c]\).






Figure 13.1: One camera frame as a height × width × channels tensor: each pixel of the grid is three 8-bit intensities, and the frame is a single 480 × 640 × 3 array indexed by row, column, and channel.



The shape is also a bill, and it is worth paying in full once. As delivered — one byte per value — a frame costs
\[
\begin{aligned}
480 \times 640 \times 3 &= 921{,}600\ \text{values} = 921{,}600\ \text{bytes} \approx 0.92\ \text{MB},\\
\text{at 30 frames/s:}\quad 921{,}600 \times 30 &\approx 27.6\ \text{MB/s}.
\end{aligned}
\]
That 27 MB/s is the same number Part I used to prove the imagery cannot leave the aircraft; it now reappears as the load the onboard pipeline must absorb continuously. And the bill grows before the model ever sees the frame: networks compute in floating point, and converting each 1-byte integer to a 4-byte float32 quadruples the footprint to about 3.7 MB per frame. Multiply by the buffering a real pipeline needs — the frame being captured, the frame being processed, the intermediate results — and image memory starts to compete for the companion computer’s RAM in earnest. The source constraint the next chapter makes precise is already visible in outline: in an embedded vision system, the activations — the tensors flowing between layers — often cost more memory than the model’s own weights, and every one of them scales with the input resolution chosen here.
The channel axis is where the tensor view starts earning its generality. Nothing about axis 2 says “colour”; it says “measured quantities per pixel,” and the running example’s Intel RealSense D455 makes the point physically. Alongside the RGB stream it produces a depth stream — a plane of the same spatial layout whose value at \((v, u)\) is the measured range, in millimetres, to whatever surface that pixel sees, delivered as 16-bit integers because 256 levels cannot span centimetre precision over tens of metres. Aligned to the colour frame, depth is simply a fourth channel a pipeline may stack on: \(C = 4\), shape 480 × 640 × 4. A thermal camera delivers \(C = 1\) — one radiometric plane. The tensor formalism absorbs all of these without modification, which is exactly why every vision framework speaks it.
Two bookkeeping conventions complete the picture, and both bite in practice. First, axis order: cameras and OpenCV deliver channels-last (\(H, W, C\) — the three colour values of one pixel adjacent in memory), while PyTorch expects channels-first (\(C, H, W\) — each colour plane contiguous), so every pipeline contains an explicit transpose, and supplying the wrong order fails silently or loudly but never correctly. Second, the batch axis: models process inputs in batches, adding a leading axis \(N\) for “which image,” so the tensor a PyTorch model actually receives is rank-4 with shape \((N, C, H, W)\) — for onboard inference, almost always \(N = 1\). A short exchange with a live frame makes all of this concrete:
import cv2
import numpy as np
import torch

frame = cv2.imread("field_frame.png")     # any 640x480 capture
print(frame.shape, frame.dtype)           # (480, 640, 3) uint8  -- H, W, C
print(frame[240, 320])                    # centre pixel, e.g. [ 84 148  96]
print(frame.nbytes)                       # 921600 bytes

x = torch.from_numpy(frame).float() / 255.0   # uint8 -> float32 in [0, 1]
x = x.permute(2, 0, 1).unsqueeze(0)           # (H,W,C) -> (1, C, H, W)
print(x.shape)                            # torch.Size([1, 3, 480, 640])
print(x.element_size() * x.nelement())    # 3686400 bytes -- the float bill
(One trap for the record: OpenCV orders the channels blue–green–red for historical reasons, so frame[240, 320] above prints B, G, R — a pipeline mixing OpenCV capture with a model trained on RGB images must swap channels explicitly, and this single silent mismatch has degraded more deployed detectors than any exotic failure.)

title: 13  Images as Data: From Pixels to Tensors
section: 13.5 Spatial Structure: Why the Grid Is Not Just a List
text:
13.5 Spatial Structure: Why the Grid Is Not Just a List
A 480 × 640 × 3 tensor holds 921,600 numbers, and nothing so far prevents treating it as a flat vector of that length — forgetting the grid, keeping the values. What would be lost? Everything, and the argument is worth making precisely, because it is the founding argument of convolutional processing.
Consider a thought experiment. Take every frame the camera will ever produce and shuffle its pixels by one fixed permutation — the same scrambling applied to every frame. No information is destroyed: the permutation is invertible, and every pixel value survives. Yet the scrambled frames are meaningless to the eye, because what the eye reads is not the set of values but their arrangement: an edge is a coherent intensity change between neighbouring pixels, a texture is a repeating local pattern, a goose is a particular composition of curves and contrasts spanning a compact region. Adjacent pixels sample adjacent patches of the physical world, so nearby values are strongly correlated and jointly meaningful in a way that distant values are not. That is spatial structure, and the shuffle preserves the data while annihilating it.
Now count what ignoring it costs. The generic way to wire a flattened image into a network is a fully-connected layer: every input value connected, with its own weight, to every unit of the next layer. Even a modest first layer of 1,000 units costs
\[
\begin{aligned}
921{,}600 \times 1{,}000 &= 9.216 \times 10^{8}\ \text{weights} \\
\text{at 4 bytes each:}\quad &\approx 3.7\ \text{GB},
\end{aligned}
\]
which is essentially the Jetson Nano’s entire 4 GB of memory spent before the network has a second layer — for a layer that, by construction, could learn the scrambled images exactly as easily as the real ones, because it assigns independent weights to every position and encodes no notion of “neighbouring.” Worse, whatever it learns it learns per location: the weights that come to recognize a goose centred in the frame say nothing about a goose near the edge, so every appearance position must be learned separately, from separate examples. The fully-connected layer is simultaneously too large to fit and too weak to generalize, and both failures have the same cause — it treats the image as a list.
The repair is to process the image the way its structure suggests: locally, and identically everywhere. A convolution takes a small grid of weights — a kernel, typically 3 × 3 per channel — and slides it across the image. At each position, the kernel is multiplied element-wise with the window of pixels beneath it and the products are summed to a single number; sliding over all positions produces a new plane, the feature map, aligned with the image, whose value at each location measures how strongly the kernel’s pattern is present there. Figure 13.2 traces one position through the operation with a classic hand-designed kernel that responds to vertical edges; in a network the kernel’s weights are not designed but learned, exactly as Part II’s reader learned that a PID gain is tuned rather than guessed — the mechanism is fixed, the numbers come from data.






Figure 13.2: Convolution slides one small kernel across the whole image: at each position the 3 × 3 window is multiplied element-wise by the kernel and summed to a single value of the feature map, so 28 parameters examine every neighbourhood of a 307,200-pixel frame.



The arithmetic reverses spectacularly. A 3 × 3 kernel spanning all three input channels holds \(3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27\) weights plus one bias — 28 parameters — and those same 28 numbers examine every one of the roughly 300,000 window positions in the frame. Against the fully-connected layer’s \(9 \times 10^8\) weights, that is a reduction of seven orders of magnitude, purchased by an assumption the thought experiment just validated: the patterns that matter are local, and a pattern worth detecting at one position is worth detecting at every position. The second half of that assumption buys the generalization the flat layer lacked — because the kernel slides, a goose-shaped response learned from geese in the training set’s frame centres fires just as well on a goose in the corner. The property is called translation equivariance: shift the input, and the feature map shifts with it, rather than the detection failing.
One kernel yields one feature map, and one pattern detector does not make a perception system, so a convolutional layer learns a bank of \(F\) kernels and stacks their maps: an \(H \times W \times C\) input becomes an \(H' \times W' \times F\) output. Read that shape carefully, because it is the moment the tensor formalism pays for itself: the output is again a rank-3 tensor of the same form as the input, but its channel axis no longer counts colours — it counts features found. Layer two convolves over layer one’s feature maps and finds patterns of patterns; by the depth of a real network the channels encode fragments like “textured round body” and “long curved neck,” still organized on a spatial grid that remembers where. Every tensor between the camera and the answer has the same three-axis anatomy established in Figure 13.1 — which is why this chapter’s representation, and not any particular network, is the true foundation of Part III. How many layers, how many kernels, and how the whole stack is trained and squeezed into the Jetson’s power budget is the business of the next chapter, on TinyML; what cannot change, whatever those answers are, is the shape of the data flowing through.

title: 13  Images as Data: From Pixels to Tensors
text:
13.6 Three Tasks, One Tensor
Everything so far concerns the input. The output side has its own taxonomy, and choosing from it is a mission decision, not a modelling detail. Inference — running the trained model forward on a live frame — always consumes the same \((1, 3, H, W)\) tensor; what distinguishes the classical vision tasks is the structure of what comes back. Figure 13.3 puts the three that matter for this book side by side on the same scene.






Figure 13.3: Three vision tasks distinguished by output structure: classification returns one label and confidence for the whole frame, object detection returns a list of bounding boxes each with class and confidence, and pose estimation returns named keypoint coordinates within each detected animal.



Classification answers one question about the whole frame: which class is this? The model’s final output is a vector of scores, one per class — here perhaps just two, goose and no goose — normalized so they read as confidences. It is the least structured output, the cheapest to compute, and the cheapest to train, because labelling a training image requires only a word. Its limitation is exactly its economy: a classification of the running example’s frame asserts that a goose exists somewhere in 307,200 pixels. For a wildlife survey counting animals in archived imagery frame by frame, that can suffice. For a vehicle that must close on the animal, it is a fact without a direction.
Object detection answers what is present, and where — for every instance. The output is a variable-length list: for each object found, a bounding box — an axis-aligned rectangle, parameterized as a centre \((u, v)\) with width and height, or equivalently by two corners, in pixel coordinates — plus a class label and a confidence. The structural leap from classification is real and it is the reason detection is harder to train and to run: the model must produce zero, one, or many answers per frame, each tied to a location, and its training data must contain drawn boxes, not just words. (The loss that trains such a model correspondingly combines a classification term, a box-geometry term, and a confidence term — a composite the next chapters return to; for now the point is that output structure dictates training structure.)
Pose estimation — keypoint detection — answers how the object is arranged: it locates named structural points as pixel coordinates, head and neck-base and tail for a bird, joints for a person. It recovers geometry within the object that a box discards — which way the animal faces, whether wings are spread — at the price of still more computation and far more expensive labels, every training image needing every keypoint clicked.
The running example needs the middle column, and it is worth stating the reasoning as engineering rather than as taste, because the Building a Detection Pipeline chapter builds directly on it. The deterrence behavior of Part II’s state machine needs a target to steer toward: a direction, updated at frame rate. A detection’s box centre \((u, v)\) provides exactly that — through camera geometry, a pixel position is a bearing from the camera — and this is where the D455’s fourth channel closes the loop Part I promised: the depth value at that same \((v, u)\) supplies the missing range, and bearing plus range is a 3D target position in the vehicle’s frame. That triple — detect, look up depth, transform — is the target-position topic the mission logic has consumed since Part II, finally traced back to its pixels. Classification cannot feed it, for want of a location. Pose estimation could enrich it — a bird’s heading would help predict its escape direction — but it costs compute the Jetson’s budget will be shown (next chapter) to need elsewhere, and the deterrence maneuver as designed needs a position, not a posture. Richer output structure is bought with computation and labelled data; buy what the mission needs.

13.6.1 Pixels on target
One more quantity binds the input representation to the task, and it was promised in Part I: the search altitude is “fixed from below by the pixels-on-target requirement.” That requirement can now be computed. The Commercial Drone Landscape chapter’s ground-sample-distance relation, \(\text{GSD} = pH/f\), says one pixel spans a ground distance set by pixel pitch, height, and focal length; the ratio \(p/f\) is just the angle one pixel subtends, so for a camera viewing a target at range \(R\) the same relation reads: one pixel covers \(R \, \theta_{\text{pix}}\) metres, where \(\theta_{\text{pix}}\) is the per-pixel angle. The D455’s colour camera spans a horizontal field of view of about \(90^\circ\); in the 640-column mode,
\[
\theta_{\text{pix}} = \frac{90^\circ}{640} = 0.141^\circ = 2.45\ \text{mrad per pixel}.
\]
A Canada goose’s body is roughly 0.35 m long. At a range of 20 m,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{metres per pixel} &= R\,\theta_{\text{pix}} = 20 \times 2.45\times 10^{-3} = 4.9\ \text{cm} \\
\text{pixels on goose} &= \frac{0.35}{0.049} \approx 7\ \text{pixels};
\end{aligned}
\]
at 10 m the same goose spans about 14 pixels. Seven pixels is a smudge — a detector fed smudges produces confidences barely above its false alarms — while double that begins to be a bird, with a visible neck and body to compose features from. The number explains, quantitatively, why the running example’s search leg flies at a few tens of metres and not at the legal ceiling, and it plants a warning the preprocessing section is about to pay off: resolution spent at the camera can be silently un-spent before the model ever sees the frame.

title: 13  Images as Data: From Pixels to Tensors
section: 13.7 From Camera Frame to Model Input
text:
13.7 From Camera Frame to Model Input
Between the USB cable and the network sits a short, unglamorous, load-bearing stage the source pipeline names in one word: preprocess — resize, crop, normalize. A trained network’s first layer has a fixed input shape, almost never the camera’s: detection models commonly expect a square input such as 640 × 640 or smaller, chosen (next chapter) to fit a compute budget. The camera’s 640 × 480 frame must be resized to that shape — and because 640 × 480 is not square, either non-uniformly stretched (distorting every goose) or, standardly, scaled uniformly and padded with dead bands to fill the square (letterboxing), in which case every box the detector reports lives in the model’s coordinates and must be mapped back through the same scale and offset before it means anything in camera pixels. An alternative to shrinking everything is cropping a region of interest: once a target is being tracked, feeding the model a full-resolution crop around its last known position spends the whole input budget where the target is — more pixels on goose from the same camera — at the risk that a second bird outside the crop goes unseen. Finally the values are normalized — converted to float and scaled to \([0,1]\), often further shifted and scaled per channel to match the statistics the network was trained under — and the axes transposed to \((1, C, H, W)\), exactly the permute/unsqueeze lines of the earlier code block.
The resize step deserves respect rather than habit, because it is where this chapter’s threads knot together. Computation and activation memory both scale with the pixel count of the model’s input — halve each side and both fall by four, which is the single most powerful lever the next chapter has for fitting perception into the Jetson’s budget. But the pixels-on-target arithmetic runs on the resolution the model sees, not the resolution the sensor captured: downsample a frame in which a goose spans 14 pixels by two, and the detector receives a 7-pixel smudge — the camera’s resolution silently discarded in a line of preprocessing. Input resolution is thus a genuine design variable with a constraint from each side: pushed down by power, memory, and frame-rate, pushed up by detection range at mission altitude. Setting it is not a preprocessing detail; it is the first negotiation between this chapter’s representation and the next chapter’s constraints, and the Building a Detection Pipeline chapter will settle it with measurements rather than defaults.
That is the foundation laid. An image is a tensor; the tensor’s grid carries the spatial structure that convolution — a few shared weights, slid everywhere — is shaped to exploit; feature maps carry that structure through a network, layer by layer, in the same three-axis form; and out the far end comes an answer whose structure was a mission decision, made here: the running example detects, because deterrence needs a bearing. What remains is everything the word trained has been holding back — how the kernels’ numbers are learned, and how a network of them is compressed until it runs, at frame rate, inside a 10-watt computer bolted to a 2.2-kilogram aircraft. That is TinyML, and it is the next chapter.
