title: 13  Images as Data: From Pixels to Tensors
text:
13.8 Check Your Understanding

The running example is considered for an upgrade to a camera mode of 1280 × 720 at 30 frames/s. Compute the per-frame memory as delivered (uint8, 3 channels) and after conversion to float32, and the raw delivered data rate. State one quantity in the perception pipeline that this upgrade quadruples besides the frame itself.







TipShow answer





Per frame: \(720 \times 1280 \times 3 = 2{,}764{,}800\) values — about 2.76 MB as uint8, and \(\times 4 = 11.1\) MB as float32. At 30 frames/s the camera delivers \(2{,}764{,}800 \times 30 \approx 83\) MB/s, three times the 640 × 480 mode’s ~27.6 MB/s. Beyond the frame itself, the activations — the feature-map tensors between network layers — scale with input pixel count, so if the model’s input resolution is raised to exploit the new camera, every layer’s activation memory and compute grow in proportion (quadrupling if both input sides are doubled). A sharper camera whose frames are downsampled back to the old model input, by contrast, buys nothing at all.




Every frame the camera produces is scrambled by the same fixed, invertible pixel permutation before being stored. Exactly as much information survives as before. Explain why a fully-connected network could in principle learn to classify the scrambled frames as well as the originals, why a convolutional network could not, and what this asymmetry reveals about what convolution assumes.







TipShow answer





A fully-connected layer assigns an independent weight to every input position and encodes no notion of neighbourhood; relabelling the positions (which is all a fixed permutation does) just relabels the weights, so its learning problem is unchanged. A convolutional network, by contrast, hard-codes the assumption that meaningful patterns are local — its kernels only ever see small contiguous windows — and the permutation destroys locality: pixels that were neighbours in the world are scattered across the grid, so no small window contains a coherent pattern to detect. The asymmetry shows that convolution is not a generic function approximator but a structural commitment: it wins on images precisely because, and only because, images really do concentrate their meaning in local spatial arrangements. Where that assumption fails, so does the architecture’s advantage.




Compute the parameter count of (a) a fully-connected layer from a flattened 480 × 640 × 3 image to 1,000 units, and (b) a convolutional layer of 32 kernels, each 3 × 3 spanning all 3 input channels, with one bias per kernel. State the output tensor shape of (b) (assume the spatial size is preserved) and what its channel axis now means.







TipShow answer






\(921{,}600 \times 1{,}000 = 9.216 \times 10^8\) weights (plus 1,000 biases) — about 3.7 GB in float32. (b) Each kernel holds \(3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27\) weights plus 1 bias, so 32 kernels hold \(32 \times 28 = 896\) parameters — six orders of magnitude fewer, independent of image size. The output shape is \(480 \times 640 \times 32\): one feature map per kernel, spatially aligned with the input. The channel axis no longer indexes colours but features — each of the 32 planes maps where one learned local pattern occurs in the frame.





For each requirement, name the vision task (classification, detection, or pose estimation) whose output structure is the minimum sufficient, and say what the output supplies that the next-cheaper task cannot. (a) Post-flight review flags which archived frames contain any goose, for a human to audit. (b) The deterrence behavior steers toward the nearest goose in view. (c) A researcher asks whether deterred geese take off away from the aircraft’s approach direction.







TipShow answer






Classification — a per-frame label and confidence is exactly the required output; location within the frame is unused because a human will look at flagged frames anyway. (b) Detection — steering needs a per-instance location; the box centre gives a bearing (and, with the depth channel, a range), and “nearest” requires distinguishing instances, which a whole-frame label cannot do. (c) Pose estimation — take-off direction relative to approach requires the animal’s orientation, geometry within the object; a bounding box records extent but not which end is the head, so detection cannot answer it. The pattern: each step up buys structure — location, then internal geometry — and should be bought only when the mission question actually consumes it.





Using the chapter’s numbers (90° across 640 columns, goose body 0.35 m), find the maximum range at which a goose still spans at least 15 pixels. The pipeline then letterboxes the 640-wide frame into a 320 × 320 model input. What does the effective per-pixel angle become, and what happens to your range?







TipShow answer





At \(\theta_{\text{pix}} = 2.45\) mrad, the goose spans \(0.35/(R \times 2.45\times10^{-3})\) pixels; setting that to 15 gives \(R = 0.35/(15 \times 2.45\times10^{-3}) \approx 9.5\) m. Letterboxing 640 columns into 320 halves the horizontal pixel count across the same 90° field, so the effective per-pixel angle doubles to 4.9 mrad — and the 15-pixel range halves to about 4.8 m. The camera did not change; a preprocessing line halved the detection range. This is why input resolution is negotiated against the mission’s required detection range, not defaulted — and why the running example’s search altitude and its model input size are coupled decisions.




The detection pipeline reports a goose with box centre \((u, v) = (400, 300)\) in the 640 × 480 colour frame. Part I claimed the depth camera “earns its mass” at this moment. State precisely what the detector’s output alone determines about the goose’s position, what single additional lookup the aligned depth stream provides, and why a monocular (colour-only) camera would instead have to maneuver to recover the same information.







TipShow answer





The box centre fixes only a direction: through the camera geometry, pixel \((400, 300)\) corresponds to a ray from the camera — a bearing — with the goose lying somewhere along it at unknown range; a nearby goose and a distant large object can produce the same pixels. The aligned depth stream turns position into one array lookup: the depth value at \((v, u) = (300, 400)\) is the range along that ray, and bearing plus range fixes the goose’s 3D position in the vehicle’s frame — the content of the target-position topic the mission logic consumes. A monocular camera measures no range, so it would have to triangulate: observe the goose from two or more separated viewpoints and intersect the bearings, which costs maneuvering time against a moving animal and couples perception accuracy to flight precision. The depth camera converts that flight problem into memory access.

13.9 Try It
Part 1 — hold the tensor in your hands. Take any outdoor photograph (a field with birds is ideal; failing that, any scene with a distinct subject) and open it in Python with OpenCV or PIL. Verify the claims of this chapter against it one by one: print the shape and dtype and identify \(H\), \(W\), and \(C\); index a pixel you can point to in the image and check the value ordering (is it RGB or BGR?); split and display the three channel planes separately and find a feature visible in one channel but weak in another. Then run the chapter’s thought experiment for real: build one fixed random permutation, apply it to the pixels, and display the result — then invert it and confirm the image returns. Finally, downsample the image by factors of 2, 4, 8, and 16 and find the factor at which you can no longer identify the subject; measure the subject’s size in pixels at that scale. You have just located your own pixels-on-target threshold — keep the number in mind when a detector’s is discussed.
Part 2 — convolve by hand, then size the mission. Implement 2D convolution yourself in a dozen lines of NumPy — loops are fine, clarity over speed — and apply the vertical-edge kernel from Figure 13.2 and its transpose to a grayscale version of your image. Display both feature maps and check they are bright where you predicted. Convince yourself of translation equivariance: shift the input a few pixels, re-convolve, and compare. Then put the chapter’s last relation to work for the running example: tabulate metres-per-pixel and pixels-on-goose (0.35 m body) at ranges of 5, 10, 20, and 40 m for the 640-column mode, and repeat for model input widths of 640, 416, and 320 after letterboxing. Pick the lowest model resolution that still keeps at least 15 pixels on a goose at your chosen search range, and write two sentences defending the choice — one about detection, one about what the saved computation buys, which the next chapter will make quantitative.

title: 14  TinyML: Deploying Neural Networks on Embedded Hardware
text:
14.1 Learning Objectives
The Images as Data chapter closed on a promise with two halves: how a network’s kernel weights are learned, and how a network of them is compressed until it runs, at frame rate, inside a 10-watt computer bolted to a 2.2-kilogram aircraft. This chapter takes the second half first, and the order is deliberate. Learning the weights — the data, the labels, the training loop — is the business of the next chapter, on building a detection pipeline; but what can usefully be trained is dictated by where the result must run, and an engineer who trains first and asks deployment questions afterward routinely produces a model that is accurate, elegant, and unflyable. The discipline that takes the deployment constraints as the starting point of model design has a name: TinyML — machine learning made useful under physical constraints of memory, compute, power, and time. Its founding observation is a mismatch. Mainstream deep learning grows by every axis at once — more parameters, more data, more accelerator hours — while an aircraft’s budget is fixed by battery chemistry and payload mass before any model is chosen. Someone must move, and it will not be the battery.
The constraints themselves are not new to this book. Part I priced the wireless link and found it could not carry the camera stream, which is why the pixels are understood onboard at all; the Anatomy of a Multirotor chapter allotted roughly 12 W to the entire avionics complement and showed that every added gram reappears as lost loiter time; and the previous chapter left a warning on the table: the tensors flowing between a network’s layers often cost more memory than the network’s own weights. What this chapter adds is the machinery that lives inside those constraints. It maps the three places a model can run and why the choice among them precedes every other choice; it itemizes the real memory bill of onboard inference — weights, activations, buffers — rather than the datasheet’s flattering summary; it develops quantization, the single most consequential compression technique, from its arithmetic up through a worked accounting of what it saves; it surveys pruning and distillation, the other members of the compression toolbox; and it follows a trained model down the deployment pipeline — convert, optimize, deploy — through the runtimes that execute it, ending with a comparison of the two toolkits that dominate the smallest tier of that pipeline, TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers and Edge Impulse.

14  TinyML: Deploying Neural Networks on Embedded Hardware

title: 14  TinyML: Deploying Neural Networks on Embedded Hardware
text:
14.2 Key Vocabulary

TinyML — the discipline of designing, compressing, and deploying machine-learning models to run under tight physical constraints — memory in kilobytes to megabytes, power in milliwatts to watts — on hardware at or near the sensor that produces the data.
Quantization — replacing a model’s high-precision numbers (typically 32-bit floats) with low-precision ones (typically 8-bit integers) related by a stored scale factor, cutting memory, memory bandwidth, and usually latency at a small cost in accuracy.
Post-training quantization (PTQ) — quantizing an already-trained float model by measuring the ranges of its weights and activations on a small calibration dataset and choosing scale factors from them; no retraining required.
Quantization-aware training (QAT) — training (or fine-tuning) a model with simulated quantization in the loop, so the weights settle into values that survive rounding; costlier than PTQ but recovers most of its accuracy loss.
Pruning — removing weights, channels, or whole neurons that contribute little to a network’s output; shrinks the parameter count, but yields speed only when the runtime and hardware can exploit the resulting sparsity or reduced structure.
Knowledge distillation — training a small student model to reproduce the outputs of a large teacher model, transferring capability into a deployable size; the teacher stays on the workstation, the student flies.
Model footprint — the storage a deployed model occupies (its weights plus metadata), as distinct from the RAM its execution consumes; the number quoted on a model card, and never the whole bill.
Activation memory — the RAM occupied at inference time by the intermediate tensors flowing between layers; it scales with input resolution and often exceeds the weights, especially on memory-poor devices.
Inference latency — the wall-clock time from presenting an input tensor to receiving the model’s output, the quantity a control loop actually waits on; measured, never assumed, and the central subject of the Real-Time Inference on the Edge chapter.
TensorFlow Lite (TFLite) — the deployment-oriented branch of the TensorFlow ecosystem: a converter that emits a compact model file and a lean runtime that executes it on phones and single-board computers; its sibling TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers (TFLM) is a C++ library that runs the same models on bare-metal microcontrollers with no operating system and no dynamic memory allocation.
Edge Impulse — a hosted end-to-end platform for embedded ML that carries a project from data acquisition through signal processing, training, and testing to an exported, compiled C++ library for a target microcontroller.
Tensor arena — in TFLM, the single statically allocated block of RAM from which all of a model’s activations and scratch buffers are carved at runtime; the developer sizes it by hand, and it is the practical measure of a model’s RAM appetite on an MCU.

title: 14  TinyML: Deploying Neural Networks on Embedded Hardware
text:
14.3 The Placement Problem
Every machine-learning system that touches a robot answers one question before any question of architecture: where does the model run? The candidate answers form a hierarchy of three tiers, separated by orders of magnitude in every resource that matters, and Figure 14.1 lays them side by side.






Figure 14.1: The three tiers a model can run on — cloud GPU, companion computer, microcontroller — separated by orders of magnitude in memory and power, with the wireless link severed from the decision path at the first step onboard.



At the top sits the cloud tier — server GPUs with tens of gigabytes of memory, drawing hundreds of watts, reachable from the aircraft only through a wireless link. Part I already disqualified that link as a pipe for imagery on bandwidth grounds; the placement argument adds two counts to the indictment. The first is latency and its variance: a round trip over a real wireless link takes tens to hundreds of milliseconds when it works, and an unbounded time when it degrades — and a deterrence maneuver steering toward a moving animal consumes a fresh target position every frame. A decision loop is only as fast as its slowest hop, and a hop through a radio makes the loop’s worst case the radio’s worst case. The second is power: transmitting data costs battery just as computing does, and streaming sensor data to remote compute spends the energy budget twice — once to send the question, once to fly while waiting for the answer. The cloud tier is not thereby useless; it is where everything that can wait belongs — training and retraining, heavy post-flight analysis, mapping, labeling, the long-term learning loop. The design rule the hierarchy enforces is exactly that split: keep urgent sensing local; offload only what can wait.
The middle tier is the companion computer, and it is where this book has been heading since Part I bolted one to the airframe. A Jetson-class single-board computer offers a few gigabytes of RAM shared between CPU and GPU, roughly a hundred GPU cores, and a power appetite near 10 W — a budget the Companion Computers chapter showed already strains the ~12 W avionics allowance. It runs a full Linux stack, ROS 2 nodes, and — decisively — GPU-shaped inference at frame rate, with no radio between the camera and the decision. This is the tier the running example’s detector occupies, and the tier whose constraints shape most of this chapter.
The bottom tier is the microcontroller (MCU) — an STM32- or Arduino-class chip clocked in megahertz, holding SRAM measured in kilobytes, drawing milliwatts. No deep vision model fits here, and none should be forced to; the tier’s genius is different. An MCU can afford to be always on: a 1-D convolutional classifier watching an accelerometer window for anomalous vibration, or an audio trigger listening for a signature, can run continuously for the cost of a status LED and wake heavier machinery only when something warrants it. The source constraint that defines this tier is worth internalizing as a single figure of merit: a MobileNet-class vision model occupies about 16.9 MB as trained, while a realistic MCU memory budget is 256 KB — a factor of sixty-six before a single activation or buffer is counted. Deployment at this tier is not a matter of trimming a model; it is a matter of designing a different, far smaller one, which is why the toolkits examined at this chapter’s end exist.
Two consequences of the hierarchy organize everything that follows. First, training and inference split across tiers. Training a network — thousands of gradient-descent passes over a dataset — is exactly the bursty, deadline-free, compute-hungry workload the cloud tier exists for, and it happens once; inference happens on every frame, forever, under a deadline, and must live onboard. The pipeline connecting the two tiers — train on a workstation, convert, optimize, deploy, infer — is this chapter’s final subject. Second, placement precedes architecture. The question “what is the smallest model and sensor configuration that is useful enough for the mission?” has a different answer on each tier, so an engineer who has not chosen the tier cannot meaningfully choose the model. The tier fixes the budget; the budget is mostly memory and time; and the memory budget deserves to be itemized before anything is compressed to fit it.

title: 14  TinyML: Deploying Neural Networks on Embedded Hardware
section: 14.4 The Memory Bill: Weights, Activations, Buffers
text:
14.4 The Memory Bill: Weights, Activations, Buffers
Ask what a model costs to run and the usual answer is its parameter count — “a 3.2-million-parameter detector” — converted at four bytes per float32 weight to a model footprint of 12.8 MB. That number is real, but treating it as the memory requirement is the embedded-ML equivalent of budgeting a vehicle by its sticker price. What the device must actually hold at the moment of inference is closer to
\[
\text{RAM peak} \approx \text{activations} + \text{input buffers} + \text{runtime workspace} + \text{application state},
\]
with the weights alongside — and on most platforms the largest term is not the weights. It is the activations: the intermediate tensors flowing between layers, which the Images as Data chapter flagged as the hidden cost of input resolution and which can now be made precise. Consider the first convolutional layer of a detector taking a 640 × 640 × 3 input: a bank of 32 kernels at stride 2 produces a 320 × 320 × 32 feature map. The layer’s weights are trivial — \(3 \times 3 \times 3 \times 32 = 864\) of them, under 4 KB as float32. Its output is not:
\[
\begin{aligned}
320 \times 320 \times 32 &= 3{,}276{,}800\ \text{values} \\
\text{as float32:}\quad 3{,}276{,}800 \times 4\ \text{B} &\approx 13.1\ \text{MB}.
\end{aligned}
\]
One layer, near the top of the network, transiently holds more than three thousand times its own weight in activations — and at least two such tensors are alive at any moment, since a layer’s input must persist while its output is written. Activation memory decays as the network’s spatial dimensions shrink deeper in, so the peak usually sits in these wide early layers, and the peak is what must fit. To the weights and activations add the buffers an application owns because it is a robot and not a benchmark: the camera frames themselves (at the 640 × 480 mode of the Images as Data chapter, 921,600 bytes each, and a capture pipeline holds more than one), the runtime’s scratch workspace, and the state of the application around the model. Figure 14.2 draws the full bill for an illustrative small detector, and its shape explains most of embedded-ML practice.






Figure 14.2: The real RAM bill of onboard inference: for a representative small detector the weights are the smallest major line item, activations dominate and scale with input resolution, and the two levers — precision and pixels — multiply to shrink the bill roughly fivefold.



Three lessons fall out of the figure. First, the two big levers multiply: quantizing values from float32 to int8 divides both weights and activations by four, and halving the model’s input side divides activations (and compute) by four again — together taking the illustrative peak from ~58 MB to ~10 MB. The resolution lever is the same one the Images as Data chapter priced from the other side: every halving also halves the pixels on a distant goose, so the lever is pulled against the mission’s detection range, not freely. Second, some terms do not move: camera frames arrive as uint8 and cannot be quantized further, so a bill dominated by buffers responds to pipeline design (fewer copies, smaller queues, streaming windows instead of stored histories) rather than model compression. Third, the tiers reprice the bill. On a 4 GB Jetson sharing memory between CPU, GPU, and the whole operating system, a 58 MB peak is affordable and the bill’s real bite is bandwidth — every byte of weights and activations must move through memory for every frame, and moving bytes costs time and energy. On a 256 KB MCU the same accounting is existential: the entire stacked bar must fit in SRAM, which is why the canonical MCU vision demonstration is a 96 × 96 grayscale classifier occupying a few hundred kilobytes, and why the slide from megabytes to kilobytes cannot be walked by compression alone. It begins, on every tier, with the same first step: giving up 24 of the 32 bits every number is carrying.

title: 14  TinyML: Deploying Neural Networks on Embedded Hardware
text:
14.5 Quantization: Trading Precision for Feasibility
A trained network’s weights are float32 values: 32 bits encoding a sign, an exponent, and 23 bits of mantissa, able to distinguish on the order of \(10^{38}\) magnitudes with seven decimal digits of precision. Training genuinely uses that dynamic range — gradient updates are tiny nudges accumulated over thousands of steps, and they vanish if the representation cannot resolve them. Inference does not. A finished network is a fixed function being evaluated, not adjusted; its decisions rest on comparisons — which class score is largest, whether a confidence clears a threshold — and comparisons survive small perturbations of every number involved. Empirically, the weights of a trained layer huddle in a narrow, roughly bell-shaped band (a range like \([-0.4, +0.4]\) is typical), occupying a sliver of float32’s range. Thirty-two bits are being spent to store values that a much coarser code could carry. Quantization is that coarser code.
The standard scheme maps each float value \(r\) to an 8-bit integer \(q\) through an affine relation:
\[
r \approx S \,(q - Z),
\]
where the scale \(S\) is a float32 constant and the zero point \(Z\) is the integer to which the real value 0.0 maps. For weights, which are centered near zero, the symmetric special case \(Z = 0\) suffices, and the scheme collapses to \(r \approx S q\): choose \(S\) so that the largest-magnitude weight lands on the integer extreme, and every weight becomes \(q = \operatorname{round}(r/S)\), an integer in \([-128, 127]\). Figure 14.3 traces the mapping for a concrete layer — the measured weight range sets \(S\), one worked weight is quantized and dequantized, and the rounding error is bounded — and then presents the bill.






Figure 14.3: int8 quantization maps a layer’s trained weight distribution onto 256 integer levels through one stored scale factor; for a 3 × 3 convolution from 128 to 256 channels, the 1.18 MB of float32 weights become 0.29 MB of integers plus a kilobyte of scales.



The accounting deserves to be walked once by hand, because it is the worked answer to a question the compression literature usually leaves qualitative. Take a mid-network detection layer: a 3 × 3 convolution from 128 input channels to 256 output channels. Its weight count and float32 cost are
\[
\begin{aligned}
3 \times 3 \times 128 \times 256 &= 294{,}912\ \text{weights} \\
\text{as float32:}\quad 294{,}912 \times 4\ \text{B} &= 1{,}179{,}648\ \text{B} \approx 1.18\ \text{MB}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Quantized, each weight is one byte — 294,912 bytes, about 0.29 MB — plus the metadata that makes the integers meaningful: one scale per output channel (per-channel scaling tracks the fact that different kernels settle into different ranges), \(256 \times 4\ \text{B} \approx 1\) KB. The overhead is a rounding error on the total; the saving is a clean factor of four, and it compounds across the model: the 16.9 MB MobileNet of the previous section is about 4.2 million float32 weights at four bytes each, and the same network quantized is about 4.2 MB. What was spent to earn it is bounded and small: each weight moved by at most \(S/2 \approx 0.0017\) — noise at the scale of the weights themselves — and in practice a well-calibrated int8 model gives up on the order of a percentage point of accuracy, often less. There is a satisfying symmetry in where this lands: the camera’s samples arrived as 8-bit integers, 256 levels, in the first place. The float32 the pipeline inflated them into was a convenience of training, not a property of the information; quantization returns the model to the precision regime its input never left.
Memory is only the first dividend. The second, less obvious and often larger, is latency and energy. The number of multiply-accumulate operations is unchanged by quantization, so a speedup cannot come from doing less arithmetic — it comes from feeding the arithmetic. Inference on an embedded processor is usually memory-bound: the cost of an operation is dominated by moving its operands from DRAM through the caches, not by the multiply itself (fetching a value from off-chip memory costs on the order of a hundred times the energy of multiplying it). Quartering every operand quarters that traffic, quadruples the number of weights that fit in cache, and — because a processor’s vector unit is a fixed number of bits wide — lets each instruction process four times as many int8 values as float32 ones. Embedded CPUs and the DSP extensions of Cortex-class MCUs are explicitly designed around this, which is why int8 inference commonly runs two to four times faster than float32 on the same silicon, at correspondingly lower energy per frame. For an aircraft whose compute is billed in watts against loiter time, quantization is not only how the model fits; it is how each inference costs less flight.
What quantization asks in return is care with ranges, and this is where the two practical routes diverge. Weights are easy — they are known, fixed numbers, and their ranges can simply be read off. Activations are not: their ranges depend on what data flows through the network, so they must be estimated by running the trained float model over a small calibration dataset — a few hundred representative inputs — and recording the ranges each layer produces. That is post-training quantization: measure, choose scales, round, done, with no retraining. Its failure mode is a calibration set that misrepresents flight data — ranges set too narrow clip real activations at the integer extremes, ranges set too wide squander the 256 levels on values that never occur — which is one more reason the dataset work of the next chapter is deployment work, not preamble. When PTQ’s accuracy loss is too large — common for small models, which have less redundancy to absorb rounding — quantization-aware training closes the gap: the model is fine-tuned with simulated rounding inside the training loop, so the weights themselves learn to sit where quantization will not hurt them. The practical doctrine is to try the cheap route first and escalate: PTQ costs minutes, QAT costs a training run, and the running example’s detector — a small model, but not a tiny one — is a typical PTQ success.






NoteFor More



int8 is a resting point, not a floor. Mixed-precision schemes keep sensitive layers (often the first and last) at higher precision while quantizing the rest harder; 4-bit and even 1-bit (binary) networks push the same logic further at growing accuracy cost; and float16, halving memory with almost no accuracy risk, is the preferred cheap step on GPUs — including Jetson-class hardware — whose tensor units execute it natively. The engineering habit transfers unchanged: choose the coarsest representation the task’s accuracy floor tolerates, and measure rather than assume where that floor is.

title: 14  TinyML: Deploying Neural Networks on Embedded Hardware
section: 14.6 The Rest of the Toolbox: Pruning, Distillation, and System-Level Tricks
text:
14.6 The Rest of the Toolbox: Pruning, Distillation, and System-Level Tricks
Quantization shrinks every number; the remaining compression techniques shrink the count of numbers, and each carries a caveat that matters in practice.
Pruning exploits the redundancy of trained networks: many weights end up near zero and contribute almost nothing, and removing them — weight by weight, or channel by channel, typically by magnitude, with a brief fine-tune afterward to let the survivors compensate — can cut a model’s parameter count substantially at modest accuracy cost. The caveat is the gap between a smaller file and a faster model. Unstructured pruning turns dense weight matrices into sparse ones, and sparse arithmetic is only faster on hardware and runtimes built to skip zeros — which most embedded stacks are not; a dense matrix with zeros scattered through it multiplies in exactly the time the full matrix did. Structured pruning — removing whole channels or filters — keeps the arithmetic dense and delivers real speedups everywhere, at the price of coarser, more accuracy-costly cuts. The drone framing from the source material is the right discipline: prune until the model still catches the mission-critical cases, and validate that boundary on the mission’s own hard examples, not on average benchmarks.
Knowledge distillation attacks the problem from above. A large teacher model — too big to fly, living happily on the cloud tier — is trained first; a small student, sized for the aircraft, is then trained to match the teacher’s outputs rather than (or in addition to) the raw labels. The teacher’s full output distribution carries more information than a hard label — how confidently it rates each class, which alternatives it considers plausible — and students trained on it reliably outperform identical architectures trained on labels alone. For a drone program the technique has a clean division of labor: the teacher absorbs the expensive learning offline, the student carries a distilled copy of it onboard, and the two tiers of the placement hierarchy each hold the model shaped for them.
The toolbox’s remaining members are system-level rather than model-level, and Part III has already met most of them. Input reduction is the resolution lever of the previous section, plus region-of-interest cropping — the Images as Data chapter’s trick of spending the input budget where the target was last seen. Cascades put a cheap model in front of an expensive one: an MCU-tier trigger or a small classifier runs always-on, and the heavyweight detector runs only when summoned — the architecture of the compute hierarchy expressed inside a single perception pipeline. Offloading completes the set by sending summaries — detections, thumbnails, hard cases — rather than raw data to the ground, keeping the safety path local while still feeding the cloud tier’s retraining loop. None of these is exclusive; a deployed system typically stacks quantization and an efficient architecture and a reduced input and a cascade, because the tiers’ budgets are not met by any single factor of four.

title: 14  TinyML: Deploying Neural Networks on Embedded Hardware
section: 14.7 From Trained Model to Flying Model
text:
14.7 From Trained Model to Flying Model
The techniques above act on a model; a deployment moves one. The path from a training run to a decision on the aircraft is a pipeline with named stages, and every embedded-ML project walks it:
\[
\text{dataset} \rightarrow \text{train} \rightarrow \text{convert} \rightarrow \text{optimize} \rightarrow \text{deploy} \rightarrow \text{infer}.
\]
Training happens on the cloud tier, in a full framework — PyTorch or TensorFlow — whose comforts (autograd, dynamic graphs, a Python interpreter) exist for experimentation and are dead weight in flight. Conversion strips that weight: the trained network is exported to a compact, execution-oriented format — a .tflite flatbuffer, or the framework-neutral ONNX interchange format — that records just the graph of operations and the weights. Optimization is where this chapter’s techniques are applied to the converted artifact: quantization with a calibration set, pruning, operator fusion. Deployment hands the optimized artifact to a runtime on the target — and the runtime is chosen by the tier. On a Jetson, the natural road runs through TensorRT, the inference engine bundled with the JetPack image the Companion Computers chapter flashed: it ingests an ONNX or TFLite model, fuses and re-plans its layers for the specific GPU on the board, selects int8 or float16 kernels, and emits an engine tuned to the silicon. On a Raspberry Pi–class CPU, TFLite’s own interpreter with its optimized ARM kernels is the standard path. On an MCU, the runtime must fit in kilobytes, which is the niche the next section’s toolkits occupy.
Two doctrines govern the walk. The first is portability before efficiency: prototype in the portable formats with clear interfaces, measure on the real target, and reach for hardware-specific machinery only where profiling shows it pays — prototype, measure, optimize, then verify safety behavior on hard cases. Premature hand-optimization welds a project to one board and one vendor before the design has settled. The second is that the model is a component, not the system. On the aircraft, the ML runtime sits in a stack — application logic above it, ROS 2 middleware and MAVLink beside it, Linux or an RTOS below — and competes with flight control, telemetry, and logging for the same cores, memory bandwidth, and watts. A model that benchmarks beautifully in isolation can still fail in integration: a blocking call in the wrong thread drops camera frames; an unthrottled logger steals the bus; a memory spike evicts the very buffers the capture pipeline needs. The perception system the running example is building is, in the end, software engineering with a model inside it — and the measurement discipline that proves the assembled stack meets its deadline is the subject of the Real-Time Inference on the Edge chapter.

section: 14.8 Two Toolkits for the Smallest Tier
text:
14.8 Two Toolkits for the Smallest Tier
On the companion tier, deployment tooling is a menu of interchangeable parts. On the MCU tier — kilobytes of SRAM, no operating system, no allocator — the tooling is the project, and two names dominate it. They are best understood not as competitors on a feature checklist but as two answers to the question of who owns the pipeline, and Figure 14.4 walks both roads stage by stage.






Figure 14.4: The two dominant MCU deployment toolkits walked stage by stage: with TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers the developer owns every step from data collection to on-target profiling; with Edge Impulse the hosted platform owns the middle of the pipeline and hands back a compiled C++ library for integration.



TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers is a library — an open-source C++ inference engine, a few tens of kilobytes compiled, designed for bare metal. It assumes nothing: no operating system, no filesystem, no dynamic allocation. The model arrives as a byte array compiled into the firmware; the developer instantiates an interpreter, registers only the operators the model actually uses (unused kernels never cost flash), and hands it a tensor arena — one statically allocated block, sized by hand through trial and profiling, from which every activation and scratch buffer is carved. Everything upstream of that integration — collecting data, training, converting, calibrating the quantization — is the developer’s own pipeline, in ordinary TensorFlow. The contract is maximal control and maximal responsibility: any target with a C++ toolchain, no vendor in the loop, and every one of the six pipeline stages on the team’s shoulders.
Edge Impulse is a platform — a hosted service in which the pipeline itself is the product. Data is acquired into a browser studio (uploaded, or streamed from a phone or a supported development board); a signal-processing block and a model are composed visually, with a Keras “expert mode” underneath for teams that outgrow the defaults; training runs on the platform’s cloud with quantization handled as a default; and the export is a compiled C++ library for the chosen target, with per-target latency and RAM estimates attached. Two details make it more than a convenience wrapper. Its DSP-block-first design reflects real MCU practice, where a feature extractor (a spectrogram, a filter bank) in front of a tiny network routinely beats a bigger network on raw samples. And its EON compiler emits the network as generated source code rather than a flatbuffer walked by an interpreter, saving meaningful RAM and flash on chips where both are counted in kilobytes. The contract is the mirror image of TFLM’s: a working prototype in days and guided resource estimates, in exchange for a pipeline that lives on someone else’s servers, is easiest on supported hardware, and yields deep customization reluctantly.
The choice between them is an engineering-situation question, not a quality ranking — the more so because the roads share pavement: Edge Impulse builds on TensorFlow and the TFLite model format, and both roads end in int8 C++ on the same silicon. A team that must own, reproduce, and audit every stage — a research group whose experiment is the pipeline, a product team with compliance obligations, a project targeting an unsupported chip — takes the library. A team whose scarce resource is embedded-ML engineering time — a field-robotics group that needs a vibration trigger working this month, a classroom, a prototype racing a funding deadline — takes the platform, and graduates to the library if and when its needs outgrow the defaults. For the running example, this entire comparison lives at the MCU tier — the always-on trigger of a cascade, should the system grow one. The goose detector itself, resident on the Jetson, takes the third road already described: trained in PyTorch, exported, quantized, and handed to TensorRT, with no MCU ceiling in sight.
That closes the frame this chapter opened. The placement hierarchy assigns the detector to the companion tier; the memory bill says what fitting there means; quantization and its siblings are how the fit is achieved; and the pipeline and its toolkits are how the result travels from a training run to a process consuming camera tensors inside the running example’s Detector node. What the frame still lacks is its center: the trained model itself — the dataset of geese and not-geese, the labeled boxes, the training runs and their failure modes. That is the next chapter, and it is where Part III stops preparing and starts building.

title: 14  TinyML: Deploying Neural Networks on Embedded Hardware
text:
14.9 Check Your Understanding

A detection head ends in a 1 × 1 convolution from 512 input channels to 21 output channels. Compute its weight count and its memory at float32 and at int8 (ignore biases). Per-channel quantization adds one float32 scale per output channel: compute the metadata overhead as a percentage of the int8 weight memory, and state why the overhead was negligible for the chapter’s 128-to-256-channel example but is less so here.







TipShow answer





Weights: \(1 \times 1 \times 512 \times 21 = 10{,}752\). At float32: \(10{,}752 \times 4 = 43{,}008\) B ≈ 43 KB; at int8: 10,752 B ≈ 10.8 KB — the factor of four as always. Metadata: 21 scales × 4 B = 84 B, about 0.8 % of the int8 weights. The chapter’s example carried 256 scales against 294,912 int8 weights (≈ 0.35 %). The general rule: per-channel overhead is (4 B × output channels) against (1 B × weights per channel × channels), so it grows as layers get thinner — fewer weights per output channel. For very small layers the metadata fraction rises, which is one reason tiny models benefit proportionally less from quantization than their headline parameter counts suggest.




Quantization does not reduce the number of multiply-accumulate operations a model performs, yet int8 inference commonly runs two to four times faster than float32 on the same embedded CPU. Give the two main mechanisms, and explain why the same reasoning predicts that quantization speeds up a memory-bound workload more than a compute-bound one.







TipShow answer





First, memory traffic: embedded inference is usually limited by moving weights and activations through DRAM and cache, not by arithmetic; int8 quarters every operand, so the memory system delivers the same layer in a quarter of the bytes, and four times as much of the model stays cache-resident. Second, vector width: a SIMD unit is a fixed number of bits wide, so each instruction processes 4× as many int8 values as float32 values. Both mechanisms accelerate the supply and throughput of operands, not the operation count — so a workload already bottlenecked on memory gains nearly the full factor, while a compute-bound workload (small model, fast memory) gains only what wider integer SIMD provides. This is also why the energy saving tracks the speedup: the dominant energy cost is data movement, and quantization is a data-movement optimization.




Assign each task to a tier of the compute hierarchy — cloud, companion computer, or MCU — and justify with the chapter’s criteria (latency, bandwidth, power, link reliability, privacy): (a) deciding, within one frame time, whether the deterrence target’s position has updated; (b) retraining the detector on last month’s hard cases; (c) monitoring motor vibration continuously for bearing wear, including while the main computer is under full perception load.







TipShow answer






Companion computer: the decision is consumed at frame rate by the control loop, so it cannot tolerate a radio’s variable latency or failure modes — the urgent path stays local, and only this tier has the GPU to run the detector. (b) Cloud: retraining is compute-hungry, deadline-free, and needs the accumulated dataset — exactly the “can wait” workload; only summaries and hard cases need to cross the link, and in batch. (c) MCU: an always-on 1-D classifier on accelerometer windows costs milliwatts and kilobytes, runs regardless of what the companion computer is doing (a key point — the Jetson under full perception load is exactly when a competing monitor would be starved), and needs only to raise a flag when something is anomalous. The pattern is the chapter’s cascade: cheap and always-on at the bottom, capable and framewise in the middle, heavy and offline at the top.





Using the chapter’s accounting, estimate the RAM peak for the running example’s detector deployed as int8 with a 320 × 320 model input: weights 3.2 MB, peak activations 2.3 MB, a capture pipeline holding two 640 × 480 × 3 uint8 camera frames, and 1 MB of runtime workspace. Then explain why a further halving of the model input to 160 × 160 shrinks one term by four but two of the terms not at all — and which mission quantity, from the Images as Data chapter, the halving would damage.







TipShow answer





Frames: \(2 \times 921{,}600 \approx 1.84\) MB. Peak ≈ \(3.2 + 2.3 + 1.84 + 1.0 \approx 8.3\) MB. Halving the input side to 160 × 160 divides activation memory (and per-frame compute) by four — activations scale with the model’s input pixel count — but the weights are fixed by the architecture, and the camera buffers are fixed by the sensor’s resolution, which does not change when the model’s input does. The damaged quantity is pixels on target: the Images as Data chapter showed the pixels a goose subtends scale with the model-input resolution the detector actually sees, so halving the input halves pixels-on-goose and with it the usable detection range — the resolution lever is always pulled against the mission’s geometry.




Post-training quantization calibrates a layer’s activation scale from representative inputs. Suppose the calibration set for the goose detector was collected indoors, and a layer’s activations there span \([0, 6]\), so \(S\) is chosen as \(6/255 \approx 0.024\) — but in bright field conditions the same layer’s activations reach 24. What happens numerically to the flight-time activations, why does the damage not show up on the calibration data, and what does this imply about who should assemble the calibration set?







TipShow answer





Every activation above 6 quantizes to \(q = 255\) and is clipped: the top three-quarters of the layer’s real dynamic range collapses onto a single level, so exactly the strong responses — the layer’s most confident feature detections — become indistinguishable from one another, and the layers downstream inherit saturated, information-poor inputs. On the calibration data the model is bit-for-bit healthy, because no calibration input ever exceeds the measured range; the failure is invisible until deployment conditions diverge from calibration conditions. The implication: the calibration set is mission data, not convenience data — it must span the lighting, altitude, and scene conditions of flight, which makes calibration a dataset-engineering task belonging to the same discipline (and the same chapter, the next one) as the training set itself.




A university field-robotics group wants an acoustic trigger on a drone that wakes the main perception stack when it hears geese; one member has embedded experience, none has ML-pipeline experience, and the demonstration is in six weeks on a supported development board. A second group is building a certifiable agricultural product on a custom STM32 board and must reproduce every build from version-controlled sources. Recommend a toolkit for each, and state why neither recommendation applies to the goose detector itself.







TipShow answer





First group: Edge Impulse — the constraint is embedded-ML engineering time, the board is supported, and the platform’s owned pipeline (acquisition, DSP block, training, compiled C++ export with resource estimates) converts six weeks into a plausible schedule; the DSP-first design suits an acoustic trigger particularly well. Second group: TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers — a custom board is outside any platform’s supported list, and certifiability demands that every pipeline stage (data, training, conversion, calibration, integration) be owned, version-controlled, and reproducible in-house, which is precisely the library’s contract. Neither applies to the goose detector because it runs on the companion tier, not an MCU: a Jetson-class board with gigabytes of RAM takes the TFLite/ONNX-to-TensorRT road, and the MCU toolkits’ defining constraints — kilobyte arenas, no OS, interpreter-free execution — are constraints it does not have.

14.10 Try It
Part 1 — quantize a real model and audit the damage. In a notebook, take any small trained vision model (a Keras MobileNet variant, or the small CNN you built for the previous chapter’s exercises) and walk it through post-training quantization with the TFLite converter: export it once as float32 and once as full-int8 with a calibration generator that yields a few hundred representative inputs. Compare the two files’ sizes on disk against this chapter’s factor-of-four prediction (and explain any shortfall — which parts of a .tflite file are not weights?). Then run both models over a held-out set and measure the damage directly: the maximum absolute difference in output scores, and the number of inputs on which the predicted class actually changes. Finally, sabotage the calibration deliberately — calibrate on a single image, or on blank frames — re-export, and watch the failure mode of Check question 5 appear in your own accuracy numbers.
Part 2 — itemize a memory bill. Using a model-summary tool (torchinfo in PyTorch, model.summary() in Keras), tabulate for the same model, layer by layer: parameter count, parameter bytes at float32 and int8, and output-activation bytes at float32 for a 640 × 640 input. Identify where the activation peak sits, and compare peak activations to total weights — then repeat at a 320 × 320 input and confirm the activations quarter while the weights do not move. Add realistic buffer terms (two camera frames at your sensor’s resolution, 1 MB of workspace) and produce your own version of this chapter’s memory-bill chart. Close with two sentences: one stating which single change most reduces your model’s RAM peak, and one stating what that change costs the mission, in the currency of the Images as Data chapter’s pixels-on-target arithmetic.

title: 15  Building a Detection Pipeline: Data, Labeling, and Training
text:
15.1 Learning Objectives
The TinyML chapter left its own frame deliberately unfinished. It laid out the deployment pipeline — dataset → train → convert → optimize → deploy → infer — then spent all of its pages on the second half, on the grounds that what can usefully be trained is dictated by where the result must run. The constraints are now settled: the running example’s detector lives on the companion tier, quantized to int8, its input resolution negotiated against the pixels-on-target arithmetic of the Images as Data chapter. What is still missing is the center of the frame — the trained model itself, which means the dataset of geese and not-geese, the labeled boxes, the training run, and the numbers that say whether any of it worked. This chapter builds that center, and it is where Part III stops preparing and starts building.
One reorientation is needed at the outset, because it decides where the effort goes. Every previous quantitative chapter of this book has been about computation: control laws, memory bills, quantization arithmetic. A detection pipeline is the first piece of the system whose behavior is fixed not by code but by data — the model’s kernels take whatever values the dataset teaches them, and no amount of downstream engineering recovers what the dataset failed to contain or, worse, mislabeled. The practical consequence is an inversion of where a newcomer expects the time to go. Training a small detector is minutes of rented GPU time and five lines of Python; collecting and labeling the images it learns from is days of unglamorous work, and it is the bottleneck of every real detection project. The chapter therefore walks the pipeline in the order the work actually happens — collect, label, split, train — and then dwells, longer than practical guides usually do, on the demand such guides state in three words and leave undefined: show evaluation metrics. Precision, recall, and mAP are the vocabulary in which a detector’s fitness for a mission is argued, and this chapter works all three from raw counts up.

title: 15  Building a Detection Pipeline: Data, Labeling, and Training
text:
15.2 Key Vocabulary

Ground-truth annotation — the labeled fact a training example carries: for detection, a hand-drawn bounding box plus a class identity for every object of interest in the image, treated by training and evaluation alike as the truth against which the model is measured.
YOLO format — the plain-text label convention used by the YOLO family: one .txt file per image, one line per object, each line a class index followed by the box’s center coordinates, width, and height, all normalized to the range \([0,1]\) by dividing by the image’s dimensions.
Train/validation split — the division of a dataset into images the optimizer learns from and images reserved for measurement only; the validation side exists to estimate performance on data the model has never seen, and is honest only if nothing resembling it leaked into training.
Data augmentation — synthetically varying training images (flips, crops, color shifts, mosaics) each time they are shown to the model, so a small dataset teaches invariances — lighting, viewpoint, scale — that it is too small to demonstrate with real examples.
Transfer learning — initializing a model from weights pretrained on a large general dataset and fine-tuning on a small task-specific one, so the early layers’ general visual features (edges, textures, shapes) are inherited rather than relearned from scratch.
IoU (Intersection over Union) — the overlap score between two boxes: the area of their intersection divided by the area of their union, ranging from 0 (disjoint) to 1 (identical); a predicted box matches a ground-truth box when their IoU clears a chosen threshold, conventionally 0.5.
Precision — of all the detections the model reported, the fraction that were real: \(\text{TP}/(\text{TP}+\text{FP})\); low precision means false alarms.
Recall — of all the objects actually present, the fraction the model found: \(\text{TP}/(\text{TP}+\text{FN})\); low recall means misses.
mAP (mean Average Precision) — the standard single-number summary of a detector: for each class, the area under the precision–recall curve swept out by varying the confidence threshold (that class’s AP), averaged over all classes; reported at a fixed IoU threshold (mAP@0.5) or averaged over a range (mAP@0.5:0.95).
Confidence threshold — the score cutoff below which a detection is discarded at inference time; an operating-point choice that trades precision against recall and belongs to the system designer, not the model.

title: 15  Building a Detection Pipeline: Data, Labeling, and Training
text:
15.3 The Shape of the Work
Figure 15.1 lays the whole pipeline out, with the two stages the TinyML chapter already built shown in outline at the far end. Reading it left to right gives the order of operations; reading where its emphasis falls gives the order of importance. The amber stages — labeling, training, evaluation — are this chapter’s center of mass, and the red return arrow along the bottom is its most important single edge: a deployed detector’s mistakes are not merely failures to be lamented but a precise, prioritized specification of what data to collect next. A detection pipeline is not a line; it is a loop that happens to be drawn as one.






Figure 15.1: The detection pipeline from raw footage to a flying detector: this chapter builds collection, labeling, splitting, training, and evaluation; conversion, optimization, and deployment were the previous chapter’s subject; and flight-time mistakes feed the next round of data collection.



The tier assignments come straight from the placement argument of the TinyML chapter and need no re-litigating: everything up to and including evaluation is bursty, deadline-free, compute-hungry work that belongs on a workstation or the cloud tier, and only the final inference stage runs on the aircraft. What the figure adds is a budget for attention. The stages that look like machine-learning work — picking an architecture, running the optimizer — are the most automated and least decisive parts of the pipeline. The stages that look like clerical work — choosing which frames to keep, drawing boxes tightly, deciding what counts as which class — are where the detector’s ceiling is set. The sections that follow take the stages in order, spending effort in proportion to that budget.

title: 15  Building a Detection Pipeline: Data, Labeling, and Training
text:
15.4 Collecting the Data
The raw material of a detection dataset is footage: recorded flight video from the platform’s own camera is best, because it samples the exact viewpoint, altitude, optics, and scene statistics the deployed model will face, but phone or action-camera footage of the same subjects, and public video of comparable scenes, all serve — particularly early, when the goal is a first working model rather than a final one. What matters far more than the source is the spread. A detector generalizes only across variation it has seen: a dataset collected in one session, at one altitude, under one sky, produces a model superbly calibrated to that hour and brittle everywhere else. The collection checklist is therefore written in the mission’s terms — multiple lighting conditions, multiple altitudes and therefore target scales (the pixels-on-target arithmetic of the Images as Data chapter says a goose at 20 m is a 7-pixel object in the 640-column mode, so if the mission will fly at 20 m the dataset must contain 7-pixel geese, not just the flattering close-ups), multiple backgrounds, and — easy to forget — frames containing no targets at all, plus frames containing the confusable near-misses the model must learn to reject. For the running example that last category has a name: other birds. A detector that has only ever seen geese labeled as geese has never been taught that a duck is not one.
Video becomes a dataset by frame extraction, and the step carries one non-obvious decision: the sampling interval. Thirty frames per second of the same scene are not thirty examples; they are one example, photocopied. Consecutive frames are near-duplicates, and a dataset padded with them is smaller than it looks and — as the splitting section will show — dangerous in a specific way. Sampling every second or two of footage, then culling blurred and empty-sky frames by eye, turns an afternoon of flying into a few hundred genuinely distinct images:
import cv2

cap = cv2.VideoCapture("flight_a.mp4")
fps = cap.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FPS)            # e.g. 30.0
step = int(fps * 2)                        # keep one frame every 2 s
i = saved = 0
while True:
    ok, frame = cap.read()
    if not ok:
        break
    if i % step == 0:
        cv2.imwrite(f"raw_frames/flight_a_{saved:04d}.jpg", frame)
        saved += 1
    i += 1
How many images are enough? A useful floor for a first fine-tuned model is a few dozen labeled images per contributor and a hundred-odd overall — enough, with transfer learning and augmentation carrying the rest, to demonstrate the workflow and produce a model that visibly works on footage like its training data. A model to rely on wants an order of magnitude more, gathered iteratively as the loop at the bottom of Figure 15.1 reveals what is missing. The number that matters is never the count; it is the coverage.

title: 15  Building a Detection Pipeline: Data, Labeling, and Training
text:
15.5 Labeling: Drawing the Ground Truth
Labeling is where a pile of images becomes a dataset: a human looks at each frame and records, in machine-readable form, what a perfect detector would have said about it. For object detection that record is a set of ground-truth annotations — one bounding box, as tight as the pixels allow, plus one class identity, for every object of interest in the frame. The tooling is mature and interchangeable: LabelImg (a lightweight desktop annotator), CVAT (a self-hostable web tool built for team-scale annotation), Roboflow (a hosted platform that adds dataset management, format conversion, and augmentation), and makesense.ai (a no-install browser tool) all present the same core interaction — drag a rectangle, pick a class — and all export the standard interchange formats. Which format is a detail worth pinning down precisely once, because every training framework speaks one of two dialects: COCO format, a single JSON file describing every image, box, and category in pixel coordinates; and YOLO format, the one this pipeline uses, which Figure 15.2 specifies down to the arithmetic.






Figure 15.2: One labeled image in YOLO format: the image keeps its name, a sibling text file holds one line per object, and each line stores the class index and the box’s center, width, and height as fractions of the frame’s dimensions.



The format rewards a close reading. Each line is five numbers: a class index (from a data.yaml file that maps goose to 0 and other_bird to 1), then the box’s center \((x_c, y_c)\) and its width and height — the same center-plus-extent parameterization the Images as Data chapter introduced for detector outputs, which is no coincidence: the label format mirrors what the model must learn to produce. All four coordinates are normalized — divided by the image’s width or height — so the figure’s 112 × 72-pixel box centered at pixel \((400, 180)\) in a 640 × 480 frame becomes the line 0 0.625 0.375 0.175 0.150. Normalization is what lets the label survive the preprocessing gauntlet: the frame will be resized and letterboxed on its way into the model, and a label stored in fractions of the frame needs no rewriting when the frame changes size.
The mechanical format is the easy half of labeling; the hard half is consistency, and it is worth three rules, prefaced by the blunt truth that motivates all of them: the model learns from the labels it is given, and if the labels are wrong, it learns the wrong lesson — with full confidence, every epoch. First, boxes are tight: the annotation convention is the smallest axis-aligned rectangle containing the visible object, and a labeler who leaves generous margins is teaching the model that geese include a halo of grass, which will surface months later as systematically loose predicted boxes and depressed mAP@0.5:0.95. Second, class boundaries are written down before labeling begins: is a swimming goose with a hidden body a goose? A bird too distant to identify? Two labelers who answer differently produce a dataset that disagrees with itself, and the model splits the difference. Third, nothing is skipped silently: an unlabeled goose in a training image is not a missing label — it is a negative label, an assertion that this patch of pixels is background, and every such assertion actively teaches the model to ignore exactly what it is supposed to find. Auditing a sample of teammates’ labels before training, tedious as it sounds, is the highest-leverage hour in the pipeline — and visualizing the dataset with its boxes drawn before any training run is the same discipline in single-person form.






NoteFor More



Manual labeling costs about a minute per box, which prices a ten-thousand-image dataset in weeks of human attention — and that arithmetic is why automated labeling pipelines are the standard advanced extension of this material. Two foundation models changed the economics. Grounding DINO performs open-vocabulary detection: given an image and a text prompt (“goose”, “bird”), it proposes bounding boxes for the named concept without any task-specific training. SAM (Segment Anything Model) and its video-capable successor SAM2 do the complementary job: given a point, box, or rough prompt, they produce a pixel-precise mask of the indicated object, and SAM2 can propagate that mask through subsequent video frames — so one click on a goose in frame 1 can yield boxes for the next several hundred frames. Chained together — Grounding DINO proposes, SAM refines, a human verifies and corrects rather than draws — such semi-supervised pipelines reduce manual effort by an order of magnitude. The human is not removed: foundation-model proposals inherit their own biases (Grounding DINO will happily box gulls under the prompt “goose”), so the pipeline’s output is a set of initial annotations for refinement, and the audit step becomes the labeling job. The trade is the same one every chapter of this Part has priced: these models are enormous and run on the cloud tier — offline labeling assistance is precisely the deadline-free workload that tier exists for.

title: 15  Building a Detection Pipeline: Data, Labeling, and Training
section: 15.6 Splitting the Data: The Honest Held-Out Set
text:
15.6 Splitting the Data: The Honest Held-Out Set
Before training, the labeled dataset is divided: most images (a customary 80%) become the training set the optimizer grinds against; the remainder becomes the validation set, which the optimizer never touches and which exists solely to answer one question — how does the model do on images it has not seen? The question matters because a neural network with millions of parameters and a few hundred training images can, in the limit, simply memorize the answers; performance on the training set is therefore evidence of nothing. Only the validation score estimates the quantity the mission cares about, which is performance on the next flight’s footage.
That estimate is honest only if the split is, and video-derived datasets fail the honesty test in one specific, near-universal way. Figure 15.3 shows it. Shuffle all extracted frames and split randomly, and every validation frame has near-duplicate siblings — same flock, same light, same background, seconds apart — sitting in the training set. The model is then graded on questions it has effectively already seen; validation scores come back gratifyingly high, and they are a lie, one that stays hidden until the first flight over new ground. The failure has a name — leakage — and a simple fix: the unit of splitting is the recording session, never the frame. Whole flights, whole sessions, ideally whole days and sites, are assigned to one side or the other, so the validation set is footage the model has never seen a neighbour of.






Figure 15.3: Two ways to split video frames: a random frame-level split leaks near-duplicate frames across the boundary and inflates the validation score; splitting by whole recording session keeps validation footage genuinely unseen.



The session-level split usually lowers the validation score, sometimes sharply — and that drop is not a cost but a correction: the number was wrong before. The same reasoning, incidentally, has already appeared in this Part wearing different clothes: the TinyML chapter’s warning that a quantization calibration set must span flight conditions, not convenience conditions, is the same principle applied one pipeline stage later. Held-out data is a measuring instrument, and an instrument contaminated by its subject measures nothing.
What the split takes away in flattery, data augmentation partially gives back in substance. Each time a training image is shown to the model, it is randomly perturbed — flipped horizontally, scaled and cropped, jittered in hue and brightness, or composited into a mosaic of four training images at once, a YOLO-family staple that manufactures scale variation and crowded scenes from sparse data. A hundred images become, in effect, an endless stream of variants, and the invariances the dataset is too small to demonstrate with real examples — geese face either way, sunlight is not part of goosehood — are taught synthetically. Two cautions keep the technique honest. Geometric augmentations must transform the labels along with the pixels (flip the image, flip every \(x_c\) — the frameworks handle this, but only for the augmentations they know about), and augmentation applies to the training set only: a validation set that is also augmented is measuring performance on the augmenter, not the world.

title: 15  Building a Detection Pipeline: Data, Labeling, and Training
text:
15.7 Training: Borrowed Features, New Classes
With images/, labels/, and data.yaml in place, the training itself is almost anticlimactic — deliberately so, because the hard decisions were made upstream. The pipeline fine-tunes YOLOv8n, the nano variant of a widely used single-stage detector family: about 3.2 million parameters, which the alert reader will recognize as the previous chapter’s illustrative memory bill made flesh — roughly 12.8 MB of float32 weights, 3.2 MB after the int8 quantization that same chapter developed, comfortably inside the companion tier’s budget. “Single-stage” means the network maps the input tensor to boxes in one forward pass, predicting, at every position of its final feature maps, box coordinates and per-class scores directly — the output structure the Images as Data chapter’s task taxonomy assigned to detection, produced at the frame rates the aircraft needs.
The decisive move is where the initial weights come from. Training a 3.2-million-parameter network from random initialization on a hundred-image dataset fails outright — there are vastly more parameters than facts to constrain them. Transfer learning sidesteps the arithmetic: training starts from weights pretrained on a large general-purpose detection dataset, and the small custom dataset only has to adapt them. The division of labor falls along the network’s depth, exactly as the Images as Data chapter’s feature-map story predicts: the early layers’ kernels — edge, texture, and shape detectors — are generic visual machinery that transfers unchanged, while the later layers and the detection head, which compose those features into class-specific evidence, are what fine-tuning actually rewrites. The pretrained model already knows a great deal about birds; the dataset’s job is only to teach the difference between goose and other_bird, and a few hundred images genuinely suffice for that. Running the pretrained model on the validation images before fine-tuning makes the point empirically — it boxes the birds competently and calls them all bird, class 14 of somebody else’s dataset — and provides the baseline against which the fine-tuned model’s improvement is the pipeline’s key teaching moment.
from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("yolov8n.pt")        # pretrained weights: the borrowed features
model.train(data="data.yaml", epochs=50, imgsz=640)
metrics = model.val()             # precision, recall, mAP50, mAP50-95
What the optimizer minimizes is the composite loss the Images as Data chapter promised to return to: a classification term scoring the per-class predictions at each output position, and a box-geometry term scoring predicted rectangles against ground-truth ones by their overlap (some detector families carry a third, a standalone objectness/confidence term). The training run emits the curves of both falling epoch by epoch, alongside validation metrics rising — and the reflex for reading them is the one Part II taught for PID tuning: curves are diagnostics, not decoration. Training loss falling while validation metrics stall or reverse is overfitting, the memorization failure the held-out set exists to catch, and the standard responses — stop earlier, augment harder, collect more data — all amount to re-balancing parameters against facts. But “validation metrics rising” presumes the metrics mean something to the reader, and this is exactly the point where most practical treatments go quiet. The next section does not.

title: 15  Building a Detection Pipeline: Data, Labeling, and Training
section: 15.8 Did It Work? Precision, Recall, and mAP
text:
15.8 Did It Work? Precision, Recall, and mAP
A classifier is easy to score: its answer is right or wrong, and accuracy is a percentage. A detector’s answer is a list of localized boxes, and scoring it requires two decisions a classifier never faces: what counts as “found” (a box in roughly the right place? exactly the right place?), and how to trade the two distinct ways of being wrong — crying goose at empty grass, and staying silent over a real one. The standard machinery resolves both, and it is worth building from the ground up because every number a training framework prints is made of it.
The first decision is settled by IoU — Intersection over Union — the overlap score between a predicted box and a ground-truth box: the area both cover divided by the area either covers. Figure 15.4 works one case through: a prediction and a truth box of 8,000 px² each, overlapping in a 4,900 px² region, giving
\[
\text{IoU} = \frac{4{,}900}{8{,}000 + 8{,}000 - 4{,}900} = \frac{4{,}900}{11{,}100} = 0.44.
\]
Against the conventional matching threshold of 0.5, that detection — which a human would call “basically right, a bit off” — does not count. The strictness is deliberate: for the running example, the box centre becomes a steering bearing and indexes the depth map, so a box half-off the goose is operationally a miss. With matching defined, every detection and every ground-truth object receives exactly one verdict. A detection matching an unclaimed truth box at IoU ≥ 0.5 with the correct class is a true positive (TP); a detection with no match — wrong place, wrong class, or a duplicate box on an already-claimed object — is a false positive (FP); a labeled object no detection matched is a false negative (FN). One verdict is conspicuously absent: the true negative, all the background correctly left unboxed, is uncountable — there are indefinitely many rectangles a detector correctly did not draw — which is why detection is scored by precision and recall rather than accuracy, and why the detection confusion matrix has a permanently empty cell.






Figure 15.4: Scoring one detection: IoU against the ground-truth box decides whether it matches, every detection and labeled object receives a TP, FP, or FN verdict, and the counts fill a confusion matrix from which precision and recall are computed.



The figure’s right panel runs the counts for a deliberately tiny worked example that the rest of this section will reuse: a validation set containing 5 labeled geese, against which the detector, keeping only detections with confidence ≥ 0.5, reports 6 boxes — 4 of them matching geese, 2 of them false alarms, with 1 goose found by nothing. The confusion matrix holds TP = 4, FP = 2, FN = 1, and the two headline numbers follow:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{precision} &= \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP}+\text{FP}} = \frac{4}{6} = 0.67, \\
\text{recall} &= \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP}+\text{FN}} = \frac{4}{5} = 0.80.
\end{aligned}
\]
Read them as sentences, because that is how they are used in a design meeting: when this detector cries goose, it is right two times in three (precision), and of the geese actually present, it finds four in five (recall). Neither number alone characterizes the detector, because each can be bought at the other’s expense with a single knob — the confidence threshold. Raise it to 0.9 and only the surest detections survive: precision climbs, recall collapses. Lower it to 0.1 and everything vaguely birdlike gets a box: recall climbs, precision collapses. The threshold is an operating point, chosen by the system designer against mission costs — and for the running example the costs are asymmetric in an instructive way. A false positive sends the aircraft to harass an empty patch of grass: wasted battery, mild embarrassment. A false negative leaves a goose unharassed in a protected field: the mission’s entire purpose, unmet. The running example therefore operates deliberately down-threshold of the precision-recall balance point, accepting more false alarms to miss fewer geese — a choice no training framework can make, because it is written in the currency of the mission, not the model.
Because the threshold is arbitrary, a fair comparison between detectors must not depend on it — and that requirement is exactly what AP exists to satisfy. The construction, worked in Figure 15.5 on the same 5-goose validation set, is mechanical: take every detection the model offers, sorted by confidence descending, and walk down the list, treating each rank as an operating point and recording cumulative precision and recall there. The full ranking for the worked example — seven detections, the six already seen plus one low-confidence false positive at 0.42 — traces the table in the figure: recall rises stepwise as each TP is absorbed (topping out at 0.80, since the fifth goose is never detected at any threshold), while precision sawtooths, dropping at each FP and partially recovering at each TP. Plot precision against recall and the sawtooth becomes the precision–recall curve; AP is the area under it, computed against the curve’s upper envelope (at each recall level, the best precision achievable at that recall or beyond — the convention smooths the sawtooth and rewards what an optimally chosen threshold could get). For the worked example the envelope holds precision 1.0 out to recall 0.4, then 0.75 to recall 0.6, then 0.67 to recall 0.8, then falls to zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{AP}_{50} &= (0.4)(1.0) + (0.2)(0.75) + (0.2)(0.67) \\
               &= 0.400 + 0.150 + 0.133 = 0.68.
\end{aligned}
\]






Figure 15.5: From a ranked list of detections to AP: each rank down the confidence ordering is one operating point contributing a precision–recall pair; the area under the resulting curve’s upper envelope is that class’s average precision, and mAP averages AP over classes.



Two averaging steps turn AP into the numbers a training run actually prints. Averaging AP over classes gives mAP — if goose scores 0.68 and other_bird a weaker 0.52, then mAP@0.5 is 0.60 — a convention that matters when classes are imbalanced, since a detector can post a handsome average on the abundant class while quietly failing the rare one, which is a reason to always read the per-class table, not just the mean. Averaging over IoU thresholds gives the stricter mAP@0.5:0.95: the entire computation repeated at matching thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05 and averaged, so that a detector earns full credit only when its boxes are not merely on the object but tight — which is why this is always the lower of the two numbers reported, and why sloppy training labels, which teach loose boxes, damage it first. When the validation call in the training snippet returns its four columns — precision, recall, mAP50, mAP50-95 — every one of them is now legible as a specific computation over TP, FP, and FN counts, and a statement like “the fine-tuned model reached 0.85 mAP@0.5” has become checkable engineering rather than incantation.
