title: 15  Building a Detection Pipeline: Data, Labeling, and Training
text:
15.9 Closing the Loop
The validation table says how good the model is; it does not say why it is bad where it is bad, and the last discipline of the pipeline is extracting that answer. The method is unglamorous: run the trained detector over the validation set and over fresh footage, and look at the failures one by one. They will cluster — and each cluster is a sentence in the specification for the next dataset. Misses at long range: the dataset lacks small-scale geese, or the input resolution is below the pixels-on-target floor of the Images as Data chapter — collect high-altitude footage, or revisit the resolution negotiation. Ducks boxed as geese: the other_bird class is underpopulated — collect confusers. Failures against a specific background or lighting: a coverage gap, named precisely by the failing frames themselves. Small datasets guarantee such mistakes, and the correct response is neither despair nor another architecture, but the red arrow of Figure 15.1: mistakes are the cheapest, most accurate data-collection guidance the project will ever get. Even the deployed model keeps contributing — the TinyML chapter’s offloading pattern, shipping hard cases and low-confidence detections back from the aircraft as summaries, exists precisely to keep this loop turning after launch.
The pipeline is now complete end to end, in the only sense that matters: every stage from raw footage to a validated, deployable model has been built, and the two stages beyond — quantize, hand to TensorRT, run inside the Detector node — were the previous chapter’s work. Two threads remain open, both deliberate. The numbers this chapter computed were a worked miniature; the Wildlife Detection from the Air case study, which closes this Part, holds the whole pipeline against the published record — a real research team detecting sheep from 80 m, and the waterfowl literature’s own goose detectors — reading their datasets, labeling compromises, and reported failures with exactly the instruments built here. And a model that is accurate is not yet a model that is fast enough: proving the deployed detector meets its frame-rate deadline inside the aircraft’s stack is a measurement discipline of its own, taken up in the Real-Time Inference on the Edge chapter.

title: 15  Building a Detection Pipeline: Data, Labeling, and Training
text:
15.10 Check Your Understanding

A labeler produces a box for a goose occupying pixels from \((u, v) = (200, 300)\) to \((280, 360)\) in a 640 × 480 frame. Write the YOLO-format label line (class goose = 0), showing the arithmetic for all four coordinates.







TipShow answer





The box’s center is at \(u_c = (200+280)/2 = 240\), \(v_c = (300+360)/2 = 330\); its width is 80 px and height 60 px. Normalizing: \(x_c = 240/640 = 0.375\); \(y_c = 330/480 = 0.6875\); \(w = 80/640 = 0.125\); \(h = 60/480 = 0.125\). The line is 0 0.375 0.6875 0.125 0.125. Note the divisor differs per axis — horizontal quantities are divided by the width (640), vertical by the height (480) — a mismatch here is a classic silent labeling bug that displaces every box vertically.




On a validation set containing 40 labeled geese, a detector at confidence ≥ 0.5 reports 35 boxes, of which 28 match a goose at IoU ≥ 0.5. Fill in the confusion matrix (TP, FP, FN), compute precision and recall, and state — in mission terms for the running example — what each of the two error counts costs.







TipShow answer





TP = 28; FP = 35 − 28 = 7; FN = 40 − 28 = 12 (TN is undefined for detection). Precision = 28/35 = 0.80: one alert in five sends the aircraft to investigate something that is not a goose — wasted battery and flight time. Recall = 28/40 = 0.70: 12 of the 40 geese present go undetected and undeterred — a direct failure of the mission’s purpose. For a deterrence mission the FN cost dominates, which argues for lowering the confidence threshold (trading precision away to recover recall) rather than raising it.




Explain why a random frame-level split of video-derived data inflates validation metrics, why the inflation is invisible during development, and how the same failure mode reappeared in the previous chapter in a different pipeline stage.







TipShow answer





Frames extracted seconds apart from one video are near-duplicates; a random split scatters them across both sides, so nearly every validation image has a close sibling in training and the model is scored partly on memorization. The inflation is invisible because every number the developer sees — computed on that contaminated validation set — is self-consistently high; the truth only surfaces on genuinely new footage, i.e., in the field. The TinyML chapter’s quantization-calibration failure is the same principle one stage later: a calibration set drawn from convenient (e.g., indoor) data yields activation ranges that look perfect on calibration data and clip catastrophically on flight data. In both cases held-out data is a measuring instrument, and it measures only what it was sampled from.




A pretrained YOLOv8n detects the birds in the validation images but labels them all bird. Fine-tuning on 130 labeled images produces a model that reliably distinguishes goose from other_bird. Explain, in terms of which layers change and what they encode, why 130 images suffice here when training the same architecture from random initialization would fail.







TipShow answer





The pretrained network’s early convolutional layers already encode general visual features — edges, textures, part-like patterns — learned from a large general dataset; these transfer to the new task essentially unchanged, because low-level visual structure is shared across image domains. Fine-tuning mainly has to adjust the later layers and detection head, which compose those features into class evidence — teaching the (comparatively few) parameters that separate goose-shaped feature combinations from other-bird-shaped ones. 130 images carry enough information for that small adaptation, but nowhere near enough to constrain all 3.2 million parameters from scratch: with random initialization the network must learn edge detectors and class boundaries simultaneously from a dataset thousands of times too small, and it memorizes instead of generalizing.




A detector’s ranked output on a validation set with 4 ground-truth geese is: 0.92 TP, 0.85 TP, 0.71 FP, 0.63 TP, 0.50 FP. Compute cumulative precision and recall at each rank, then AP@0.5 using the upper-envelope convention. What is the maximum recall, and why does it fall short of 1.0?







TipShow answer





Ranks: (1) P = 1/1 = 1.00, R = 1/4 = 0.25; (2) P = 2/2 = 1.00, R = 0.50; (3) P = 2/3 = 0.67, R = 0.50; (4) P = 3/4 = 0.75, R = 0.75; (5) P = 3/5 = 0.60, R = 0.75. Envelope: precision 1.00 holds for recall in (0, 0.50] (best precision at or beyond those recalls is 1.00); precision 0.75 for (0.50, 0.75]; zero beyond 0.75. AP = (0.50)(1.00) + (0.25)(0.75) = 0.50 + 0.1875 ≈ 0.69. Maximum recall is 0.75: the fourth goose is matched by no detection at any confidence, and no threshold choice can recover an object the model never proposed.




mAP@0.5:0.95 for a trained model comes back much lower than its mAP@0.5, and inspection shows the predicted boxes systematically include a margin of grass around each goose. Trace the likely cause backward through the pipeline, and state which pipeline stage — not which hyperparameter — the fix belongs to.







TipShow answer





mAP@0.5:0.95 re-scores the same detections at IoU thresholds up to 0.95, so it punishes boxes that find the object but fit it loosely — precisely the symptom described. The model learned loose boxes because it was taught them: training annotations drawn with generous margins shift the box-geometry loss’s target, and the model reproduces the margin faithfully. The fix belongs to the labeling stage — re-audit the annotations against the tight-box convention and correct them — not to training hyperparameters, which would be tuning the optimizer to better fit wrong answers. The general lesson: metric pathologies whose pattern is systematic (every box loose in the same way) usually indict the dataset; random pathologies more often indict the model or the data volume.

text:
15.11 Try It
Part 1 — build a labeled dataset and audit it. Collect two or three minutes of video containing a target class of your choosing (birds at a pond, cars from a footbridge — anything with multiple instances and confusers). Extract frames at a 2-second interval with the chapter’s snippet, cull the useless ones, and label 40–60 images in a browser tool (makesense.ai requires no installation), exporting in YOLO format. Before doing anything else, audit: write a short script that draws every label file’s boxes back onto its image, page through all of them, and count your own labeling errors — missed objects, loose boxes, class inconsistencies. Fix what you find, then write down your class-boundary rules (what did you decide about occluded, distant, or ambiguous instances?) as the labeling spec you should have written first. Finally, split by session, not by frame: hold out footage from a different time or vantage point if you have it, and state in one sentence what your validation set does and does not test.
Part 2 — train, evaluate, and compute one AP by hand. Fine-tune yolov8n.pt on your dataset for 50 epochs (any free GPU notebook service suffices) and run validation. First reproduce the baseline comparison: run the pretrained weights on your validation images, then your fine-tuned weights, and save one side-by-side pair that shows the difference. Then interrogate the metrics: from the validation output, read precision, recall, mAP@0.5, and mAP@0.5:0.95, and check the per-class table for imbalance. Finally, verify the machinery yourself: pick 8–10 of your model’s detections on a handful of validation images, determine each one’s TP/FP verdict at IoU ≥ 0.5 (compute one IoU by hand from box coordinates while you are at it), build the ranked table as in Figure 15.5, and compute AP with the envelope convention. Compare your hand-computed value against the framework’s per-class AP — and if they disagree wildly, find out which of you is matching detections to ground truth differently. That disagreement, run to ground, teaches more than the training run did.

title: 16  Real-Time Inference on the Edge: Latency and Trade-offs
text:
16.1 Learning Objectives
The previous chapter ended with a validated detector and an unpaid debt. The pipeline it built runs from raw footage to a model with a measured mAP, and the chapter before it carried that model through quantization and into TensorRT on the companion computer — but every number produced so far describes accuracy, and accuracy says nothing about time. A detector that finds nineteen geese in twenty is useless to the running example if each answer arrives half a second after the frame that prompted it, because the target-position topic the mission logic has consumed since Part II is only worth publishing while the goose is still near the position being published. The demand the deployment stage places on the system is usually compressed into one hyphenated word — the system must detect targets in real-time — and this chapter’s first job is to take that word apart, because it names not one requirement but two, each measured differently, each failed differently.
The second job is the trades. When measurement says the deadline is missed — and on a first attempt it usually does — the engineer holds a small set of levers, and every one of them buys time by spending something the mission also wants: a smaller model spends accuracy, a lower input resolution spends detection range, a skipped frame spends freshness. The previous two chapters built the levers themselves — quantization, resolution, model choice; this chapter is about pulling them deliberately: reading an accuracy-versus-speed frontier, pricing a model-size step in both currencies, and measuring the result honestly, which turns out to be its own discipline with its own failure modes. The chapter then follows the deployed detector into two subjects that only exist after deployment. The first is time-smoothing: a per-frame detector flickers, and the machinery that turns flickering boxes into stable, trackable objects — and the decision delay that stability costs — is what lets the state machine act on perception without overreacting to one noisy frame. The second is robustness: the gap between the validation set and the world, which widens on a vibrating, altitude-changing, weather-exposed aircraft faster than on any other deployment platform a vision model is likely to meet.

title: 16  Real-Time Inference on the Edge: Latency and Trade-offs
text:
16.2 Key Vocabulary

FPS (frames per second) — the throughput of a perception pipeline: how many frames complete processing per second of wall-clock time, sustained; set by the pipeline’s slowest stage, not by the sum of its stages.
End-to-end latency — the age of the information at the moment it is acted on: the wall-clock time from the instant light left the scene to the instant the pipeline’s output is available to the consumer, summed across every stage in between — of which model inference is only one.
Tail latency — the high-percentile behavior of a latency distribution (the 95th or 99th percentile frame); the number a control deadline actually cares about, since a loop that misses its deadline one frame in twenty misses it every second at 20 FPS.
Thermal throttling — an embedded processor’s self-protection under sustained load: as die temperature rises, clock speeds are cut and latency rises, minutes into exactly the kind of continuous inference a mission demands and a short benchmark never sees.
Model size trade-off — the family-wide pattern that detection accuracy rises with parameter count while latency rises with it too, at sharply diminishing accuracy returns; choosing a variant is choosing a point on that frontier, not maximizing either axis.
Object tracking — associating per-frame detections across time so that the same physical object keeps a stable identity from frame to frame; the output is tracks — object histories with IDs, positions, and motion — rather than isolated boxes.
Persistence threshold — the number of consecutive frames (or the duration) a track must survive before the system treats it as real and acts on it; the standard defense against acting on one spurious detection, purchased at a computable delay.
Robustness — a deployed model’s ability to keep performing as conditions drift away from those of its training data: different lighting, motion blur, partial occlusion, new backgrounds.
Distribution shift — the statistical name for that drift: the deployed input distribution no longer matches the distribution the training and validation data were drawn from, so the validation score silently stops predicting field performance.
Responsible AI — the engineering obligation that follows from deploying a model whose errors move a physical machine through public airspace: privacy, safety, bias, and accountability treated as design requirements rather than afterthoughts.

title: 16  Real-Time Inference on the Edge: Latency and Trade-offs
text:
16.3 What “Real-Time” Actually Requires
“Real-time” is not a synonym for “fast.” It is a relationship between the pipeline and two clocks. The first clock is the camera’s: frames arrive every 33.3 ms at the 30 frames-per-second mode the running example’s camera delivers, and a pipeline that takes longer than that per frame cannot keep up. If it tries anyway — queuing every frame and processing them in order — the queue grows without bound and so does the age of the frame being processed: after a minute, the detector is diligently finding geese where they were a minute ago. The practical discipline is to drop stale frames and always process the newest one, which caps the damage but concedes the point: a pipeline slower than the arrival rate sees only a fraction of what the camera saw. The first condition, then, is a throughput condition: sustained FPS must meet the rate at which the mission needs fresh answers.
The second clock belongs to the consumer. The deterrence behavior steers toward the target position at frame rate, and a position is useful only while the goose is still near it. That is a latency condition — from photons to published position must be short enough that the answer is still true — and it is genuinely independent of the first. The independence is worth one concrete illustration, because it is the most common confusion in performance claims. A pipeline whose stages run concurrently — frame \(n\) being captured while frame \(n-1\) is preprocessed while frame \(n-2\) is in the network — completes one frame per duration of its slowest stage, so its FPS can be excellent while each individual answer still takes the sum of all stages to emerge. A vendor demo showing smooth 30 FPS detection overlays can be carrying 150 ms of pipeline depth, and for a control loop those are entirely different numbers: FPS says how often a new answer arrives; latency says how old each answer is on arrival. A surveillance dashboard cares about the first. A vehicle steering toward a moving animal cares about both.
How stale is too stale? Arithmetic the reader has done since Part I settles it. A goose that has decided to relocate moves at several metres per second — call it 5 m/s walking-to-flapping. In 50 ms it moves 25 cm, comfortably inside the deterrence maneuver’s tolerance; in 500 ms it moves 2.5 m, several body lengths, and the published position is fiction. The freshness requirement is therefore mission-derived, not universal — a crop-survey pipeline mapping static fields could tolerate seconds — and stating it explicitly, in milliseconds, is the first act of real-time engineering. For the running example this chapter adopts a round budget: end-to-end latency under 100 ms, sustained throughput matching the camera’s 30 FPS or degrading gracefully below it.

title: 16  Real-Time Inference on the Edge: Latency and Trade-offs
text:
16.4 The Latency Budget
Where do the milliseconds go? The instinctive answer — “inference” — is wrong in the same way the previous Part’s instinctive answer to memory (“the weights”) was wrong, and the correction is the same: itemize the whole bill. Figure 16.1 walks one frame through a representative deployment of the running example’s detector — YOLOv8n, int8, TensorRT, on the companion computer — and then shows the same stages pipelined.






Figure 16.1: One frame’s journey through the inference pipeline, itemized in milliseconds, and the same stages pipelined across consecutive frames: end-to-end latency is the sum of the stages, while sustained FPS is set by the slowest stage alone.



The numbers are representative rather than universal — the whole point of the next section is that they must be measured, not copied — but their shape is typical and instructive. Inference, the stage every optimization guide obsesses over, is half the bill. Capture is a heavy line item that no model compression touches: the sensor must expose (longer in low light — a robustness thread picked up later), read out, and push 921,600 bytes over USB before software sees anything. Preprocessing is the resize-letterbox-normalize gauntlet of the Images as Data chapter, cheap but not free. Postprocessing covers non-maximum suppression, the depth lookup, and the pixel-to-vehicle-frame transform that turns a box into the target position. Summed: 50 ms of age on every published position — within the 100 ms budget, with room for the degradation that field conditions will impose.
The pipelined view yields the throughput verdict. With stages overlapped, a new result emerges once per slowest stage — 25 ms here, a 40 FPS ceiling — so the camera’s 30 FPS is sustained with headroom. But the same figure shows how quickly the ledger can flip: swap in a model whose inference takes 40 ms, and the bottleneck stage exceeds the 33.3 ms frame interval; the pipeline now completes at most 25 frames per second, frames drop, and — if the queueing discipline is wrong — latency compounds frame over frame. One stage’s overrun degrades both conditions at once, which is why the budget is kept as a table of stages and re-measured whenever any stage changes. The habit should feel familiar: it is Part I’s power budget and the TinyML chapter’s memory bill, transposed into milliseconds.

title: 16  Real-Time Inference on the Edge: Latency and Trade-offs
text:
16.5 Measuring Honestly
The latency budget is only as good as its numbers, and timing a neural network is strewn with ways to get flattering, wrong ones. Four disciplines separate a measurement from an anecdote.
Exclude warm-up. The first inference after a model loads pays one-time costs — kernel compilation, memory allocation, cache population — that can run to hundreds of milliseconds and will never recur in flight. A benchmark that includes them overstates latency; a benchmark of only the first few frames can also understate steady-state FPS while the GPU’s clocks ramp. Run tens of inferences before recording anything.
Report the tail, not just the mean. Latency is a distribution, and control deadlines are violated by its worst cases, not its average. A pipeline averaging 30 ms with a 99th-percentile of 80 ms misses a 60 ms deadline about once every hundred frames — at 30 FPS, several times every ten seconds, each miss a stale position published to the steering loop. The mean hides this entirely; the percentiles are the honest summary, and the maximum over a long run is worth recording besides.
Run long enough to get hot. An embedded computer under sustained inference load heats up, and when it reaches its thermal limit it protects itself by cutting clock speeds — thermal throttling — at which point latency quietly rises. The effect takes minutes to appear and a 30-second benchmark will never see it, which is exactly why it surfaces in the field instead: the mission’s twentieth minute, a warm afternoon, a heatsink sized for the bench. Benchmarks intended to clear a flight readiness bar run for the duration of a flight, and log temperature alongside latency so the correlation is visible.
Measure on the target, under the mission’s load. The Jetson’s GPU shares memory bandwidth, power budget, and (for some stages) CPU cores with everything else Part II put on the aircraft — the ROS 2 graph, the MAVLink bridge, logging, the camera driver itself. A model benchmarked alone on the bench inherits resources the mission will take back. The previous chapter’s doctrine — the model is a component, not the system — becomes a measurement rule here: the number that matters is the latency of the assembled stack, measured at the output topic, while everything else runs.
The measurement itself needs no framework, only care with what is timed:
import time
import numpy as np

lat = []
for i in range(1000):
    frame = get_latest_frame()          # drops stale frames; returns newest
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    boxes = detector.infer(frame)       # preprocess + model + NMS inside
    lat.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000.0)

lat = np.array(lat[50:])                # discard warm-up
print(f"mean {lat.mean():.1f} ms   p50 {np.percentile(lat, 50):.1f}"
      f"   p99 {np.percentile(lat, 99):.1f}   max {lat.max():.1f}")
Note what this loop measures and what it does not: it times preprocess-through-postprocess — the software stages — but starts its clock after capture, so the capture line of the latency budget must be measured separately (typically from the frame’s hardware timestamp, which the camera driver attaches, to the moment get_latest_frame returns). Timing from the hardware timestamp to the published topic, inside the running ROS 2 graph, is the full end-to-end figure; the snippet’s figure is the part the model choice controls. Keeping the two straight — and saying which one a reported “latency” is — is half of measurement honesty.

title: 16  Real-Time Inference on the Edge: Latency and Trade-offs
text:
16.6 The Accuracy–Speed Frontier
Suppose the measurement disappoints: the tail latency blows the budget, or the sustained FPS sags under load. Two of the levers are inherited from earlier chapters and need only naming: quantization (the TinyML chapter’s factor of two-to-four, already spent if the deployment followed that chapter) and input resolution (the Images as Data chapter’s quadratic lever, pulled against pixels-on-target and detection range). The third lever is the one this Part has so far held fixed: the model itself. Modern detector families are published as a ladder of sizes — the same architecture scaled in depth and width — and the YOLOv8 family the pipeline trains is typical: nano, small, medium, large, extra-large, from 3.2 million parameters to 68.2 million. The published benchmarks of the family, plotted in Figure 16.2, form the curve on which every model-size decision is made.






Figure 16.2: The YOLOv8 family’s published COCO accuracy against computational cost: accuracy climbs with model size at sharply diminishing returns, while latency grows roughly in proportion to compute, so the mission’s accuracy floor — not the top of the curve — selects the variant.



Three readings of the curve matter more than any point on it. First, its shape: accuracy saturates while cost does not. The step from nano to small buys 7.6 points of COCO mAP for 3.3× the compute — a defensible trade; the step from large to extra-large buys 1.0 point for 1.6× the compute on top of an already-unflyable base. The saturation is not an accident of this family but the general pattern of scaling within a task: the easy accuracy is bought first, cheaply, and each further point costs more than the last. Second, the latency axis is the binding one onboard: on the companion computer’s fixed compute budget, a model’s GFLOPs translate roughly into its inference time, and somewhere along the curve — the shaded region of the figure — the frame-rate condition of the first section fails outright, making the upper family members not slower options but non-options. Third, and most important, the question the curve answers: not “which model is best” — the top of the curve is best, uselessly — but “which is the smallest model that clears the mission’s accuracy floor at the mission’s frame rate.” That is the same question the TinyML chapter’s placement problem asked of hardware tiers, now asked within a tier, and it explains the deployment folklore the source material compresses into a tip: start with the nano model and scale up only when measurement says the accuracy floor is unmet. Starting large and shrinking under schedule pressure runs the same search from the expensive end.
Two refinements keep the frontier honest in practice. The published mAP figures are COCO numbers — eighty everyday object classes — and a two-class goose detector fine-tuned per the previous chapter will not match them numerically; the ordering and the shape transfer, the absolute values do not, so the family comparison worth trusting is run on the mission’s own validation set. And the frontier interacts with the resolution lever: a larger model at a smaller input can land at the same latency as a smaller model at full input with different accuracy — the small model preserving small-object range (more pixels on the distant goose), the large one classifying what it sees more reliably. The two-lever grid — family member × input size — is small enough to measure exhaustively in an afternoon of benchmarking, and for a mission whose targets are 7-pixel smudges at range, the pixels usually win. There is no closed-form answer here, which is the section’s real lesson: the frontier tells the engineer where to look; only the stopwatch and the validation set say where to land. The “best” model, as the source material puts it, is a system-level trade-off — accuracy, latency, energy, memory, robustness, and the cost of being wrong, negotiated together.

title: 16  Real-Time Inference on the Edge: Latency and Trade-offs
text:
16.7 From Frames to Decisions: Tracking
Everything so far treats each frame as an isolated question. But the mission does not consume frames — it consumes decisions: begin the deterrence run, steer toward this goose, break off. And between per-frame detections and sound decisions sits a gap that latency and accuracy numbers do not describe. A detector operating deliberately down-threshold — as the previous chapter argued the running example should, trading precision for recall — emits occasional false positives by design; even on true geese, boxes flicker as confidence hovers near threshold, vanish for a frame of motion blur, and reappear. A state machine wired directly to raw detections inherits every flicker: it would launch a deterrence run at a shadow, abort when a real goose blinks out for two frames, and re-acquire the same bird as a new target ten times a minute. The missing machinery is object tracking: associating detections across frames so that the same physical goose keeps the same identity over time, converting a stream of stateless boxes into a set of object histories. Figure 16.3 shows the transformation on a strip of frames.






Figure 16.3: Per-frame detections are noisy — boxes flicker, drop out, and false-alarm — while a tracker’s association across frames produces stable object identities, and a persistence threshold converts them into decisions at a computable delay.



The mechanics are lighter than the word “tracking” suggests. Each frame, the tracker matches the detector’s new boxes against its live tracks using cheap evidence — box overlap with the track’s last position, a constant-velocity prediction of where the track should be now, detection confidence — then extends matched tracks, lets unmatched tracks coast on their predicted motion for a few frames before retiring them, and opens tentative tracks for unmatched detections. Standard lightweight implementations such as ByteTrack and BoT-SORT do exactly this with no neural network of their own and no training: their cost is microseconds of bookkeeping per frame, which is why the tracking line of the latency budget was near-zero. For that price the mission logic gains three things it cannot get from any single frame: stability (one goose is one object, not a re-detected stranger every frame), motion (a track has a velocity — where the goose is heading, which the deterrence approach can lead), and evidence accumulation — the ability to require that an object persist before acting on it.
That last item is where tracking rejoins this chapter’s subject, because persistence is bought with time. A persistence threshold of \(N\) consecutive frames means a track is confirmed — and the deterrence decision fires — only after the object has survived \(N\) association rounds, which at frame interval \(\Delta t\) adds a decision delay of \(N \Delta t\): five frames at 30 FPS is 167 ms between first genuine sighting and action. That delay is not overhead to be minimized to zero; it is the price of not chasing shadows, and it is tuned, like the confidence threshold it complements, in mission currency. A spurious deterrence run costs a full flight leg of battery; 167 ms of deliberation costs 80 cm of goose travel. The running example takes that trade — and takes the symmetric one on the way out, coasting a confirmed track through several missed frames before declaring the goose gone, so one blurred frame does not abort a deterrence run in progress. Both thresholds lengthen the effective latency between the world changing and the system’s model of it changing; both are the reason the raw pipeline latency needed headroom under its 100 ms budget rather than merely meeting it.
Tracking earns its keep, and then it fails in its own ways, worth naming because each corrupts a different downstream consumer. An ID switch — the same goose re-identified as a new object after a blur or a crossing with another bird — corrupts counting and re-triggers per-target logic. A duplicate track — one goose carried as two flickering identities — inflates counts and can split the deterrence logic’s attention. A lost track — the track dying while the goose remains — silently ends a deterrence run early. None of these appear in detector metrics; they are evaluated on video with track-level checks — identity consistency, count stability over a sequence with known ground truth — one more instance of this chapter’s refrain that the deployed system must be measured at the level its consumers consume.

section: 16.8 Robustness: When the World Leaves the Dataset
text:
16.8 Robustness: When the World Leaves the Dataset
The previous chapter’s split discipline produced an honest validation score — honest, that is, about footage statistically like the dataset. The field makes no such promise. A deployed model’s inputs drift away from its training distribution — the phenomenon called distribution shift — and when they do, the validation score stops predicting anything without announcing that it has stopped: the model still runs, still emits confident boxes, and is simply wrong more often. A drone is close to the worst platform imaginable on this axis. Its viewpoint changes continuously with altitude and attitude; its scenes change with weather, season, and site; its own propulsion vibrates the camera; and its mistakes cost energy and, in the limit, safety. The maxim from the source material deserves its italics: a model that works in a notebook is not necessarily ready to fly. Figure 16.4 catalogs the three failure modes a flying camera meets first, with the symptom each produces and the mitigations each admits.






Figure 16.4: Three robustness failure modes of onboard vision — lighting change, motion blur, and occlusion — each an instance of distribution shift, each with a distinct symptom in the detector’s output and a distinct set of mitigations spanning data, hardware, and system design.



The three columns share a structure worth extracting. Each failure mode is, at bottom, a coverage statement about the dataset — the conditions under which the detector degrades are precisely the conditions the training distribution undersampled — which is why the first mitigation in every column is data: targeted augmentation for the perturbation’s cheap approximations, targeted collection for the real thing. The distinction between those two matters and the source material states it exactly: augmentation simulates small variations around known examples — a brightness shift, a synthetic blur — and cannot conjure missing domains; no augmentation of daytime meadow footage produces the statistics of dusk, rain, or a new site. Augmentation stretches coverage; only collection extends it. This is the closing loop of the previous chapter wearing its field clothes: failures cluster by condition, and the cluster names the next collection flight. The second mitigation in every column is system design rather than model design — stabilization hardware, flight profiles that respect the camera (slower, smoother legs while detecting), tracker persistence carrying identity through transient dropouts — a reminder that the perception system extends well beyond the network. And the third is evaluation design: reporting metrics per condition (morning versus noon, calm versus windy, near versus far) rather than as one pooled number, so that a model strong on average and blind at dusk cannot hide inside its own mean. The habit of building that per-condition table before collecting data — deciding what the mission envelope contains and measuring coverage against it — is the cheapest robustness tool in the kit.
One mitigation belongs to no column because it belongs to all of them: admitting, at runtime, that the model may currently be wrong. A perception system cannot detect its own distribution shift directly, but it can watch proxies — detection confidence trending down, detection rate collapsing or spiking, track churn rising, inputs statistically unlike anything calibrated for — and treat sustained anomaly as a signal to degrade gracefully: widen persistence thresholds, slow the search, hold position, or hand the decision back to the operator, rather than continue steering on fiction. Part II built exactly this reflex into the flight stack — the watchdog, the failsafe ladder, the principle that every autonomous behavior needs a defined behavior for its own failure — and the perception system, as the newest autonomous behavior aboard, owes the same contract. The Detector node that publishes target positions should also publish its own health, and the state machine that consumes the first should consume the second.

title: 16  Real-Time Inference on the Edge: Latency and Trade-offs
text:
16.9 A Note on Responsibility
There is a last trade-off in this chapter’s territory that is not measured in milliseconds. The system now assembled — a camera, a detector, a tracker, an aircraft that acts on what they say — watches a physical place continuously, and its errors move a machine through that place. That raises obligations beyond engineering correctness. On-device inference, adopted in Part I for bandwidth and here for latency, turns out to carry a privacy dividend — raw imagery of whoever walks through the protected area never leaves the aircraft, and the system can be designed to transmit and retain only derived summaries — but the dividend is not automatic and it is not absolution: what is stored, for how long, who may access it, and what the system does about people it was never meant to watch are design decisions, made explicitly or made badly. Dataset bias has already appeared in this Part as an accuracy problem; it returns as a fairness and safety problem when the failures cluster on particular conditions, places, or bystanders. And a wildlife-deterrence system in particular owes an account of its effects on the animals themselves. These questions get a chapter of their own — The Ethics and Ecology of Autonomous Wildlife Management, in Part V — with the full treatment of privacy-by-design, bias auditing, and the ecology of deterrence. They are flagged here, before the system flies, for one reason: responsible AI is a set of design requirements, and design requirements bind earliest, when the logging format, the retention policy, and the evaluation table are still cheap to change.
The Part’s arc is now complete: pixels became tensors, tensors met budgets, budgets shaped a trained detector, and this chapter held the assembled pipeline to the two clocks the mission runs on — then smoothed its output into objects worth acting on and armored it against the field. What the running example’s perception stack now publishes is exactly what Part II’s state machine was built waiting for: a confirmed, tracked, health-annotated target position, fresh to within a measured bound. One chapter remains before Part IV takes up the autonomy that decides what to do with that position: a case study that holds this Part’s entire approach against the published record of detecting animals from the air — and against the measured behavior of the geese themselves.

title: 16  Real-Time Inference on the Edge: Latency and Trade-offs
text:
16.10 Check Your Understanding

A vendor demo shows a detection overlay updating smoothly at 30 FPS, and the vendor claims the system is “real-time.” State the two separate conditions a real-time perception pipeline must satisfy, and describe a stage structure under which this demo passes one condition while carrying 150 ms of end-to-end latency. Which condition does the smooth overlay actually demonstrate?







TipShow answer





The conditions are throughput — sustained FPS at least the rate at which the mission needs fresh answers (bounded by the slowest pipeline stage) — and freshness: end-to-end latency (the sum of all stages) within the mission’s staleness budget. A five-stage pipeline whose stages each take 30 ms, run concurrently, emits a new result every 30 ms (33 FPS — smooth overlay) while each result is 150 ms old on arrival. The overlay demonstrates only throughput: it shows how often a new answer appears, not how old each answer is. For a display, age barely matters; for a loop steering toward a moving animal, 150 ms is 75 cm of goose travel at 5 m/s, and the latency condition must be verified separately, by measuring from the frame’s hardware timestamp to the published output.




A pipeline’s measured stages are: capture 15 ms, preprocess 5 ms, inference 40 ms, postprocess 3 ms, track-and-publish 2 ms, with a 30 FPS camera (33.3 ms frame interval). Compute the end-to-end latency and the sustained throughput ceiling, state which real-time condition fails, and explain what happens to latency over time if the pipeline naively queues every frame instead of dropping stale ones.







TipShow answer





Latency is the sum: \(15 + 5 + 40 + 3 + 2 = 65\) ms. Throughput is set by the slowest stage: one result per 40 ms, a ceiling of 25 FPS. The freshness condition can still pass (65 ms is under a 100 ms budget), but the throughput condition fails: 25 FPS cannot keep up with 30 FPS arrival. With naive queueing, frames arrive every 33.3 ms and leave every 40 ms, so the queue grows by one frame every ~200 ms and the age of the frame being processed grows without bound — after a minute the detector is analyzing footage from seconds ago, and the published positions are systematically stale even though each individual frame still takes only 65 ms of processing. Dropping stale frames caps latency at the pipeline depth but concedes that only ~25 of every 30 frames are seen; fixing the condition properly requires shrinking the 40 ms bottleneck stage (smaller model, lower resolution) or accepting a lower target rate.




Using the published YOLOv8 family figures (n: 8.7 GFLOPs / 37.3 mAP; s: 28.6 / 44.9; m: 78.9 / 50.2; l: 165.2 / 52.9; x: 257.8 / 53.9), compute the compute-cost multiplier and the mAP gain for the steps n→s and l→x, and state the general shape of the frontier these two numbers illustrate. Then explain why the absolute mAP values should not drive the running example’s model choice, and what should.







TipShow answer





n→s: \(28.6/8.7 \approx 3.3\times\) the compute for \(44.9 - 37.3 = 7.6\) mAP. l→x: \(257.8/165.2 \approx 1.6\times\) the compute for \(53.9 - 52.9 = 1.0\) mAP. The frontier rises steeply at the small end and flattens at the large end — accuracy saturates while cost does not, so each further point of accuracy costs more than the last. The absolute values are COCO benchmarks: eighty everyday classes, a distribution unlike a two-class aerial goose task, so a fine-tuned goose detector’s numbers will differ; only the ordering and shape transfer. The choice should be driven by measurements on the mission’s own validation set and hardware: the smallest family member whose measured accuracy clears the mission’s floor at the mission’s frame rate — starting from nano and scaling up on evidence, not down from the top under schedule pressure.




A detector benchmarks at a mean latency of 28 ms over a 30-second bench test, and the team declares a 60 ms deadline comfortably met. Give two distinct reasons this conclusion can be wrong in flight even if the measurement was performed correctly as far as it went, and state the benchmarking discipline that catches each.







TipShow answer





First, the mean hides the tail: a distribution with mean 28 ms can carry a 99th percentile above 60 ms, and at 30 FPS a 1-in-100 violation recurs several times every ten seconds, each one a stale position published to the control loop. Discipline: report percentiles (p95/p99) and the maximum, not the mean alone. Second, 30 seconds is too short and too idle: thermal throttling appears minutes into sustained load — the processor cuts clocks as it heats, raising latency — and a bench test without the mission’s competing processes (ROS 2 graph, logging, camera driver, MAVLink bridge) lends the model memory bandwidth and cores the mission will reclaim. Discipline: benchmark for a flight’s duration, on the target, with the full stack running, logging temperature alongside latency. (Warm-up is the symmetric error in the other direction — including the first inferences’ one-time costs overstates latency — excluded by discarding initial iterations.)




The running example’s tracker requires 5 consecutive frames of persistence at 30 FPS before confirming a track, and coasts a confirmed track for up to 4 missed frames before retiring it. Compute the decision delay on first sighting and the maximum blindness the coasting rule tolerates, and explain — in mission currency — what each threshold purchases and what raising each further would cost.







TipShow answer





Confirmation delay: \(5 \times 33.3 \approx 167\) ms between first genuine detection and the deterrence decision — during which a goose at 5 m/s moves about 80 cm. Coasting: \(4 \times 33.3 \approx 133\) ms of continuous dropout tolerated before a confirmed track dies. Confirmation purchases immunity to acting on single-frame false positives — a spurious deterrence run costs a flight leg of battery, far more than 167 ms of deliberation. Coasting purchases immunity to aborting a deterrence run over one or two blurred frames — a lost track mid-run silently ends the mission’s core behavior. Raising the confirmation threshold further delays every legitimate response (and a fast-moving goose may exit the frame before confirmation); raising the coasting window further means steering longer on a motion prediction rather than a measurement — the track can drift arbitrarily far from the real animal, and a genuinely departed goose keeps consuming deterrence effort.




During an evening flight, the detector’s confidence scores sag across the whole flight and recall drops sharply, though the model performed well on the validation set. A teammate proposes fixing it by adding synthetic brightness reduction to the training augmentation. Diagnose the failure mode, evaluate the proposal — including what augmentation can and cannot fix — and name the runtime behavior the system should have exhibited in the meantime.







TipShow answer





This is distribution shift, lighting-change column: dusk imagery is statistically unlike the (presumably daytime) training and validation distribution, so the validation score stopped predicting field performance — and did so silently. Brightness augmentation is a partial, legitimate first step: it simulates small photometric variations around known examples and can recover some robustness cheaply. But dusk is closer to a missing domain than a perturbation — changed color balance, longer exposures adding motion blur, different backgrounds and animal behavior — and augmentation cannot conjure a domain the dataset lacks; the durable fix is targeted collection of evening footage (with the per-condition evaluation table extended to report dusk performance separately, so the gap is visible rather than pooled into a mean). At runtime, the sustained confidence anomaly should have triggered graceful degradation — widened persistence thresholds, a slowed search, holding position, or handing back to the operator — because a perception system that cannot notice its own degradation steers the vehicle on fiction.

text:
16.11 Try It
Part 1 — build the latency budget, then break it. Take the detector you trained in the previous chapter’s exercise (any YOLOv8n fine-tune serves) and benchmark it honestly on the most constrained hardware you have: time 1,000 inferences with time.perf_counter, discard the first 50, and report mean, p50, p99, and max. Then extend the measurement outward into a full budget: time preprocessing separately, time capture by comparing frame timestamps against arrival times if your camera exposes them, and lay out your own version of Figure 16.1. Now stress it: run the benchmark again for ten sustained minutes while logging latency per 10-second window (and processor temperature, if exposed) and look for the throttling drift; then run it once more with a competing CPU load (a video encode, a compile) and quantify what contention costs your p99. Finally, sweep the two levers: benchmark the n and s family members at input sizes 640, 416, and 320 — a 3 × 2 grid — and plot your own accuracy-latency frontier from the grid’s validation mAP and measured p99, marking which cells meet a 30 FPS throughput condition on your hardware. Write one sentence naming the cell you would fly and the two numbers that justify it.
Part 2 — add a tracker and measure what it buys. Run your detector over two or three minutes of continuous video containing your target class and log raw per-frame detections. First quantify the flicker: count single-frame false positives and 1–3-frame dropouts of genuinely present objects — the noise a state machine wired to raw detections would inherit. Then add tracking: either integrate a standard lightweight tracker (ByteTrack via the Ultralytics model.track() interface is a one-line change) or implement the chapter’s loop yourself — associate by IoU against a constant-velocity prediction, confirm after \(N\) frames, coast for \(M\). Measure the transformation: how many false positives survive to confirmed tracks at \(N = 5\); how many dropouts are bridged by coasting at \(M = 4\); how the object count over the clip compares, raw versus tracked, against a hand count. Then find the failure modes: engineer an occlusion (two targets crossing, or one passing behind cover) and observe whether you get an ID switch or a lost track, and at what coasting window the track survives. Close by computing your decision delay \(N \Delta t\) and writing two sentences: one defending your \(N\) and \(M\) in mission currency, one stating which tracking failure mode your consumer — count, alert, or pursuit — is most sensitive to, and why.

title: 17  Case Study: Wildlife Detection from the Air
text:
17.1 Learning Objectives
Every quantitative claim in this Part so far has been the book’s own: worked miniatures, illustrative budgets, published benchmark tables read at a distance. That was the right way to build the machinery, but machinery built entirely from first principles carries a standing risk — that the problems it prepares for are not quite the problems the field actually has. The corrective is a case study, and this chapter conducts one. Its primary text is a real research paper: a team at a New Zealand university spent years trying to detect sheep from a drone at 80 m, built their own dataset because none existed, compared five detector architectures head to head, and published what worked, what failed, and how fast each ran (Sarwar et al. 2020). Around that paper sits a wider literature — cattle counted from quadrotors (Barbedo et al. 2020), seabird colonies censused by the tens of thousands (Hayes et al. 2021), waterfowl surveys that include Canada geese by name (Zhai et al. 2025) — and a smaller, sharper literature on the other side of the camera: field measurements of what geese do when a drone approaches them (Bech-Hansen et al. 2019).
Reading published work is a skill this book has not yet asked for, so the chapter models it. The questions an engineer puts to a paper are the ones Part III has spent four chapters making precise: What are the problem’s constants — altitude, target size in pixels, background? Where did the dataset come from, how big is it, and how was it split? What does the headline metric actually compute, and at what operating point? And what did the authors not do — which claims are measurements and which are projections? Asked of the sheep paper, those questions return a study that lands with almost uncanny precision on the running example’s own territory: small whitish blobs against pasture, a detector meant for the aircraft, precision and recall argued over in percentage points. Asked of the goose literature, they return the constants the running example will actually face — including one, set by the geese themselves, that no previous chapter has priced.

title: 17  Case Study: Wildlife Detection from the Air
text:
17.2 Key Vocabulary

Onboard detection — running the detector on the aircraft’s own computer rather than on the ground or in the cloud; the deployment mode Part III has argued for throughout, and the stated (but not demonstrated) goal of the sheep study.
Aerial survey — a systematic overflight flown to detect, count, or map animals over an area; the observational mode of wildlife work, where the deliverable is a census rather than an intervention.
Scale variation — the change in a target’s apparent pixel size with altitude and terrain: the same animal spans a few pixels or tens of pixels depending on range, so a detector must either see all scales in training or have the scale pinned by flight discipline.
Small-object detection — the regime in which targets span roughly twenty pixels or fewer, too few to exhibit the internal detail general-purpose detectors rely on; the regime every high-altitude animal detector lives in.
Animal clustering — the tendency of animals to group until their bodies touch or overlap in the image, merging distinct individuals into one blob and defeating both segmentation and box-based non-maximum suppression; the dominant reported error source across species.
Centroid annotation — a ground-truth label consisting of a single point at each object’s center rather than a bounding box; natural for counting tasks and for small, overlapping targets, at the cost of the box-based metric machinery.
False negative (missed detection) — an animal present but not detected; in a survey it biases the count low, in the running example’s mission it leaves a goose undeterred.
False positive (false alarm) — a detection with no animal behind it — a rock, a fence post, a shed roof; in a survey it biases the count high, in the running example’s mission it spends a flight leg harassing grass.
Disturbance response — the measurable behavioral reaction of animals to an approaching aircraft, from raised-head vigilance to flushing (the whole flock taking flight); a function of altitude and approach distance that field studies quantify and flight plans must respect.

title: 17  Case Study: Wildlife Detection from the Air
section: 17.3 The Problem the Literature Keeps Meeting
text:
17.3 The Problem the Literature Keeps Meeting
Why is finding an animal from a drone hard, when finding a face in a phone photo is solved? A camera trap bolted to a tree answers by contrast. The trap’s viewpoint never changes; its scale is fixed, so a deer is always roughly the same size in pixels; and its background is the same background, every frame, so the oldest trick in computer vision — model the background, subtract it, and whatever remains is the animal — works. A drone forfeits all three properties at takeoff. Every frame arrives from a different pose and altitude, under a different lighting angle, over a different patch of ground, and the aerial-animal literature is, at bottom, the record of what that forfeiture costs. Five challenges recur across it — across cattle, seabirds, waterfowl, and sheep, across a decade of architectures — with a regularity that marks them as properties of the problem rather than of any one study. Figure 17.1 collects them.






Figure 17.1: The five recurring challenges of animal detection from a UAV, each quantified by the published literature, and the static-camera contrast that explains why all five are aerial-specific.



Three of the five deserve a sentence beyond the figure, because they will drive everything that follows. Scale variation is Part I’s ground-sample-distance relation acting as an adversary: a cattle-counting team reported a nominal 1 cm-per-pixel resolution at 30 m that wandered by ±20% with terrain relief alone, enough to break any size-based filtering until they built an explicit correction into the pipeline (Barbedo et al. 2020). Background contrast is not a fixed difficulty but a seasonal, lighting-dependent variable — the same team documented pasture ranging from bright green to pale yellow across a season — which is the field-scale version of the distribution-shift lesson the previous chapter drew, and it produces the single most consistent quantitative pattern in this literature: detection in the high 90s against simple backgrounds, dropping ten to twenty points wherever vegetation intrudes. And clustering is the failure that survives every architecture: animals bunch until their bodies touch, at which point a segmenter merges them, a box detector’s overlapping predictions get collapsed by the very non-maximum suppression step meant to clean duplicates — a seabird study watched legitimate penguin detections eliminated exactly this way (Hayes et al. 2021) — and a counting pipeline undercounts. Cattle F1 falls from 99.1% for isolated animals to 89.3% in four-animal clusters (Barbedo et al. 2020); geese, which raft together on water and graze in dense flocks, sit squarely in the danger zone.
The remaining two — motion, and structural false positives — round out the budget. Animals move between overlapping frames, so surveys double-count; the pragmatic mitigation in the cattle work is to fly when the animals are least active, a reminder that flight planning is part of the perception system. And at fifteen pixels, an animal is a shape and a color, which means everything sharing that shape and color is a candidate: white shed roofs depressed cattle F1 from 97.4% to 92.4% on the images containing them (Barbedo et al. 2020), rocks and shadows were logged as penguins (Hayes et al. 2021), and the sheep study’s own networks — the case this chapter now turns to — false-alarmed on fences.

title: 17  Case Study: Wildlife Detection from the Air
text:
17.4 Sheep at Eighty Metres
The sheep study’s problem statement is one sentence long and contains, on inspection, most of Part III. Detect sheep from a UAV flying at 80 m, where an adult sheep in a 2048 × 1080 video frame is “a rather nondescript whitish blob about 20 pixels long and 10 pixels wide” (Sarwar et al. 2020). Every number in that sentence is a decision. The altitude is a three-way compromise the authors state explicitly: 80 m — well under the 120 m legal ceiling that New Zealand shares with much of the world — bought enough detail on each sheep, enough paddock per frame to be useful, and minimal disturbance to the animals. The pixel count is that altitude passed through the pixels-on-target relation of the Images as Data chapter, and it is worth checking their arithmetic against ours, because the check teaches something. The platform was a consumer quadrotor whose camera family has a wide field of view of roughly 94°; spread over 2,048 columns that is about 0.8 mrad per pixel, so at 80 m each pixel covers about 6.5 cm of paddock, and a sheep roughly 1.2 m long by 0.6 m wide spans about 19 × 9 pixels — the paper’s 20 × 10, recovered from first principles. The same relation exposes the uncomfortable comparison: the running example’s depth camera in its 640-column mode subtends roughly 2.45 mrad per pixel, three times coarser, which is why its 0.35 m goose gets only 7 pixels at 20 m. The sheep team could fly at 80 m because their sensor spent 2,048 columns on the scene; angular resolution, not courage, sets the survey altitude.
Fifteen-ish pixels puts the task deep in small-object detection, and the paper’s literature review is a catalog of why that regime breaks the standard toolkit: small objects lack the internal detail — texture, parts, structure — that convolutional features feed on, and the authors note the YOLO family’s own documentation of its localization weakness on small targets, concluding that (as of the study’s writing) no off-the-shelf single-stage detector was good enough for the job (Sarwar et al. 2020). The claim has aged — the waterfowl literature below fields modern detectors against comparably small birds with strong results — but the underlying physics has not: a detector asked about a 15-pixel blob is reasoning from a few dozen informative values, and every design choice in the study flows from that scarcity.
The dataset had to be built, because — to the authors’ knowledge — no public dataset of drone imagery of sheep existed. This is the collect-and-label stage of the Building a Detection Pipeline chapter, executed for real, and the study’s choices read like that chapter’s checklist: video recorded at different times of day and in different weather, deliberately capturing the diversity of illumination, shadow, and background color; frames cut to 256 × 256 tiles; and, after augmentation, 22,742 labeled images split 80/10/10 into train, validation, and test. One labeling decision matters more than it first appears: every image was annotated twice, with bounding boxes and with centroid annotations — a point per sheep — because the five architectures under comparison consume different ground truth. The double labeling is the tell that this is a genuine comparison study: the same images, the same split, the same training budget, and only the detector varies.

title: 17  Case Study: Wildlife Detection from the Air
text:
17.5 Five Detectors, One Question
The comparison spans the two-stage/one-stage divide this Part has met twice already. On the two-stage side, the authors trained four networks through a modified R-CNN procedure — generate candidate regions, classify each — trimmed for the task: 1,000 region proposals per image instead of the classic 2,000, overlap thresholds tuned so that proposals count as positive examples more readily (small targets need every positive they can get), and a softmax-plus-cross-entropy classifier in place of the traditional support-vector-machine stage, purely to save training time. Two of the four were the era’s standard pretrained backbones, AlexNet and GoogLeNet, retrained on sheep. The other two were built for the occasion, and their design logic is the paper’s quiet thesis about small objects. Network-I is one convolutional layer, one fully connected layer, and a softmax — very nearly the smallest CNN that can exist — testing whether a tiny network suffices when the objects themselves carry so little detail. Network-II is seven convolution–batch-norm–ReLU–maxpool blocks that halve the spatial dimension at every step, 256 × 256 down to 2 × 2, deliberately densifying the features toward the end so that what survives is essentially the objects’ contour information — the authors’ explicit bet that a 15-pixel sheep is a contour and nothing else.
The one-stage entrant is the interesting one. Rather than YOLO or SSD — dismissed for their small-object record — the authors adopted a UNet: an encoder–decoder network with skip connections, producing not boxes but a full-resolution probability map, trained with the weighted Hausdorff distance as its loss (Sarwar et al. 2020). The ground truth here is the centroid labels, and the loss is built from the geometry of point sets — for estimated locations \(x\) with probabilities \(p_x\) and true centroids \(Y\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
L_T(p, Y) \;=\;& \frac{1}{|X|+\varepsilon} \sum_{x \in \Omega} p_x \, \min_{y \in Y} d(x,y) \\
&+ \frac{1}{|Y|} \sum_{y \in Y} \min_{x \in \Omega} \frac{d(x,y)+\varepsilon}{\,p_x^{\alpha} + \varepsilon/d_{\max}\,} \\
&+ L_1\!\left(C - \hat{C}\right),
\end{aligned}
\]
whose two main terms are a conversation between prediction and truth: the first says everywhere you claim a sheep, a true centroid should be nearby — it penalizes confident probability mass far from any real sheep, which is the false-positive direction; the second says every true centroid should have confident probability mass nearby — it penalizes real sheep that no prediction approaches, the false-negative direction. The third term trains a count: a scalar regressed from the network’s deepest features, passed through a SoftPlus, \(\hat{C} = \log(1 + e^{s})\), and rounded to give the number of sheep directly. The architecture’s stated limitation is single-class operation — one species, no more, without modification — but for small, complexly shaped, overlapping objects, centroids have a structural advantage over boxes: two touching sheep have two distinct centers even when no line separates their pixels, and there is no non-maximum suppression step to collapse them.
All five networks trained under identical conditions — stochastic gradient descent, 500 epochs, on a single desktop GPU (an NVIDIA GTX 1080) — and the results are unambiguous:

Figure 17.2 plots the table the way the previous chapter taught — accuracy against time — and the shape of the result is its own lesson. The previous chapter’s frontier forced a trade: more accuracy for more milliseconds, pick your point. Here there is no trade to make. The UNet wins every column at once — most accurate, fastest by a wide margin, tightest localization — because the four R-CNN-trained networks pay a structural tax it does not: a thousand region proposals per image, each classified separately, against the UNet’s single forward pass. Frontiers are properties of scaling within an architecture; across architectures, one design can simply dominate another for a given task, and finding the dominant design for this task — not the best-known design for tasks in general — is what the comparison bought.






Figure 17.2: The five detectors’ reported F1-score against time per image: the centroid-based UNet dominates on both axes at once, and every timing is a desktop-GPU measurement, not a flight measurement.



The failure modes are as instructive as the rankings, because they are the challenge taxonomy of Figure 17.1 reporting for duty. The two custom networks false-alarmed on fences — linear, high-contrast structures that share edge statistics with a sheep’s contour: structural false positives, exactly as the cattle and seabird studies predicted. The two pretrained backbones produced duplicate detections on the same sheep — several boxes on one animal — the pathology the detection-pipeline chapter’s matching rules would score as one true positive plus a string of false positives. And the winning UNet’s only reported failure is that it errs “when sheep are very close together” (Sarwar et al. 2020) — clustering, the challenge that survives even the architecture built to resist it. The best detector in the study fails exactly where the whole literature fails, which is the strongest evidence the chapter has that the taxonomy is real.

section: 17.6 Reading the Results with Part III’s Instruments
text:
17.6 Reading the Results with Part III’s Instruments
Now put the paper under this Part’s instruments, starting with a question a careful reader should already have: where is mAP? The Building a Detection Pipeline chapter presented mean average precision as the standard detector summary, yet this study reports precision, recall, and F1 at a single operating point, and never mentions it. The answer is structural, and it generalizes. The entire mAP construction stands on IoU — box-overlap matching between prediction and ground truth — and the winning network has no boxes: a centroid detector’s output is a set of points, so matching must be by distance (is there a predicted point near enough to this true centroid?), localization quality becomes the root-mean-square error of matched locations — the table’s RMSE column, under one pixel for the UNet — and the natural summary becomes the precision/recall/F1 triple computed at the model’s operating point. The lesson is not that the paper is deficient; it is that the metric follows the output representation, and an engineer comparing this study against a box-detector paper must down-convert both to the common currency — TP, FP, FN — before believing any comparison. The counts, and the two ways of being wrong they encode, survive every change of representation; the summary statistics on top of them do not.
The operating point itself repays reading. Precision 96.2%, recall 90.1%: when this detector says sheep, it is right 24 times in 25, and it finds nine sheep in ten. That asymmetry — precision comfortably above recall — is well suited to the study’s implicit mission, which is counting: false positives corrupt a census as badly as false negatives, and a follow-up count-regression head makes systematic over-detection actively harmful. The running example’s mission prices the same two errors differently, as the detection-pipeline chapter argued: an unharassed goose is a mission failure, an investigated patch of empty grass a battery expense, so the goose detector deliberately trades precision for recall. Same machinery, opposite operating point — chosen, in both cases, in mission currency. A survey counts; a deterrence system must not miss.
Then there is the claim in the title, and the word doing quiet work in it: towards detection of sheep onboard a UAV. Nothing in the paper runs on an aircraft. Every timing in Table 17.1 was measured on a desktop GTX 1080; the onboard argument is a closing projection — the UNet’s 0.14 s per image, about 7 FPS, is fast enough that the authors are “confident” the task could run in real or near-real time on an embedded board such as the Jetson Nano, whose specifications (128 CUDA cores, 4 GB of shared memory, 5 W) they cite (Sarwar et al. 2020). The previous chapter equips the reader to see precisely what stands between that confidence and a flight: a Jetson Nano is not a GTX 1080 with fewer fins — it is an order-of-magnitude step down in cores, memory bandwidth, and power, sharing its memory with an operating system and (on a real aircraft) a full sensing stack. The measure-on-the-target discipline, the tail-latency question, thermal behavior under sustained load, the capture-and-preprocess stages that the 0.14 s figure does not include — every honest-benchmarking rule of the Real-Time Inference chapter names a gap between this paper’s last section and a working onboard system. None of this is a criticism of the study, which claims exactly what it demonstrates and flags the rest as future work; the same group’s journal follow-up reports a refined multi-scale U-Net variant reaching approximately 98% F1 on the sheep task (Sarwar et al. 2021). It is, rather, a calibration for reading: a paper’s conclusions section is where measurement ends and projection begins, and the reader is responsible for knowing which side of that line each claim lives on. The gap between “towards onboard” and onboard is, not coincidentally, the exact territory the previous two chapters of this Part were written to cross.

title: 17  Case Study: Wildlife Detection from the Air
text:
17.7 From Sheep to Geese
How hard is the running example’s problem, relative to the case just studied? The cross-species literature gives a calibrated answer, and Figure 17.3 assembles it. White sheep on green pasture sit near the easy pole of aerial animal detection — the highest animal-background contrast the problem ever offers, no vegetation tall enough to occlude, modest flock densities in the imagery. Geese offer none of those mercies, and the waterfowl literature quantifies what their absence costs. The most directly on-point study is a drone-based waterfowl survey system whose detection classes include Canada, Brant, and Emperor geese by name: it reports detection accuracy above 95% for birds sitting on open water — a background as clean as pasture — falling to 80–85% in vegetated and cropped habitat where birds overlap with cover (Zhai et al. 2025). That ten-to-fifteen-point drop is the background-contrast challenge measured on geese, and it forecasts the running example’s own validation table: strong over mown grass, weakest exactly where geese actually loiter — pond margins, reed beds, crop stubble.






Figure 17.3: Reported accuracy across five aerial animal-detection studies, easy condition against hard condition within each: the recurring ten-to-twenty-point drop is the background and clustering cost, measured independently across species.



Two more bars on that figure locate the goose problem’s other axes. Where the task is a single visually distinct species against varied backgrounds, modern box detectors do well: a predecessor waterfowl effort — from the group behind the goose-inclusive survey system — assembled aerial duck datasets running to roughly 197,000 annotations and reported a Faster R-CNN baseline at 95.38% mAP (Zhang et al. 2022). Where the task becomes fine-grained — sixteen visually similar waterbird species on the Texas coast — reported mAP falls to 67.9% for the best model in a Faster R-CNN-versus-RetinaNet comparison (Kabra et al. 2022). The running example lives between those poles: two classes, goose and other_bird, which is fine-grained enough to be non-trivial (a distant duck and a distant goose are a few dozen pixels of brown each) but far from a sixteen-way identification. And on the sensing side, the literature has an answer the running example’s current payload does not exploit: for warm-bodied animals against cool backgrounds, thermal imaging substantially outperforms visible light alone — a wildlife-detection benchmarking effort reports large gains from thermal and fused streams over RGB (Chang et al. 2023) — and an open-source waterfowl identification tool built for management agencies pairs a thermal and an RGB sensor precisely to get detection from one and species identity from the other (Loken et al. 2025). Thermal is a payload and cost decision, not a free upgrade, but it is the standard escape hatch when visible-light contrast runs out — dusk, dawn, and vegetation — and worth holding in reserve against the robustness failure modes the previous chapter cataloged.
One more contrast between the sheep study and the goose problem is about time, and it is good news. The sheep team’s first act was building a dataset from nothing, because in their sub-field nothing public existed. The waterfowl sub-field, a few years on, is different: the goose-inclusive survey work publishes a companion dataset — reported at some nine thousand high-resolution aerial images carrying over half a million machine-assisted box annotations, Brant and Canada and Emperor geese among the classes, hosted in an open conservation-imagery repository (Zhai et al. 2025). For the running example’s collect stage, that changes the opening move the detection-pipeline chapter prescribed: public aerial goose imagery now exists at a scale no field campaign will match, ideal for pretraining and for populating the easy conditions — with the usual caveat that a dataset collected over an Alaskan lagoon shares neither the altitude profile, the optics, nor the backgrounds of the running example’s protected field, so the session-split discipline and the fly-your-own-camera collection round remain exactly as necessary as that chapter argued.

title: 17  Case Study: Wildlife Detection from the Air
text:
17.8 The Altitude the Animals Set
Every constraint on flight altitude so far in this book has come from physics or law: pixels-on-target from below, the 122 m ceiling from above, battery and coverage in between. The wildlife literature adds a constraint from an unexpected authority — the animals — and for geese specifically, it has been measured. A field study flew a consumer quadrotor toward 24 wild goose flocks of five species, at 50 m and 100 m altitude, and recorded the birds’ response (Bech-Hansen et al. 2019). The results draw a sharp line in the sky: approaches at 100 m overflew the flock without flushing it 74% of the time, while approaches below 100 m succeeded only 20% of the time — four flights in five, the flock was airborne before the aircraft arrived. Vigilance behavior began when the drone was still 200–300 m away, and the authors’ operational recommendation is blunt: to survey geese without disturbing them, launch about 500 m out and fly at about 100 m.
Set that finding against the pixels-on-target arithmetic and the bind is immediate. At the disturbance-safe altitude, with the running example’s camera in its 640-column mode,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{metres per pixel at } 100\ \text{m} &= R\,\theta_{\text{pix}} = 100 \times 2.45 \times 10^{-3} = 24.5\ \text{cm} \\
\text{pixels on a } 0.35\ \text{m goose} &= \frac{0.35}{0.245} \approx 1.4\ \text{pixels}.
\end{aligned}
\]
One and a half pixels is not a small target; it is no target at all. The altitude band the geese tolerate and the altitude band the detector needs do not overlap — for this sensor configuration — and Figure 17.4 draws the squeeze. The sheep study threaded the same needle without remarking on it: 80 m was gentle enough for sheep (a species far more drone-tolerant than wild geese) while its 2,048-column sensor still delivered 20-pixel animals. The general lesson is the one the figure’s footer states: the reconciling lever is angular resolution, not altitude. Feeding the detector from the camera’s full sensor width rather than the reduced mode, cropping a full-resolution region of interest around a candidate before classifying it — the Images as Data chapter’s trick — or carrying a longer lens all raise the detection floor toward the tolerance band, each at memory, compute, and field-of-view prices this Part has already taught the reader to itemize.






Figure 17.4: The altitude negotiation for the running example: detection range pushes the aircraft down, measured goose disturbance responses push it up, regulation caps it, and angular resolution is the lever that reconciles them.



A deterrence mission complicates the picture in an interesting way: flushing the flock is not a failure mode, it is the deliverable. But it is the deliverable on command — an uncommanded flush, triggered by the search pattern itself, scatters the flock before it has been localized and before the system can drive it in a chosen direction, and it habituates the birds to exactly the stimulus the mission depends on. Disturbance, in other words, is a resource to be spent deliberately, not leaked; and the broader literature on drone disturbance of wildlife — now substantial enough to support systematic review (Afridi et al. 2025) — is the reference the mission’s ethics chapter in Part V will draw on when it prices that spending properly. The nearest thing the published record offers to the running example as a whole system is instructive to name here: a field-tested agricultural drone that detects deer with a YOLO-family model, plans coverage paths over the protected crop, and returns to an autonomous charging station between sorties (Temesgen et al. 2025) — detection, planning, and endurance engineering composed into one loop. That composition — what the detector node publishes, who consumes it, and how the mission logic, planner, and platform close around it — is precisely the subject the System Architecture chapter of Part V takes up for the running example itself.
