title: 17  Case Study: Wildlife Detection from the Air
text:
17.9 What the Case Study Settles
Six findings travel from this chapter’s reading directly into the running example’s design file. First, the challenge taxonomy is real: scale variation, background contrast, clustering, motion, and structural false positives recur, quantified, across every species and architecture surveyed, so a goose pipeline budgets for all five or rediscovers them in the field. Second, the small-object regime governs architecture: below about twenty pixels, standard detectors weaken and task-shaped designs — up to and including abandoning boxes for centroids — can dominate the general-purpose toolkit on accuracy and speed at once. Third, the metric follows the output representation, and comparisons across papers are made in the common currency of TP, FP, and FN, at stated operating points, or not at all. Fourth, easy and hard conditions differ by ten to twenty points everywhere in this literature; the running example should plan for that spread — per-condition evaluation, targeted collection at the reedy margins — rather than be surprised by it. Fifth, “towards onboard” and onboard are separated by exactly the disciplines of the previous two chapters: target-hardware measurement, latency budgets, and the quantize-convert-deploy pipeline; a desktop-GPU timing is the beginning of that argument, never its end. And sixth, the animals are a stakeholder in the flight plan: measured disturbance responses set an altitude band as binding as any regulation, and reconciling it with pixels-on-target is a sensor-resolution problem the design must solve on purpose.
The Part’s story is now complete twice over — once as machinery, built across four chapters, and once as corroboration, read out of the published record of people solving the same problem for sheep, cattle, seabirds, and geese. What remains is everything the detector’s output feeds: the search patterns that put the camera over the right field, the pursuit behaviors that spend the detections, and the coordination that makes several aircraft more than the sum of their cameras. That is Part IV’s territory.

title: 17  Case Study: Wildlife Detection from the Air
text:
17.10 Check Your Understanding

The sheep study reports its animals as roughly 20 × 10 pixels at 80 m, while the running example’s goose spans only about 7 pixels at 20 m — four times closer, yet fewer pixels. Reconstruct the arithmetic that explains the apparent paradox, and state the general design lesson.







TipShow answer





Pixels on target depend on range and per-pixel angle: pixels ≈ (target size)/(R·θpix). The sheep platform spreads a ~94° field of view over 2,048 columns, giving θpix ≈ 0.8 mrad, so at 80 m each pixel covers ~6.5 cm and a 1.2 m sheep spans ~19 pixels. The running example’s 640-column mode spreads ~90° over 640 columns — θpix ≈ 2.45 mrad, three times coarser — so at 20 m each pixel covers ~4.9 cm and a 0.35 m goose spans ~7. The sheep is also simply a bigger animal. Lesson: angular resolution (sensor columns per degree) is as decisive as altitude, and it is a design variable — full-sensor capture, region-of-interest crops, or a longer lens buy detection range without descending.




The sheep study never reports mAP, the metric the detection-pipeline chapter called the standard detector summary. Explain the structural reason, name what the study reports instead for localization quality, and state the rule for comparing its results against a box-detector paper’s mAP.







TipShow answer





mAP is built on IoU matching, and IoU requires boxes; the winning UNet predicts centroids — points — so box overlap is undefined. Matching must instead be by distance (a predicted point close enough to a true centroid is a TP), and localization quality is reported as the RMSE of matched locations (0.783 px for the UNet). Precision, recall, and F1 survive unchanged because they are computed from TP/FP/FN counts, which any matching rule produces. The comparison rule: reduce both papers to counts and stated operating points before comparing — F1 at one threshold and mAP (an area over all thresholds) are not directly comparable numbers, and the matching criteria beneath them differ besides.




The sheep detector operates at precision 96.2%, recall 90.1%; the detection-pipeline chapter argued the goose detector should operate with recall above precision. Explain why both choices are correct, in the currency each mission uses.







TipShow answer





The operating point prices the two error types against mission costs. The sheep system’s implicit mission is counting: a false positive inflates the census exactly as a false negative deflates it, and the paper’s count-regression head makes systematic over-detection actively corrupting — so precision is kept high, accepting that one sheep in ten is missed in any single frame. The goose mission is deterrence: a false negative is a goose left undeterred (the mission’s purpose unmet), while a false positive costs battery and time investigating grass — so the threshold moves down, trading precision for recall. Same machinery, opposite corners: the confidence threshold belongs to the mission, not the model.




The winning UNet’s only reported failure is on sheep “very close together” — and clustering is also the dominant reported error for cattle, penguins, and vegetated waterfowl. Explain why clustering defeats box detectors and centroid detectors through different mechanisms, and name the machinery from the Real-Time Inference chapter that partially compensates in the running example.







TipShow answer





Box detectors on clustered animals produce heavily overlapping predictions, and non-maximum suppression — the step that removes duplicate boxes on one object — cannot distinguish “two boxes, one animal” from “two boxes, two touching animals,” so it collapses legitimate detections (the seabird study’s penguin failure). Centroid detectors avoid NMS but fail when the probability map’s peaks merge: two animals close enough that their predicted probability mass fuses into one blob yield one centroid. Both mechanisms undercount. In the running example, tracking helps at the margins: animals that separate even briefly across frames get distinct track identities that persistence and coasting can maintain through subsequent merges — though a flock that never separates remains undercounted, which is one reason flock-level behavior (Part IV) matters more than per-bird counts for deterrence.




The sheep paper concludes that detection “should be able” to run in real or near-real time onboard, citing the UNet’s 0.14 s per image and the Jetson Nano’s specifications. Using the previous chapter’s disciplines, list what this projection has not yet established, and estimate the first-order concern.







TipShow answer





The 0.14 s (~7 FPS) was measured on a desktop GTX 1080; the projection target is an order of magnitude weaker in cores, memory bandwidth, and power. Unestablished: (1) on-target latency — measured on the Nano, not inferred from spec sheets; (2) the full budget — 0.14 s covers inference, not capture, preprocessing, or postprocessing; (3) tail latency, not just a mean; (4) sustained thermal behavior at 5–10 W in an enclosure; (5) contention with the rest of a flight stack sharing the same memory and cores. First-order concern: raw throughput — a conservative scaling of a 0.14 s desktop-GPU inference onto Nano-class hardware lands at whole seconds per frame, far from frame rate, which is why the deployment chapters’ quantization, resolution, and runtime-optimization levers (int8, TensorRT) are not optional refinements but the difference between the projection and a working system.




The goose-inclusive waterfowl study reports >95% detection accuracy on open water but 80–85% in vegetated habitat. Restate this result in the vocabulary of the previous chapter’s robustness section, and derive from it two concrete rows in the running example’s evaluation plan.







TipShow answer





It is a quantified, condition-dependent performance gap: background composition is a dimension of the input distribution, and pooled accuracy hides a ten-to-fifteen-point spread between its easy and hard regions — exactly the argument for per-condition evaluation rather than one averaged number. Evaluation-plan rows: (1) report the goose detector’s metrics separately for open-ground/open-water backgrounds versus vegetated-margin backgrounds (reed beds, pond edges, crop stubble), so the gap is measured before deployment rather than discovered during it; (2) weight the next collection round toward the hard condition — vegetated-margin footage with partially occluded geese, labeled under the written class-boundary rules for partial visibility — since that is where both the literature and the mission’s geese concentrate the failures.

17.11 Try It
Part 1 — read a paper with the instruments. Choose one study from this chapter’s literature — the cattle, seabird, waterfowl, or multi-species waterbird paper — and extract it into a one-page engineering brief using this chapter’s template: the problem’s constants (altitude or GSD, target size in pixels, background types); the dataset (source, size, annotation type, split discipline — and whether the split would pass the detection-pipeline chapter’s leakage test); the method (architecture, one-stage or two-stage, loss, ground-truth representation); the evaluation (which metrics, at what operating point or threshold, and what the matching criterion was); and the claims ledger — two columns, measured versus projected, with every conclusion in the paper assigned to one. Close with three sentences: the result most transferable to the goose problem, the result least transferable and why, and the one experiment you would run that the authors did not.
Part 2 — reproduce the small-object cliff. Take the detector you fine-tuned in the detection-pipeline chapter’s exercise and measure how its accuracy degrades as targets shrink toward the sheep paper’s regime. Downsample your validation images by factors of 2 and 4 (then upsample back to the model’s input size, so input resolution is constant and only target scale changes — this simulates flying 2× and 4× higher), and run validation at each scale. Plot mAP@0.5 against median target size in pixels, and find your detector’s cliff — the target size at which mAP falls below half its full-scale value. Compare your cliff against the pixels-on-target table for your own camera: what is the maximum altitude at which your detector’s targets stay above the cliff? Finally, test one mitigation from this chapter: crop full-resolution regions of interest around targets in the downsampled-by-4 condition and re-run validation on the crops — and report, in two sentences, how much of the lost accuracy the resolution lever recovered and what the crop cost you in field of view.

title: 18  Coordinate Frames: From Camera to World
text:
18.1 Learning Objectives
Part III ended with a detector that works: a network on the companion computer that draws a box around a goose, and a depth camera whose aligned range image turns that box’s centre into a distance. The Building a Detection Pipeline chapter was explicit about what those two numbers buy — the box centre fixes a bearing, the depth value fixes a range along it, and together they pin the goose’s position in three dimensions. What that chapter deliberately left unexamined is the fine print on the word position. Position relative to what? The camera reports the goose relative to its own lens, in axes that tilt every time the airframe rolls and pivot every time it yaws. The autopilot, meanwhile, accepts Offboard setpoints in the local North-East-Down frame introduced in the PX4 Autopilot Stack chapter — axes nailed to the world, origin frozen at the launch point — and that chapter promised that the frame conventions behind its “z is down, so altitude is negative” sign discipline would get a chapter of their own in Part IV. This is that chapter.
The gap it closes is not a technicality. A detection expressed in camera coordinates is unusable as a navigation target: “6 metres out along the lens axis” means a different world location every few milliseconds as the aircraft moves, and handing it raw to the flight controller would command the drone toward wherever its own nose happens to point. Between the perception system and the navigation system there must sit a piece of mathematics — small, exact, and utterly load-bearing — that re-expresses the same physical point in the world’s coordinates. In the running example that mathematics lives in one module, frames.py, whose entire public surface is eight short functions; this chapter derives what those functions compute. The material is the first genuinely geometric machinery of the book, and it will be spent again immediately: every planner in this Part consumes targets and waypoints in the NED frame this chapter learns to reach.

text:
Name the three coordinate frames a vision-guided drone must reconcile — camera optical, body FRD, and local NED — and state each frame’s axis convention, what it is attached to, and why no two of them can be conflated.
Derive the optical-to-body transformation for a forward-facing camera as an axis remapping composed with a mounting-pitch rotation, and verify that the remapping is a proper rotation rather than a reflection.
Convert a PX4 attitude quaternion into a rotation matrix, and explain why quaternions rather than Euler angles carry the attitude across the body-to-NED step.
Carry a real detection numerically through the complete chain — pixel and depth to camera point, to body frame, to relative NED, to absolute NED — and sanity-check the result against physical expectations.
Express the full pipeline as a product of homogeneous transformations, and quantify the dominant error sources — extrinsic calibration, attitude error, synchronization latency, and depth uncertainty — as position error at the mission’s working ranges.

title: 18  Coordinate Frames: From Camera to World
text:
18.2 Key Vocabulary

Camera optical frame — the coordinate frame attached to the camera lens under the ROS REP-103 convention: x to the right of the image, y downward in the image, z forward along the viewing direction; the frame in which a depth camera reports every detected point.
FRD (Forward-Right-Down) — PX4’s body frame convention: x out the nose, y out the right side, z down through the belly; attached to the airframe and rotating with it, so a fixed world point has constantly changing FRD coordinates in flight.
NED (North-East-Down) — the local world frame in which PX4 navigates: x North, y East, z Down, origin at the point where the state estimator initialized (the launch point); the frame of every Offboard position setpoint, where altitude appears as negative z.
Rotation matrix — a 3 × 3 orthogonal matrix with determinant +1 that re-expresses a vector in a rotated frame without changing its length; its inverse is its transpose, which makes reversing any frame transformation computationally free.
Quaternion — a four-component representation of 3D orientation, written \([w, x, y, z]\) in PX4’s convention, that encodes an axis and an angle of rotation without the singularities of three-angle representations; the native attitude output of the flight controller’s estimator.
Gimbal lock — the degeneracy of Euler-angle representations in which two of the three rotation axes align (at ±90° pitch), collapsing a degree of freedom; the classical argument for carrying attitude as a quaternion.
Homogeneous transformation — a 4 × 4 matrix \(T = \begin{bmatrix} R & t \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) packaging a rotation and a translation so that chains of frame changes compose by ordinary matrix multiplication.
Camera intrinsics — the parameters of the camera’s own projection (focal lengths \(f_x, f_y\) and principal point \(c_x, c_y\), in pixels) that convert between a pixel coordinate and a direction in the optical frame.
Extrinsic calibration — the fixed rigid transform between the camera and the airframe — where the camera sits and how it is tilted — measured once at build time; an error here biases every detection the system will ever make, in the same direction.

title: 18  Coordinate Frames: From Camera to World
text:
18.3 One Point, Three Frames
Every sensor bolted to an aircraft measures in its own private coordinate system, and before any two measurements can be combined — or a measurement handed to a controller — they must be re-expressed in a common frame. The running example’s navigation pipeline threads exactly three. Figure 18.1 draws them side by side, and the differences among them are worth reading closely, because each difference is a transformation the software must perform.






Figure 18.1: The three coordinate frames of the vision-to-navigation pipeline: the camera optical frame attached to the lens, the FRD body frame attached to the airframe, and the local NED frame fixed to the world at the launch point.



The camera optical frame is the convention ROS standardizes in REP-103 and the one the running example’s Intel RealSense reports in: x points to the right of the image, y points down the image, and z points out of the lens along the viewing direction. The choice looks eccentric until it is set beside the image-coordinate convention from the Images as Data chapter — column index \(u\) increasing rightward, row index \(v\) increasing downward from a top-left origin. The optical frame is that screen convention extruded into 3D: x tracks \(u\), y tracks \(v\), and z carries the one thing a depth camera adds, range outward. A detected goose enters the pipeline as a point in this frame,
\[
P_C = \begin{bmatrix} x_C \\ y_C \\ z_C \end{bmatrix},
\]
and getting from the detector’s actual output — a pixel and a depth — to \(P_C\) is the projection geometry that chapter deferred. A pinhole camera maps a 3D point to the pixel \(u = f_x \, (x_C / z_C) + c_x\), where \(f_x\) is the focal length measured in pixels and \(c_x\) the image centre; run backward, with the depth value supplying \(z_C = Z\) directly (the RealSense reports perpendicular distance to the image plane, not slant range):
\[
x_C = \frac{(u - c_x)\, Z}{f_x}, \qquad y_C = \frac{(v - c_y)\, Z}{f_y}.
\]
The intrinsics come from the camera’s factory calibration, but a serviceable estimate falls out of geometry: a 90° horizontal field of view spread across 640 columns means the 320 columns on either side of centre span 45°, so \(f_x = 320/\tan 45^\circ = 320\) pixels. Take the goose the Images as Data chapter boxed at \((u, v) = (400, 300)\) in the 640 × 480 frame, and let the aligned depth lookup at that pixel return 6.00 m:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_C &= \frac{(400 - 320)(6.00)}{320} = 1.50\ \text{m} \\
y_C &= \frac{(300 - 240)(6.00)}{320} \approx 1.13\ \text{m} \\
P_C &= [\,1.50,\ 1.13,\ 6.00\,]\ \text{m}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The goose sits 6 m out along the lens axis, 1.5 m to the right of it, 1.13 m below it. That is a complete, correct 3D position — and it is useless to the autopilot, because every one of those numbers is measured against a lens that moves.
The drone body frame is PX4’s FRD convention: x forward out the nose, y right, z down. It is rigidly attached to the airframe and rotates with it. The camera is bolted to this frame — in the running example, tilted downward so the search pattern’s forward flight keeps the ground in view — so the relationship between optical and body coordinates is fixed at build time: a constant rotation, part of the system’s extrinsic calibration, that never changes in flight.
The local NED frame is the one the reader has been flying in since Part II: x North, y East, z Down, origin wherever the flight controller’s state estimator initialized — the launch point, which is why the very first Offboard example commanded -5.0 to mean five metres up. Unlike the other two frames it never rotates; it is the closest thing the system has to “the world.” Every position the autopilot publishes, and every setpoint it accepts, lives here.
Three frames, and two fundamentally different kinds of separation between them. Optical-to-body is a constant transform, knowable in advance to whatever precision the tape measure and the mounting jig allow. Body-to-NED is the aircraft’s attitude — it changes with every gust and every commanded turn, and no measurement made at build time can supply it. Something on the aircraft must estimate it continuously, and something does: the flight controller’s EKF, whose construction from gyroscope, accelerometer, and magnetometer evidence the Sensing the World chapter told in full. This chapter does not reopen that story. It stands on its result — the estimator publishes the vehicle’s attitude, as a quaternion, many times per second — and asks only what to do with it.

title: 18  Coordinate Frames: From Camera to World
text:
18.4 The Pipeline in One Equation
The complete journey from detection to navigation target is a single line of algebra:
\[
P_{NED} \;=\; P_{Drone} \;+\; R^{NED}_{Body}\, R^{Body}_{Camera}\, P_{Camera}.
\]
Read it right to left, the order in which the operations act. \(P_{Camera}\) is the detected point in the optical frame — the \([1.50, 1.13, 6.00]\) just computed. \(R^{Body}_{Camera}\) is the fixed extrinsic rotation that re-expresses it in the body frame; the superscript–subscript notation names the frames, “from Camera coordinates into Body coordinates.” \(R^{NED}_{Body}\) is the attitude rotation, built fresh from the EKF’s current quaternion, that re-expresses the body-frame vector in world axes. At that point the vector is world-aligned but still measured from the aircraft — a displacement, “the goose is 3.4 m East of me” — so the final step adds \(P_{Drone}\), the drone’s own EKF position, translating the origin from the aircraft to the launch point. Rotations first, translation last: rotations act on directions, and only after the directions are world-aligned does adding a world-frame position make sense. Figure 18.2 lays the chain out stage by stage, with the worked example’s numbers riding alongside; the two sections that follow derive its two rotations.






Figure 18.2: The full transformation pipeline from goose detection to navigation target, with the chapter’s worked example carried through every stage.

title: 18  Coordinate Frames: From Camera to World
section: 18.5 Optical to Body: A Relabeling and a Tilt
text:
18.5 Optical to Body: A Relabeling and a Tilt
Suppose first that the camera is mounted perfectly level, looking straight out the nose. Then the optical and body frames are the same physical directions wearing different labels, and the transformation is pure bookkeeping. Where does the camera’s z-axis point? Out of the lens — which is out of the nose: the body’s x. Where does the camera’s x point? Right in the image — the body’s y. The camera’s y? Down the image — the body’s z. Three questions, three answers, and the transformation is written:
\[
x_B = z_C, \qquad y_B = x_C, \qquad z_B = y_C,
\]
or as a matrix acting on \(P_C\),
\[
\Pi \;=\;
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 0 & 1 \\
1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 0
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
P'_B = \Pi\, P_C .
\]
\(\Pi\) deserves one check before it is trusted: is it a rotation? Its columns are orthonormal, and its determinant is \(+1\) — it is the cyclic permutation \((x, y, z) \to (z, x, y)\), and cyclic permutations of a right-handed triad are genuine rigid rotations. Had the mapping instead swapped exactly two axes, the determinant would be \(-1\): a reflection, which no physical mounting of a rigid camera can produce. A determinant check is thirty seconds of arithmetic that catches an entire class of frame bugs — coordinate systems accidentally mirrored — that otherwise surface as a drone that turns left toward geese on its right.
Real mountings are not level. The running example’s camera is pitched downward by a fixed angle \(\theta\) so that forward flight sweeps the ground; that tilt is a rotation about the body’s y-axis, applied after the relabeling:
\[
R_y(\theta) =
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos\theta & 0 & -\sin\theta \\
0 & 1 & 0 \\
\sin\theta & 0 & \cos\theta
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
P_B = R_y(\theta)\, P'_B .
\]
Sign conventions in rotation matrices are where frame code quietly goes wrong, so verify this one physically rather than trusting it. A goose dead ahead of the camera at distance \(d\) has \(P'_B = [d, 0, 0]\) after relabeling. If the camera is tilted down by \(\theta\), that goose is really below the aircraft’s horizontal plane — forward and down. Apply the matrix: \(R_y(\theta)\,[d, 0, 0]^T = [\,d\cos\theta,\ 0,\ d\sin\theta\,]^T\). Forward component \(d\cos\theta\), downward component \(d\sin\theta\) — positive z, and z is down in FRD. The matrix passes: positive \(\theta\) means a downward-looking camera, exactly the convention the mounting drawing uses. Together, \(R^{Body}_{Camera} = R_y(\theta)\,\Pi\), the fixed extrinsic rotation of the master equation.
Now run the worked example through, with the camera pitched down \(\theta = 45^\circ\) (\(\cos\theta = \sin\theta \approx 0.7071\)). Relabeling first:
\[
P'_B = \Pi \begin{bmatrix} 1.50 \\ 1.13 \\ 6.00 \end{bmatrix}
     = \begin{bmatrix} 6.00 \\ 1.50 \\ 1.13 \end{bmatrix},
\]
then the tilt:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_B &= 0.7071\,(6.00) - 0.7071\,(1.13) = 0.7071 \times 4.87 \approx 3.44 \\
y_B &= 1.50 \\
z_B &= 0.7071\,(6.00) + 0.7071\,(1.13) = 0.7071 \times 7.13 \approx 5.04 \\
P_B &= [\,3.44,\ 1.50,\ 5.04\,]\ \text{m}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The goose is 3.44 m ahead of the aircraft, 1.50 m to its right, and 5.04 m below it. Notice what the tilt did: most of what the camera called “forward” became, in the body’s honest axes, depth below the aircraft — which is exactly what a 45°-down camera looking at a ground target should report.

title: 18  Coordinate Frames: From Camera to World
section: 18.6 Body to NED: The Quaternion Does the Work
text:
18.6 Body to NED: The Quaternion Does the Work
The second rotation cannot be measured with a jig, because it is the aircraft’s attitude and it changes continuously. The flight controller’s estimator publishes it as a unit quaternion \(q = [w, x, y, z]\) — four numbers with \(w^2 + x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1\), encoding a single axis in space and a single angle of rotation about it (via \(w = \cos(\alpha/2)\), with \([x,y,z]\) the rotation axis scaled by \(\sin(\alpha/2)\)). The standard expansion converts it to the rotation matrix that carries body-frame vectors into NED:
\[
R(q) =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 - 2(y^2 + z^2) & 2(xy - wz) & 2(xz + wy) \\
2(xy + wz) & 1 - 2(x^2 + z^2) & 2(yz - wx) \\
2(xz - wy) & 2(yz + wx) & 1 - 2(x^2 + y^2)
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
P^{rel}_{NED} = R(q)\, P_B .
\]
Why a quaternion, when three Euler angles — roll, pitch, yaw — seem so much more legible? Four reasons, in ascending order of practical weight. Singularity: Euler angles represent attitude as three chained rotations, and at ±90° pitch two of the three axes align — gimbal lock — collapsing a degree of freedom, so the representation cannot even express which way the vehicle is turning; an acrobatic or wind-thrown multirotor visits that neighborhood, and estimator mathematics must not blow up when it does. Numerical stability: accumulated floating-point error pushes a quaternion slightly off unit length, and the fix is one renormalization — divide four numbers by their norm — whereas a drifting 3 × 3 matrix must be re-orthogonalized, an expensive and delicate repair. Interpolation: blending smoothly between two attitudes (needed whenever measurements must be aligned across time, as the error-budget section will want) is well defined for quaternions and badly behaved for Euler angles. And nativeness: the estimator the Sensing the World chapter described carries its attitude state as a quaternion; PX4 publishes it in exactly the \([w, x, y, z]\) order used here, so consuming it directly avoids a conversion — and every conversion between attitude conventions is an opportunity for a sign error that flies the aircraft somewhere surprising.
The matrix \(R(q)\), like every rotation matrix, is orthogonal: its inverse is its transpose. That property is worth pausing on because the software leans on it. Transforming a NED vector back to the body frame — which the mission logic needs whenever it asks “which way, in my own axes, is that world point?” — requires no matrix inversion at all, just \(R^T\), numerically exact and nearly free.
Put the worked example’s aircraft in a definite attitude: level flight, nose due East — a yaw of \(\psi = 90^\circ\), so \(q = [\cos 45^\circ, 0, 0, \sin 45^\circ] = [0.7071, 0, 0, 0.7071]\). Substituting \(w = z = 0.7071\), \(x = y = 0\) into \(R(q)\):
\[
R(q) =
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & -1 & 0 \\
1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix},
\]
which reads as a sanity check in matrix form: body-forward \([1,0,0]\) maps to \([0,1,0]\) — East, where the nose points; body-right maps to \([-1,0,0]\) — South, which is indeed to the right of an eastbound aircraft; body-down maps to down. Applying it:
\[
P^{rel}_{NED} = R(q) \begin{bmatrix} 3.44 \\ 1.50 \\ 5.04 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} -1.50 \\ 3.44 \\ 5.04 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
The goose is 3.44 m East of the drone, 1.50 m South of it (negative North), and 5.04 m below it — the same displacement as before, now expressed in axes that will not move when the aircraft does.

title: 18  Coordinate Frames: From Camera to World
text:
18.7 From Relative to Absolute
One step remains, and it is an addition. The vector just computed is world-aligned but drone-centred; the autopilot navigates toward absolute positions, measured from the EKF origin at the launch point. The drone knows its own position in that frame — the same estimate the Offboard examples of Part II consumed — so:
\[
P_{Goose} = P_{Drone} + P^{rel}_{NED}.
\]
Give the worked example’s aircraft the position \(P_{Drone} = [20.0,\ 5.0,\ -5.50]\) — 20 m North and 5 m East of launch, at the 5.5 m mission altitude the Part II survey plan flew:
\[
P_{Goose} = \begin{bmatrix} 20.0 \\ 5.0 \\ -5.50 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} -1.50 \\ 3.44 \\ 5.04 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 18.50 \\ 8.44 \\ -0.46 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
And here the chain hands back its first reward: a physical sanity check. \(D = -0.46\) m puts the computed goose 0.46 m above the launch-pad ground plane — about the height of a standing goose’s body. Had a sign been wrong anywhere in the chain — the pitch matrix transposed, the quaternion order scrambled, the remap mirrored — this number would come out as a goose 10 m underground or hovering at altitude, and the error announces itself. Checking the D-component of transformed ground targets against “roughly zero” is the cheapest regression test the perception-to-navigation boundary has, and the running example’s integration tests use exactly it.

18.7.1 The Same Chain as One Matrix
The pipeline was derived as rotate, rotate, add — but there is a standard notation that folds all three steps into products of a single object, and it is the notation every robotics text and every ROS transform library speaks. Append a 1 to each position vector, \(\tilde{P} = [x, y, z, 1]^T\), and package each frame change as a 4 × 4 homogeneous transformation:
\[
T = \begin{bmatrix} R & t \\ \mathbf{0}^T & 1 \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
T\,\tilde{P} = \begin{bmatrix} R P + t \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
The appended 1 is the whole trick: it multiplies the translation column \(t\), so a single matrix–vector product now performs rotate-and-translate. Chains of frames compose by plain matrix multiplication, in the same right-to-left reading order as before:
\[
\tilde{P}_{W} = T^{World}_{Drone}\; T^{Drone}_{Camera}\; \tilde{P}_C,
\]
where \(T^{Drone}_{Camera}\) carries the extrinsic rotation \(R_y(\theta)\,\Pi\) together with the camera’s mounting offset from the vehicle centre (a few centimetres this chapter has quietly neglected — the homogeneous form is where it stops being neglectable), and \(T^{World}_{Drone}\) carries the attitude rotation \(R(q)\) together with \(P_{Drone}\). The subscript-cancellation reading — Camera cancels against Camera, Drone against Drone — makes long chains auditable at a glance, and inverting any link is mechanical: \(T^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} R^T & -R^T t \\ \mathbf{0}^T & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). For a two-link chain the explicit form of this chapter and the homogeneous form are the same arithmetic; the homogeneous form wins the moment a third frame appears — a gimbal between camera and body, a second aircraft, a map frame above NED — which is precisely the direction this Part is headed.

title: 18  Coordinate Frames: From Camera to World
text:
18.8 The Module in Code
All of the above compiles down to remarkably little software. The running example’s frames.py exposes the two rotations, their inverses, and the composed chain — eight functions, each a few lines of NumPy:



Table 18.1: The frame-conversion module’s public surface.









Function
Computes




quat_to_rot(q)
\(R(q)\): the body-to-NED rotation matrix from a PX4 \([w,x,y,z]\) quaternion


optical_to_body(v, pitch)
\(R_y(\theta)\,\Pi\,v\): axis remap plus mounting-pitch correction


body_to_ned(v, q)
\(R(q)\,v\): attitude rotation into world axes


body_to_optical(v, pitch) / ned_to_body(v, q)
the inverses, via transposes — no matrix inversion anywhere


optical_to_ned_point(p, q, drone, pitch)
the full chain: \(P_{Drone} + R(q)\,R_y(\theta)\,\Pi\,p\)


ned_point_to_optical(p, q, drone, pitch)
the full chain backward






The composed forward function is the master equation verbatim:
def optical_to_ned_point(p_opt, q_wxyz, drone_ned, camera_pitch_rad=0.0):
    """Detected point (optical frame) -> absolute local NED position."""
    rel_ned = body_to_ned(optical_to_body(p_opt, camera_pitch_rad), q_wxyz)
    return np.asarray(drone_ned, dtype=float) + rel_ned
Two design choices in the module repay attention. First, every inverse is computed by transpose, never by np.linalg.inv — the orthogonality of rotation matrices, cashed in as both speed and numerical exactness. Second, the module ships its own inverse chain, ned_point_to_optical(), whose stated consumers are simulation and testing: plant a synthetic goose at a known NED position, run the inverse chain to compute what the camera should see, feed that to the pipeline as a fake detection, and the forward chain must reproduce the planted position to machine precision, for randomized attitudes and camera angles. A transform library that round-trips thousands of random points is trustworthy in a way no amount of staring at sign conventions can establish — geometry code fails silently, so it must be tested loudly.
Where this module sits in the running system is a story for later: the Systems Architecture chapter in Part V draws the full ROS 2 node graph, with the frame conversion living between the Detector’s camera-frame output and the Mission Manager’s world-frame target topic — the position it must occupy, since it is the only component that consumes both the perception stream and the flight controller’s state estimate at once.

title: 18  Coordinate Frames: From Camera to World
text:
18.9 Where the Centimetres Go
The derivations above are exact; the numbers fed into them are not, and a frame chain is an error amplifier with a specific, predictable structure. The governing approximation: a small angular error \(\delta\theta\) (in radians) anywhere in the rotation chain displaces a target at range \(r\) by roughly \(r\,\delta\theta\) — angle errors become position errors in proportion to distance. Four sources dominate, and each is worth pricing at the worked example’s 6 m range.
Extrinsic calibration error. If the mounting pitch entered as 45.0° is really 47.0°, every detection is rotated 2° wrong: \(6 \times 0.035 \approx 21\) cm — and systematically, always the same direction, so no amount of averaging removes it. This is why extrinsics are calibrated rather than read off the CAD drawing, and why a camera knocked in a hard landing must be recalibrated.
Attitude estimation error. The EKF’s attitude is good but not perfect; a 1° error displaces the 6 m target by about 10 cm. This error the transform chain simply inherits — the Sensing the World chapter’s error budget, resurfacing as position error on every target the perception system reports.
Synchronization latency. The subtlest source: the attitude used must be the attitude when the frame was exposed, not when the transform runs. Detection inference takes tens of milliseconds; if the aircraft is yawing at 30°/s and the transform naively grabs the latest quaternion 60 ms after exposure, it applies an attitude 1.8° stale — \(6 \times 0.031 \approx 19\) cm — and the drone’s own position is stale too: at 3 m/s, another 18 cm. The mitigation is bookkeeping, not mathematics: timestamp every image at exposure, buffer the state estimates, and transform with the attitude interpolated to the image’s timestamp (interpolation being one of the quaternion’s four advantages, now earning its keep).
Depth uncertainty. Stereo depth error grows roughly quadratically with range; at 6 m the running example’s camera is credibly a couple of percent off — 12 cm or more, along the ray.
Stack the worst cases and the transformed goose position carries perhaps half a metre of error at 6 m — larger than the goose itself. Whether that is a crisis depends entirely on the consumer, and for the running example it is not: the mission requires flying toward a goose closely enough to deter it, a metre-scale task, and the errors shrink as range closes. But the budget explains two design facts. It is why the module’s documentation flags vision/PX4 synchronization and calibration as its leading limitations, ahead of anything algorithmic; and it is why a target position is treated downstream as an estimate to be refined — re-detected, re-transformed, and filtered as the aircraft approaches — rather than a coordinate to be trusted once. What the planner does with a stream of imperfect world-frame targets is exactly where this Part goes next.

title: 18  Coordinate Frames: From Camera to World
text:
18.10 Check Your Understanding

Name the three coordinate frames of the vision-to-navigation pipeline, state each one’s axis convention and what it is attached to, and explain in one sentence why a detection expressed in the first frame cannot be sent to the autopilot directly.







TipShow answer





Camera optical frame (ROS REP-103): x right in the image, y down in the image, z forward out of the lens; attached to the camera. Body FRD frame (PX4): x forward, y right, z down; attached to the airframe and rotating with it. Local NED frame: x North, y East, z Down; fixed to the world with origin where the EKF initialized (the launch point). A detection in the optical frame is measured against axes that translate and rotate with the aircraft, so the same numbers describe a different world location every instant — while PX4’s Offboard setpoints are interpreted in the world-fixed NED frame; without the transformation the drone would be commanded toward wherever its lens happens to point.




The optical-to-body relabeling maps \((x_C, y_C, z_C) \to (z_C, x_C, y_C)\). Show that this is a proper rotation, and explain what it would mean — mathematically and physically — if a proposed axis mapping had determinant \(-1\).







TipShow answer





Write the mapping as the permutation matrix \(\Pi\) with rows \([0,0,1]\), \([1,0,0]\), \([0,1,0]\). Its columns are orthonormal and its determinant is \(+1\) (expanding along the first row: \(1 \times (1\cdot 1 - 0) = +1\)), so it is orthogonal with determinant \(+1\) — a proper rotation; equivalently it is a cyclic permutation of a right-handed triad, which is always achievable by rigid rotation. A determinant of \(-1\) would make the map a reflection: it would turn a right-handed frame into a left-handed one, which no physical re-orientation of a rigid camera can do. In code, such a matrix signals a bug — typically two axes swapped or one sign dropped — and its symptom in flight is mirrored behavior, such as steering left toward a target on the right.




A goose is detected dead centre in the image at depth 10.0 m, with the camera pitched down 30°. Compute its body-frame position and interpret each component.







TipShow answer





Dead centre means \(P_C = [0, 0, 10.0]\). Relabeling: \(P'_B = [10.0, 0, 0]\). Pitch correction with \(\cos 30^\circ = 0.866\), \(\sin 30^\circ = 0.5\): \(x_B = 0.866 \times 10.0 = 8.66\), \(y_B = 0\), \(z_B = 0.5 \times 10.0 = 5.00\), so \(P_B = [8.66, 0, 5.00]\) m. The goose is 8.66 m ahead of the aircraft along its nose, dead on the centreline, and 5.00 m below it — the 10 m of “camera forward” split by the 30° tilt into forward and down components, as a downward-pitched camera watching a ground target requires.




The aircraft flies level with its nose due West, so \(q = [0.7071, 0, 0, -0.7071]\). Build \(R(q)\), transform \(P_B = [4, 1, 2]\) m into relative NED, and check the result against compass intuition.







TipShow answer





With \(w = 0.7071\), \(z = -0.7071\), \(x = y = 0\): the off-diagonal terms give \(2(xy - wz) = -2wz = +1\) and \(2(xy + wz) = -1\), so \(R(q) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Then \(P^{rel}_{NED} = [\,0\cdot4 + 1\cdot1,\ -4,\ 2\,] = [1, -4, 2]\). Intuition check: body-forward maps to \([0,-1,0]\) — due West, where the nose points — so 4 m ahead becomes 4 m West (East \(= -4\)) ✓; the right side of a westbound aircraft faces North, so 1 m right becomes 1 m North ✓; 2 m below stays 2 m down ✓.




Give the two strongest practical reasons the body-to-NED rotation is carried as a quaternion rather than as roll-pitch-yaw Euler angles, and one reason specific to integrating with PX4.







TipShow answer






No singularities: Euler angles suffer gimbal lock at ±90° pitch, where two rotation axes align and a degree of freedom vanishes — an attitude a wind-thrown or aggressively maneuvering multirotor can reach, and one at which Euler-based mathematics degenerates. (2) Cheap numerical hygiene and well-defined interpolation: floating-point drift is repaired by renormalizing four numbers, and blending between two attitudes — needed when interpolating the attitude to an image’s exposure timestamp — is well behaved for quaternions and pathological for Euler angles. The PX4-specific reason: the flight controller’s EKF represents and publishes attitude natively as a \([w, x, y, z]\) quaternion, so consuming it directly eliminates a convention conversion — and every attitude-convention conversion is a classic source of sign and ordering bugs.





The detector’s inference takes 80 ms, the transform uses the latest attitude rather than the attitude at exposure, and the aircraft is yawing at 45°/s while tracking a goose at 5 m range. Estimate the resulting position error, and name the fix.







TipShow answer





The attitude is stale by \(45 \times 0.08 = 3.6^\circ = 0.063\) rad; at 5 m range the target displaces by roughly \(r\,\delta\theta = 5 \times 0.063 \approx 31\) cm — comparable to the whole goose, from timing alone (and if the aircraft is also translating, its stale position adds directly on top). The fix is synchronization, not better math: timestamp each frame at exposure, buffer the flight controller’s attitude and position estimates, and evaluate the transform with the state interpolated to the frame’s timestamp — quaternion interpolation making the attitude half of that well defined.

title: 19  Path Planning on the Edge: Search Grids and Coverage Algorithms
text:
19.1 Learning Objectives
The Coordinate Frames chapter closed by handing this Part a stream of imperfect world-frame targets and asking what a planner does with them. Before that question can be answered, there is an older debt to pay. Back in Part II, the Mission Scripting chapter flew a lawnmower survey that had been clicked out by hand on QGroundControl’s map — and admitted, in the same breath, that the pattern was not an aesthetic choice but a computable one: the row pitch is a sensor parameter, and “the entire pattern can be computed from the field polygon and the sensor footprint.” This chapter performs that computation. It is the first planning algorithm of the book, and deliberately the simplest: a function that takes a bounding box and a sweep spacing and returns the ordered NED waypoint list the Mission Scripting chapter’s state machine already knows how to fly.
The chapter then does something the hand-drawn version never had to: it asks what the algorithm is for, and when it is the wrong tool. A lawnmower path answers one specific question — how does a drone with a finite sensor footprint guarantee it has seen every point of an area? — and it answers it without a map, without obstacles, and in microseconds of arithmetic. The other canonical planning question — how do I get from here to there, past things in the way? — belongs to a different family entirely: graph search, whose standard-bearer is A*. The running example needs both. Searching an open field for geese is a coverage problem; closing on a detected goose, re-routing when the world changes, and threading obstacles are point-to-point problems. Knowing which question is being asked, before reaching for an algorithm, is most of what “path planning” means in practice — and both algorithms here are chosen for the same reason the rest of the stack was: they run comfortably on the low-power companion computers of Part I, where planning shares a processor with inference and telemetry.

title: 19  Path Planning on the Edge: Search Grids and Coverage Algorithms
text:
19.2 Key Vocabulary

Coverage algorithm — a path planner whose goal is not to reach a point but to pass a sensor’s footprint over every point of a region; its output is judged by completeness of coverage, not by path length to a destination.
Lawnmower search pattern (parallel sweep, boustrophedon) — the canonical coverage path: long parallel legs spaced at most one sensor swath apart, joined by short row steps, flown in alternating directions so each leg begins where the last one ended.
Search bounding box — the axis-aligned rectangle \([x_{\min}, x_{\max}] \times [y_{\min}, y_{\max}]\), expressed here in local NED coordinates, that defines the region a search must cover; together with the spacing, the complete parameterization of a lawnmower path.
Swath width (\(w\)) — the width of ground a downward-looking sensor images along one leg, set by altitude and field of view; the physical quantity the sweep spacing must not exceed.
Sweep spacing (\(s\)) — the perpendicular distance between adjacent legs; chosen as the swath width derated by a deliberate overlap fraction, so that imperfect flying still leaves no unseen strip.
Cross-track error (\(e_{ct}\)) — the perpendicular distance from the vehicle’s actual position to the straight line of its current leg; the along-track coordinate measures progress, the cross-track coordinate measures straying.
A* search — best-first graph search that expands nodes in order of \(f(n) = g(n) + h(n)\), the cost incurred so far plus a heuristic estimate of the cost remaining; with an admissible heuristic it returns a minimum-cost path.
Admissible heuristic — a heuristic that never overestimates the true remaining cost (straight-line distance is the standard example for spatial planning); the property that upgrades A* from “usually good” to provably optimal.
Dynamic re-routing — re-planning in flight when the world model changes — a new obstacle, a moved target, an updated cost map — either by re-running the planner or by incremental methods that repair the previous solution instead of discarding it.

title: 19  Path Planning on the Edge: Search Grids and Coverage Algorithms
section: 19.3 The Spacing Comes from the Sensor
text:
19.3 The Spacing Comes from the Sensor
Every parameter of a lawnmower path except one is geometry the operator already owns: the bounding box is the field to be searched, the altitude is fixed by the mission (5.5 m for the running example’s survey, comfortably under the regulatory ceiling), and the leg length falls out of the box. The one genuinely new number is the sweep spacing, and it comes from the camera.
A camera looking straight down from altitude \(h\) with a horizontal field of view \(\theta_{\text{fov}}\) images a strip of ground — the swath — whose width is a single line of trigonometry: half the swath subtends half the field of view, so
\[
w = 2\,h \tan\!\left(\frac{\theta_{\text{fov}}}{2}\right).
\]
The running example’s depth camera was estimated in the Coordinate Frames chapter to have roughly a 90° horizontal field of view. At the survey altitude:
\[
w = 2 \times 5.5 \times \tan 45^\circ = 11.0\ \text{m}.
\]
Flying adjacent legs exactly 11 m apart would tile the field with zero margin: any imperfection — a metre of GNSS scatter, a gust, a goose at the seam between swaths imaged too obliquely to detect — opens an unseen strip. The standard remedy is to derate the spacing by an overlap fraction \(\beta\):
\[
s = w\,(1 - \beta),
\]
and \(\beta = 0.4\) — a common choice when detection reliability at the swath edges is doubtful — gives \(s = 11.0 \times 0.6 = 6.6\) m. Here the book’s threads tie together pleasingly: the real hand-drawn survey that the Mission Scripting chapter dissected had a row pitch of roughly 6.5 m, drawn by eye on a map. The eye was right, and now it is clear why it was right: 6.5 m is what a 90° camera at 5.5 m altitude with 40 % overlap requires. The hand and the arithmetic agree — but only the arithmetic scales, transfers to a new altitude, and can run on board.
Two caveats keep the model honest. First, the formula assumes a nadir-pointing camera; the running example’s camera is pitched 45° forward (the extrinsic the Coordinate Frames chapter calibrated), which projects a trapezoidal footprint ahead of the aircraft rather than a rectangle below it. The conservative practice is to use the footprint’s narrowest cross-track extent as \(w\), and the nadir formula is a serviceable stand-in at survey altitudes. Second, the formula is the reason the search flies at constant altitude: \(w\) scales linearly with \(h\), so an altitude that wanders makes the swath width wander with it, and a spacing chosen for 5.5 m silently loses its overlap margin at 4 m. Constant altitude is not a stylistic requirement — it is what holds \(w\), and therefore the coverage guarantee, still.

section: 19.4 The Generator: Two Parameters In, a Mission Out
text:
19.4 The Generator: Two Parameters In, a Mission Out
With \(s\) in hand, generating the path is a short exercise in careful bookkeeping. The region is an axis-aligned bounding box in local NED — \([x_{\min}, x_{\max}]\) north–south, \([y_{\min}, y_{\max}]\) east–west — and the legs will run north–south (the long axis), stepping east between legs. Three decisions make the algorithm correct rather than merely plausible:

Round the leg count up, never the spacing. The box width \(W = y_{\max} - y_{\min}\) is rarely an exact multiple of \(s\). Taking \(n = \lceil W / s_{\max} \rceil + 1\) legs and then recomputing the actual step as \(W / (n - 1)\) shrinks the spacing to fit — the step can only come out at or below the maximum the sensor allows, so rounding can tighten coverage but never loosen it.
Alternate leg directions. Even-indexed legs fly south-to-north, odd-indexed legs north-to-south. Each leg then begins where the previous one ended, and the row step between legs needs no waypoint of its own — it is simply the flight from one leg’s last waypoint to the next leg’s first.
Emit waypoints, not trajectories. The output is an ordered list of \((N, E, D)\) triples — exactly the data structure the Mission Scripting chapter’s NAVIGATE state consumes, streaming each waypoint as an Offboard setpoint and advancing on the acceptance-radius arrival test. The planner plans; the machinery that flies is already built.

import math

def lawnmower(x_min, x_max, y_min, y_max, s_max, altitude):
    """Parallel-sweep (lawnmower) coverage path over a NED bounding box.

    Legs run north-south (along x); the sweep steps east (along y).
    Returns an ordered list of (north, east, down) waypoints.
    """
    width = y_max - y_min
    n_legs = max(2, math.ceil(width / s_max) + 1)
    step = width / (n_legs - 1)      # actual spacing: <= s_max by construction
    z = -altitude                    # NED: down is positive, so up is negative
    waypoints = []
    for i in range(n_legs):
        y = y_min + i * step
        if i % 2 == 0:               # even legs: fly south -> north
            waypoints.append((x_min, y, z))
            waypoints.append((x_max, y, z))
        else:                        # odd legs: fly north -> south
            waypoints.append((x_max, y, z))
            waypoints.append((x_min, y, z))
    return waypoints
Twenty lines, no dependencies beyond ceil, and a run time measured in microseconds — a planner that could re-run every second on the smallest computer in Part I’s inventory without anyone noticing. Figure 19.1 traces a worked call: a fresh illustrative search area, a 60 m × 33 m box north-east of the launch point, at the survey’s 5.5 m altitude with \(s_{\max} = 6.6\) m.






Figure 19.1: The lawnmower generator’s output for a 60 m × 33 m bounding box with 6.6 m sweep spacing: six alternating legs, twelve waypoints, and the swath-overlap geometry that justifies the spacing.



Follow the arithmetic through. \(W = 33\) m and \(s_{\max} = 6.6\) m give \(n = \lceil 5.0 \rceil + 1 = 6\) legs, and the recomputed step is \(33 / 5 = 6.6\) m exactly. Six legs of 60 m and five row steps of 6.6 m make the total track
\[
d = nL + (n-1)\,s = 6(60) + 5(6.6) = 393\ \text{m},
\]
and the track length immediately audits the schedule, the same trick the Mission Scripting chapter played on its plan file. At that survey’s camera-friendly 1.5 m/s:
\[
t = \frac{393}{1.5} = 262\ \text{s} \approx 4.4\ \text{min},
\]
which busts the 3.5-minute search-leg allocation in Part I’s mission time budget. At 2.0 m/s the same path takes 197 s ≈ 3.3 min and fits. This is the kind of trade a generator surfaces before anything flies: spacing is quantized (the \(\lceil\cdot\rceil\) means widening \(s_{\max}\) only drops a whole leg at discrete thresholds — here, not until \(s_{\max} \ge 8.25\) m, a 25 % overlap), while speed is continuous, so speed is usually the first lever pulled. Whether the detector still performs at 2.0 m/s of motion blur is a question for the frame-rate and latency budgets of Part III — planning decisions ripple into perception, and the budget arithmetic is where the ripple shows up.
The computed version also settles an audit the hand could not. The Mission Scripting chapter’s real survey put four legs at 6.5 m pitch — spanning about 19.5 m — inside a fenced field nearly 39 m across. Run the generator on that fence and it asks for seven legs, not four: the hand-drawn mission swept roughly half its field, a shortfall invisible on the map view and instant in the arithmetic. Nothing about the flight was wrong; the coverage claim was, and only the computation noticed.
Two practical notes complete the generator. Real search areas are rarely aligned with north: the standard treatment is to rotate the region’s corner coordinates into an axis-aligned frame, generate the path there, and rotate the waypoints back — a single 2D rotation matrix each way, machinery the Coordinate Frames chapter made routine. And the bounding box must sit strictly inside the geofence polygon of the Geofencing and Fail-Safes chapter, with margin for the cross-track error the next section budgets — a generated path that grazes the fence line is a generated failsafe trigger.

title: 19  Path Planning on the Edge: Search Grids and Coverage Algorithms
section: 19.5 Cross-Track Error Is a Coverage Budget
text:
19.5 Cross-Track Error Is a Coverage Budget
The generator’s output is a guarantee written in pencil: if the aircraft flies each leg where the arithmetic put it, every point of the box passes under the camera. The quantity that measures “where the arithmetic put it” is cross-track error. For the leg from waypoint \(A\) to waypoint \(B\), define the unit tangent and normal
\[
\hat{t} = \frac{B - A}{\lVert B - A \rVert},
\qquad
e_{ct} = (p - A) \cdot \hat{n},
\]
where \(p\) is the vehicle’s estimated position and \(\hat{n}\) is \(\hat{t}\) rotated 90° in the horizontal plane. The projection onto \(\hat{t}\) is the along-track coordinate — how far down the leg the vehicle has progressed; the projection onto \(\hat{n}\) is the cross-track coordinate — how far it has strayed off the line. A signed \(e_{ct}\) (positive right of track, negative left) is more useful than a distance, because its sign says which way to steer back.






Figure 19.2: Cross-track error defined on a single leg, and its consequence across adjacent legs: opposing drifts larger than the swath overlap open a strip of ground the camera never sees.



Figure 19.2 shows why this number owns a line in the mission requirements rather than a footnote. The swath of a leg flown with error \(e_i\) is displaced by \(e_i\); adjacent swaths, planned to overlap by \(w - s\), stop overlapping when the two legs drift apart by more than that margin:
\[
e_{i+1} - e_i > w - s \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{a strip between legs is never imaged.}
\]
For the worked numbers, \(w - s = 11.0 - 6.6 = 4.4\) m, and the worst case — adjacent legs drifting in opposite directions — splits the budget evenly: each leg may stray at most \((w - s)/2 = 2.2\) m before the coverage claim fails. Now the budget can be spent, item by item, and the items are all familiar. The position estimate itself carries metre-scale GNSS scatter — the same scatter that set the floor under the Mission Scripting chapter’s acceptance radius — and the vehicle can only hold the line as well as it knows where the line is. Steady wind adds a systematic offset: the position controller flies crabbed into the wind, converging to the leg with some residual bias rather than tracking it exactly. And the acceptance radius contributes at the leg ends: with the 1.5 m radius that chapter chose, each corner is cut up to 1.5 m before the turn begins, shaving the swath short at the box’s north and south edges. Metre-scale error against a 2.2 m budget is not comfortable — it is roughly half the budget spent before the wind blows — which is precisely why the requirement is phrased minimize cross-track error, and why the overlap fraction \(\beta\) exists at all: \(\beta\) is the coverage guarantee’s insurance policy, priced in extra legs and minutes of battery.
One subtlety separates good leg-tracking from naive waypoint-chasing. A controller that simply steers at the next waypoint from wherever it currently is will happily fly a diagonal back to the corner after a gust — correct arrival, wrong swath, since the diagonal’s camera footprint is not the planned leg’s. Tracking the line — feeding the controller a setpoint that advances along the leg while nulling \(e_{ct}\) — keeps the flown swath congruent with the planned one. The cascaded position controller of Part II does this well when the streamed setpoints march down the leg at the commanded ground speed rather than jumping to the far corner in one step; the distinction costs a few lines in the NAVIGATE state and buys back most of the wind’s share of the budget.

title: 19  Path Planning on the Edge: Search Grids and Coverage Algorithms
text:
19.7 Two Planners, One Mission
Set side by side, the two algorithms are less rivals than answers to different questions, and the running example’s mission asks both in sequence:



Table 19.1: Coverage search versus point-to-point search: the same word “planning,” two different problems.











Lawnmower coverage
A* graph search




Question answered
“Have I seen every point of the area?”
“What is the shortest way to that point?”


World model required
None — a bounding box and a sensor footprint
An occupancy grid or graph with costs


Obstacles
Assumed absent (open field)
The entire point


Output
Fixed waypoint list, known length in advance
Path dependent on the map; length known only after search


Guarantee
Complete coverage, if cross-track error stays within the overlap margin
Minimum-cost path, if the heuristic is admissible


Compute cost
Microseconds, independent of world size
Milliseconds and up, scales with map size and clutter


Mission phase
Systematic search for a target
Transit, approach, and re-routing around obstructions






The handoff between them is the mission’s hinge, and it is worth being precise about the mechanics. The lawnmower list is flown by the Mission Scripting chapter’s state machine — stream the current waypoint, advance on the acceptance test — inside a state the Finite State Machines and Behavior Trees chapter will name SEARCH_GRID. The search-phase requirement is that a detection immediately preempts the sweep: the machine abandons the current leg mid-flight and transitions to pursuit, exactly the event-driven preemption the state-machine formalism was built for. Two design consequences follow for the planner. First, because the path is data — a list and an index — abandoning it costs nothing and resuming it costs one integer: store the index, chase the goose, and re-enter the list at the stored leg when the pursuit resolves, rather than re-sweeping ground already covered. Second, the pursuit target arrives from the perception stack as a NED position — the very stream of imperfect world-frame targets the Coordinate Frames chapter delivered — and whether the pursuit needs A* at all depends on the world between drone and goose: over the open field, the answer is usually a straight line and no planner; near the treeline or a geofence boundary, it is a grid query. The next chapters take up what happens after arrival — the deterrence patterns flown at the target, and the state machinery that sequences search, pursuit, and escape into one mission.






NoteFor More



The lawnmower over a rectangle is the base case of a richer theory. Boustrophedon cellular decomposition extends complete coverage to regions with obstacles: the free space is sliced into obstacle-free cells by sweeping a line across the region and splitting wherever an obstacle interrupts it; each cell gets its own lawnmower, and the cells are visited in an order that minimizes transit — a traveling-salesman flavored sequencing problem. Energy-aware variants choose leg orientation as well: legs aligned with the prevailing wind trade fewer turns against asymmetric headwind/tailwind legs, a measurable difference in battery on large fields. On the graph-search side, the D* Lite algorithm mentioned for re-routing maintains its search rooted at the goal, so that when the vehicle moves or costs change, most of the computed structure survives — the reason it became the standard for planetary rovers and remains the default answer when A* must run inside a tight replanning loop.

title: 19  Path Planning on the Edge: Search Grids and Coverage Algorithms
text:
19.8 Check Your Understanding

A drone searches at 8 m altitude with a nadir camera whose horizontal field of view is 90°, and the mission requires 30 % swath overlap. Compute the swath width and the sweep spacing, then the number of legs the generator emits for a bounding box 50 m wide.







TipShow answer





Swath: \(w = 2 \times 8 \times \tan 45^\circ = 16\) m. Spacing: \(s = 16 \times (1 - 0.3) = 11.2\) m. Legs: \(n = \lceil 50 / 11.2 \rceil + 1 = \lceil 4.46 \rceil + 1 = 6\), and the recomputed step is \(50 / 5 = 10\) m — tighter than the 11.2 m maximum, as the ceiling guarantees. The generator never widens the spacing to fit the box; it adds a leg and shrinks the step.




Trace lawnmower(0, 100, 0, 20, 7.0, 6.0) by hand: how many legs and waypoints result, what is the actual step, in which direction does the third leg (index 2) fly, and what is the final waypoint?







TipShow answer





\(W = 20\), so \(n = \lceil 20/7 \rceil + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4\) legs and \(8\) waypoints, with step \(20/3 \approx 6.67\) m. Leg index 2 is even, so it flies south-to-north (\(x\) from 0 to 100) at \(y \approx 13.33\) m. The last leg (index 3, odd) flies north-to-south at \(y = 20\), so the final waypoint is \((0, 20, -6.0)\) — northing 0, easting 20 m, 6 m above the launch altitude in NED’s negative-down convention.




A survey flies \(w = 11\) m swaths at \(s = 8\) m spacing. GNSS scatter alone contributes about 1 m of cross-track error per leg. How much additional systematic drift (wind bias) per leg can the coverage guarantee absorb in the worst case, and what are the two remedies when the answer is judged too thin?







TipShow answer





The overlap margin is \(w - s = 3\) m, and the worst case is adjacent legs drifting oppositely, so each leg’s total budget is \((w-s)/2 = 1.5\) m. With 1 m already spent on GNSS scatter, only about 0.5 m per leg remains for systematic wind bias — thin, since steady crosswind residuals can exceed that. The remedies pull opposite levers: tighten the spacing (more overlap, more legs, more time and battery) or reduce the error itself (track the leg line rather than chase corners, feed the controller setpoints that march along the leg, accept the time cost of flying slower in wind).




A* with the Euclidean heuristic returns an optimal path. A colleague proposes doubling the heuristic — using \(h'(n) = 2\,h(n)\) — because it makes the planner visibly faster on the companion computer. What property is lost, what is the worst case for the returned path, and why might the trade still be accepted on a drone?







TipShow answer





Doubling breaks admissibility: \(h'\) can now overestimate the true remaining cost, so the goal can be expanded while a cheaper route is still unexplored, and optimality is lost. This is weighted A* with \(\varepsilon = 2\); the returned path is at most \(2\times\) the optimal cost (bounded suboptimality), and in open maps typically far closer. The trade is often right on a drone because the planner shares a small processor with inference and telemetry, and a path 10–20 % long that arrives in a fifth of the compute — and therefore replans at a higher rate as the world changes — beats a perfect path delivered late.




For each task, name the appropriate planner — lawnmower coverage, A*, or neither — and justify in one sentence: (a) sweep a 70 m × 40 m open field to find any geese present; (b) fly from the field’s corner to a detected goose on the far side of a treeline; (c) fly from hover directly to a detected goose 15 m away over open grass.







TipShow answer






Lawnmower coverage: the question is “see everything,” there are no obstacles, and the box-plus-spacing parameterization guarantees completeness. (b) A: the question is point-to-point and the treeline is an obstacle, so a shortest path must be searched on a map that represents it. (c) Neither: with a straight, obstacle-free line to a known NED target, the answer is the straight line itself — streaming setpoints toward the target — and invoking a planner adds latency and code for nothing. Choosing no algorithm* when the question doesn’t require one is also a planning decision.





Mid-sweep on leg 3 of 6, the detector reports a goose and the mission preempts the search. Ten minutes later the pursuit resolves and the search must continue. Compare the cost and the coverage consequences of (a) restarting the lawnmower from leg 0, (b) resuming at the stored index on leg 3, and (c) regenerating a fresh bounding box over only the unswept remainder.







TipShow answer






Restarting re-flies roughly half the track — minutes of battery the time budget almost certainly cannot spare — for ground already covered; its only virtue is that staleness of the earlier sweep is refreshed. (b) Resuming at the stored index costs one integer of state and a transit back to the abandoned leg; coverage of the remainder is exactly as planned, and the only gap risk is the partial leg 3, which should be resumed at its start (or at the recorded abandon point) rather than skipped. (c) Regenerating over the unswept sub-box costs one more generator call — microseconds — and produces the cleanest plan when the pursuit ended far from leg 3, trading a slightly different leg layout for a shorter transit. In practice (b) and (c) are the real candidates, and the choice turns on where the pursuit left the vehicle; (a) is defensible only if enough time has passed that geese may have re-landed on swept ground.

19.9 Try It
Part 1 — build the generator and audit it. Implement lawnmower() exactly as specified — bounding box, maximum spacing, altitude in, ordered NED waypoint list out — plus a swath(altitude, fov_deg, overlap) helper that computes \(s_{\max}\) from sensor geometry. Reproduce the chapter’s worked example (60 × 33 m box, 90° field of view, 5.5 m altitude, 40 % overlap) and confirm 6 legs, 12 waypoints, a 6.6 m step, and 393 m of track; then write a track_length() function and a time audit at 1.5 and 2.0 m/s. Plot the path (matplotlib, equal axes, north up) with the swath of each leg drawn as a translucent band — the plot makes coverage gaps visible by eye. Then feed the waypoint list into the Mission Scripting chapter’s state-machine node in SITL and fly it in Offboard mode: the NAVIGATE state needs no changes at all, which is the point — the planner and the executor meet at a list. Finally, log cross-track error each tick (the signed-distance formula of this chapter, against the current leg) and, after landing, plot its histogram; compare the spread against your overlap margin \((w-s)/2\) and state whether your coverage claim survived the flight.
Part 2 — A* on a grid, then make it dynamic. Implement a_star() on a 2D occupancy grid with 8-connectivity and diagonal cost \(\sqrt{2}\), and verify optimality on hand-checkable cases: an empty grid (path length must equal the octile distance) and this chapter’s 14 × 9 wall-with-gap grid (the figure’s 12-cell path). Instrument the node-expansion count and compare three heuristics on a 200 × 200 grid with random obstacles: \(h = 0\) (Dijkstra), Euclidean, and \(2\times\) Euclidean — report expansions and path cost for each, and confirm the weighted variant’s path is never worse than twice optimal. Then make it dynamic: after finding a path, mark a random free cell on that path as an obstacle and re-plan from a point midway along the path. Measure re-plan time, and write three sentences on whether full re-planning is affordable at this grid size and replan rate on your target hardware — and at what map size or rate you would reach for an incremental planner instead.

title: 20  Vector-Based Threat Evasion: The Math of Escape
text:
20.1 Learning Objectives
The previous chapter closed on the mission’s hinge: a detection preempts the search grid, the drone closes on its target, and the deterrence work begins. This chapter is about the moment that plan inverts — when something starts closing on the drone. A territorial goose breaking off from the flock to defend it, another aircraft blundering into the working volume, any object whose track ends where the drone is hovering: the roles of pursuer and pursued swap in a frame or two, and the vehicle that was maneuvering at a target must instantly maneuver away from one. The response has a hard real-time character that nothing earlier in this Part had. A coverage path is computed before takeoff; an A* query tolerates a few milliseconds of thought. An incoming threat at bird speeds allows roughly the time between two heartbeats to notice, decide, and move.
That tempo dictates the mathematics. There is no grid, no graph, no search: the entire computation is a handful of dot products and cross products on six numbers — the threat’s position and velocity relative to the drone’s — cheap enough to re-run at the estimator’s full update rate. And every one of those numbers lives in the local North-East-Down frame the Coordinate Frames chapter established: the threat’s position arrives from the perception stack as a world-frame point (one more of the imperfect world-frame targets that chapter’s pipeline delivers), its velocity is estimated by differencing successive positions, and the escape command leaves as an NED velocity setpoint. Two questions organize the chapter. First, is this thing actually going to hit me? — a prediction problem, answered by a dot product. Second, which way is out? — a geometry problem, and the answer, perpendicular or opposite to the threat’s trajectory, is constructed with a cross product. Both answers are then handed to the state machinery of the next chapter, where they will live inside a state the Finite State Machines and Behavior Trees chapter names EVADE_THREAT — the highest-priority behavior in the mission, entitled to preempt everything else the drone is doing.

title: 20  Vector-Based Threat Evasion: The Math of Escape
text:
Form the threat vector and the relative velocity from two position–velocity pairs in local NED, and apply the dot-product test \(\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{rel} < 0\) to decide whether the threat is closing.
Derive the time of closest approach \(t^*\) by minimizing the squared separation, compute the miss vector and miss distance, and state the three-part trigger — closing, soon, and inside the safety radius — that starts an evasion.
Explain, via the danger-cylinder picture, why a direction perpendicular to the threat’s trajectory is the geometrically sound escape when the threat is fast, and when a straight retreat (opposite the approach) is the better choice.
Construct a full 3D evasion vector with two cross products — one perpendicular to both the track and the line of sight, one pointing away from the predicted passing side — including the NED sign check that prevents commanding a dive and the fallback when the geometry degenerates.
Verify an escape by recomputing the closest approach under the commanded velocity, and state the two assumptions (instant velocity change, non-maneuvering threat) whose failure motivates bounded-acceleration commands and, for a pursuing threat, potential fields or rapid re-planning.

title: 20  Vector-Based Threat Evasion: The Math of Escape
text:
20.2 Key Vocabulary

Threat vector (\(\mathbf{r}\)) — the position of the threat relative to the drone, \(\mathbf{r} = P_{threat} - P_{drone}\), expressed in local NED; a single vector carrying both the bearing and the range of the danger.
Relative velocity (\(\mathbf{v}_{rel}\)) — the threat’s velocity minus the drone’s, \(\mathbf{v}_{rel} = \mathbf{v}_t - \mathbf{v}_d\); it collapses two moving trajectories into one straight-line track flown past a drone pinned at the origin.
Collision course — an encounter that is closing (\(\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{rel} < 0\)) and whose predicted point of closest approach falls inside the safety radius; either condition alone is not yet an emergency.
Closest point of approach (CPA) — the moment \(t^* = -(\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{rel})/\lVert\mathbf{v}_{rel}\rVert^2\) at which the separation between drone and threat is smallest, and the miss vector \(\mathbf{m} = \mathbf{r} + \mathbf{v}_{rel}\,t^*\) describing where the threat passes and by how much.
Safety radius (\(R_{safe}\)) — the minimum separation the mission is willing to accept between the drone and any uncooperative mover; a predicted miss distance below it is the evasion trigger.
Evasion vector — the commanded escape direction: perpendicular to the threat’s trajectory when the threat is fast, opposite the approach when the drone can outrun it, and always biased away from the side on which the threat will pass.
Cross product (\(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}\)) — the vector perpendicular to both of its operands, with magnitude \(\lVert\mathbf{a}\rVert \lVert\mathbf{b}\rVert \sin\theta\); the constructor of perpendicular escape directions, and identically zero when its operands are parallel — the degenerate case the code must catch.
Safe altitude — a designated altitude, above the encounter, that the escape maneuver climbs toward; giving the evasion state a fixed destination turns “flee” into a bounded, resumable behavior.
Potential field — a control technique that sums a repulsive gradient pushed out by each threat with an attractive gradient pulled toward a goal, and commands the net downhill direction; the standard first answer when the threat pursues rather than flying a straight line.
