title: 20  Vector-Based Threat Evasion: The Math of Escape
section: 20.3 The Threat Vector and the Closing Test
text:
20.3 The Threat Vector and the Closing Test
Everything begins by subtracting. The perception pipeline delivers the threat’s position \(P_t\) in local NED — the same camera-to-world chain of the Coordinate Frames chapter, pointed now at something the mission fears instead of something it seeks — and the flight controller’s estimator supplies the drone’s own position \(P_d\) and velocity \(\mathbf{v}_d\). The threat vector
\[
\mathbf{r} = P_t - P_d
\]
compresses the situation into one arrow: its norm \(\lVert\mathbf{r}\rVert\) is the range, its direction is the bearing. But a position, however close, is not yet a threat — a goose ten metres away flying away is scenery. Danger lives in the motion, and the motion that matters is relative. Estimate the threat’s velocity \(\mathbf{v}_t\) (in practice by differencing its last few world-frame positions over their timestamps) and form the relative velocity
\[
\mathbf{v}_{rel} = \mathbf{v}_t - \mathbf{v}_d .
\]
This subtraction performs a conceptual simplification worth pausing on: it pins the drone at the origin of a relative frame and lets the threat do all the moving. Two curved, coupled trajectories become one straight line — the threat travels along \(\mathbf{r} + \mathbf{v}_{rel}\,t\) — and every question about the encounter becomes a question about how close that line passes to a fixed point.
The first question is binary: is the gap shrinking? The separation’s rate of change has the sign of the dot product \(\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{rel}\) — differentiate \(\lVert\mathbf{r}(t)\rVert^2\) and the term \(2\,\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{rel}\) is what comes out. The test reads directly:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{rel} &< 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{closing}, \\
\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{rel} &> 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{opening}, \\
\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{rel} &= 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{abeam}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The intuition is the dot product’s usual one: it measures alignment. A negative value means the relative motion points back along the line of sight — the threat is eating range. Run continuously, this three-way test is the cheapest early-warning system in robotics: three multiplications, two additions, and a sign check per update.
Numbers make it concrete, and the encounter they describe will run through the whole chapter. Mid-mission, the drone holds \(P_d = (30.0,\ 10.0,\ {-10.0})\) — 10 m up, in NED’s negative-down convention — drifting north at \(\mathbf{v}_d = (1, 0, 0)\) m/s. A goose breaks toward it from ahead and to the right: \(P_t = (38.0,\ 12.0,\ {-10.0})\), flying south at \(\mathbf{v}_t = (-3, 0, 0)\) m/s, at the same altitude. Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{r} &= (8,\ 2,\ 0), \qquad \lVert\mathbf{r}\rVert = \sqrt{68} \approx 8.25\ \text{m}, \\
\mathbf{v}_{rel} &= (-3-1,\ 0,\ 0) = (-4,\ 0,\ 0)\ \text{m/s}, \\
\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{rel} &= (8)(-4) + (2)(0) + (0)(0) = -32 \;<\; 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]
Closing — at \(-(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{rel})/\lVert\mathbf{r}\rVert = 32/8.25 \approx 3.9\) m/s, the drone’s 1 m/s of northward drift and the goose’s 3 m/s of southward flight pooled into one number. (The speeds are deliberately leisurely so the arithmetic stays legible; the geometry, not the tempo, is the lesson, and it survives unchanged when the incomer is three times faster.)

title: 20  Vector-Based Threat Evasion: The Math of Escape
text:
20.4 Predicting the Near Miss
Closing is necessary but not sufficient: two aircraft can close for a while and still pass comfortably wide. The evasion decision needs the future minimum of the separation, and for a straight-line relative track that minimum has a closed form. The squared separation at time \(t\) is
\[
d^2(t) = \lVert \mathbf{r} + \mathbf{v}_{rel}\,t \rVert^2
       = \lVert\mathbf{r}\rVert^2 + 2\,(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{rel})\,t + \lVert\mathbf{v}_{rel}\rVert^2\,t^2,
\]
an upward-opening parabola in \(t\). Setting its derivative to zero gives the time of closest approach
\[
t^* = -\,\frac{\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{rel}}{\lVert\mathbf{v}_{rel}\rVert^2},
\]
which is positive exactly when the encounter is closing — the dot-product test and the CPA formula agree by construction. Substituting \(t^*\) back gives the miss vector, the threat’s position relative to the drone at that worst moment:
\[
\mathbf{m} = \mathbf{r} + \mathbf{v}_{rel}\,t^* .
\]
Its norm is the predicted miss distance, and one property of \(\mathbf{m}\) will earn its keep shortly: it is always perpendicular to \(\mathbf{v}_{rel}\) (at the closest point, the relative motion is exactly sideways — that is what “closest” means).
For the running encounter:
\[
\begin{aligned}
t^* &= \frac{32}{(-4)^2 + 0 + 0} = \frac{32}{16} = 2.0\ \text{s}, \\
\mathbf{m} &= (8,\ 2,\ 0) + (-4,\ 0,\ 0)(2.0) = (0,\ 2,\ 0), \\
\lVert\mathbf{m}\rVert &= 2.0\ \text{m}.
\end{aligned}
\]
In two seconds, the goose passes 2.0 m to the drone’s east, at the same altitude. Whether that is an emergency is a mission parameter, not mathematics: the safety radius \(R_{safe}\) encodes how much separation the operator demands from an uncooperative mover — 3 m here, roughly the drone’s rotor span plus a wingspan plus turbulence margin. The full trigger is a three-part conjunction, and each part guards against a different false alarm:

Closing: \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{rel} < 0\) — otherwise the threat is departing and any maneuver is wasted battery.
Soon: \(t^* \le T_{horizon}\) (a few seconds) — a threat predicted to arrive in forty seconds will be re-predicted forty times before it matters; acting on distant extrapolations of a noisy velocity estimate produces a drone that flinches at everything.
Close: \(\lVert\mathbf{m}\rVert < R_{safe}\) — the pass must actually violate the radius.

Here: closing (yes), \(t^* = 2.0\) s (soon), miss \(2.0 < 3\) m (inside). Evade — with two seconds in hand. Figure 20.1 lays the whole prediction out to scale.






Figure 20.1: The threat vector, the closing test, and the predicted near miss for the chapter’s running encounter: a goose 8.25 m out closes at 3.9 m/s and will pass 2.0 m east of the drone in 2.0 s — inside the 3 m safety radius.



The two-second warning is the entire argument for prediction over reaction, and it deserves the emphasis the numbers give it. A purely reactive system — one that maneuvers when the range gets small — would begin its escape with the goose a wingbeat away, spending its maneuver on desperation. The predictive system starts the same escape 2 s and 8 m earlier, which at quadrotor accelerations is the difference between a brisk sidestep and a stall-the-airframe emergency. The prediction costs almost nothing (the formulas above are a dozen floating-point operations) but it leans on estimates that do cost something: the threat’s position carries the half-metre-scale error the Coordinate Frames chapter budgeted at these ranges, and differencing noisy positions to get \(\mathbf{v}_t\) amplifies that noise. A miss predicted at 2.9 m against a 3 m radius is not meaningfully different from one predicted at 3.1 m — which is why \(R_{safe}\) is chosen with slack in it, and why the assessment re-runs every update rather than trusting any single prediction.

title: 20  Vector-Based Threat Evasion: The Math of Escape
section: 20.5 Why Perpendicular Is the Way Out
text:
20.5 Why Perpendicular Is the Way Out
The trigger has fired; the drone owns 2.0 seconds. Which way should it go? The lab-honed rule of thumb — escape perpendicular or opposite to the threat’s trajectory — sounds like folklore until it is drawn in the relative frame, where it becomes a theorem about cylinders.
Pin the drone at the origin. The threat travels the straight line \(\mathbf{r} + \mathbf{v}_{rel}\,t\); inflate that line by the safety radius and it becomes a danger cylinder of radius \(R_{safe}\) around the threat’s relative track — the set of every position that will, at some moment, be within \(R_{safe}\) of the threat. The drone is currently inside this cylinder (that is precisely what miss distance \(2.0 < 3\) m means), and escaping is now a literal geometric task: get outside the tube before the threat arrives.
Seen this way, the candidate maneuvers sort themselves:

Motion parallel to the cylinder’s axis — directly away along the threat’s line of approach — never exits the tube at all. It changes when the threat arrives, not where it passes. If the drone can sustain a higher speed than the threat’s closing rate, this straight retreat opens the range forever and is a perfectly good escape; if it cannot, retreat merely postpones the same near miss. Running from a faster pursuer down its own track is the one provably losing move.
Motion perpendicular to the axis exits through the nearest wall, and converts every metre-per-second of drone speed into miss distance. Crucially, its effectiveness does not depend on the speed ratio: the threat’s velocity has no component in the perpendicular plane (that is what perpendicular means), so a straight-flying threat cannot contest the sidestep at all. This is the escape that still works when the incomer is faster — and the threats worth engineering for, a territorial goose in full flight or a rogue aircraft, generally are. Rerun the encounter with the goose replaced by a 12 m/s incomer on the same track: \(t^*\) collapses to roughly 0.6 s and the miss distance stays 2.0 m (the miss depends on the track’s direction, not its speed); retreat at any achievable quadrotor speed loses, but the perpendicular exit — 1 m to the nearest wall, as computed next — remains a fraction of a second’s work.

So “perpendicular or opposite” decodes to: opposite if you are faster (it maximizes range and buys time), perpendicular if you are not (it is the only direction the threat cannot defend). A small autonomous drone facing birds and aircraft should assume it is not.
One question remains: perpendicular which way? The perpendicular directions form a whole plane — from inside a tube you can aim at any point of the wall — and they are far from equivalent. The drone sits 2.0 m from the cylinder’s axis (the miss distance is exactly the drone’s distance from the relative track), in a tube of radius 3 m. Exit toward the side the threat will pass on — east, through the axis — and the wall is \(R_{safe} + \lVert\mathbf{m}\rVert = 5.0\) m away, crossing in front of the danger on the way. Exit away from the passing side — west — and the wall is \(R_{safe} - \lVert\mathbf{m}\rVert = 1.0\) m away. Exit straight up, at right angles to the miss, and the chord gives \(\sqrt{R_{safe}^2 - \lVert\mathbf{m}\rVert^2} = \sqrt{9-4} \approx 2.24\) m. The ranking is general: the cheapest exit is directly away from the miss vector — dodge away from the side on which the threat will pass, the matador’s move — with the perpendicular-to-the-miss directions (for a co-altitude encounter, straight up) a respectable second that buys vertical separation and ground clearance. Figure 20.2 makes the picture exact.






Figure 20.2: The danger cylinder in the relative frame: motion along the axis never exits the tube, motion perpendicular does — and the cross-section shows the exits are not equivalent: 1.0 m away from the passing side, 2.24 m straight up, 5.0 m across the axis.

title: 20  Vector-Based Threat Evasion: The Math of Escape
section: 20.6 Building the Escape with Cross Products
text:
20.6 Building the Escape with Cross Products
The geometry says: move in the plane perpendicular to \(\mathbf{v}_{rel}\), biased away from the passing side, and preferably upward. The tool that constructs such directions from the vectors already in hand is the cross product. For \(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}\), the essentials: the result is perpendicular to both operands; its magnitude is \(\lVert\mathbf{a}\rVert\lVert\mathbf{b}\rVert\sin\theta\); its sign follows the right-hand rule and flips if the operands swap; and it vanishes when the operands are parallel — a failure mode, not a curiosity, that the implementation below must detect. Componentwise,
\[
\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} =
\big(a_y b_z - a_z b_y,\;\; a_z b_x - a_x b_z,\;\; a_x b_y - a_y b_x\big).
\]
The construction uses it twice, and each application answers one of the geometry’s demands.
First cross product — perpendicular to everything. The two vectors that define the encounter are the relative track \(\mathbf{v}_{rel}\) and the line of sight \(\mathbf{r}\). Their cross product
\[
\mathbf{u}_1 = \mathbf{v}_{rel} \times \mathbf{r}
\]
is perpendicular to both: it leaves the collision plane entirely, at right angles to the track (so the threat cannot contest it) and at right angles to the line of sight (so every unit of motion is pure lateral separation). For the running encounter,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{u}_1 &= (-4,\ 0,\ 0) \times (8,\ 2,\ 0) \\
  &= \big( (0)(0)-(0)(2),\;\; (0)(8)-(-4)(0),\;\; (-4)(2)-(0)(8) \big) \\
  &= (0,\ 0,\ -8), \qquad \hat{\mathbf{u}}_1 = (0,\ 0,\ -1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Both defining vectors were horizontal, so their mutual perpendicular is vertical — and in NED, a \(D\)-component of \(-1\) points up. That sign was luck, and luck is not a control law: swap the operand order and the same arithmetic yields \((0, 0, +8)\), a command to dive at the ground. The implementation therefore checks the \(D\)-component and negates the vector if it is positive — both \(\mathbf{u}_1\) and \(-\mathbf{u}_1\) are equally perpendicular, and the mission’s preference between them is not geometric but physical: climb, never dive. Climbing moves away from the ground, the obstacles, and (for an avian threat defending ground it considers its own) usually the contested airspace; it is also the direction of the designated safe altitude the maneuver ultimately makes for.
Second cross product — away from the passing side. \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1\) solves the vertical axis of the escape plane; the horizontal axis should point away from the miss. Crossing the track with \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1\) produces the remaining perpendicular direction:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{u}_2 &= \mathbf{v}_{rel} \times \hat{\mathbf{u}}_1
= (-4, 0, 0) \times (0, 0, -1)
= (0,\ -4,\ 0), \\
\hat{\mathbf{u}}_2 &= (0,\ -1,\ 0)
\end{aligned}
\]
— due west, which is exactly \(-\hat{\mathbf{m}}\), the direction away from the goose’s predicted 2 m-east pass. That is not a numerical coincidence. The vector triple product identity \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{a}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}) - \mathbf{c}\lVert\mathbf{a}\rVert^2\), applied with \(\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{v}_{rel}\) and \(\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{r}\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{v}_{rel}\times(\mathbf{v}_{rel}\times\mathbf{r})
  &= \mathbf{v}_{rel}\,(\mathbf{v}_{rel}\cdot\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{r}\,\lVert\mathbf{v}_{rel}\rVert^2 \\
  &= -\lVert\mathbf{v}_{rel}\rVert^2 \left( \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{v}_{rel}\,
      \frac{-(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{rel})}{\lVert\mathbf{v}_{rel}\rVert^2} \right)
   = -\lVert\mathbf{v}_{rel}\rVert^2\, \mathbf{m},
\end{aligned}
\]
since the parenthesized quantity is precisely \(\mathbf{r} + \mathbf{v}_{rel}\,t^*\). The double cross product is always anti-parallel to the miss vector: the construction does not merely find some perpendicular — it automatically finds the matador’s side, for any encounter geometry, with no case analysis. This is the quiet payoff of doing the escape with vector algebra instead of hand-tuned rules.
One wrinkle rewards a careful look, because it is invisible in this example and a wrong-way dodge in others. The climb-never-dive negation propagates: negating \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1\) negates \(\mathbf{v}_{rel} \times \hat{\mathbf{u}}_1\) as well, which would land the sidestep on the wrong side precisely in the encounters where the climb check fired. The implementation therefore pins \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_2\) against the miss directly — negate it whenever \(\mathbf{u}_2 \cdot \mathbf{m} > 0\) — a check that is a no-op here (the climb check was too) but load-bearing in half of all geometries. Sign conventions compose, and every sign in a control law earns an explicit test.
The evasion vector. Sum the two unit directions and renormalize — an equal blend of “climb” and “away from the pass,” both lying in the plane the threat cannot contest — and scale by the escape speed \(v_{esc}\) the airframe can honestly deliver:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\mathbf{e}} &= \frac{\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1 + \hat{\mathbf{u}}_2}{\lVert \hat{\mathbf{u}}_1 + \hat{\mathbf{u}}_2 \rVert}
= \left(0,\ -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\ -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right), \\
\mathbf{v}_{cmd} &= 5\,\hat{\mathbf{e}} = (0,\ -3.54,\ -3.54)\ \text{m/s}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The escape trajectory: from \((30, 10, -10)\), the drone breaks due west while climbing at 45°, perpendicular to the goose’s north–south track, opening toward the safe altitude (15 m, \(D = -15\)) it will hold until the threat clears. Figure 20.3 draws the full construction in three dimensions.






Figure 20.3: The cross-product construction of the 3D evasion vector for the running encounter: \(\mathbf{u}_1 = \mathbf{v}_{rel}\times\mathbf{r}\) points straight up, \(\mathbf{u}_2 = \mathbf{v}_{rel}\times\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1\) points west — exactly away from the predicted miss — and their blend sends the drone climbing west at 45°, in the plane the threat cannot contest.



Verify, don’t hope. The construction is only as good as its effect on the number that triggered it, so recompute the closest approach under the commanded velocity. The new relative velocity is \(\mathbf{v}_{rel}' = \mathbf{v}_t - \mathbf{v}_{cmd} = (-3,\ 3.54,\ 3.54)\), and with \(\mathbf{r}\) unchanged at the moment the maneuver begins:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{rel}' &= (8)(-3) + (2)(3.54) + 0 = -16.93, \\
t^{*\prime} &= \frac{16.93}{(-3)^2 + (3.54)^2 + (3.54)^2} = \frac{16.93}{34.0} = 0.498\ \text{s}, \\
\mathbf{m}' &= (8, 2, 0) + (-3,\ 3.54,\ 3.54)(0.498) = (6.51,\ 3.76,\ 1.76), \\
\lVert\mathbf{m}'\rVert &= \sqrt{42.3 + 14.1 + 3.1} \approx 7.72\ \text{m}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The predicted miss climbs from 2.0 m to 7.72 m — from well inside the safety radius to comfortably outside it — and the miss vector’s positive \(D\)-component says the goose now passes 1.76 m below the climbing drone. The encounter still “closes” briefly (the geometry guarantees some approach), but its closest point is a non-event. One honest caveat rides along: this verification assumed the drone’s velocity changed instantly, which no airframe delivers. The next section pays that debt.
The degenerate case. The construction has one hole, and it is the most dangerous geometry of all: a dead-ahead collision. When the threat comes straight down the line of sight, \(\mathbf{r}\) and \(\mathbf{v}_{rel}\) are anti-parallel, \(\mathbf{u}_1 = \mathbf{v}_{rel}\times\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}\), and the miss vector is zero too — there is no “side it will pass on” because it will not pass, it will arrive. Geometrically the symmetry is real (every perpendicular is equally good), but code cannot normalize a zero vector, so the implementation substitutes an arbitrary perpendicular: \(\mathbf{v}_{rel} \times \hat{\mathbf{d}}\), with \(\hat{\mathbf{d}} = (0,0,1)\) the NED down axis, gives a horizontal sidestep at right angles to the approach — and if the threat is coming straight down or straight up (making that cross product vanish as well), any horizontal direction serves.

title: 20  Vector-Based Threat Evasion: The Math of Escape
text:
20.7 From Vector to Maneuver
The mathematics compresses into a function small enough to audit line by line — and it must be auditable, because it will run inside the highest-priority behavior in the mission:
import numpy as np

D_HAT = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0])          # NED down axis

def evasion_command(p_d, v_d, p_t, v_t,
                    r_safe=3.0, horizon=5.0, v_esc=5.0):
    """Assess a threat and, if it triggers, return an NED escape
    velocity command; return None if no evasion is required."""
    r = np.asarray(p_t, float) - np.asarray(p_d, float)   # threat vector
    v_rel = np.asarray(v_t, float) - np.asarray(v_d, float)
    closing = r @ v_rel
    if closing >= 0.0:
        return None                        # opening or abeam: no threat
    t_star = -closing / (v_rel @ v_rel)    # time of closest approach
    if t_star > horizon:
        return None                        # closing, but not soon
    miss = r + v_rel * t_star              # CPA miss vector (perp. to v_rel)
    if np.linalg.norm(miss) >= r_safe:
        return None                        # passes outside the radius
    u1 = np.cross(v_rel, r)                # perp. to track and line of sight
    if np.linalg.norm(u1) < 1e-6:          # dead-ahead: no unique side
        u1 = np.cross(v_rel, D_HAT)        # fall back: horizontal sidestep
        if np.linalg.norm(u1) < 1e-6:      # threat vertical: any direction
            u1 = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0])
    if u1[2] > 0.0:                        # NED sign check:
        u1 = -u1                           #   climb, never dive
    u1 /= np.linalg.norm(u1)
    u2 = np.cross(v_rel, u1)               # perp. to the track, in the escape plane
    if u2 @ miss > 0.0:                    # flipping u1 above flips this product too:
        u2 = -u2                           #   re-pin it away from the miss
    n2 = np.linalg.norm(u2)
    e = u1 if n2 < 1e-6 else u1 + u2 / n2
    return v_esc * e / np.linalg.norm(e)   # commanded NED escape velocity
Three implementation realities separate this function from a flying escape.
Bound the command the airframe can honor. The verification above assumed the commanded velocity took effect instantly; a real quadrotor must pitch over and accelerate, and an evasion command that demands an instant 5 m/s reversal — or worse, a naive implementation that converts the evasion vector into an extreme attitude target — will spend its two seconds of warning saturating motors instead of moving. The remedy is the same discipline the cascaded controllers of Part II imposed everywhere else: command velocity, let the position/velocity cascade generate attitudes, and slew the commanded velocity toward \(\mathbf{v}_{cmd}\) under an acceleration cap rather than stepping it. The margin the prediction bought is exactly what pays for the ramp — which is one more argument for triggering on the forecast, not the flinch. One further bound belongs to the mission rather than the airframe: when the threat will pass overhead, the away-from-the-miss direction points downward, and the construction will honestly spend part of the escape descending — correct geometry that the mission’s minimum-altitude margin must be allowed to cap.
Re-run everything, every update. The escape vector is computed from one snapshot of a noisy world. The threat’s velocity estimate wobbles; the threat itself may turn. The evasion state therefore loops the entire assessment at the estimator rate — recompute \(\mathbf{r}\), \(\mathbf{v}_{rel}\), the trigger, and the vector; re-slew toward the fresh command — so that a curving threat faces a continuously re-aimed escape rather than a stale one. Against a straight-flying threat the recomputed vector barely moves and the loop costs nothing; against a maneuvering one, the loop is the difference between a control law and a wish.
Define done. A behavior that can preempt everything needs an exit condition as crisp as its entry: the encounter has cleared when the closing test goes positive and the range exceeds the safety radius with margin — the threat is behind, opening, and far — or when the drone reaches its safe altitude and the threat is no longer tracked. Where control goes next (resume the abandoned search leg? return home?) is sequencing, not geometry, and it is precisely the job of the next chapter: the Finite State Machines and Behavior Trees chapter builds the EVADE_THREAT state around this function — its preemption of every other state on trigger, its guard conditions, and the bookkeeping that lets the interrupted mission resume — turning this chapter’s arithmetic into the reflex arc of the whole system.






NoteFor More



Everything above assumes the threat flies straight: the CPA formula extrapolates a line, and the perpendicular escape works because a non-maneuvering threat cannot contest the sideways plane. A pursuing threat breaks both assumptions at once — it re-aims at the drone every instant, so there is no fixed track to be perpendicular to, and any single precomputed escape vector is stale the moment the pursuer turns. The graduate-track extension of this problem replaces the one-shot vector with a continuously recomputed field or plan. The classic tool is the potential field: the threat emits a repulsive potential that grows steeply inside the safety radius, the safe altitude or rally point emits an attractive one, and the drone commands the negative gradient of the sum — recomputed every tick, so the escape direction automatically rotates as the pursuer curves. Potential fields are cheap (a few vector operations per threat, so multiple simultaneous threats just sum) but carry known pathologies: local minima where attraction and repulsion cancel, and oscillation in narrow passages. The heavier alternative is rapid re-planning — re-running a short-horizon planner several times a second over predicted threat positions, in the spirit of the dynamic re-routing discussed with A* in the previous chapter. Between the two sit velocity obstacles, which characterize the set of drone velocities that lead to collision with each mover and choose outside it, and upstream of all of them sits estimation: a pursuer’s future position deserves better than differenced detections, which is where a Kalman filter over the threat’s state earns its place. Against a stochastic pursuer — one that maneuvers unpredictably — the guarantees get weaker and the margins must get correspondingly fatter: the safety radius and trigger horizon absorb what the mathematics no longer promises.

title: 20  Vector-Based Threat Evasion: The Math of Escape
text:
20.8 Check Your Understanding

A detected mover sits at \(\mathbf{r} = (12, -5, 0)\) m with relative velocity \(\mathbf{v}_{rel} = (2, 1, 0)\) m/s. Apply the closing test and state, in one sentence, what the drone should do about this object.







TipShow answer





\(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{rel} = (12)(2) + (-5)(1) + 0 = 24 - 5 = +19 > 0\): the separation is growing — the object is departing. The drone should do nothing but keep watching: the test re-runs every update, and a mover that turns will announce itself with a sign change; maneuvering against an opening track wastes battery and interrupts the mission for scenery.




A threat has \(\mathbf{r} = (10, 0, 0)\) m and \(\mathbf{v}_{rel} = (-3, 1, 0)\) m/s, with \(R_{safe} = 3\) m. Compute \(t^*\), the miss vector, and the miss distance, and make the evade/no-evade call — then say why an engineer might distrust the call either way.







TipShow answer





\(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{rel} = -30\) (closing); \(\lVert\mathbf{v}_{rel}\rVert^2 = 10\), so \(t^* = 3.0\) s. \(\mathbf{m} = (10,0,0) + (-3,1,0)(3) = (1, 3, 0)\), giving \(\lVert\mathbf{m}\rVert = \sqrt{10} \approx 3.16\) m. Strictly \(3.16 \ge 3\): no evade. But the margin is 16 cm against a position estimate carrying half-metre-scale error and a velocity estimate built by differencing it — well inside the noise. This is exactly why the safety radius is chosen with slack, why the prediction re-runs continuously rather than being trusted once, and why a mission designer might add hysteresis (trigger at 3 m, stand down at 4 m) so the decision doesn’t chatter across the boundary.




For the encounter of question 2, compute \(\mathbf{u}_1 = \mathbf{v}_{rel}\times\mathbf{r}\) and \(\mathbf{u}_2 = \mathbf{v}_{rel}\times\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1\) (after the NED sign check), and confirm that \(\mathbf{u}_2\) points away from the miss vector you found.







TipShow answer





\(\mathbf{u}_1 = (-3,1,0)\times(10,0,0) = \big((1)(0)-(0)(0),\ (0)(10)-(-3)(0),\ (-3)(0)-(1)(10)\big) = (0,0,-10)\). The \(D\)-component is already negative (up), so the sign check passes: \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1 = (0,0,-1)\). Then \(\mathbf{u}_2 = (-3,1,0)\times(0,0,-1) = \big((1)(-1)-0,\ 0-(-3)(-1),\ 0\big) = (-1,-3,0)\) — exactly \(-\mathbf{m}\) for the miss \(\mathbf{m} = (1,3,0)\) of question 2, as the triple-product identity guarantees: the construction dodges away from the side the threat passes on, with no case analysis.




A threat approaches with \(\mathbf{r} = (5, 5, 0)\) and \(\mathbf{v}_{rel} = (-2, -2, 0)\). Compute the miss vector and \(\mathbf{v}_{rel}\times\mathbf{r}\), explain what has happened geometrically, and state what the implementation does about it.







TipShow answer





\(t^* = 20/8 = 2.5\) s and \(\mathbf{m} = (5,5,0) + (-2,-2,0)(2.5) = (0,0,0)\): a predicted dead-center collision. The cross product also vanishes — \(\mathbf{v}_{rel}\times\mathbf{r} = (0, 0, (-2)(5)-(-2)(5)) = \mathbf{0}\) — because \(\mathbf{r}\) and \(\mathbf{v}_{rel}\) are anti-parallel: the threat is coming straight down the line of sight, so there is no “side it will pass on” and every perpendicular is equally good. Code cannot normalize a zero vector, so the implementation falls back to \(\mathbf{v}_{rel}\times\hat{\mathbf{d}}\) (a horizontal sidestep perpendicular to the approach), and if the threat’s track is itself vertical, to any fixed horizontal direction. The most symmetric geometry is the most dangerous one, and it is handled by explicit fallback, not by hoping the norm is never small.




The chapter’s escape blended “climb” and “away from the pass” equally, yielding a 7.72 m verified miss — yet a pure westward sidestep at the same 5 m/s yields about 7.9 m, slightly better. Why might the mission still prefer the blend?







TipShow answer





Because miss distance against this threat is not the only currency. The climb component buys vertical separation (the goose passes below, not beside), moves the drone away from the ground and low obstacles just as an aggressive lateral maneuver makes position error most likely, and makes progress toward the designated safe altitude that defines the maneuver’s endpoint — turning “flee” into a bounded behavior with a destination. The pure sidestep optimizes a single scalar; the blend spends a fraction of a metre of miss distance on robustness. Both live in the plane perpendicular to the threat’s track, which is the property that actually defeats the threat.




Explain why the evasion vector is recomputed at the estimator’s full rate rather than executed once, giving one reason rooted in estimation and one rooted in the threat’s behavior — and name the class of threat for which even a recomputed vector is not enough.







TipShow answer





Estimation: the threat’s velocity comes from differencing noisy world-frame positions, so any single snapshot can be badly wrong; re-running the assessment averages the decision over many estimates instead of betting the airframe on one. Behavior: the CPA extrapolation assumes a straight track, so if the threat turns, the old escape vector points the wrong way; the recomputation loop continuously re-aims the escape at the current geometry. The class that defeats both: a pursuing threat, which re-aims at the drone every instant — there is then no fixed track to be perpendicular to, and the tools become potential fields, velocity obstacles, or rapid re-planning, with a filter (e.g., Kalman) improving the threat-state estimate underneath all of them.

title: 20  Vector-Based Threat Evasion: The Math of Escape
text:
20.9 Try It
Part 1 — implement, reproduce, then attack it with randomness. Implement evasion_command() exactly as specified, plus a helper cpa(r, v_rel) returning \((t^*, \mathbf{m})\). Reproduce the chapter’s encounter — drone \((30,10,-10)\) at \((1,0,0)\) m/s, threat \((38,12,-10)\) at \((-3,0,0)\) m/s — and confirm every intermediate: \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{rel} = -32\), \(t^* = 2.0\) s, miss 2.0 m, \(\mathbf{u}_1 = (0,0,-8)\), \(\mathbf{v}_{cmd} = (0,-3.54,-3.54)\), and a verified post-maneuver miss of 7.72 m. Then Monte Carlo it: generate ten thousand random encounters (positions in a 40 m cube, speeds up to 15 m/s), and assert three invariants on every triggering case — the returned command is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{v}_{rel}\) to numerical precision; its sidestep opposes the predicted pass, \(\mathbf{v}_{cmd} \cdot \mathbf{m} \le 0\); and, for encounters that begin from hover, the recomputed miss under the command is never smaller than the unassisted miss. Then relax the hover restriction and study the violations that appear rather than suppressing them: a drone already moving fast in a favorable direction can lose ground when the command discards that velocity for a fixed-speed escape (a case for scaling \(v_{esc}\), not for trusting momentum), and a threat passing far overhead draws a descending dodge that a mission altitude floor must cap. Log the near-degenerate geometries (smallest \(\lVert\mathbf{u}_1\rVert\) before fallback) and check the fallback fired. A control law that survives ten thousand random geometries — including the ones that expose its assumptions — is trustworthy in a way a worked example alone is not.
Part 2 — close the loop in simulation. Move the function into a simulated encounter: propagate a straight-flying threat and a drone that, on trigger, slews its velocity toward the command under a 3 m/s² acceleration cap (the bound a real airframe imposes), re-running the full assessment at 20 Hz. Plot both 3D trajectories and the separation-versus-time curve, marking the trigger instant, the unassisted CPA prediction, and the actual minimum separation achieved — then sweep the trigger horizon from 0.5 s to 5 s and plot achieved miss distance against warning time, which makes the price of late detection quantitative. Finally, make the threat pursue: re-aim its velocity at the drone’s current position each tick and watch the fixed-vector escape degrade as pursuit speed rises. Three sentences: at what pursuer speed does the perpendicular escape stop clearing the safety radius, and which For More technique would you reach for first, and why? In SITL, the same loop runs against PX4 with the command streamed as an Offboard velocity setpoint — the configuration the related lab’s threat-injection exercise grades.
Related Lab: See Appendix B for the lab assignment that applies this chapter’s concepts.

title: 21  Finite State Machines and Behavior Trees for Mission Logic
text:
21.1 Learning Objectives
The previous chapter ended holding a velocity command and a question. The escape vector was built, verified, and bounded — and then the Vector-Based Threat Evasion chapter stopped, deliberately, at the observation that where control goes next — resume the abandoned search leg? return home? — is sequencing, not geometry. This chapter is the sequencing. The mission now owns three genuine competences, each built in its own chapter: it can sweep an area with coverage guarantees (the lawnmower generator of the Path Planning on the Edge chapter), it can flee along a mathematically sound escape vector (the previous chapter’s evasion_command), and — with the deterrence patterns the Harassment Pattern Generation chapter supplies — it will be able to work a detected goose once it finds one. It also still knows how to take off and land, machinery that has been solid since Part II. What it lacks is an arbiter: the piece of software that decides, twenty times a second, which of these things the aircraft is doing right now, and that changes the answer safely when the world changes it first.
The reader has built that arbiter’s ancestor already. The Mission Scripting chapter rebuilt a waypoint mission as a finite state machine — IDLE, TAKEOFF, NAVIGATE, LAND, DONE, with a failsafe check evaluated before everything else — and closed with a promise: add a detection event and a pursuit state, add an evasion state guarded by a proximity test, and “the machine expresses the whole reactive repertoire of Part IV — every addition a new box and its arrows, every existing box untouched.” This chapter cashes that promise, and it is worth being clear about what is new. That earlier machine executed a fixed list; its guards asked “am I there yet?” The machine built here arbitrates among behaviors that watch the world; its guards ask “what matters most right now?” Same formalism, higher stakes — a wrong transition in the list-flying machine wastes a leg, while a wrong transition here can leave the aircraft harassing a goose while a threat closes on it. The chapter therefore spends its effort where mission machines actually fail: on guard conditions that deserve the name, on the race conditions that live at state boundaries, on what the machine does when its sensors go quiet, and — when the flat machine begins to creak under its own arrows — on the Behavior Tree, the architecture that scales past it.

Specify the five-state mission machine — IDLE/TAKEOFF, SEARCH_GRID, HARASS_TARGET, EVADE_THREAT, LAND/RETURN-TO-HOME — including each state’s single job, the data it owns, and the machinery from earlier chapters it wraps.
Draw and read a state-transition diagram as a design contract: states, transitions, guard conditions, fail-safe exits, and the override transition that grants one state preemptive priority over every other.
Write guard conditions that are deterministic and robust — hysteresis on thresholds, persistence on detections, staleness checks on telemetry — and match each technique to the specific failure it prevents.
Identify race conditions at state boundaries, defuse them with a single-writer, priority-ordered tick, and bound and measure state-transition latency from logged telemetry.

title: 21  Finite State Machines and Behavior Trees for Mission Logic
text:
21.2 Key Vocabulary

Finite state machine (FSM) — mission logic structured as a set of discrete states with exactly one active at a time, plus transitions between them that fire when their guard conditions become true; everything not drawn as a transition is impossible by construction.
State transition — the change of active state, taken when a guard becomes true; in a disciplined machine it is the only mechanism by which the vehicle’s behavior changes, which is what makes logged transitions a complete flight narrative.
Guard condition — the boolean test, computed from observed and estimated data, that gates a transition; a well-written guard is deterministic (same inputs, same answer), reads a consistent snapshot of the world, and never tests elapsed time when it could test state.
Preemption — the interruption of the active behavior by a higher-priority one, with enough context saved — the stashed state and leg index here — that the interrupted work can later resume rather than restart.
Race condition — a situation in which two or more triggers become true within the same update interval, so the outcome depends on the order or timing of their evaluation; defused by making that order explicit and singular rather than accidental.
Hysteresis — the use of separate trigger and release thresholds around a decision boundary, so that a noisy signal crossing the boundary cannot chatter a transition on and off many times a second.
Transition latency — the elapsed time between a guard’s condition becoming true in the world and the first command of the new state reaching the flight controller; the reflex time of the whole autonomy stack, and a quantity worth logging on every transition.
Behavior Tree (BT) — a control architecture in which conditions and actions sit at the leaves of a tree, internal nodes sequence or select among their children, and the whole tree is re-evaluated from the root each tick; priority and preemption emerge from child ordering rather than explicit transition arrows.
Tick — one periodic evaluation cycle of the mission logic — the FSM’s loop iteration or the BT’s root-to-leaf traversal — during which triggers are checked in a fixed order and exactly one behavior acts.

section: 21.3 Five States, Three Chapters of Machinery
text:
21.3 Five States, Three Chapters of Machinery
The machine has five states, and the first useful observation is that none of them is new work. Each state is a thin wrapper around something a previous chapter already built and tested; the machine’s job is not to do anything but to decide which already-working thing runs. That division of labor — behaviors in their own functions, arbitration in one small loop — is the single most important structural decision in the chapter, because every pathology examined later (spaghetti transitions, races, lock-ups) is a symptom of letting the two mix.



Table 21.1: The five mission states, the machinery each wraps, and their entry and exit events.












State
Its one job
Wraps
Enters when
Leaves when




IDLE/TAKEOFF
Arm, establish Offboard, climb to mission altitude
Part II’s warm-up and climb sequence
Power-on
Climb complete: \(\lvert z - z_{sp}\rvert < 0.5\) m


SEARCH_GRID
Fly lawnmower waypoint \(i\) of \(N\) at constant altitude
The Path Planning on the Edge chapter’s generated list and arrival test
Climb complete, or sweep resumed
Detection confirmed, sweep exhausted, or preempted


HARASS_TARGET
Close on the target and fly the deterrence pattern inside a standoff radius
The Harassment Pattern Generation chapter’s pattern generators
Detection confirmed
Target dispersed or track lost, or preempted


EVADE_THREAT
Slew onto the evasion vector, recomputed every tick; climb toward the safe altitude
The previous chapter’s evasion_command
Threat trigger, from any flying state
Threat cleared (resume) or will not clear (go home)


LAND/RETURN-TO-HOME
Climb to return altitude, fly home, descend, disarm
Part II’s RTL machinery
Sweep done, battery reserve, mission clock, or break-off
Landed and disarmed






Two of the state names are compound, and the merging is deliberate. IDLE/TAKEOFF fuses what the Mission Scripting chapter kept separate because, from the mission’s point of view, “getting airborne” is one job with one exit condition; the internal arm-then-climb sequence is the state’s private business. LAND/RETURN-TO-HOME fuses the two ways a flight ends for the same reason: whether the vehicle lands where it is or transits home first is a parameter of one recovery behavior, not two different situations the arbiter must distinguish. A state is a job, not a moment — the test for whether two candidate states should merge is whether the machine would ever need to make a different decision in one than in the other.
The second observation is about data. Each state owns the variables it needs and no others: SEARCH_GRID owns the waypoint list and the index \(i\); HARASS_TARGET owns the target track; EVADE_THREAT owns the stash — the (state, leg index) pair recorded at the moment of preemption — and the safe-altitude setpoint. The Path Planning on the Edge chapter made the case that abandoning a coverage path costs nothing because the path is data, “a list and an index”: store the index, chase the goose, re-enter the list at the stored leg. The stash generalizes that trick to the whole machine. Preemption without a stash is amnesia — the drone that flees a threat and then hovers, mission forgotten, has a working evasion vector and a broken machine.

title: 21  Finite State Machines and Behavior Trees for Mission Logic
text:
21.4 The Diagram Is the Design
For a mission machine, the state-transition diagram is not documentation drawn after the fact; it is the design artifact itself, and it earns that status through what it excludes. Every arrow in Figure 21.1 is a claim — “the system may change behavior here, under this condition” — and every absent arrow is a stronger one: this change of behavior cannot happen, no matter what the code’s author forgot. Reviewing a mission means reviewing this drawing. If a transition cannot be drawn without ambiguity — two arrows from one state whose guards can be true simultaneously, with no stated priority — the machine has a bug before a line of code exists.






Figure 21.1: The five-state mission machine: the normal sequence runs left to right, the return arcs resume the sweep, and the EVADE_THREAT override (dashed amber) may preempt any flying state — a transition evaluated before the state dispatch on every tick.



Walk the drawing the way the mission runs. The solid left-to-right chain is the flight everything is supposed to be: climb, sweep, find, harass, and eventually home. The upper arcs are the loops that make it a search rather than a script — harassment that disperses its target hands control back to the sweep at the stored leg, and a sweep that exhausts its list with nothing found goes home with a clear conscience. So far this is the Mission Scripting chapter’s machine with better-traveled boxes.
The dashed amber arrows are what is genuinely new, and they encode the requirement the previous chapter’s mathematics was built to serve: the threat trigger — closing, soon, and inside the safety radius, the three-part conjunction derived there — must be able to fire from any flying state and take the aircraft instantly. Structurally, this is the same move the Mission Scripting chapter made with its failsafe check: the question is evaluated before the state dispatch, every tick, so no state’s own logic can shadow it, including states added later by someone who never read the original design. One override, drawn once per state, evaluated in one place. When it fires, EVADE_THREAT’s entry action stashes the interrupted state and the sweep index; when the encounter clears — the previous chapter’s exit test, opening and beyond the safety radius with margin — the dashed teal arrow gives back what was taken. And when the encounter refuses to clear, or the battery reaches its floor mid-evasion, the machine does not loiter in a fight it cannot win: it breaks off for home, which is the arrow from EVADE_THREAT to LAND.
One box is conspicuously absent: there is no FAILSAFE state, even though the Mission Scripting chapter’s machine had one. That is because this machine is the middle layer of authority, not the top. The geofence, battery, and link-loss failsafes of the Geofencing and Fail-Safes chapter live in PX4 itself and preempt this machine the way this machine preempts its own states — when they fire, the mission node’s opinion stops mattering entirely. The grey note in the figure records that hierarchy. Mission logic that pretends to be the last line of defense is mission logic that will one day fight its own autopilot; the correct posture is to stay inside the envelope those failsafes police, and to treat their firing as a verdict, not a negotiation.

title: 21  Finite State Machines and Behavior Trees for Mission Logic
text:
21.5 Guards That Deserve the Name
The classic warning about mission machines — don’t build a spaghetti machine — is not about the number of states. Five states can be spaghetti; twenty can be clean. The difference is discipline about transitions, and the discipline has three parts.
One writer, one place, every change logged. The state variable is written by exactly one function, called from exactly one place — the tick — and never from a sensor callback, a timer, or a thread that happens to know better. Callbacks write data (positions, detections, timestamps); the tick reads that data and makes every decision. The corollary costs one line and pays for itself the first debugging session: every transition emits a log line — [STATE CHANGE] SEARCH_GRID -> HARASS_TARGET (detection) — so the flight’s entire behavioral history is grep-able. A machine whose transitions are all logged can be debugged from a transcript; a machine that changes state silently, from three call sites, can only be debugged by luck.
Thresholds get hysteresis; events get persistence. Every guard in the diagram compares a noisy estimate against a threshold, and a noisy signal near a single threshold is a transition oscillator. The previous chapter computed miss distances against a 3 m safety radius using position estimates carrying half-metre-scale error; a predicted miss wobbling between 2.9 m and 3.1 m would enter and exit EVADE_THREAT several times a second, each entry re-stashing context and re-slewing the velocity command — chatter that is expensive in logic and violent in flight. The remedy is two thresholds with a gap wider than the noise: trigger the evasion when the predicted miss drops below 3 m, but release it only when the range exceeds the radius plus a margin — say 4 m — and the closing test has gone positive. The same idea, applied to events instead of thresholds, is persistence: a single-frame detection is noise until it survives \(k\) consecutive frames (the SEARCH_GRID exit guard), and a target is not lost until the track has been silent for a dwell time (the 3 s in the HARASS_TARGET return arc), because a detector that misses two frames should not, by itself, end a deterrence run. Persistence trades a bounded, chosen delay for immunity to single-sample lies — and the delay is honest: a \(k\)-frame confirmation at the detector’s frame rate still preempts the sweep within a few hundred milliseconds, immediate on the timescale of a mission, deliberate on the timescale of noise.
Dead data is worse than no data. The requirement that the machine “gracefully handle sensor drops without crashing the aircraft” is a design constraint on guards, and it starts with an observation: a guard evaluated against a stale estimate is not conservative, it is wrong with confidence. The telemetry stream stops; the last position says the drone is mid-leg; the arrival guard keeps failing; the machine happily streams setpoints computed from a world snapshot growing older by the second. The fix is to make freshness itself the first guard of the tick. Every message carries a timestamp; the tick begins by computing the age of the newest estimate, and the response is graded: beyond a short staleness bound (half a second, matching the Offboard dead-man’s-switch timescale from Part II), the machine stops trusting derived guards and simply holds position — freeze, don’t guess; beyond a longer bound (a couple of seconds), it gives up on the mission and goes home on the flight controller’s own navigation, which does not depend on the companion computer’s dying data path. The same logic applies per-stream: a threat whose track has gone stale is treated as unknown, not as gone — EVADE_THREAT holds its climb rather than declaring victory on silence.

title: 21  Finite State Machines and Behavior Trees for Mission Logic
section: 21.6 Races, Edges, and the Latency Budget
text:
21.6 Races, Edges, and the Latency Budget
The advice to simulate the unexpected comes with a specific scenario worth taking literally: inject the threat at the exact moment the drone is turning at the edge of the search grid. It is a well-chosen needle. At that instant three things are true at once — the arrival guard for waypoint \(i\) has just fired, the leg index is mid-increment, and the threat trigger is newly true — and any looseness in how the machine orders its decisions becomes visible. Suppose detections arrive in one callback, positions in another, and both callbacks write self.state directly. The arrival callback advances the index and begins the turn; the threat callback, running between two lines of the other, stashes a state that is half-updated — an index pointing at a leg the machine never actually started. Weeks later, an evasion resumes the sweep one leg early and the coverage claim silently loses a swath. That is a race condition, and its defining cruelty is that it is invisible in every test where events arrive politely one at a time.
The defense is architectural, and it was already stated as the first guard discipline: a single-threaded tick in which all triggers are evaluated, in a fixed priority order, and at most one transition is taken per tick. Priority resolves simultaneity by decree rather than by accident: health first, threat second, the active state’s own exit guard last. When the threat trigger and the arrival guard are both true on the same tick, the threat wins, the arrival is simply re-evaluated on the next tick after the encounter clears, and nothing about the outcome depends on which callback happened to run first — because callbacks no longer decide anything. Edge cases are where state machines love to lock up; the lock-ups almost always trace to two authorities disagreeing about the current state, and a machine with one authority cannot disagree with itself.
Ordering makes the machine correct; the tick rate makes it fast enough, and that claim should be numbers, not adjectives. Define the reaction chain for the SEARCH_GRID → HARASS_TARGET transition: a goose enters the camera’s view; the detector, running at 5 Hz with 80 ms of inference latency (the kind of budget Part III’s edge-inference chapters made routine), reports it; the tick, at 20 Hz, evaluates the guard. The worst case stacks every wait end to end:
\[
\begin{aligned}
t_{\text{react}} &\le T_{\text{det}} + t_{\text{inf}} + T_{\text{tick}} \\
                 &= 200 + 80 + 50 = 330\ \text{ms},
\end{aligned}
\]
plus \((k-1)\) further detector periods if the guard demands \(k\)-frame persistence — a deliberate, legible trade between reflex and false alarms. The same arithmetic run on the threat trigger explains why the evasion chapter insisted its assessment was cheap enough to re-run at the estimator’s full rate: the trigger rides the 50 Hz estimator, not the 5 Hz detector, so the override’s worst-case reaction is dominated by the tick alone. Logging turns the bound into a measurement: stamp the moment a guard’s input first satisfied it and the moment the new state’s first command left the node, and the difference — the transition latency — lands in the telemetry log next to position, velocity, and active state, where a histogram of it after each flight verifies that the machine’s reflexes match its design.
One more physical reality belongs to transitions. A state change is a command discontinuity: SEARCH_GRID was streaming a gentle leg-following setpoint, and one tick later EVADE_THREAT wants 5 m/s toward the escape plane. The previous chapter’s warning applies at every boundary, not just the dramatic one — a commanded velocity that steps instantly exists only in simulation, and an aircraft asked to honor the step responds by saturating motors and shedding tracking accuracy exactly when precision matters most. Every state’s output therefore passes through the same slew limiter, the bounded-acceleration ramp built for the evasion command; transitions change the target of the ramp, never the command itself. The machine decides in discrete jumps; the airframe must never feel them.

title: 21  Finite State Machines and Behavior Trees for Mission Logic
text:
21.7 The Machine in Code
The whole design compresses into one loop that reads like the diagram — which is the test of both:
from enum import Enum, auto

class MissionState(Enum):
    IDLE_TAKEOFF = auto()
    SEARCH_GRID = auto()
    HARASS_TARGET = auto()
    EVADE_THREAT = auto()
    LAND_RTH = auto()

FLYING = {MissionState.IDLE_TAKEOFF, MissionState.SEARCH_GRID,
          MissionState.HARASS_TARGET, MissionState.EVADE_THREAT}

def transition(self, new_state, reason):
    self.log(f"[STATE CHANGE] {self.state.name} -> {new_state.name}"
             f" ({reason})")
    self.t_guard_true = self.guard_stamp    # transition-latency bookkeeping
    self.state = new_state

def tick(self):                             # 20 Hz; the only writer of state
    # 1. never act on dead data
    age = self.now() - self.last_estimate_stamp
    if age > 2.0:
        self.transition(MissionState.LAND_RTH, "telemetry stale")
    elif age > 0.5:
        self.hold_position()                # freeze, don't guess
        return

    # 2. the override: evaluated before any state's own logic
    cmd = evasion_command(self.pos, self.vel,
                          self.threat_pos, self.threat_vel)
    if cmd is not None and self.state in FLYING and self.airborne():
        if self.state != MissionState.EVADE_THREAT:
            self.stash = (self.state, self.leg_index)
            self.transition(MissionState.EVADE_THREAT, "threat trigger")

    # 3. one state, one job; at most one transition per tick
    match self.state:
        case MissionState.IDLE_TAKEOFF:
            self.fly_takeoff()
            if self.at_mission_altitude():
                self.transition(MissionState.SEARCH_GRID, "climb complete")
        case MissionState.SEARCH_GRID:
            self.fly_leg(self.leg_index)    # lawnmower list + arrival test
            if self.detection_confirmed():  # k consecutive frames
                self.transition(MissionState.HARASS_TARGET, "detection")
            elif self.sweep_exhausted():
                self.transition(MissionState.LAND_RTH, "sweep done")
        case MissionState.HARASS_TARGET:
            self.fly_pattern()              # the Harassment Pattern Generation chapter's business
            if self.target_gone(dwell=3.0): # persistence, not one frame
                self.transition(MissionState.SEARCH_GRID, "resume sweep")
        case MissionState.EVADE_THREAT:
            self.slew_toward(cmd or self.last_evasion_cmd)
            if self.threat_cleared():       # opening AND far, with margin
                prev, self.leg_index = self.stash
                if (prev == MissionState.HARASS_TARGET
                        and self.target_gone(dwell=3.0)):
                    prev = MissionState.SEARCH_GRID   # stale track: sweep
                self.transition(prev, "threat cleared")
        case MissionState.LAND_RTH:
            self.fly_home_and_land()
Every principle of the chapter is visible as a line. Freshness is step 1; the override is step 2, before the dispatch, stashing context on the way in; each state performs one action and tests its own exits; every transition passes through one function that logs and stamps it. The resume logic carries the chapter’s one subtle guard: EVADE_THREAT gives back the state it took unless that state’s own preconditions have rotted while the drone was busy fleeing — a harassment target not seen for the whole encounter is a track, not a target, and the honest resume is the sweep, from which a fresh detection will re-enter HARASS_TARGET through the front door. Guards compose; a resume is just a transition, and it gets guarded like one.

title: 21  Finite State Machines and Behavior Trees for Mission Logic
section: 21.8 When the Flat Machine Runs Out
text:
21.8 When the Flat Machine Runs Out
Look back at Figure 21.1 and count what the override costs: one dashed arrow per flying state. Now add the global concerns hiding in the grey note — staleness, battery, geofence margin — each of which is also, logically, an arrow from every state. A flat machine with \(S\) states and \(G\) always-on concerns owes \(S \times G\) transitions, and every new state signs up for all \(G\) of them while every new concern must be wired into all \(S\) states. At five states and a handful of concerns the diagram is legible because this chapter cheated deliberately — hoisting the override and the health checks out of the states and into the tick’s preamble. That hoisting is the insight: priorities that apply everywhere want to be structure, not arrows. The Behavior Tree is what that insight looks like when it is taken all the way.
A BT turns the arrangement inside out. There are no states and no transitions; there is a tree whose leaves are conditions (instant tests) and actions (behaviors that may run for many ticks), and whose internal nodes compose them: a sequence (→) ticks its children in order and needs all of them to succeed, a selector (?) ticks its children in order and takes the first that does not fail. Every tick, evaluation starts at the root and flows down. Figure 21.2 rebuilds the whole mission this way: the root selector tries “defend” first (threat closing? then evade), “energy” second (battery at reserve? then return home), and only then the mission sequence — take off, then harass if the goose is in view, else search, then land. Preemption is no longer drawn anywhere, because it is not a feature — it is a consequence. The tick that finds “threat closing?” true never reaches the mission branch at all; whatever action was RUNNING there is halted by the traversal itself. The five-state machine needed one dashed arrow per state to say “the threat outranks you”; the tree says it once, by putting the defend branch first.






Figure 21.2: The mission rebuilt as a Behavior Tree: a root selector tries defend, then energy, then the mission sequence, and child ordering alone gives the threat branch preemptive priority — no override arrows required.



The tree’s second virtue is that recovery composes as naturally as preemption. Watch what happens after a successful deterrence run, with no special code: the goose leaves, so “goose in view?” starts returning FAILURE, so the inner selector falls through to SEARCH_GRID — which has kept its leg index, because actions own their data here exactly as states did — and the sweep resumes. The flat machine needed an explicit return arc with a resume guard; the tree gets the same behavior from a condition ceasing to hold. Adding a new always-on concern — say, a rule that icing conditions ground the mission — is one new branch inserted at the right priority, touching nothing else; in the flat machine it would be a visit to every state. This is what “cleaner modularity and preemption handling” means concretely, and it is why BTs displaced giant FSMs first in game AI and then across robotics.
None of which retires the five-state machine. At this mission’s scale the FSM is arguably the better artifact: its diagram is a complete, auditable enumeration of everything the system can do, its stash-and-resume semantics are explicit rather than emergent, and its code is a page. The honest engineering rule is about derivatives, not absolutes: when each new behavior or concern costs a constant amount of drawing and wiring, the flat machine is fine; when the cost starts scaling with the number of existing states — when the arrows begin to multiply — the structure is asking to become a tree. The running example sits, by design, right at that boundary, which is why this chapter builds the machine flat and shows the tree beside it.






NoteFor More



The graduate-track version of this mission replaces the flat FSM with a formal Behavior Tree outright, and the formalism rewards a closer look. Each node returns one of three statuses per tick — SUCCESS, FAILURE, or RUNNING — and RUNNING is the ingredient that makes the tree a control structure rather than a decision tree: a long action holds its branch across many ticks while the higher-priority branches keep being re-checked above it. Beyond sequence and selector, production trees add decorators (single-child modifiers: inverters, retry-N-times, rate limiters, timeouts) and a parallel node that ticks several children at once — a monitor-while-acting pattern, e.g. stream the deterrence pattern while a watchdog child tracks the target’s freshness. A subtlety worth knowing before writing one: classic sequence/selector nodes come in reactive and with-memory variants. A reactive sequence re-ticks its earlier children every tick (so “take off” must be idempotent — return SUCCESS instantly once airborne), while a with-memory sequence resumes at the child that was RUNNING (cheaper, but it gives up the continuous re-checking that makes preemption automatic); choosing wrongly produces either wasted work or a tree that cannot be interrupted, and the standard advice is reactive composites at the safety-critical top of the tree, memory where re-checking is genuinely redundant. The ecosystem is mature: BehaviorTree.CPP powers the ROS 2 Nav2 stack’s mission logic, with a graphical editor (Groot) for authoring and live tree inspection, and py_trees (with py_trees_ros) offers the same ideas in Python at prototyping speed. The companion graduate extension — a threat that actively pursues rather than flying straight — slots into this architecture cleanly: the evade action’s internals swap the one-shot escape vector for the potential-field or replanning methods sketched in the previous chapter’s For More, while the tree above it does not change at all. That separation — behaviors evolve, structure holds — is the whole argument.

title: 21  Finite State Machines and Behavior Trees for Mission Logic
text:
21.9 Check Your Understanding

The five-state machine merges IDLE with TAKEOFF and LAND with RETURN-TO-HOME, yet keeps SEARCH_GRID and HARASS_TARGET separate even though both are “fly a pattern and watch the sensors.” Using the chapter’s test for state identity, justify both decisions.







TipShow answer





The test: two candidate states deserve to merge when the machine would never make a different decision in one than in the other. IDLE and TAKEOFF share every exit and every override response — nothing preempts differently mid-arm versus mid-climb, and both exist only to reach “airborne at mission altitude” — so they are one job with private phases. The same holds for LAND versus RETURN-TO-HOME: one recovery behavior, parameterized by whether a transit precedes the descent. SEARCH_GRID and HARASS_TARGET fail the test everywhere: different exit guards (detection versus dispersal/track-loss), different data owned (list and index versus target track), different resume semantics after an evasion (the sweep resumes unconditionally; harassment resumes only if the track is fresh). Merging them would force one state to carry flags distinguishing its two personalities — which is the flag-pile the FSM formalism exists to abolish.




The threat trigger fires when the predicted miss drops below \(R_{safe} = 3\) m, but the release guard demands range greater than 4 m and a positive closing test. The position estimate near the boundary carries roughly 0.5 m of noise. Explain what a single 3 m threshold for both directions would do in flight, and why the 1 m gap is sized correctly relative to the noise.







TipShow answer





With one threshold, an encounter hovering near 3 m would cross it many times a second as the noisy estimate wobbles: each crossing enters or exits EVADE_THREAT, re-stashing context, re-aiming the slew, and jerking the commanded velocity — chatter that degrades tracking exactly when margin is thinnest, and floods the log with meaningless transitions. Hysteresis works when the gap between trigger and release comfortably exceeds the noise: 1 m against 0.5 m-scale scatter means a genuine geometry change, not a noise excursion, is required to reverse the decision (roughly a two-sigma separation). The release also demands the closing test go positive because range alone is not safety — a threat can be far and inbound; requiring opening and far makes the release a statement about the encounter, not about one noisy sample.




A teammate wires the detection callback to write self.state = HARASS_TARGET directly “to save a tick of latency.” Describe the race this creates at the search grid’s corner turn, and what the single-writer tick buys that the 50 ms costs.







TipShow answer





At a corner, the tick’s SEARCH_GRID case is mid-flight through advancing the leg index and issuing the turn when the callback, running asynchronously, overwrites the state. The tick’s remaining lines execute in a state they were not written for: the index may be half-updated (stashed or resumed wrong later), the turn setpoint may be issued after the state changed (a search command leaking into harassment), and if the threat trigger also fires that tick, the priority ordering is bypassed entirely — the callback’s write wins over the override that is supposed to outrank it. The single-writer tick makes every decision at one point in time, against one consistent snapshot, in one stated priority order; outcomes stop depending on callback scheduling. The cost is bounded and known — at most one 50 ms tick of added latency — and the reaction budget already carries far larger terms (the detector’s 200 ms period, 80 ms of inference), so the trade buys determinism for a marginal share of the total.




A mission runs its tick at 20 Hz, its detector at 4 Hz with 120 ms inference latency, and requires 2-frame persistence before leaving SEARCH_GRID. Bound the worst-case time from a goose entering the camera’s view to the first HARASS_TARGET command, and identify which term dominates and what that implies about where engineering effort should go.







TipShow answer





Worst case, the goose appears just after a frame is captured: wait one full detector period (250 ms), plus inference (120 ms) for the first report; persistence demands a second consecutive frame, adding one more period plus inference is not needed — the second report arrives one period after the first, so add 250 ms; then up to one tick (50 ms) before the guard is evaluated. Total: \(250 + 120 + 250 + 50 = 670\) ms. The persistence and detector-period terms dominate — 500 of the 670 ms — so raising the tick rate is nearly worthless, while raising detector frame rate (or triggering the guard on the inference timestamp rather than arrival time) attacks the real budget. Reflex time lives in perception, not in the state machine; the machine’s job is merely not to add to it.




During a harassment run, EVADE_THREAT preempts and the encounter takes 20 seconds to clear. Explain why the machine resumes SEARCH_GRID at the stored leg rather than HARASS_TARGET, and why this is a guard on the resume transition rather than a special case inside EVADE_THREAT’s escape logic.







TipShow answer





The stash records where control was, but HARASS_TARGET’s precondition is a fresh target track, and twenty seconds of fleeing is far beyond the track’s dwell time — the goose has moved, possibly dispersed by the commotion itself. Resuming harassment would aim a deterrence pattern at a twenty-second-old coordinate. Resuming the sweep is honest: it re-covers the area, and if the goose is still present, a fresh confirmed detection re-enters HARASS_TARGET through its normal entry guard, with a current track. Placing the check on the resume transition keeps the architecture’s separation intact: EVADE_THREAT’s job is escape geometry, and it should know nothing about targets; the resume is a transition like any other, so it gets a guard like any other. Guards compose — that is the design’s whole economy.




Express, in one sentence each, how the flat FSM and the Behavior Tree encode the rule “evasion outranks everything,” and then compute the wiring cost in each architecture of adding a new always-on concern (icing conditions ground the mission) to a system that has grown to 12 states or action branches.







TipShow answer





The FSM encodes the rule as one dashed override arrow per flying state, all funneling into EVADE_THREAT, evaluated before the state dispatch; the BT encodes it by making the defend branch the root selector’s first child, so every tick checks it before any other branch can run. Adding the icing concern to the flat machine means a new guard reachable from all 12 states — either 12 new arrows or another hoisted preamble check, plus a review of every state’s resume/stash semantics against the new exit: cost proportional to \(S\). In the tree it is one new sequence — condition “icing?” then action “return home” — inserted at the appropriate priority between defend and the mission branch: cost constant, existing branches untouched. That derivative — per-addition cost constant versus proportional to system size — is the practical boundary where the tree earns its keep.

21.10 Try It
Part 1 — build the machine and hunt its races. Extend the Mission Scripting chapter’s state-machine node into the full five-state mission in SITL. Wire SEARCH_GRID to the lawnmower generator’s waypoint list and arrival test; stub HARASS_TARGET as a fixed-radius orbit about the reported target (the Harassment Pattern Generation chapter supplies the real patterns, closing the loop with the target-centering law the Target Tracking and Visual Servoing chapter supplies in between); wire the threat trigger and EVADE_THREAT around evasion_command(), evaluated in the tick’s preamble with the stash-and-resume bookkeeping of this chapter; route every state’s output through one shared slew limiter. Script the world: a simulated detection event partway through leg 3, a threat injected during the harassment orbit. Log every transition as [STATE CHANGE] A -> B (reason) with a timestamp, and log telemetry — position, velocity, active state — at full rate. Fly the complete lifecycle: takeoff, sweep, detection, harassment, threat, evasion, resume or return, land. Then torture it: inject the threat on the exact tick the drone turns at a grid corner (script the injection off the arrival guard’s own log line to guarantee the collision) and confirm the stash resumes the correct leg; kill the detection stream mid-harassment and confirm the dwell guard, not a crash, ends the run; freeze the telemetry stream and confirm the staleness ladder holds, then goes home. Every torture case should end with the machine in a defensible state and a log that explains itself.
Part 2 — measure the reflexes, then grow the tree. From Part 1’s logs, compute transition latency for every transition in the flight — guard-true timestamp to first new-state command — and plot the histogram per transition type; check the threat override’s latency against the tick-period bound and the detection transition against the persistence arithmetic of this chapter, and explain any outlier. Then rebuild the same mission as a Behavior Tree in py_trees: root selector, defend branch, energy branch, mission sequence with the harass-else-search selector inside it, reusing Part 1’s behavior functions as action nodes unchanged. Verify the same scripted flight produces the same trajectory. Finally, run the chapter’s scaling argument as an experiment: add one new always-on concern — a wind limit that grounds the mission when estimated wind exceeds a threshold — to both implementations, and count the sites each change touched. Two sentences: which architecture would you trust a teammate to extend without you reviewing the diff, and what, concretely, made the difference?

title: 22  Target Tracking and Visual Servoing
text:
22.1 Learning Objectives
The previous chapter built the arbiter and left one box running on credit. HARASS_TARGET earned its full citizenship in the five-state machine — an entry guard with \(k\)-frame persistence, a dwell-time exit, stash-and-resume semantics under preemption — while its actual flying stayed deliberately thin: the Try It stubbed it as a fixed-radius orbit about the reported target, and the deterrence patterns themselves arrive in the next chapter. But between the arbiter and the patterns sits a premise that neither supplies. Every tick that HARASS_TARGET runs, it consumes a target track, and everything downstream — the dwell guard, the orbit stub, the swooping and circling patterns to come — assumes that track stays fresh for tens of seconds while the aircraft maneuvers aggressively around the very animal it is tracking. Nothing built so far makes that true. A track is fed by detections; detections come from a camera with a finite field of view; and the aircraft’s own motion is constantly working to carry the goose out of that field of view.
The Coordinate Frames chapter is why this gap carries a price tag rather than a vague unease. That chapter turned a bounding box and a depth value into a world-frame NED position — and then priced the result honestly: calibration, attitude error, synchronization, and depth uncertainty stack to perhaps half a metre at 6 m range, which is why it closed by insisting the transformed position be treated as an estimate to be refined — re-detected, re-transformed, and filtered as the aircraft approaches. Refinement has a precondition the transform cannot enforce: the goose must still be in the frame when the next image arrives. Fly toward a half-metre-wrong estimate of a moving bird, with a camera whose 640 columns span 90°, and a few seconds of accumulated error, target motion, and attitude transients will walk the bounding box to the image border and off it — at which point the detector goes silent, the track goes stale, and the position estimate that navigation depends on stops updating precisely when it is needed most. The machinery that prevents this is visual servoing: closing a control loop directly on what the camera sees, so that “keep the target in view” is not a hope but a feedback law. This chapter builds that law — a proportional controller whose error signal is measured in pixels — and makes the architectural argument the running example depends on: the image-plane loop and the world-frame estimate are not two answers to one question but answers to two different questions, and the system needs both.

Distinguish position-based visual servoing (PBVS) from image-based visual servoing (IBVS) — what kind of sensor each treats the camera as, which space its error signal lives in, and which failure modes each inherits — and classify the running example’s existing detection-to-waypoint pipeline within that taxonomy.
Derive the decoupled proportional centering law from first principles: pixel error from the image centre, normalization that makes the gains resolution-independent, the sign discipline that keeps the loop negative-feedback in PX4’s FRD/NED conventions, and deadband and saturation as the practical guards around it.
Predict the closed-loop behavior of the centering loop quantitatively — its exponential time constant from the gain, the steady-state lag it leaves against a moving target, and the gain ceiling imposed by perception latency — using the same machinery as the Closed-Loop Control chapter, with pixel error as a new kind of error signal.
Explain, at an introductory level, what the interaction matrix (image Jacobian) is, and why rotational centering channels are depth-independent while translational channels have loop gain that scales inversely with target range.
Argue the “complementary, not redundant” two-loop architecture: an outer position-based loop that navigates on the Coordinate Frames chapter’s world-frame estimate, an inner image-based loop that keeps the target centered at frame rate — and why the inner loop is what keeps the outer loop’s estimate alive.
