title: 22  Target Tracking and Visual Servoing
text:
22.2 Key Vocabulary

Visual servoing — controlling a robot’s motion by closing a feedback loop directly on live camera measurements, as opposed to look-then-move, in which vision is consulted once to plan a motion that then executes open-loop.
Position-based visual servoing (PBVS) — the scheme that treats the camera as a 3D sensor: image measurements are first converted into a Cartesian position or pose estimate of the target, and the control error is computed in that 3D task space — “fly to where the goose is.”
Image-based visual servoing (IBVS) — the scheme that treats the camera as a 2D sensor: the control error is computed directly in the image plane, as the offset between where a feature is and where it should be, with no 3D reconstruction inside the loop — “put the goose back in the middle of the picture.”
Pixel error (centering error) — the image-plane offset \((e_x, e_y)\) between a detected feature’s pixel coordinates and its desired location, here the image centre; the error signal of the centering loop, and the only measurement it needs.
Interaction matrix (image Jacobian) — the matrix \(\mathbf{L}\) relating the velocity of image features to the camera’s velocity, \(\dot{\mathbf{s}} = \mathbf{L}\,\mathbf{v}_c\); its entries depend on the target’s depth, which is why translational visual-servo channels need at least a rough range estimate to scale their gains.
Deadband — a small zone around zero error inside which the controller commands nothing, so that a target already near-centered does not keep the aircraft hunting against detector noise.
Gain scheduling — adjusting a controller gain as an operating condition changes; here, scaling the translational centering gain with the depth estimate so the loop behaves the same at 3 m as at 12 m.
Target-following control loop — the complete cycle detection → pixel error → velocity/yaw-rate command → aircraft motion → new detection; a closed loop whose total latency sets how hard its gains can be pushed.

title: 22  Target Tracking and Visual Servoing
section: 22.3 Two Ways to Use a Camera
text:
22.3 Two Ways to Use a Camera
The field’s standard taxonomy, established in the two tutorial papers every treatment of this subject descends from (Hutchinson, Hager, and Corke 1996; Chaumette and Hutchinson 2006), splits visual servo control by a single question: in which space does the error live?
Position-based visual servoing treats the camera as a 3D sensor. Image measurements — feature points, marker corners, a bounding box plus a depth value — are first pushed through a calibrated camera model into an estimate of the target’s position or pose in Cartesian space, and the controller drives a 3D error: the vector from where the vehicle is to where the estimate says it should be. The reader has already built one. The pipeline of the Coordinate Frames chapter — pixel and depth, through the intrinsics, through the fixed extrinsic rotation, through the attitude quaternion, out to a NED coordinate handed to navigation — is PBVS in everything but name. Its virtues are exactly the ones that chapter cashed in: the output is a geometrically meaningful world position, directly usable for waypoint navigation, standoff-distance logic, geofence checks, and logging where the goose was on a map. Its weakness was priced in the same chapter’s error budget: every link in the reconstruction — intrinsics, extrinsics, attitude, synchronization, depth — feeds its error straight into the commanded destination, with nothing inside the loop to notice or correct. And one more weakness went unstated there because no chapter yet needed it: nothing in a PBVS loop knows about the image border. The controller reasons entirely in world coordinates; it will happily command a maneuver that is correct in 3D and sweeps the target out of the camera’s field of view on the way.
Image-based visual servoing treats the camera as a 2D sensor and refuses the reconstruction step entirely. The error is computed where the measurement lives — in the image — as the offset between the feature’s current pixel coordinates and its desired ones, and that offset maps through a control law directly to motion commands. No pose estimate exists inside the loop, so no pose-estimation error can bias it: if the camera’s focal length is 5% wrong, or the mounting pitch is 2° off, an IBVS loop’s path to the goal bends, but its destination does not move, because the loop keeps pushing until the thing it actually measures — pixel error — reaches zero. The general IBVS control law, given in both tutorials, is a proportional law:
\[
\mathbf{v}_c = -\lambda\, \mathbf{L}^{+}\, \mathbf{e},
\]
where \(\mathbf{e}\) is the stacked image-feature error, \(\mathbf{L}^{+}\) is the pseudoinverse of the interaction matrix, and \(\lambda > 0\) is the gain. The interaction matrix is where IBVS keeps its one debt to 3D geometry: \(\mathbf{L}\)’s entries depend on the target’s depth \(Z\), so even a scheme that never reconstructs a pose needs a rough range to scale its commands sensibly — a point the next section makes concrete. IBVS’s classical pathologies are the mirror image of its virtues: it is only locally stable in general, and for large errors — especially large rotations — the commanded 3D trajectory can be strange, including the well-known camera retreat, where the camera backs away unnecessarily while sorting out a rotation (Chaumette and Hutchinson 2006).



Table 22.1: The classical trade-offs between the two visual-servoing schemes (Chaumette and Hutchinson 2006; Hutchinson, Hager, and Corke 1996).

Two cautions before the table hardens into dogma. First, the “IBVS is robust, PBVS is fragile” summary is a statement about error structure, not a guaranteed performance ranking: in a direct head-to-head on a real robotic assembly task, a well-calibrated PBVS system converged faster and slightly more accurately than its IBVS counterpart, because once calibration is trustworthy, PBVS’s clean Cartesian trajectory wins and IBVS’s theoretical robustness edge has little left to pay for (Peng and Radke 2020). The trade-offs are real; their sign, in any given system, is an empirical question. Second, the schemes are endpoints of a spectrum, not a binary: hybrid formulations that blend a partial 3D estimate with image-plane features in one control law exist precisely because each pure scheme has failure modes the other lacks (Chaumette and Hutchinson 2006) — a fact the two-loop architecture later in this chapter exploits at the systems level rather than the control-law level.
For the specific task in front of the running example — keep a detected goose centered in the frame while the aircraft works around it — the choice is not close. “Target at image centre” is an image-space objective; reconstructing a 3D pose to answer “is the goose left or right of centre, and by how much” would launder a two-subtraction question through the entire error budget of the frame chain and hand back a worse answer, later. Applied UAV target-following systems make the same call, defining the error as the pixel offset between the detected feature and the desired (centered) position (Chen et al. 2021) and, in the simplest implementations, driving it with proportional or PID control. PBVS keeps the jobs it is actually good at — approach, standoff, mapping — and IBVS takes the one it was born for.

title: 22  Target Tracking and Visual Servoing
text:
22.4 The Centering Law
The construction needs three ingredients: an error, a sign discipline, and two guards. All three fit in Figure 22.1.






Figure 22.1: The pixel-error geometry of the centering loop: the detected bounding-box centroid, the image centre, the two error components, and the commands they produce under the running example’s gains.



The error. Let the image be \(W \times H\) pixels with the origin at the top-left — the convention the Images as Data chapter fixed, \(u\) increasing rightward, \(v\) increasing downward — so the centre sits at \((c_x, c_y) = (W/2,\, H/2)\). The Part III detector reports a bounding box; its centroid \((u, v)\) is the feature. The pixel error is the componentwise offset,
\[
\begin{aligned}
e_x &= u - c_x \qquad \text{(positive: target right of centre)} \\
e_y &= v - c_y \qquad \text{(positive: target below centre),}
\end{aligned}
\]
and dividing each component by its half-frame dimension normalizes it into \([-1, 1]\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{e}_x &= \frac{e_x}{W/2} \\
\hat{e}_y &= \frac{e_y}{H/2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The normalization looks cosmetic and is not. It makes the gains resolution-independent: a target one-quarter of the way to the frame edge produces \(\hat{e}_x = 0.5\) whether the camera is running its 640 × 480 depth-aligned mode or a 1280 × 720 mode, so a tuning session survives a camera-mode change, and the gains acquire honest physical units — radians per second of yaw, metres per second of climb, at full-scale error.
The law. The full IBVS machinery would build the interaction matrix for the centroid feature and invert it. For this task, the matrix collapses. One feature, near the image centre, at a roughly known working distance, controlled through two nearly decoupled channels — horizontal error corrected by yaw, vertical error corrected by vertical velocity — makes \(\mathbf{L}\) effectively constant and near-diagonal, so its pseudoinverse folds into two per-axis constants, and the general law \(\mathbf{v}_c = -\lambda \mathbf{L}^{+}\mathbf{e}\) specializes to two independent proportional controllers:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\omega_z &= K_{\text{yaw}}\, \hat{e}_x \\
v_D &= K_{\text{alt}}\, \hat{e}_y,
\end{aligned}
\]
with \(\omega_z\) the commanded yaw rate, \(v_D\) the commanded vertical velocity in NED (positive down), and \(K_{\text{yaw}}, K_{\text{alt}} > 0\). This decoupled-proportional pattern is exactly the simplified form applied UAV tracking systems fly before the controller is upgraded (below); the justification for the simplification is the near-constancy of \(\mathbf{L}\) for this one-feature, small-error, known-ranges regime — push outside that regime (large errors, features far off-axis, unknown depth) and the full matrix earns its keep.
The signs. The alert reader will notice the minus sign of \(-\lambda \mathbf{L}^{+}\mathbf{e}\) has vanished, and the explanation is worth a paragraph because a wrong sign here is the single most common visual-servoing bug. What the general law’s minus sign encodes is negative feedback — commands must shrink the error — and whether that surfaces as a plus or minus in code depends entirely on the axis conventions at both ends of the loop. Trace the horizontal channel in the book’s conventions. In PX4’s FRD body frame, positive yaw rate swings the nose right. A camera panning right drags the whole scene left across the image: for a target near the centre, \(\dot{u} \approx -f_x\, \omega_z\), with \(f_x\) the focal length in pixels playing its geometric role as pixels per radian. So a target right of centre (\(\hat{e}_x > 0\)) commanded through \(\omega_z = K_{\text{yaw}}\hat{e}_x > 0\) yaws the nose right, slides the image left, and shrinks the error — two sign conventions (image-\(u\) rightward, FRD-yaw rightward) composing into a positive gain. The vertical channel composes the same way: positive \(\hat{e}_y\) (target below centre) commands positive \(v_D\) (descend, in down-positive NED), the descending camera slides the image up, and \(e_y\) shrinks. In a z-up convention — common in the literature — the same physics surfaces with minus signs, which is why published control laws disagree about signs while agreeing about everything real. The invariant to verify is never the symbol; it is the loop: does each channel’s command move the target toward the centre? Get one sign backwards and the loop is positive feedback — every correction pushes the goose farther out, exponentially, until it exits the frame in under a second. The Coordinate Frames chapter’s warning that a reflection in the transform surfaces in flight as mirrored behavior — steering left toward a target on the right — has a control-loop twin here, and the bench test in this chapter’s Try It exists to catch it before flight ever does.
The guards. Two practical amendments, both standard in fielded systems, complete the law. First, a deadband: inside a small normalized radius of the centre — 5% is typical, about 16 columns and 12 rows here — command zero. Detector centroids jitter by pixels frame to frame even on a stationary bird; without a deadband the loop dutifully chases that jitter, and the aircraft hunts — small perpetual yaw and climb oscillations that waste battery, smear the camera, and accomplish nothing, since a goose 15 pixels off-centre is exactly as tracked as one dead-centre. (One refinement worth knowing: commanding zero inside the band and \(K\hat{e}\) outside it puts a step discontinuity at the band’s edge, so implementations often subtract the band instead — command proportional to \(\hat{e}\) beyond the deadband — trading the step for a smooth ramp.) Second, saturation: clip each command to a ceiling well inside the airframe’s capability, for the same reason every state’s output in the previous chapter passed through the shared slew limiter — a bounding box appearing at the frame edge should produce a brisk turn, not a full-authority lunge that trades tracking accuracy for drama. The centering loop’s output joins every other behavior’s output at that same limiter; the loop decides direction and urgency, the limiter keeps the airframe’s experience continuous.
One structural fact about this law deserves to be stated before the numbers, because the whole architecture argument rests on it: the law says nothing about distance. Both channels rotate or translate the camera to re-point it; neither knows how far away the goose is, whether the aircraft is closing or retreating, or when to stop. A pure centering loop would keep a goose perfectly framed from 400 m away, forever. Approach and standoff belong to the world-frame estimate — which is the “complementary, not redundant” section’s business.

title: 22  Target Tracking and Visual Servoing
text:
22.5 The Loop, Run by Numbers
Take the frame in Figure 22.1: the running example’s 640 × 480 camera, a confirmed track whose bounding-box centroid sits at \((u, v) = (480, 180)\) — upper right, a goose lifting away to the right of the aircraft’s nose. With gains \(K_{\text{yaw}} = 0.8\) rad/s and \(K_{\text{alt}} = 1.2\) m/s at full-scale error and a 0.05 deadband:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{e}_x &= \frac{480 - 320}{320} = +0.50 \\
\hat{e}_y &= \frac{180 - 240}{240} = -0.25,
\end{aligned}
\]
both far outside the deadband, so the loop acts:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\omega_z &= 0.8 \times 0.50 = +0.40\ \text{rad/s} \approx 23^{\circ}/\text{s (yaw right)} \\
v_D &= 1.2 \times (-0.25) = -0.30\ \text{m/s (negative D: climb).}
\end{aligned}
\]
Yaw right at 23°/s, climb at 0.3 m/s — a firm, unhurried correction, reproducible on paper from four numbers and two gains.
What happens next is where the Closed-Loop Control chapter’s machinery takes over, because a pixel error is just an error signal, and this is just a P controller wearing a camera. Combine the image kinematics with the control law: \(\dot{e}_x = \dot{u} \approx -f_x \omega_z\) and \(\omega_z = K_{\text{yaw}} e_x / (W/2)\) give
\[
\dot{\hat{e}}_x = -\frac{f_x}{W/2}\, K_{\text{yaw}}\, \hat{e}_x,
\]
a first-order exponential decay. The running example’s camera makes the constant memorable: a 90° horizontal field of view over 640 columns gave \(f_x = 320\) pixels in the Coordinate Frames chapter — exactly \(W/2\) — so the ratio is 1 and the normalized gain is the closed-loop bandwidth: time constant \(\tau = 1/K_{\text{yaw}} = 1.25\) s. From \(\hat{e}_x = 0.50\) the error decays to the 0.05 deadband in \(\tau \ln(0.50/0.05) \approx 2.9\) s, and the yaw rate decays with it — the proportional controller’s signature soft landing, no overshoot, no ringing, provided the gain respects the loop’s delay.
That proviso is the tuning story in one inequality. The error the controller acts on is old: roughly 50 ms of capture-to-publish pipeline (the Real-Time Inference chapter’s budget) plus up to one 20 Hz mission tick, call it a delay \(T_d \approx 0.1\) s. A proportional loop with pure delay, \(\dot{e}(t) = -K\,e(t - T_d)\), goes formally unstable when \(K\,T_d\) reaches \(\pi/2\) — here \(K \approx 15\) — but degrades long before: as \(K T_d\) grows past a few tenths, the controller is forever correcting an error that no longer exists, overshooting centre and swinging back, the same phase-lag mechanism the Closed-Loop Control chapter exposed. At \(K_{\text{yaw}} = 0.8\), \(K T_d = 0.08\) and the delay is invisible; crank the gain to 5 for “snappier” tracking and \(K T_d = 0.5\) buys visible hunting. The engineering rule is the usual one: the closed-loop time constant should sit an order of magnitude above the total loop delay, and the way to make the loop faster is to shrink the delay — a faster detector, a tick that reads fresher boxes — not to raise the gain into the oscillation regime.
Two more inherited results round out the analysis. A moving target turns the P controller’s steady-state error loose: a goose crossing the line of sight at 2.5 m/s at 10 m range subtends an angular rate of 0.25 rad/s, and holding the nose on it requires \(\omega_z = 0.25\) rad/s forever — which a proportional law only produces at a standing error \(\hat{e}_x = 0.25/0.8 \approx 0.31\), about 100 pixels. The goose rides a third of the way toward the frame edge, tracked but off-centre: the Closed-Loop Control chapter’s constant-disturbance standoff, re-materialized in pixels. The remedies are also that chapter’s — an integral term to grind the standing error away (with windup guards when the target accelerates), or feedforward of the track’s estimated angular rate — and the running example accepts the lag instead, because 100 pixels off-centre still leaves 220 pixels of margin, and simplicity is worth more here than perfection. Finally, depth: the yaw channel’s loop gain contains only \(f_x\) — rotation moves pixels at the same rate whatever the range, which is one reason yaw-based centering is the robust default. But the vertical channel is translational, and a translating camera moves a target’s image in proportion to \(f_y/Z\): the same 0.3 m/s climb that nudges a goose at 12 m nudges one at 3 m four times harder. A vertical gain tuned crisp at long range rings at short range. This is the interaction matrix’s depth-dependence stripped to one fraction, and the practical fix is one line of gain scheduling — scale \(K_{\text{alt}}\) with the depth estimate the outer loop already computes — or the conservative alternative, tuning at the closest working range and accepting sluggishness far out.

title: 22  Target Tracking and Visual Servoing
text:
22.6 Complementary, Not Redundant
The system now holds two complete answers to “a goose was detected — do something”: the Coordinate Frames chapter’s transform, which produces a world position to navigate toward, and this chapter’s law, which produces re-pointing commands to keep the detection in frame. It is tempting to see them as rivals — the fast cheap loop versus the slow rigorous one — and to ask which the running example should use. The correct answer is that they are not answering the same question, and Figure 22.2 draws the architecture that uses both.






Figure 22.2: The two-loop tracking architecture: the outer position-based loop navigates on the world-frame estimate, the inner image-based loop re-points the aircraft at frame rate, and both consume — and protect — the same detection stream.



Run the failure analysis in both directions. A system with only the outer, position-based loop inherits the full error budget with no in-loop correction — the half-metre at 6 m is commanded, not just estimated — and, worse, nothing anywhere enforces that the target stays visible while the vehicle flies its correct-in-3D trajectory. One noisy depth sample, one aggressive correction, one goose that flaps ten metres during the estimate’s latency, and the bounding box crosses the image border. At that moment the failure compounds: the position estimate is built from detections, so losing sight doesn’t degrade the estimate, it stops it — the aircraft is now navigating to where a goose used to be, on a track aging toward the FSM’s 3 s dwell cutoff. You cannot localize what you cannot see. A system with only the inner, image-based loop fails in the complementary direction: it can hold the goose in frame from any distance, indefinitely, but it has no notion of range, closure, or standoff — it cannot approach, cannot stop approaching, cannot log where the goose is for the sweep planner, cannot answer a single question that the mission’s other consumers ask in world coordinates.
So the architecture stacks them, each at the rate its data supports. The outer loop runs at detection-plus-transform rate: box, depth, frame chain, filtered NED estimate, approach and standoff commands — the camera as 3D sensor, PBVS in spirit, feeding everything downstream that thinks in world coordinates. The inner loop runs every frame on raw pixel error — no depth lookup, no transform, nothing between the detector and the command but two subtractions and two multiplies — continuously absorbing exactly the errors the outer loop is blind to: target motion since the last estimate, attitude transients, the accumulated bias of calibration. The split is also an honest division by what can hurt each loop: the inner loop is immune to the calibration budget (it measures pixels and commands until pixels say centered) but knows nothing of the world; the outer loop knows the world but believes its calibration. Chained, the inner loop’s centering keeps the detection stream — the outer loop’s raw material — flowing, while the outer loop supplies the two things the inner loop structurally lacks: a range (which the vertical channel’s gain scheduling already wanted) and a destination.
This two-loop pattern is not an invention of convenience. At the control-theory level it is the systems-engineering cousin of hybrid visual servoing, which combines partial 3D estimates with image-plane features in one law precisely because the pure schemes fail differently (Chaumette and Hutchinson 2006). At the applied level it is how working UAV systems are built: a monocular precision-landing system for a moving platform, for instance, runs a fiducial-based localization stage to get the vehicle to the platform’s vicinity and image-plane PID corrections to keep the marker centered through the terminal approach (Salagame, Govindraj, and Omkar 2022) — coarse navigation from reconstruction, fine correction from pixels, the same architecture with a landing pad in place of a goose. And when the stakes or the dynamics outgrow proportional control, the error definition survives even as the controller is upgraded: a published UAV target-following system defines its objective as exactly this chapter’s centered-feature error and drives it with nonlinear model-predictive control (Chen et al. 2021) — the production-grade descendant of the same loop, solving for the command sequence rather than multiplying by a gain.
For the mission machine, the division of labor lands cleanly on the FSM’s states. SEARCH_GRID consumes the outer loop’s output at the moment of detection — the world-frame position that tells HARASS_TARGET where to go. HARASS_TARGET flies on both: the outer loop’s estimate governs approach and standoff radius, while the inner loop, ticking underneath, keeps the goose in frame so the track that entry guard confirmed stays fresh — feeding the dwell guard, feeding the estimate, and feeding the pattern generators the next chapter builds, every one of which (“swoop toward, circle around, feint away”) presumes the aircraft continuously knows which way the goose is. Harassment Pattern Generation will spend its pages on what to fly around a target; this chapter is why, throughout those maneuvers, there will still be a target to fly around.

title: 22  Target Tracking and Visual Servoing
text:
22.7 The Centering Loop in Code
The law, its guards, and its conventions compress into one plain function, shaped — like everything the mission machine calls — to be invoked from the tick:
IMG_W, IMG_H = 640, 480   # the depth-aligned mode from Part III
DEADBAND = 0.05           # normalized: 5% of the half-frame
K_YAW = 0.8               # rad/s of yaw rate at full-scale error
K_ALT = 1.2               # m/s of vertical rate at full-scale error
MAX_YAW_RATE = 0.6        # rad/s   } ceilings well inside the airframe;
MAX_VERT_RATE = 0.8       # m/s     } the shared slew limiter still applies

def _p_channel(err, gain, limit):
    """One axis: deadband, then proportional, then saturation."""
    if abs(err) < DEADBAND:
        return 0.0                     # near-centered: don't hunt
    cmd = gain * err
    return max(-limit, min(limit, cmd))

def centering_command(bbox_center, image_size=(IMG_W, IMG_H)):
    """Pixel centroid of the tracked target -> (yaw_rate, vertical_rate).

    Signs follow PX4 conventions: positive yaw rate is nose-right (FRD),
    positive vertical rate is downward (NED). Both channels are negative
    feedback: each command moves the target's image toward the centre.
    """
    u, v = bbox_center
    w, h = image_size
    e_x = (u - w / 2) / (w / 2)        # [-1, 1], + = right of centre
    e_y = (v - h / 2) / (h / 2)        # [-1, 1], + = below centre
    yaw_rate = _p_channel(e_x, K_YAW, MAX_YAW_RATE)
    vert_rate = _p_channel(e_y, K_ALT, MAX_VERT_RATE)
    return yaw_rate, vert_rate
Wiring it into the previous chapter’s machine changes a handful of lines in the HARASS_TARGET case. The state’s action asked fly_pattern() to close on the target and work it; the centering loop now supplies the aim underneath whatever pattern is flown:
case MissionState.HARASS_TARGET:
    if self.track_is_fresh():          # measured or briefly coasted box
        yaw_rate, vert_rate = centering_command(self.track.bbox_center)
        self.fly_pattern(yaw_rate, vert_rate)  # pattern: next chapter
    else:
        self.hold_pattern()            # no fresh pixels: freeze the aim
    if self.target_gone(dwell=3.0):
        self.transition(MissionState.SEARCH_GRID, "resume sweep")
Three disciplines from the previous chapters carry over unchanged and are worth naming, because each guards a real failure. Freshness first: centering_command must only ever see a measured box — or one the Part III tracker is coasting through a few missed frames — never a stale one; servoing on a track that has been silent for a second steers the aircraft by a fiction, and the honest response to missing pixels is to freeze the aim and let the dwell guard, not the servo, decide what happens next (dead data is worse than no data, exactly as the FSM chapter argued for guards). One writer: the loop computes commands, but only the tick issues them — the centering law is a pure function called from the state’s action, not a callback with opinions about self.state. One limiter: its output merges with the pattern generator’s and passes through the same shared slew limiter as every other behavior, so a bounding box that jumps (an ID switch, a second goose) produces a bounded swing of the nose, not a snap.






NoteFor More



The full interaction matrix is worth meeting once, even though this chapter’s task never inverts it. For a single image point at normalized coordinates \((x, y)\) and depth \(Z\), the classic result is a 2 × 6 matrix mapping the camera’s full velocity screw — three translations, three rotations — to the feature’s image velocity; its translational columns all carry \(1/Z\) while its rotational columns carry none, which is the general form of this chapter’s observation that yaw centering is depth-free and vertical-velocity centering is not (Chaumette and Hutchinson 2006). Stacking the matrices of several features and pseudoinverting yields servo laws that control all six degrees of freedom from imagery alone — the machinery behind precision manipulation and marker-based docking — at the price of the singularity and local-minimum pathologies the tutorials catalogue. The mature open-source implementation of all of it, PBVS and IBVS and the hybrid schemes, is INRIA’s ViSP library, which ships ROS integration and is a sensible next stop for a reader who wants to fly more than two channels. On the estimation side, production trackers rarely feed raw centroids to the servo: a constant-velocity Kalman filter over the track smooths detector jitter and supplies the angular-rate feedforward that eliminates the moving-target lag computed in this chapter — the same filter-then-control layering the reader has now seen at every level of the stack.

title: 22  Target Tracking and Visual Servoing
text:
22.8 Check Your Understanding

Classify each within the IBVS/PBVS taxonomy, with one sentence of justification: (a) the running example’s detection → depth → frame chain → NED waypoint pipeline from the Coordinate Frames chapter; (b) this chapter’s centering loop; (c) a precision-landing system that estimates a known-size fiducial marker’s full 3D pose and flies to a fixed offset above it.







TipShow answer






PBVS: the camera is used as a 3D sensor — image measurements are reconstructed into a Cartesian target position, and the error driven to zero (vehicle-to-waypoint) lives in task space. (b) IBVS: the error is the pixel offset from image centre, computed and controlled entirely in the image plane with no pose reconstruction in the loop. (c) PBVS, and a well-chosen use of it: the marker’s known geometry and the trusted calibration make the 3D reconstruction reliable, and the objective — a fixed spatial offset from the pad — is inherently a Cartesian goal, exactly the regime where PBVS’s clean, predictable trajectory is the advantage (Peng and Radke 2020).





A camera runs at 1280 × 720. The tracked centroid is at \((u, v) = (400, 500)\), the gains are \(K_{\text{yaw}} = 0.6\) rad/s and \(K_{\text{alt}} = 1.0\) m/s at full-scale error, and the deadband is 0.08. Compute both commands, state each one’s physical direction, and then show what the same physical scene would command if the camera were switched to 640 × 360.







TipShow answer





Centre is \((640, 360)\). \(\hat{e}_x = (400 - 640)/640 = -0.375\); \(\hat{e}_y = (500 - 360)/360 = +0.389\). Both magnitudes exceed the 0.08 deadband. Yaw: \(\omega_z = 0.6 \times (-0.375) = -0.225\) rad/s — negative is nose-left in FRD, correct for a target left of centre. Vertical: \(v_D = 1.0 \times 0.389 = +0.39\) m/s — positive D is downward, a descent toward a target below centre. At 640 × 360 the same scene puts the centroid at \((200, 250)\): pixel errors halve to \((-120, +70)\), but the half-frame normalizers halve too, so \(\hat{e}_x = -0.375\) and \(\hat{e}_y = +0.389\) exactly as before — the commands are identical. That invariance is what the normalization buys: gains tuned in one camera mode survive a mode change.




A teammate ports a published centering law verbatim — yaw_rate = -K * e_x_norm — onto the running example’s PX4 stack. Predict the flight behavior on the first confirmed detection, explain the mechanism in feedback terms, and describe a ground test that would have caught it.







TipShow answer





The published law was almost certainly written for a z-up yaw convention; under PX4’s FRD (positive yaw = nose right) the minus sign turns the loop into positive feedback. A goose detected right of centre commands nose-left, the image slides right, the error grows, and the command grows with it: the error compounds exponentially and the goose exits the frame edge within a second or two, every correction accelerating the departure. The FSM survives — track lost, dwell expires, resume sweep — but harassment becomes structurally impossible, and the log shows the same signature every time: detection, brief yaw away, track lost. The catch-it-first test needs no flight: on the bench (or in SITL with a planted target), present a detection right of centre and assert the sign of the commanded yaw rate is positive — “target right must command nose right.” One assertion per channel, run against synthetic boxes at all four frame edges, pins all the sign conventions at once.




The perception pipeline delivers boxes with 50 ms of end-to-end latency and the mission tick runs at 20 Hz, so the centering loop acts on errors up to about \(T_d = 0.1\) s old. For \(K_{\text{yaw}} = 0.8\) and for an impatient retune to \(K_{\text{yaw}} = 6\), evaluate \(K T_d\), describe the qualitative closed-loop behavior in each case, and state where the formal stability boundary lies. Which chapter’s machinery is this?







TipShow answer





At \(K = 0.8\): \(K T_d = 0.08\), a factor of twenty below the instability boundary \(K T_d = \pi/2 \approx 1.57\) (i.e. \(K \approx 15.7\) for this delay); the closed-loop time constant \(\tau = 1/K = 1.25\) s dwarfs the delay, and the response is a clean exponential settle. At \(K = 6\): \(K T_d = 0.6\) — still formally stable but badly damped: the controller keeps acting on 100 ms-old error, repeatedly overshooting centre and swinging back, visible as the aircraft hunting left-right across the target. This is the Closed-Loop Control chapter’s phase-lag story with a new error signal: delay in the loop converts gain into oscillation, and the honest route to a faster loop is shrinking the delay (faster detector, fresher reads), not raising the gain toward the boundary.




During a harassment run a goose walks steadily across the line of sight at 2 m/s at 8 m range. With \(K_{\text{yaw}} = 0.8\), compute where in the frame the P-only loop holds the goose at steady state, explain why the offset cannot decay to zero, and name the two standard remedies and the cost of each.







TipShow answer





Required tracking rate: \(\omega = v/r = 2/8 = 0.25\) rad/s. A proportional law produces that only at a standing normalized error \(\hat{e}_x = 0.25/0.8 = 0.3125\) — about \(0.3125 \times 320 = 100\) pixels right of centre on the 640-wide frame, a steady lead the aircraft never closes. It cannot decay because zero error would mean zero commanded yaw rate, and a nose that stops turning immediately falls behind a target that does not stop moving — the same structural standoff as the Closed-Loop Control chapter’s proportional controller against a constant disturbance. Remedies: an integral term, which winds up the extra yaw rate until the error truly zeros but must be guarded against windup when the target reverses or the command saturates; or feedforward of the track’s estimated angular rate (e.g., from a Kalman filter over the track), which removes the lag without integral dynamics but is only as good as the rate estimate it is fed.




Explain why \(K_{\text{yaw}}\) can be tuned once and trusted from 3 m to 30 m, while a \(K_{\text{alt}}\) tuned for crisp response at 12 m may oscillate as the aircraft closes to 3 m. Connect the explanation to the structure of the interaction matrix, and give the one-line fix.







TipShow answer





Yaw is a rotational channel: a rotation sweeps every pixel at \(f_x\) pixels per radian regardless of how far away the scene is, so the loop gain contains no depth and the tuning is range-invariant. Vertical velocity is a translational channel: a camera translating at \(v\) moves a target’s image at \(f_y\,v/Z\) pixels per second, so the loop gain scales as \(1/Z\) — closing from 12 m to 3 m multiplies it by four, shrinking the effective time constant fourfold and pushing a crisply tuned loop toward the hunting regime. This is the interaction matrix’s structure in miniature: its translational columns carry \(1/Z\), its rotational columns do not — the precise reason IBVS needs at least a rough depth estimate even though it never reconstructs a pose. The fix is one line of gain scheduling: scale \(K_{\text{alt}}\) proportionally with the outer loop’s depth estimate (or, conservatively, tune at the closest working range and accept sluggishness far out).

22.9 Try It
Part 1 — build the law and pin its signs. Implement centering_command() exactly as in this chapter, then test it before any aircraft is involved. First, unit tests: boxes planted at all four frame edges and at centre must produce the four correct command signs and one all-zeros result; a centroid just inside the deadband must command zero on that channel while the other still acts; commands at full-scale error must clip at the ceilings. Second — the test that catches convention bugs — generate the inputs with the Coordinate Frames chapter’s inverse chain: plant a synthetic goose at a known NED position, use ned_point_to_optical() plus the intrinsics to project it to a pixel, and assert end-to-end that a goose planted east of a north-facing drone commands positive (rightward) yaw. Then close the loop kinematically, no simulator yet: in a small script, hold the goose fixed in NED, integrate the commanded yaw rate and vertical rate into the drone’s pose at 20 Hz with a 0.1 s command delay, re-project the goose each step, and plot \(\hat{e}_x(t)\). Verify the exponential settle and measure its time constant against the predicted \(1/K_{\text{yaw}}\); then raise \(K_{\text{yaw}}\) until the trace hunts, and check the onset against the \(K T_d\) arithmetic.
Part 2 — wire it into the machine and track something that moves. In SITL, replace the previous chapter’s HARASS_TARGET stub aim with centering_command(), fed by a scripted target that the simulation projects into synthetic bounding boxes (the Part 1 projection code, now driven by a moving NED trajectory): a goose that holds still for 5 s, walks at 2 m/s across the line of sight for 10 s, then flaps away at 6 m/s. Log pixel error, commanded rates, and the FSM state at full rate. Confirm four behaviors against this chapter’s numbers: the initial centering settles with the predicted time constant; the walking phase holds the goose at the predicted steady-state offset (\(\hat{e} = \omega_{\text{target}}/K_{\text{yaw}}\) — compute it from your geometry before you fly it); the deadband keeps the aircraft quiet, not hunting, when the goose is stationary; and the flap-away phase either tracks or cleanly loses the target into the FSM’s dwell logic — kill the synthetic detections mid-run and confirm the aim freezes and the 3 s dwell, not the servo, hands control back to SEARCH_GRID with a [STATE CHANGE] line that explains itself. Finish with the sign-flip experiment from the checks: negate one gain, re-run the stationary phase, and keep the plot of the error diverging exponentially — the clearest picture of positive feedback a logbook can hold.

title: 23  Harassment Pattern Generation: Designing Deterrent Flight Paths
text:
23.1 Learning Objectives
The previous chapter closed on a promise: throughout the maneuvers this chapter designs, there will still be a target to fly around. The two-loop tracking architecture keeps the goose in frame and localized — the inner loop re-aims the camera at frame rate, the outer loop maintains a world-frame estimate — and the mission machine’s HARASS_TARGET state stands ready with an entry guard, a dwell-time exit, and stash-and-resume semantics under preemption. Every piece of scaffolding is in place except the thing being scaffolded. What, exactly, should the aircraft do once it is on station over a flock of geese it can see and localize?
The question deserves more care than “fly at them until they leave,” and this chapter’s answer has three layers. The first is behavioral: a deterrent flight path is an argument made to an animal, and it only persuades if it is phrased in the animal’s own threat grammar — which approach geometries read as danger, why a cohesive flock is easier to move than a scattered one, and why the goal is herding, not pursuit. The second is geometric: the argument is delivered as parametric trajectories — an orbit, a swoop, a figure-8, a herding vector — each with a small set of numbers (radius, speed, approach angle, minimum separation) that can be tuned, logged, and bounded. The third layer is the one that makes the other two admissible at all: a strict safety radius, which this chapter will argue is simultaneously an ethical floor and an engineering one, and — uncomfortably — a number the published literature does not supply. Along the way the chapter is candid about a second gap, this one in the running example itself: the pattern vocabulary is richer than the pattern code. The harassment node that actually flies implements one pattern, a re-centering circular orbit, and the swoop and herding designs are specified extensions built on the same skeleton. That gap — design ambition versus shipped scope — is not something to paper over; it is how real systems grow, and the chapter treats the shipped orbit as the worked foundation and the rest as engineering the reader is equipped to finish.
One more thing should be said plainly before any trajectory is drawn. This is a system designed to frighten a wild animal on purpose. Everything in this chapter — the behind-the-flock geometry, the open corridor, the separation floors, the fixed-duration exposure — exists to make that act as brief, as controlled, and as low-stress as the mission allows, and the deterrence literature is cited throughout to keep the design honest about what actually works and what merely looks aggressive. But bounding a harm is not the same as justifying it, and the justification — when deterrence is warranted at all, what the ecology of repeated disturbance costs, who decides, and by what standard — is the business of The Ethics and Ecology of Autonomous Wildlife Management chapter in Part V. This chapter builds the capability carefully; that one asks whether and when it should be used.

title: 23  Harassment Pattern Generation: Designing Deterrent Flight Paths
text:
23.2 Key Vocabulary

Deterrent pattern — a parametric flight trajectory designed to move wildlife out of an area by applying controlled, bounded pressure: enough presence to trigger the animals’ escape behavior, constrained enough never to endanger them.
Target safety radius (minimum separation) — the distance floor around the target animal that no trajectory may enter under any circumstances; enforced as a hard geometric constraint on the pattern generator, not as a tuning preference.
Standoff distance — the working range a pattern holds by design — the orbit’s radius, the swoop’s approach hold — as distinct from the safety radius, which is the never-cross floor beneath it.
Orbit pattern — a circular trajectory flown at fixed radius and altitude around the flock’s tracked center, maintaining continuous lateral presence and directional pressure without direct pursuit.
Buzzing pass (swoop) — a shallow descending approach toward the flock followed by a committed climb-out, producing a brief, visible, predator-like cue; the closest-approach point is bounded by the safety radius in both horizontal separation and altitude.
Herding vector — the direction along which the drone applies pressure: the line from a hold point behind the flock, through the flock’s center, toward the designated exit; the drone steers the flock by holding position on this line, not by chasing individuals.
Escape corridor — the deliberately unobstructed direction left open for the flock; herding works by making one route feel safest, and a design that closes every direction produces scatter, not dispersal.
Wildlife dispersal — the mission outcome: the flock leaves the protected area, intact and by its own locomotion, and does not immediately return; measured by displacement toward the exit and by return time, not by how dramatic the flight paths looked.
Flight-initiation distance (FID) — the distance at which an animal begins to flee an approaching threat; the behavioral quantity underneath every deterrence separation number, measurable, individually repeatable, and context-dependent in geese (Katsis 2025).
Habituation — the progressive weakening of a behavioral response to a stimulus that repeated exposure has taught the animal is harmless; the failure mode of every static deterrent, and the reason a deterrence pattern is designed to be varied rather than fixed.

title: 23  Harassment Pattern Generation: Designing Deterrent Flight Paths
text:
23.3 The Behavioral Contract
A deterrent pattern is only as good as its model of the animal. Four properties of goose (and, more broadly, gregarious-bird) behavior carry essentially all of the design weight, and each is worth stating with its evidence, because the evidence is what separates a defensible design from folklore.
Approach geometry is the loudest signal. The single best-replicated finding in the UAV–wildlife disturbance literature is that how an aircraft approaches matters more than almost anything else about it. A systematic review pooling results across dozens of studies found that target-oriented flight — a trajectory aimed directly at the animals — was significantly more likely to provoke an active behavioral response than lawnmower-style or tangential flight, and reads this through an antipredator lens: a threat pointed at you is a predator; one crossing your field of view is traffic (Mulero-Pázmány et al. 2017). A controlled field study on waterfowl found the same thing directly: direct approaches, especially low ones, consistently flushed birds that tangential passes left undisturbed (McEvoy, Hall, and McDonald 2016). Meanwhile an early drone-approach study on mallards, flamingos, and greenshanks found that approach speed and drone color had no measurable effect — but vertical, overhead descent provoked the strongest reactions of any geometry tested (Vas et al. 2015). For a deterrence mission this is a dial, not just a warning: the pattern generator can select response intensity by selecting geometry — tangential for presence, target-oriented for pressure, and never a vertical descent, which maximizes stress without adding any directional information the flock can act on.
Flocks flee together, and bigger flocks flee sooner. Escape in gregarious birds is contagious: a study across European flocking species found that flight-initiation distance grows with flock size — larger groups take flight earlier than small groups or singletons, consistent with many-eyes vigilance and fear spreading through the group (Morelli et al. 2019). Goose-specific work adds that the response threshold is real but plastic: individual greylag geese show repeatable FIDs that nonetheless shift with local disturbance history (Katsis 2025), and nesting snow geese ramp up vigilance well before anything flushes (Barnas et al. 2018). The design consequence is that the flock, not the bird, is the unit the pattern should address — and that a cohesive flock is the easy case. One stimulus at the right geometry moves the whole group in one direction, and a group that moves together is also a group the previous chapters’ tracker can follow as a single target. Scatter the flock and every one of those advantages inverts: multiple sub-flocks, multiple tracks, multiple directions, more flying, more stress, less dispersal.
Escape needs somewhere to go. Threatened birds move away from the threat’s line of approach toward open, unobstructed space. The chapter states this one carefully, because its evidentiary status differs from the two claims above: no published study was found testing “geese prefer open escape routes” as a specific hypothesis in those terms, and the book presents it as a design assumption consistent with general antipredator escape behavior rather than as a cited finding. But it is the assumption on which corridor design rests, and it is at least not contradicted by anything in the literature: pressure without an exit produces circling and scatter; pressure aligned with an open corridor produces directed movement.
Put the three together and the herding architecture assembles itself, drawn in Figure 23.1: position the drone behind the flock relative to the desired exit, hold a standoff distance on the line through the flock toward the corridor, and let the drone’s mere target-oriented presence — not speed, not aggression — supply the directional pressure. If the exit corridor’s direction from the flock’s center \(\mathbf{c}\) is the unit vector \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\), the drone’s hold point is simply
\[
\mathbf{p}_{\text{drone}} = \mathbf{c} - d_s\,\hat{\mathbf{u}},
\]
with \(d_s\) the standoff distance: behind the flock, on the herding vector, so that “away from the threat” and “toward the exit” are the same direction. The drone then follows the flock down the corridor at the flock’s own pace, re-evaluating \(\mathbf{c}\) from the tracker every tick. Chasing individual birds does the opposite of every line in this paragraph — it splits the flock, randomizes headings, defeats the tracker, and burns battery — which is why the herding rule is stated as the pattern family’s governing principle rather than as one option among four.






Figure 23.1: Herding, not chasing: the drone holds a standoff position behind the flock on the line through the designated exit, leaving one corridor open; its target-oriented presence closes the other directions, and the flock’s own escape behavior does the moving.



One honest addendum before the geometry hardens into confidence: pattern geometry is a strong lever, but the field evidence says it is not the only one, and possibly not the dominant one. A comparison of drone platforms hazing blackbird flocks from sunflower fields found dispersal efficacy governed by flock size and field size, not by which airframe flew (Egan et al. 2023); an industrial-site study found the multirotor outperformed the fixed-wing largely because it could fly lower and maneuver more freely — platform flexibility, not trajectory shape, was the difference (Hornain and Rosely 2024); and even hazing augmented with a chemical repellent achieved full site abandonment in only about half of trials against large flocks (Duttenhefner, Greives, and Klug 2024). A well-designed pattern earns real effect sizes, but “the right orbit radius guarantees dispersal” is not a claim the literature supports, and the running example’s metrics — displacement, return time — are there to measure what the geometry actually buys.

section: 23.4 The Safety Radius: An Ethical Floor and an Engineering One
text:
23.4 The Safety Radius: An Ethical Floor and an Engineering One
Every pattern in this chapter carries the same non-negotiable constraint: a minimum separation from the animals that the trajectory generator treats as a hard geometric floor. The requirement is ethical and it is engineering, and it is worth seeing that these are genuinely two arguments, not one argument told twice. Ethically, the mission’s entire license rests on the distinction between moving an animal and harming one: the objective is to guide geese out of a protected area, not to strike, exhaust, or panic them, and a trajectory that can pass through the space a startled goose might flap into has already failed that test before anything goes wrong. From the engineering side, the same floor protects the mission: a large Canada goose weighs 4–5 kg and spans up to 1.8 m of wing, and a collision at pattern speeds is a destroyed propeller, an uncontrolled descent, and a dead or injured animal — the worst outcome on every axis at once, including the public-trust axis on which all wildlife-management drone operations fly (Afridi et al. 2025). The floor also has to absorb the system’s own error budget: the flock-center estimate carries the half-metre-scale uncertainty priced in the Coordinate Frames chapter, the aircraft tracks its setpoints imperfectly in wind, and a bird can close several metres of separation in one startled second. A safety radius is the margin that lets all three of those misbehave at once without contact.
So what should the number be? Here the chapter must report an uncomfortable finding honestly: the published literature does not answer this question, and the numbers it does publish answer a different one. There is a substantial body of research on UAV–wildlife separation distances, and every part of it was written for missions trying not to disturb animals — surveys, counts, nest monitoring. That literature recommends: at least 40 m above individual waterfowl for multirotors (McEvoy, Hall, and McDonald 2016); 75 m or more above nesting snow geese (Barnas et al. 2018); roughly 100 m survey altitude and 500 m launch distance for non-disturbing goose observation (Bech-Hansen et al. 2019); and species-specific minimum approach distances of 50–170 m for colonial breeding birds, derived from measured flight-initiation distances across nearly 1,500 real drone flights (Velilla et al. 2025). The most influential best-practice paper in the field declines to endorse any universal number at all, arguing responses are too species- and context-dependent and recommending precautionary, species-specific protocols instead (Hodgson and Koh 2016).
None of those numbers can be imported into this chapter, because a deterrence mission inverts the design objective they were derived for. A survey standoff is the distance at which the animals fail to react; a deterrence standoff must be inside the flock’s flight-initiation distance, because being reacted to is the point. The 40–100 m figures are not a stricter version of this chapter’s numbers — they are the answer to the opposite question, and citing them as if they validated (or indicted) a close-range deterrence design would be exactly the decorative misuse of literature this book tries to avoid. And the question they leave open — what is the closest safe approach while deliberately provoking a flock to move? — appears to have no dedicated published safety standard at all.
The running example therefore does what an engineering project must do when the literature is silent: it chooses defaults, bounds them conservatively, and labels them as choices. The design bands used throughout this chapter — an orbit radius of 8–15 m, a swoop closest-approach horizontal separation of 5–8 m with a 3–5 m altitude floor, pattern altitudes of roughly 5–10 m — are engineering defaults: several body-lengths beyond any plausible flap-and-lunge envelope, sized to absorb the tracking error budget with margin, and consistent in spirit with the literature’s qualitative findings (geometry over speed, lateral over vertical, reaction provoked at tens of metres). They are not empirically validated thresholds, and the chapter will not pretend otherwise. What validation would look like is, usefully, already demonstrated in that same literature: the colonial-breeding-bird guidance derived its operational distances from measured FIDs over thousands of approach flights (Velilla et al. 2025) — the same method, run under deterrence conditions on the target population, is how these defaults would graduate into evidence. Until then, they are held wide, enforced hard, and logged every tick.
The enforcement, at least, is straightforward engineering. The safety radius enters the pattern generator as a constraint, not a hope: every candidate setpoint is checked against the current flock-center estimate before it is published, and any setpoint that would carry the aircraft inside the floor is projected back out along the line from the flock center. The check runs downstream of every pattern — orbit, swoop, herding — precisely so that no individual pattern’s bug can reach the animal.

title: 23  Harassment Pattern Generation: Designing Deterrent Flight Paths
text:
23.5 A Vocabulary of Patterns
With the behavioral contract and the safety floor in place, the patterns themselves are short work — each is a small parametric trajectory family, and each exists because it occupies a distinct point on the pressure-versus-stress curve. The taxonomy has four entries: orbit, swoop, figure-8, and herding. Herding has already been drawn (Figure 23.1); it is less a trajectory than a policy — hold the moving point \(\mathbf{c} - d_s\hat{\mathbf{u}}\) and follow — and the running example treats it as the mode the others hand off to once the flock is moving the right way. The remaining three are trajectories proper.
The orbit (Figure 23.2) is the workhorse and the one pattern the running example ships in code. The drone circles the flock’s tracked center at fixed radius \(R\), speed \(v\), and altitude, facing the center as it goes. As pressure it is deliberately moderate: continuous lateral presence from every bearing in turn, target-oriented enough to keep the flock’s attention, never closing, never overhead. Its parametrization is two lines of trigonometry. The drone’s position on the circle is
\[
\begin{aligned}
n &= c_n + R\cos\theta \\
e &= c_e + R\sin\theta,
\end{aligned}
\]
and the angle advances at the angular rate that makes the linear speed come out to \(v\):
\[
\dot{\theta} = \frac{v}{R},
\]
which for the shipped defaults (\(R = 3.0\) m, \(v = 2.0\) m/s) gives \(\dot{\theta} = 0.67\) rad/s — about 38°/s, a lap every \(2\pi R / v \approx 9.4\) s, and a gentle \(v^2/R \approx 1.3\ \text{m/s}^2\) of centripetal acceleration. The critical refinement — the difference between an orbit and a decoration — is that the center \(\mathbf{c}\) is re-read from the tracker every tick, so the circle slides with the flock rather than circling the patch of grass where the flock used to be. The design-band version of the same pattern (\(R = 8\)–15 m, \(v = 2\)–4 m/s, 5–10 m altitude) trades a longer lap for a wider margin; at \(R = 12\) m and \(v = 3\) m/s the lap stretches to 25 s and the centripetal load drops below \(0.8\ \text{m/s}^2\).






Figure 23.2: The orbit pattern: continuous lateral pressure at a fixed radius from the flock’s tracked center, re-centered every tick as the flock moves; the inset shows the figure-8 as two mirrored orbits joined at a crossover.



The swoop — the mission’s “buzzing pass” — is the escalation pattern, reserved for a flock that has looked at the orbit and gone back to grazing. It manufactures, briefly and under strict bounds, the one stimulus the literature says birds do not ignore: a committed, target-oriented, predator-like approach (Mulero-Pázmány et al. 2017; Storms et al. 2022). Its geometry (Figure 23.3) is a phase sequence rather than a closed curve: approach — hold a 10–15 m standoff behind the flock at observation altitude, matching the flock’s drift; descend — advance toward the flock along a shallow 20–30° glide slope, speed up slightly so the approach reads as deliberate; closest point — bottom out at the safety floor, no closer than 5–8 m horizontal separation and 3–5 m altitude, with no sudden direction changes; recover — turn away, climb back to observation altitude, and rejoin the orbit or the herding hold. The angle band is doing real work. Fixing the closest point at 6 m separation and 4 m altitude and starting the descent from a 15 m standoff at 8 m altitude gives a horizontal advance of 9 m against a 4 m drop:
\[
\gamma = \arctan\!\left(\frac{8 - 4}{15 - 6}\right) = \arctan\!\left(\frac{4}{9}\right) \approx 24^{\circ},
\]
squarely inside the band — a pass the flock sees coming from tens of metres out, shallow enough to stay unmistakably lateral rather than tipping toward the overhead geometry that maximizes stress without adding directional pressure (Vas et al. 2015). At 4 m/s along the roughly 9.8 m descent path, the entire committed phase lasts about 2.5 s. Steepen the slope past 30° and the pass starts to read as a dive; shallow it below 20° and it stops reading as an approach at all.






Figure 23.3: The swoop pattern in profile: a shallow 20–30° descending approach from a rear standoff, bottoming out at the safety floor — minimum horizontal separation and minimum altitude — followed by a committed climb-out; a designed extension, specified here but not part of the shipped node.



The figure-8 earns its place for a reason the next section makes precise: habituation. It is two mirrored orbits joined at a crossover (the inset of Figure 23.2 shows the geometry, which is why it gets no separate figure — it is the orbit, doubled and alternating), so the drone’s direction of travel and bearing of approach change every lap instead of never. Same radius mathematics, same safety floor, same re-centering; what it adds is variety, and for large flocks, coverage — the lobes can straddle a flock too wide for one circle to pressure evenly.
The four patterns compose through a simple selection policy, which the running example states as a heuristic rather than dressing it up as an algorithm: orbit a stationary flock; swoop a flock that ignores the orbit; herd a flock that is moving, to steer it down the corridor; rotate in the figure-8 when engagements repeat. A rule-based selector reading the tracker’s flock state (stationary, moving, direction) covers all four cases in a dozen lines, and sits exactly where fly_pattern() lives in the mission machine — inside HARASS_TARGET, below the FSM, above the trajectory math. Readers who notice that this selector is itself a little state machine nested inside a state are seeing the hierarchical-composition pattern the Finite State Machines chapter promised would recur.

section: 23.6 Habituation: Why One Pattern Is Not Enough
text:
23.6 Habituation: Why One Pattern Is Not Enough
A deterrent that works in week one and is ignored by week four has not solved the problem; it has taught the local geese a new fact about the world. Habituation — response decay to a stimulus that repeated exposure reveals as harmless — is the documented failure mode of the entire static-deterrent industry: propane cannons, scarecrows, and repeated playback all decline with exposure, a pattern reported across taxa from birds to bears to fish (Feder and Wagner 2025). A recent controlled field trial makes the contrast case cleanly: elk and deer habituated to stationary audio deterrents within a six-week deployment — and habituated more slowly when the stimulus varied, with flashing lights layered onto the audio (Rutherford, St. Clair, and Visscher 2025). The mitigation half of the claim has direct experimental support too: in a repellent study built specifically around this question, cycling the stimulus intensity fully prevented the response decline that constant exposure produced (Feder and Wagner 2025).
For drones specifically, the strongest single data point in the literature points the encouraging way. The RobotFalcon — a peregrine-shaped drone flown in predator-like pursuit of corvid, gull, starling, and lapwing flocks — cleared half its treated fields within 70 seconds, kept most fields bird-free at five minutes (against roughly 15% for untreated controls), and for several species produced return times of three to four hours where the airbase’s distress-call broadcasts bought one or two (corvids, characteristically unimpressed, returned within the hour under both); and across three months of repeated deployment it showed no evidence of habituation at all, with flight-initiation distances holding constant while static deterrents nearby were being ignored (Storms et al. 2022). The authors’ interpretation is the ethological principle this section runs on: animals cannot afford to habituate to a genuine predator, because a predator is variable, responsive, and occasionally lethal — whereas a perfectly repetitive stimulus is safe to tune out precisely because its repetition proves it harmless. A deterrent drone borrows that protection to the degree that it behaves like the former: varied approach bearings, varied patterns, movement that responds to what the flock does.
The honest boundary of the evidence: no published study has tested an orbit-versus-swoop-versus-figure-8 rotation as such, and the ordinary multirotor in the RobotFalcon study — shaped like nothing alive — still worked, just more slowly. What the literature supports is the design principle, not the specific schedule: variation and animacy delay or prevent habituation; repetition invites it. Hence the selection policy above, the figure-8’s existence, and one more running-example rule that costs nothing: never open consecutive engagements from the same bearing.

title: 23  Harassment Pattern Generation: Designing Deterrent Flight Paths
text:
23.7 The Orbit That Actually Flies
The running example’s harassment node — harassment_node.py in the mission stack — implements the orbit pattern and nothing else, and this section reads it closely, because its structure answers three questions earlier chapters left open: how HARASS_TARGET’s “fly the deterrence pattern” actually issues setpoints, how the pattern coexists with other nodes that also want to command the aircraft, and where the “target dispersed” half of the exit guard comes from. The node’s logic, lightly condensed:
class HarassmentNode(Node):
    """Circular deterrence orbit around the tracked target.
    Publishes Offboard setpoints only while it holds the
    active-controller token; reports completion on T_HARASS_DONE."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__("harassment_node")
        self.R     = self.declare_parameter("orbit_radius_m",   3.0).value
        self.speed = self.declare_parameter("orbit_speed_ms",   2.0).value
        self.hold  = self.declare_parameter("orbit_duration_s", 15.0).value
        self.alt   = self.declare_parameter("orbit_altitude_m", 3.0).value
        rate_hz    = self.declare_parameter("rate_hz",          20.0).value
        self.dt = 1.0 / rate_hz
        self.active = False          # do we own the aircraft right now?
        self.start_time = None
        self.done_sent = False
        self.center = None           # orbit center: goose (n, e)
        self.angle = 0.0
        self.create_timer(self.dt, self._tick)

    def _on_controller(self, msg):   # T_ACTIVE_CONTROLLER (String)
        self.active = (msg.data == "harassment")
        if self.active:
            self._begin()
        else:                        # token moved on: reset for next time
            self.start_time = None
            self.done_sent = False

    def _begin(self):
        if self.target is not None and self.pos is not None:
            self.center = (self.target.n, self.target.e)
            # start the orbit from wherever the drone already is:
            self.angle = atan2(self.pos.e - self.center[1],
                               self.pos.n - self.center[0])
        else:                        # no target yet: orbit in place
            self.center = (self.pos.n, self.pos.e)
            self.angle = 0.0
        self.start_time = self.now()

    def _tick(self):
        if not self.active or self.start_time is None:
            return                   # not our aircraft: publish nothing

        if self.fresh_target():      # re-center on the moving goose
            self.center = (self.target.n, self.target.e)

        # advance along the circle: linear speed -> angular rate
        self.angle += (self.speed / max(self.R, 0.5)) * self.dt
        n = self.center[0] + self.R * cos(self.angle)
        e = self.center[1] + self.R * sin(self.angle)
        yaw = atan2(self.center[1] - e, self.center[0] - n)  # face the goose

        self.pub_offboard_mode(position=True)     # every tick, or PX4
        self.pub_setpoint([n, e, -self.alt], yaw)  # drops out of Offboard

        if self.now() - self.start_time >= self.hold:
            if not self.done_sent:
                self.get_logger().info("harassment COMPLETE")
                self.done_sent = True
            self.pub_done(True)      # T_HARASS_DONE — and keep orbiting
Nearly every line is a disciplined answer to a question earlier chapters raised. The active-controller token is the distributed twin of the FSM chapter’s single-writer rule: several nodes in the stack can compute Offboard setpoints, and PX4 will obediently fly whichever arrives, so the stack shares one String topic (T_ACTIVE_CONTROLLER) naming the node that currently owns the aircraft — and this node publishes nothing unless that name is "harassment". One writer of state in a single process becomes one setpoint author in a distributed one; the tick’s first line, if not self.active: return, is the whole protocol. The activation logic in _begin() carries a small geometric courtesy with real safety value: the starting angle is computed from the drone’s current bearing off the goose, so the orbit begins from wherever the aircraft already is instead of snapping toward the circle’s \(\theta = 0\) point — no lunge across the flock’s airspace at the moment of engagement. The re-centering step is the two or three lines that make the pattern a deterrent rather than a display: each tick, a fresh target estimate slides the whole circle under the moving flock. And the angle advance — self.angle += (self.speed / max(self.R, 0.5)) * self.dt — is \(\dot{\theta} = v/R\) discretized at the 20 Hz tick, with the max(R, 0.5) guard refusing to convert a carelessly tiny radius parameter into an absurd angular rate. At the defaults, each tick advances the orbit \(0.667 \times 0.05 = 0.033\) rad — about 1.9°, a 10 cm arc step — and PX4’s position controller smooths the 20 Hz breadcrumb trail into a circle. The yaw setpoint, \(\operatorname{atan2}(\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p})\), points the nose (and the camera) at the orbit center every tick — geometry standing in for aim, a choice the next section interrogates.
Two mismatches between this code and this chapter’s own design bands deserve to be flagged rather than smoothed over. First, the shipped default radius is 3.0 m at 3.0 m altitude — inside the 8–15 m orbit band and 5–10 m altitude band the safety discussion recommended. The defaults are sized for the SITL world the node was validated in, where the “goose” is a simulation asset and the error budget is benign; a field deployment inherits the parameters as ROS 2 parameters precisely so that the deployed configuration can live in the design band without touching code. The gap is a reminder with general force: a tunable safety parameter’s default is a claim about the environment it was tuned in. Second, the node’s completion logic is time, not behavior: after orbit_duration_s (15 s — about a lap and a half) it declares the deterrence done. Which brings up the last and most architectural detail.
The node does not stop itself. After the duration elapses it latches a log line, then publishes True on the “Harass Done” topic — T_HARASS_DONE — every tick, while continuing to orbit. This looks odd until it is read against the FSM chapter, at which point it is exactly right. State transitions belong to the mission supervisor’s tick and nowhere else; a behavior node that unilaterally stopped flying would leave the aircraft commanded by no one — the distributed version of writing self.state from a callback. Instead the node reports and keeps flying, and the supervisor closes the loop: it reads T_HARASS_DONE as the “target dispersed” half of HARASS_TARGET’s documented exit guard — target dispersed or track lost — alongside the 3 s track-loss dwell it already owns, and on either condition it commands the transition back to SEARCH_GRID and reassigns the active-controller token, which resets this node for the next engagement. The honest caveat completes the picture: T_HARASS_DONE is a proxy. “Dispersed” here operationally means “the pattern ran its designed duration,” not “the flock verifiably left” — a behavior-based test would compare the tracker’s flock position against the protected-area boundary, and the Try It builds one. Fixed-duration exposure is a defensible v1 (it bounds per-engagement stress by construction, which the ethical framing wants anyway), but the reader should know which claim the topic actually makes.

title: 23  Harassment Pattern Generation: Designing Deterrent Flight Paths
text:
23.8 Aim, Meet Pattern
The previous chapter left a three-line stub inside HARASS_TARGET: centering_command() computes a yaw rate and vertical rate from pixel error, and fly_pattern(yaw_rate, vert_rate) was deferred here. The shipped node, note, uses neither — its yaw is \(\operatorname{atan2}\) toward the last known flock center, pure geometry, no pixels. So which is right? Both, in different roles, and the composition is worth spelling out because it is a miniature of the two-loop argument.
The geometric yaw is feedforward: it aims the camera where the target estimate says the goose is, and during an orbit it does the heavy rotational work — at the shipped defaults the nose must slew a continuous 38°/s just to keep facing the center, a rate the position-plus-yaw setpoint stream commands for free and that the centering loop would otherwise have to earn from accumulated pixel error. But feedforward is only as honest as its data. The orbit’s re-centering step consumes fresh target estimates; the estimates come from detections; and detections require the goose in frame while the aircraft flies a circle around it — the exact scenario the previous chapter’s inner loop exists for. If the goose walks two metres between target updates, the geometric yaw faces where it was, the bounding box drifts off-center, and without correction the drift compounds: fewer detections, staler center, worse aim, until the track dies and the dwell guard ends the engagement for the wrong reason. The centering loop’s yaw channel is the feedback trim that closes this hole — a small correction on top of the geometric aim, driven by where the goose actually sits in the image:
def fly_pattern(self, aim_yaw_rate, _aim_vert_rate):
    """HARASS_TARGET's action: orbit position from geometry,
    yaw = geometric feedforward + centering-loop trim."""
    n, e, yaw_ff = self.orbit_step(self.track.ned_estimate, self.dt)
    self.yaw_trim += aim_yaw_rate * self.dt          # integrate rate -> angle
    self.yaw_trim = clamp(self.yaw_trim, -0.35, 0.35)  # ~±20° of authority
    self.publish_position_setpoint(n, e, -PATTERN_ALT,
                                   yaw=yaw_ff + self.yaw_trim)
The trim integrates the centering law’s yaw-rate output into a bounded yaw-angle offset — ±20° of authority, enough to hold a walking goose in frame between target updates, too little to let a bad detection (an ID switch to a second goose, a gull) wrench the aircraft off its pattern. And the vertical channel — the second output of centering_command() — is deliberately dropped, which is why the parameter wears an underscore. Inside a deterrent pattern, altitude belongs to the pattern: the orbit holds its altitude band and the swoop flies a designed profile whose floor is a safety constraint, and no pixel error is entitled to override either. The centering loop’s vertical channel was built for free tracking, where nothing else claimed the axis; here something does, and the composition rule is the general one — feedback trims only the axes the trajectory has not already promised to safety. What survives of the previous chapter’s work is, in the end, its most important part: not the vertical channel, not even the yaw trim, but the guarantee underneath the re-centering step — that the detection stream the orbit’s geometry feeds on does not go dark the moment the aircraft starts maneuvering.
