title: 26  Post-Flight Diagnostics: Reading Logs and Debugging Flight Behavior
text:
26.9 Try It
Part 1 — the routine review, made routine. Fly the running example’s mission (or any Part II mission) in SITL — the simulator’s PX4 writes the same .ulg files a real flight controller does; find the newest one under the SITL working tree’s log directory, or download it from QGroundControl’s log list. Then produce a two-page post-flight report using only this chapter’s tools. Page one, vibration: ulog2csv -m vehicle_imu_status (or the pyulog snippet), plot both vibration metrics and all six clipping counters over time, and classify the flight against the chapter’s criteria — any clipping growth, metrics steady or trending, and (if you enable high-rate logging and hover deliberately for thirty seconds) where the spectral energy sits relative to your airframe’s rotation and blade-passing frequencies. Page two, power: plot voltage_v and current_a on shared time, mark every sag excursion, compute \(R_{\text{int}}\) from the largest one, and plot remaining beneath with the three tier values you recover from ulog_params (look up BAT_LOW_THR, BAT_CRIT_THR, BAT_EMERGEN_THR, and check COM_LOW_BAT_ACT) drawn as horizontal lines. Upload the same file to Flight Review and check your plots against its panels — you should now be able to say what every panel is showing and where its data lives in the file. Keep the report: it is flight one of your baseline archive, and the comparison target for everything that follows.
Part 2 — diagnose an injected fault from the log alone. Have a partner (or your future self, a week from now) prepare a SITL flight with exactly one fault injected, without telling you which: an aged battery (raise the simulated pack’s internal resistance or cut its capacity), a vibration problem (if your setup exposes IMU noise/vibration simulation parameters), a GPS degradation (PX4’s SITL failure injection can cut or degrade GNSS mid-flight when the failure-injection parameter is enabled), or a mission-layer event (a mid-flight geofence tightening that trips the running example’s watchdog). You get the .ulg file — plus the companion-side log if the mission stack was up — and nothing else. Run the full loop in writing: the first-pass checklist (did the log capture it? does the controller track its setpoints? do the sensors validate?), the signature hunt against Table 26.1 and this chapter’s traces, a named hypothesis, and the bench test you would run on real hardware to confirm it. Only then compare against what was actually injected. Score yourself not on the guess but on the chain: a wrong hypothesis reached by defensible reading of real evidence is worth more than a right one reached by luck — and either way, finish the loop: state the fix, re-fly the corrected configuration, and show the before/after pair of logs with the signature gone.
Related Lab: See Appendix B for the lab assignment that applies this chapter’s concepts.
The previous chapter assembled the machine; this one taught it to testify. A program that reviews its logs after every flight — not just the frightening ones — is running the same discipline aviation formalized decades ago, and it accumulates the one asset no amount of cleverness substitutes for: a baseline, against which the next anomaly is visible early and provably fixed. What the log cannot testify to is whether the flight should have happened at all — what a system that autonomously pursues wild animals owes the animals, the public, and the law is an account no telemetry stream records, and rendering it is the work this Part turns to next.

title: 27  Remote Sensing at Scale: Multispectral Imaging in Agriculture
text:
27.1 Learning Objectives
The previous chapter closed on a debt no log can pay — whether a flight should have happened at all is an account this Part renders in its final chapter — but before it does, an older promissory note from Part I falls due. The Commercial Drone Landscape chapter, surveying the agricultural vertical, introduced the multispectral camera and the normalized difference vegetation index, showed a real NDVI field map, and explained why the measurement is harder than the formula suggests — then explicitly deferred the hard part, promising that this chapter would develop multispectral radiometry, calibration, and index construction in full. This chapter pays that debt, and in paying it does something the book has not done since Part I: it steps outside the running example’s sensing paradigm entirely. Nearly every perception page since Part III has been about finding discrete objects — a goose, a bounding box, a confidence score — in single RGB frames. Agricultural remote sensing is the commercial drone world’s other great sensing paradigm, and it works nothing like that: no object detector, no bounding box, no target class. It is a per-pixel physical measurement, assembled across a whole field, whose “detection” is a spatial anomaly in a continuous index — and whose most interesting modern frontier is squeezing a diagnosis, not just an alarm, out of the spectrum.
That frontier is where this chapter spends its depth, because the foundation is already laid. The Commercial Drone Landscape chapter established what NDVI is, which five bands a standard agricultural multispectral array carries, why healthy vegetation reflects near-infrared strongly, and how index maps become prescription maps; none of that is repeated here. What Part I’s treatment deliberately left general is the question this chapter makes specific: NDVI’s spatial variation “reveals stress — drought, nutrient deficiency, disease, pest damage,” all lumped together. A depressed index says something is wrong. It does not say what. Telling a fungal infection apart from a dry week is a genuinely different problem — one the plant-pathology remote-sensing literature attacks with purpose-built red-edge indices and per-disease classifiers, with real head-to-head numbers against NDVI — and it comes packaged with an operational question the book is unusually well equipped to answer: how a sensing mission is actually flown, coarse survey first, targeted re-fly on what the survey flags, using precisely the coverage-pattern machinery the Path Planning on the Edge chapter built for the running example’s search grid.

title: 27  Remote Sensing at Scale: Multispectral Imaging in Agriculture
text:
Carry a multispectral image from raw digital numbers to calibrated surface reflectance — downwelling irradiance sensor, reflectance panel, solar-noon flight window — and explain why vegetation indices are computed from reflectance rather than pixel brightness, completing the radiometry the Commercial Drone Landscape chapter deferred to this chapter.
Explain why generic NDVI is a good stress detector but a poor stress classifier, and describe the red-edge mechanism — chlorophyll breakdown and cell-structure disruption in fungally colonized tissue — that disease-specific indices exploit and NDVI’s broad red/NIR contrast largely misses.
Compute NDRE and REDSI from band reflectances, and interpret REDSI’s published head-to-head accuracy against NDVI on wheat yellow rust, including what the validation platform does and does not license you to claim.
Summarize two real UAV disease-detection case studies — sugar beet Cercospora/powdery mildew and wheat stem rust — with their actual platforms, ground sample distances, classifiers, and per-class accuracies, and present early-detection lead times as a disease-specific range rather than one universal number.
Design a coarse-to-targeted two-stage crop-scouting survey: parameterize the Path Planning on the Edge chapter’s lawnmower generator for each stage, work the GSD-versus-track-length arithmetic that motivates the split, and state when adaptive sampling beats exhaustive coverage.
Contrast per-pixel continuous-index sensing with Part III’s per-frame discrete object detection precisely — same sensor category, different information-processing problem — and identify which paradigm, or which hybrid, a given sensing task calls for.

title: 27  Remote Sensing at Scale: Multispectral Imaging in Agriculture
text:
27.2 Key Vocabulary

Radiometric calibration — the conversion of a camera’s raw digital numbers into surface reflectance: a downwelling irradiance sensor records the illumination striking the scene, a panel of known reflectance imaged on the ground anchors the scale, and the ratio of reflected to incident light becomes a property of the plant rather than of the weather.
Red edge — the steep transition in vegetation reflectance between strong chlorophyll absorption in the red and strong leaf-structure scattering in the near-infrared, roughly 700–740 nm; its position and slope shift with chlorophyll content and cell condition, which makes it the recurring diagnostic region for crop disease.
Spectral signature (disease-specific sense) — beyond Part I’s general notion of a surface’s reflectance-versus-wavelength shape: the characteristic perturbation a particular stressor imposes on that shape — a fungal infection raising visible and red-edge reflectance while lowering NIR is a different signature from drought’s flatter, NIR-dominated depression, even when both depress NDVI equally.
NDRE (Normalized Difference Red Edge) — the normalized-difference index formed from NIR and red-edge reflectance, \((\rho_{\text{NIR}} - \rho_{\text{RE}})/(\rho_{\text{NIR}} + \rho_{\text{RE}})\); identical in form to Part I’s NDVI with the red band swapped for the red-edge band, less prone to saturating over dense canopy and more sensitive to early chlorophyll loss.
REDSI (Red Edge Disease Stress Index) — a purpose-built disease index computed from red and two red-edge bands, designed around the specific way wheat yellow rust distorts the red-edge region; the index with the clearest published head-to-head win over NDVI on the same plots.
Hyperspectral imaging — imaging in hundreds of contiguous narrow bands (a few nanometres each) rather than a handful of discrete filtered bands, so each pixel carries an essentially continuous spectrum; heavier, costlier, and hungrier for calibration than multispectral, but able to resolve diagnostic wavelengths a five-band filter set was not designed to isolate.
Coarse-to-targeted search (two-stage survey) — the crop-scouting flight doctrine in which a first pass covers the whole field at high altitude and coarse GSD to build an index map, anomalous sectors are flagged algorithmically, and a second pass re-flies only the flagged sectors at low altitude and fine GSD to confirm and diagnose.
Ground sample distance (GSD) — Part I’s centimetres-per-pixel measure, reappearing here as the two-stage survey’s control variable: the Commercial Drone Landscape chapter’s relation makes it linear in altitude, so each stage’s altitude choice is a resolution choice, and the coarse and targeted stages are two points on the same line.

title: 27  Remote Sensing at Scale: Multispectral Imaging in Agriculture
text:
27.3 The Measurement Beneath the Index
Part I flagged the problem in one sentence — reflectance is a ratio of reflected to incident radiance, and the incident term varies with sun angle, cloud, and haze between one flight line and the next — and this section discharges it, because every index in this chapter is meaningless without it. What a camera pixel records is a digital number proportional to the radiance entering the lens, which is the product of two things: how strongly the surface reflects at that band, and how much light was falling on it at that moment. Only the first factor is about the plant. A cloud shadow crossing the field mid-flight can depress raw NIR brightness by more than a diseased canopy does; a survey stitched from frames taken twenty minutes apart bakes the sun’s motion into the mosaic. An index computed from raw digital numbers is therefore an index of the weather as much as of the crop.
The field workflow that removes the illumination term has three standard parts, and agricultural multispectral rigs ship with the hardware for the first two. A downwelling irradiance sensor — an upward-facing light meter, filtered to the same bands as the camera — rides on top of the aircraft and logs incident illumination for every exposure, so each frame’s radiance can be divided by the illumination that produced it. A calibrated reflectance panel — a target of known, spectrally flat reflectance — is imaged on the ground before and after the flight, anchoring the ratio to an absolute scale: if the panel reflects 50 % by manufacture and reads a given digital number, the scale factor from number to reflectance follows for every band. And the flight window is scheduled near solar noon on a stable sky, not for convenience but because both corrections are approximations — the irradiance sensor measures illumination at the aircraft, not in the crop’s shadowed lower canopy, and the panel calibration holds only while the atmosphere resembles the moment it was imaged. Photogrammetry software then assembles the calibrated frames into the orthomosaic Part I defined, using generous overlap between frames so that every point on the ground is imaged several times and the stitcher has features to match; the sugar-beet study worked through below flew 80 % front and 70 % side overlap, which is representative (Koç et al. 2025).
Why go to this trouble when the index is a ratio anyway? Normalized-difference indices do cancel some illumination variation — a uniform brightening multiplies numerator and denominator alike — and that partial self-correction is a real reason the form is popular. But the cancellation is only exact if illumination shifts identically in both bands, and it does not: haze scatters blue and red far more than NIR, and canopy shadow is not spectrally neutral. The indices this chapter cares about are also being asked a harder question than Part I’s. Distinguishing a diseased pixel from a merely dry one turns on reflectance differences of a few percentage points in a 35-nanometre-wide band; that signal does not survive an uncalibrated pipeline. Calibration discipline is to this chapter what cross-track error was to the Path Planning on the Edge chapter — the unglamorous budget line the whole guarantee rests on.

title: 27  Remote Sensing at Scale: Multispectral Imaging in Agriculture
section: 27.4 A Detector Is Not a Classifier
text:
27.4 A Detector Is Not a Classifier
With calibrated reflectance in hand, Part I’s story can be sharpened into this chapter’s central distinction. NDVI works as a stress detector because nearly every way a plant can suffer eventually erodes the same contrast: less photosynthetically active tissue means less red absorption and less NIR scattering, so the index falls. That convergence is exactly what makes NDVI a poor classifier — drought, nitrogen shortage, a fungal colony, and chewing insects all arrive at the same depressed number by different routes, and by construction the index has thrown away the route. Two bands in, one scalar out: everything the spectrum knew about which stressor is at work was discarded at the moment of the subtraction.
The information NDVI discards is concentrated in a region NDVI does not sample. Between the red band’s deep chlorophyll absorption and the NIR plateau’s structural scattering lies the red edge, the steep shoulder around 700–740 nm where vegetation reflectance climbs by an order of magnitude in a few tens of nanometres. The shoulder’s position and slope are set by the two things a fungal infection attacks first: chlorophyll concentration, which the pathogen degrades as it colonizes leaf tissue, and cell structure, which collapses as mycelium spreads and pustules erupt. Both changes move and flatten the red edge before the broadband red/NIR contrast has fully deteriorated — which is the physiological reason spectral methods can beat a human scout, since the reflectance change precedes the visible pigment loss an eye detects. And the perturbation is not the same for every stressor. A multi-temporal vineyard trial in Portugal’s Vinho Verde region that tracked downy mildew across seven multispectral flights over treated and untreated vines reported the infection signature as increased reflectance in the visible and red-edge bands with a progressive decline in NIR — an opposite-signed, two-part pattern distinguishable from the flatter, NIR-dominated depression of simple water stress (Unknown (full author list not retrieved) 2025). Work on potato late blight makes the mechanism finer still: infection measurably shifts the wavelength positions of two spectral landmarks — the red-well point, where red absorption bottoms out, and the red-edge point, where the shoulder’s slope peaks — and a classifier watching those red and red-edge wavelengths reached 89.3 % accuracy at leaf scale three days after inoculation, the same day symptoms first became visible, and 89.1 % at canopy scale two days later (Fernández et al. 2020).






Figure 27.1: Representative reflectance spectra for healthy, fungally infected, and drought-stressed vegetation, with the bands NDVI samples versus the red-edge region where disease-specific indices look. Both stressors shrink NDVI’s broad red/NIR contrast toward the same depressed value; the shape of the red-edge shoulder is where their signatures separate.



Figure 27.1 draws the argument. The two teal markers under the wavelength axis are all NDVI ever sees; every curve in the figure loses contrast between them, which is why the index detects them all and distinguishes none. The amber markers sit on the shoulder, where the curves’ shapes diverge. An index built from those bands is not more sensitive in some vague sense — it is sampling the specific spectral degrees of freedom that carry the disease information. The next section builds two such indices and puts real accuracy numbers behind the claim.

title: 27  Remote Sensing at Scale: Multispectral Imaging in Agriculture
text:
27.5 Indices Built for Diagnosis
The gentlest step beyond NDVI keeps the normalized-difference form and moves one band. NDRE replaces red with red-edge:
\[
\text{NDRE} = \frac{\rho_{\text{NIR}} - \rho_{\text{RE}}}{\rho_{\text{NIR}} + \rho_{\text{RE}}},
\]
computable on any standard five-band agricultural array, since the array carries a red-edge filter precisely for indices like this one. Because red-edge reflectance — unlike deep-red reflectance, which is nearly zero for any healthy canopy — still varies with chlorophyll content in dense vegetation, NDRE keeps discriminating after NDVI has saturated over a closed canopy, and it responds to early chlorosis while the red band is still pinned near total absorption. The same one-band substitution logic produced GNDVI, the green-for-red variant introduced for chlorophyll and nitrogen estimation (Gitelson, Kaufman, and Merzlyak 1996), which reappears throughout the disease literature because disease-driven chlorophyll loss is exactly what it was built to sense.
The sharper instrument is an index designed around one disease’s signature. The Red Edge Disease Stress Index was constructed from the specific way yellow rust — the fungal disease Puccinia striiformis causes in wheat — distorts the red-edge region, and it uses three bands: red at 665 nm and two red-edge bands near 705 and 783 nm (Zheng et al. 2018):
\[
\text{REDSI} = \frac{(705-665)\,(\rho_{\text{RE3}} - \rho_{R}) \;-\; (783-665)\,(\rho_{\text{RE1}} - \rho_{R})}{2\,\rho_{R}}.
\]
The construction is a triangle: the numerator measures how far the mid-shoulder reflectance sits from the straight line joining the red trough to the upper shoulder — a direct measurement of the shoulder’s shape, which is what infection deforms. Work it through on representative reflectance values to see the leverage. A healthy wheat pixel might show \(\rho_R = 0.05\), \(\rho_{\text{RE1}} = 0.12\), \(\rho_{\text{RE3}} = 0.45\); a rust-infected one \(\rho_R = 0.09\), \(\rho_{\text{RE1}} = 0.14\), \(\rho_{\text{RE3}} = 0.28\) — red up, upper shoulder down, exactly the signature of the previous section:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{REDSI}_{\text{healthy}} &= \frac{40(0.45-0.05) - 118(0.12-0.05)}{2(0.05)} \\
                              &= \frac{16.0 - 8.26}{0.10} \approx 77 \\[4pt]
\text{REDSI}_{\text{infected}} &= \frac{40(0.28-0.09) - 118(0.14-0.09)}{2(0.09)} \\
                               &= \frac{7.60 - 5.90}{0.18} \approx 9
\end{aligned}
\]
An eight-fold contrast between the two pixels. The same two pixels’ NDVI values, computed with Part I’s formula from \(\rho_{\text{NIR}} = 0.50\) and \(0.33\) respectively, are 0.82 and 0.57 — a 1.4-fold contrast. The illustrative numbers are chosen for the arithmetic, but the separability advantage they dramatize is the published result: validated head-to-head on the same wheat plots, REDSI identified yellow rust with 84.1 % overall accuracy (kappa 0.76) at canopy scale against NDVI’s 78.8 %, and at regional scale the gap widened sharply — 85.2 % against 66.7 % (Zheng et al. 2018). Two honest caveats travel with those numbers. The validation flew on Sentinel-2 satellite imagery at 10 m per pixel, not on a drone; the index itself is sensor-agnostic — any platform carrying the three bands can compute it — and a drone’s far finer GSD would be expected to help rather than hurt, but that extrapolation was not tested in the paper. And the standard five-band agricultural array carries only one red-edge filter, so it computes NDRE but not REDSI; the full index needs a sensor with two red-edge bands, such as the dual-camera multispectral rigs the late-blight work used (Fernández et al. 2020) — a concrete instance of the sensor-selection-follows-the-question doctrine that university extension guidance on agricultural UAV sensing spells out (North Carolina State University Extension 2021).
Beyond these, the literature’s toolbox is wide, and a sampling shows the range of spectral degrees of freedom being tapped: the Photochemical Reflectance Index, PRI, built from two narrow visible bands at 531 and 570 nm, tracks xanthophyll pigment changes tied to photosynthetic efficiency; the Disease Water Stress Index couples a shortwave-infrared water-absorption band to the visible/NIR pair, at the price of a SWIR-capable sensor beyond the standard array; and the Chlorophyll Absorption Ratio Index, CARI, combines red, green, and red-edge reflectance while correcting for soil background. None of these is universally best — the wheat stem-rust study below tested fourteen candidate indices and found GNDVI, PRI, a red-edge stress index, and a chlorophyll-green index most effective for that one disease (Abdulridha et al. 2023) — and that is itself the lesson: disease-specific means the index, like the classifier, is fitted to the pathogen.

section: 27.6 Two Case Studies from Real Fields
text:
27.6 Two Case Studies from Real Fields
Numbers from real deployments discipline the enthusiasm, and two well-documented studies bracket the space — one multispectral and operational, one hyperspectral and research-grade.
Sugar beet, two diseases, one survey. A recent field trial flew a DJI Phantom 4 Multispectral — a stock quadcopter whose six-sensor head implements the same five-band architecture the Commercial Drone Landscape chapter catalogued, plus RGB — over sugar beet afflicted by two distinct fungal diseases at once: Cercospora leaf spot and powdery mildew (Koç et al. 2025). The flight parameters place it firmly in the targeted resolution regime of the next section: 15 m above ground, roughly 0.4 cm GSD, 80 % front and 70 % side overlap. NDVI maps were computed in photogrammetry software, thresholded into severity classes with the Jenks natural-breaks method, and five supervised classifiers were trained per disease. The results carry two teaching points. First, no single algorithm won: K-nearest-neighbors performed best on Cercospora (0.83 accuracy, 0.76 F1) while logistic regression performed best on powdery mildew (0.91 accuracy, 0.93 F1) — disease-specific diagnosis in practice means a separate model per disease on the same spectral data, not one universal disease index. Second, the timing evidence is concrete and honestly bounded: in a 2022 instance, the drone-derived index declined on July 20 while visual field assessment recorded no symptoms until July 24 — a directly observed four-day lead — and the authors separately describe an operational deployment in which drone-based detection ran fifteen days ahead of the farm’s usual scouting cadence, enabling earlier spraying. The four days is a measured comparison; the fifteen is an operational anecdote against habit rather than a controlled day-count, and the two should be quoted as what they are.
Wheat stem rust, hyperspectral. At the research-grade end, a 240-band hyperspectral camera (400–900 nm, 2.1 nm spectral resolution) flown on a DJI Matrice 600 Pro hexacopter at 20 m — about 3 cm GSD — surveyed 960 wheat plots for stem rust severity (Abdulridha et al. 2023). A random-forest classifier reached 85 % overall accuracy across four severity classes and 88 % on the binary healthy-versus-diseased question, and the diagnostic wavelengths the analysis singled out — clustered in the green near 530 nm and the red edge between 690 and 730 nm — are pointedly not the red/NIR pair NDVI uses, independent confirmation of this chapter’s central mechanism. The per-class breakdown deserves more attention than the headline: 84 % on healthy plots, 97 % on moderate infection, 81 % on severe — and only 76 % on mild. The early, low-severity case is simultaneously the hardest to classify and the only one worth the flight, because moderate and severe infection is what the fungicide window has already closed on. Accuracy claims in this field should be read per severity class, never as one flat number.
How much earlier than a human scout, then? The literature’s honest answer is a range, not a constant, because the physiological lead — reflectance change preceding visible pigment loss — depends on how much cellular disruption must accumulate before that particular disease is eye-visible in that particular crop. At the short end, the potato late-blight work above matched first visible symptoms at leaf scale rather than beating them (Fernández et al. 2020). The sugar-beet trial measured four days at field scale (Koç et al. 2025). At the long end, a multispectral UAV study of wheat yellow rust in Argentina reported a detection model reaching 60 % accuracy as early as 40 days after sowing — well before rust is conspicuous — climbing to 79 % by flowering, and framed the payoff as preserving an estimated 3–7 % of yield by acting inside the window the early call opens (Nguyen et al. 2023). One widely circulated figure needs a flag: a claim of “seven days before visible symptoms at ~97 % accuracy” for Septoria leaf blotch in wheat is real, but it comes from a handheld proximal hyperspectral scanner imaging individual leaves, not from any drone platform (Niu et al. 2025). The underlying mechanism is the same one that motivates UAV red-edge indices, but the number does not transfer to canopy-scale aerial sensing and should never be quoted as a drone result — a small case study in why Part III’s habit of asking what was actually measured, on what platform, at what scale follows this book’s readers everywhere.

title: 27  Remote Sensing at Scale: Multispectral Imaging in Agriculture
section: 27.7 Flying the Survey Twice: Coarse-to-Targeted Search
text:
27.7 Flying the Survey Twice: Coarse-to-Targeted Search
Everything above concerns what the pixels mean. The operational question — how a scouting mission is flown — turns out to be one the book has already mostly solved, because field-scale multispectral surveying is systematic-coverage work: the same lawnmower problem, the same boustrophedon answer, the same generator the Path Planning on the Edge chapter wrote for the running example’s search grid. What agriculture adds is a resolution dilemma the goose mission never faced, and a two-stage doctrine that resolves it.
The dilemma is the Commercial Drone Landscape chapter’s GSD relation meeting the Path Planning chapter’s track-length arithmetic. GSD is linear in altitude; so is swath width; so the total track length needed to cover a fixed area scales inversely with altitude. Diagnosis wants fine GSD — the sugar-beet study’s 0.4 cm per pixel resolves individual leaves — but fine GSD is ruinously expensive over a whole field. Work it through for a 400 m × 400 m field (16 ha) with a multispectral camera whose bands are 1,600 pixels wide and whose GSD works out to 3.2 cm per pixel at 60 m. At 60 m the swath is \(1600 \times 0.032 = 51\) m; at the 70 % side overlap photogrammetric stitching wants, the sweep spacing is 15.4 m, and the Path Planning chapter’s generator emits \(\lceil 400/15.4 \rceil + 1 = 27\) legs — about 11.2 km of track, 23 minutes at 8 m/s, one flight. Drop to 15 m for a 0.8 cm GSD and everything scales by four: a 12.8 m swath, 3.8 m spacing, 106 legs, about 42.8 km of track — and low flight is also slow flight, because motion blur is measured in pixels: at a 1/500 s shutter, 8 m/s smears 1.6 cm across the exposure, half a pixel at the coarse GSD and two full pixels at the fine one. At a blur-safe 5 m/s the fine-GSD full-field survey costs well over two hours and several battery swaps. Exhaustive coverage at diagnostic resolution does not fit in a flight day.
The two-stage pattern splits the difference, and it is documented practice, not just a neat idea: an initial pass at survey altitude maps the whole field at coarse GSD; low-index or otherwise anomalous sectors are flagged algorithmically — a threshold, a percentile cut, or the natural-breaks classing the sugar-beet study used; and the aircraft then re-flies only the flagged sectors at low altitude and fine GSD, capturing the per-leaf imagery on which a diagnosis, or a scout’s boots-on-ground visit, can stand. For the worked field: if the coarse map flags one 60 m × 60 m sector — about 2 % of the field — the targeted stage is 17 legs and roughly a kilometre of track, under four minutes at 5 m/s. Stage 1 plus Stage 2 comes to under half an hour where uniform fine coverage cost hours. The platform economics reinforce the split: extension guidance notes that a fixed-wing survey aircraft covers on the order of 200 acres in a 55-minute flight while a multirotor manages half-hour batteries — so the coarse stage suits a fast fixed-wing at altitude, and the targeted stage suits exactly the cheap, maneuverable multirotor this book has been flying all along (North Carolina State University Extension 2021).






Figure 27.2: The coarse-to-targeted two-stage crop-scouting survey: a whole-field coverage pass at high altitude and coarse GSD flags an anomalous low-index sector, and a second lawnmower at low altitude and fine GSD re-flies only that sector — the same generator the Path Planning on the Edge chapter built, called twice with different parameters.



Two connections make this more than an agricultural aside. First, both stages are literally the Path Planning chapter’s lawnmower() — a bounding box, a spacing, an altitude — called twice: once with the field polygon and the coarse spacing, once with the flagged sector’s bounding box and the fine spacing. The generator was twenty lines precisely so that it could be re-parameterized like this. Second, the flag-then-re-fly structure is the running example’s own detect-then-investigate pattern wearing different clothes: the Path Planning chapter’s search grid is preempted by a detection and the aircraft goes to look, exactly as the coarse survey’s anomaly summons the targeted stage — except that here the “detection” is a depressed patch in a continuous index map rather than a bounding box from a neural network, a distinction the next section makes precise.
The research frontier collapses the two flights into one. A reinforcement-learning scouting agent that alternates in real time between an exploration phase — covering large swaths in search of regions that contradict its current map — and denser re-scouting over flagged problem regions, steered by a learned whole-field state estimate, reached 89.8 % field-assessment accuracy while sampling only 40 % of an 80-acre field, with the authors reporting 4.8× lower labor cost than exhaustive scouting; the whole-field state mattered, since an agent reasoning only from recently visited zones managed 80.3 % at the same coverage (Zhang et al. 2020). That is the two-stage doctrine made adaptive and continuous — and it is recognizably a cousin of the coverage-versus-investigate hinge this book built into the running example’s mission logic.

title: 27  Remote Sensing at Scale: Multispectral Imaging in Agriculture
text:
27.8 Two Paradigms, One Camera Mount
The chapter’s last obligation is precision about the contrast it has been trading on. Part III’s Building a Detection Pipeline chapter and this chapter both fly a camera over the ground and both end in a georeferenced claim about what is down there. Beneath that resemblance, they are solving different information-processing problems, and an engineer choosing between them should be able to name the differences exactly.



Table 27.1: The two sensing paradigms, made precise: a discrete learned per-frame classification versus a continuous physical per-pixel measurement.











Part III: RGB object detection
This chapter: multispectral index mapping




Unit of inference
One frame at a time, onboard, at frame rate
One pixel at a time, across a whole orthomosaic


The computation
A learned function — millions of trained weights — mapping pixels to boxes and classes
A fixed arithmetic formula — a handful of band ratios — mapping reflectances to a physical index


What “detection” means
A discrete decision: this box is a goose with confidence 0.87, above threshold
A spatial anomaly: this patch’s continuous index sits below its surroundings


Output artifact
Bounding boxes and classes per frame, streamed live
A continuous scalar field over the field, assembled after landing


Ground truth required
A labeled dataset — thousands of hand-drawn boxes, the pipeline’s true bottleneck
Radiometric calibration — a panel, an irradiance sensor, a flight window


Fails when
The dataset lacked this case: unseen scale, lighting, or confusable species
Calibration breaks: cloud shadow, haze, sun angle, a skipped panel shot


Where it runs
The companion computer, subject to Part III’s latency and memory budgets
A workstation, deadline-free — photogrammetry is the cloud tier’s kind of work


Answers
“Is there a thing here, and what kind?”
“What is the condition of every point here?”






The deepest row is the ground-truth one, because it names what each paradigm’s accuracy is made of. The detector’s competence is borrowed from its dataset: it knows what a goose looks like because thousands of examples said so, and it fails on what the dataset failed to contain. The index’s competence is borrowed from physics: nobody labeled examples of “stressed”; chlorophyll absorbs red, leaf structure scatters NIR, and the formula is the mechanism written as arithmetic. That is why the index generalizes to a field it has never seen with no retraining — and why it cannot, by itself, say goose: there is no per-pixel physical formula for a species. Each paradigm is the wrong tool for the other’s question.
The boundary, though, is a place to build, and the strongest recent results live on it. The machine-learning classifiers of both case studies above are learned functions on top of physically calibrated indices — the physics supplies invariant features, the learning supplies the disease-specific decision boundary. A very recent vineyard study went further and composed the paradigms outright: a YOLO object detector — the same family the running example’s Detector node runs — trained not on RGB frames but on imagery augmented with a chlorophyll-absorption index, locating Botrytis infection sites as discrete detections at 91.1 % F1, where the identical architecture on RGB alone managed 68.1 % (Montalban-Faet et al. 2026). Read against Table 27.1, that is the whole chapter in one experiment: the learned pipeline supplied the “find the discrete thing” machinery, and the physical index supplied 23 points of F1 that no amount of RGB data was going to.






NoteFor More



The index-stack-plus-learning recipe generalizes past classification: one wheat leaf-rust study fed an algorithmically selected subset of UAV-derived vegetation indices into a neural network to predict continuous disease severity (\(R^2 \approx 0.78\) on validation), turning the healthy/diseased binary into a regression (Ju et al. 2023). On the flight-doctrine side, the incremental replanning machinery the Path Planning on the Edge chapter’s For More note introduced (D* Lite and kin) is what a single-flight adaptive scout needs when the “flagged sector” list changes mid-mission; the reinforcement-learning scouting paper is the current reference point for how far that can be pushed (Zhang et al. 2020). And for sensor selection — five-band versus dual-red-edge versus hyperspectral, fixed-wing versus multirotor per stage — the university extension literature is the practical, vendor-neutral starting point (North Carolina State University Extension 2021).

title: 27  Remote Sensing at Scale: Multispectral Imaging in Agriculture
text:
27.9 Check Your Understanding

A field’s NDVI map shows a sharply depressed patch. The farm manager asks: “drought or disease?” Explain, in terms of what NDVI computes and what fungal infection does to the reflectance spectrum, why NDVI alone cannot answer — and what additional band measurements would begin to.







TipShow answer





NDVI compresses the spectrum to one scalar per pixel from exactly two samples: red and NIR reflectance. Essentially every stressor — drought, nutrient shortage, fungal colonization, pest damage — erodes the same red/NIR contrast, so all of them converge to the same depressed index; the subtraction throws away the spectral shape that distinguishes the routes. The disease-discriminating information is concentrated in the red-edge region (~700–740 nm), which NDVI does not sample: fungal chlorophyll degradation and cell-structure collapse move and flatten the red-edge shoulder — and some diseases raise visible/red-edge reflectance while lowering NIR, an opposite-signed pattern distinct from drought’s flatter NIR-dominated depression. Measuring one or two red-edge bands (enabling NDRE, or REDSI with two of them) is the minimum addition that starts to separate the hypotheses; a targeted low-altitude re-fly or a scout’s visit confirms.




Compute REDSI and NDRE for a pixel with \(\rho_R = 0.07\), \(\rho_{\text{RE1}}(705) = 0.13\), \(\rho_{\text{RE3}}(783) = 0.36\), and \(\rho_{\text{NIR}} = 0.41\) (take \(\rho_{\text{RE}} = \rho_{\text{RE1}}\) for NDRE). Then state which standard sensor class can compute each index and why.







TipShow answer





REDSI \(= [40(0.36-0.07) - 118(0.13-0.07)]/(2 \times 0.07) = (11.6 - 7.08)/0.14 \approx 32\). NDRE \(= (0.41-0.13)/(0.41+0.13) = 0.28/0.54 \approx 0.52\). NDRE needs only NIR and one red-edge band, so any standard five-band agricultural array computes it. REDSI needs red plus two red-edge bands (≈705 and ≈783 nm); the standard five-band array carries only one red-edge filter, so REDSI requires a dual-red-edge multispectral rig (or hyperspectral, or the satellite bands it was validated on) — a concrete case of the index driving the sensor purchase.




In the head-to-head validation, REDSI beat NDVI 84.1 % to 78.8 % at canopy scale and 85.2 % to 66.7 % at regional scale. A colleague concludes: “so a drone flying REDSI detects yellow rust at 85 % accuracy.” Name two distinct corrections that claim needs.







TipShow answer





First, platform: the validation used Sentinel-2 satellite imagery at 10 m per pixel, not a drone. The index is sensor-agnostic and a UAV’s far finer GSD would plausibly do as well or better, but that was not tested — the published accuracy licenses a satellite claim, not a drone claim. Second, scope: 84–85 % is the accuracy for this disease (wheat yellow rust) with an index purpose-built for its red-edge signature, distinguishing it from background on those plots; it is not a general “disease detection accuracy,” and the same construction applied to a different pathogen or crop would need its own validation — as the stem-rust study’s different best-index set shows. (A third, finer point: quote accuracy per severity class where available; mild infection classifies worst and matters most.)




The wheat stem-rust study reported per-class accuracies of 84 % (healthy), 76 % (mild), 97 % (moderate), 81 % (severe). Why is the pattern of those numbers — not the 85 % overall figure — the operationally decisive information for a grower deciding whether to buy the survey?







TipShow answer





The economic value of the survey is concentrated in exactly one class: mild infection, the stage where fungicide intervention still preserves the crop. Moderate and severe infection are easy to classify (97 %, 81 %) precisely because the spectral perturbation is large — but by then a competent human scout sees it too, and much of the treatment window has closed. Mild is simultaneously the hardest class (76 %, the worst of the four) and the only one the flight is really for. The 85 % overall figure is an average dominated by classes that matter less; a grower should ask “how well does it catch what I can’t yet see?” — and the honest answer is the per-class number, roughly three in four. The general rule: early/low-severity detection performance, not headline accuracy, is the figure of merit for any early-warning sensing system.




Using the chapter’s worked survey numbers (400 m × 400 m field; swath 51 m and spacing 15.4 m at 60 m altitude; both linear in altitude; 70 % side overlap throughout): compute legs, approximate track, and flight time for (a) one coarse pass at 8 m/s, and (b) a full-field pass at 20 m altitude and 5 m/s. Then (c) give the two-stage total if the coarse pass flags two sectors of 50 m × 50 m each, flown at 20 m and 5 m/s, and state the time ratio of (b) to (c).







TipShow answer






Given: 27 legs, ≈11.2 km, ≈23 min at 8 m/s. (b) At 20 m, swath and spacing scale by \(20/60\): swath 17 m, spacing ≈5.1 m; legs \(= \lceil 400/5.1 \rceil + 1 = 80\); track ≈ \(80 \times 400 + 79 \times 5.1 \approx 32.4\) km; at 5 m/s ≈ 6,480 s ≈ 108 min — plus several battery swaps. (c) Each 50 m sector at 5.1 m spacing: \(\lceil 50/5.1 \rceil + 1 = 11\) legs ≈ \(11 \times 50 + 10 \times 5.1 \approx 0.60\) km, ≈2 min at 5 m/s; two sectors ≈4 min plus transits. Two-stage total ≈ 23 + 4 ≈ 27 min against ≈108 min: a factor of ≈4 — and the two-stage plan still delivers the full fine-GSD imagery over the two sectors that actually matter, while fitting comfortably into a single battery cycle.





A vendor brochure claims its drone service “detects Septoria leaf blotch seven days before visible symptoms at 97 % accuracy.” Based on this chapter, what should a careful engineer check before repeating that claim, and what is the actual provenance of those figures?







TipShow answer





Check what was measured, on what platform, at what scale. The 7-day/97 % pairing traces to a study using a handheld proximal hyperspectral scanner imaging individual leaves — not a drone, not canopy scale, not aerial GSD. The underlying mechanism (spectral change preceding visible symptoms) genuinely motivates UAV red-edge sensing, but lead time and accuracy both degrade moving from a leaf millimetres from a scanner to a canopy tens of metres below a five-band camera — the late-blight work, for instance, went from 3-days-post-inoculation performance at leaf level to 5 at canopy level. Drone-platform lead times documented in this chapter run from roughly matching first visible symptoms, through a measured four-day lead at field scale, to weeks-early detection at reduced accuracy — a disease- and platform-specific range, not a transferable headline number.

title: 27  Remote Sensing at Scale: Multispectral Imaging in Agriculture
text:
27.10 Try It
Part 1 — build both indices and compare their anomaly maps. Simulate a calibrated five-band orthomosaic as five NumPy arrays (say 400 × 400, one metre per pixel) of reflectance values: start every band from a healthy baseline (visible bands low, red ≈ 0.05, red-edge ≈ 0.15, NIR ≈ 0.48, plus a few percent of spatial noise). Inject two anomalies with different signatures: a fungal patch (raise red and red-edge reflectance, lower NIR — the downy-mildew-style opposite-signed pattern) and a broad drought gradient (depress NIR and, mildly and proportionally, red-edge, leaving the visible shape mostly intact). Compute NDVI (Part I’s formula) and NDRE per pixel, render both as images with a shared color scale, and difference each against its healthy-area median to make anomaly maps. Write down what you see before rationalizing it: both indices should flag both anomalies, but compare the contrast each index draws between the two anomaly types — then compute a third map, the NDVI-to-NDRE ratio or difference, and check whether it separates the fungal patch from the drought gradient better than either index alone. Close with three sentences on what a single-index deliverable would have told the farm manager, and what the pair tells them.
Part 2 — plan the two-stage survey with the machinery you already own. Take your Part 1 anomaly map and threshold it (a percentile cut is fine; the ambitious version implements Jenks natural breaks) to flag anomalous pixels, then compute the flagged region’s bounding box. Now reuse the Path Planning on the Edge chapter’s lawnmower() exactly as written: call it once over the full field with the coarse-stage parameters from this chapter’s worked example (compute the spacing from a 51 m swath at 70 % overlap), and once over the flagged bounding box with the targeted-stage parameters (12.8 m swath, same overlap rule). Plot both paths over the anomaly map — coarse in one color, targeted in another — and audit the plan the way that chapter audited everything: total track length and flight time per stage, batteries required at your platform’s endurance, and the time you would have spent flying the whole field at targeted resolution instead. If you flew the running example’s missions in earlier chapters, note how little new code this took: the sensing payload changed everything about the pixels and nothing about the planner.
Related Lab: No lab currently maps to this chapter.
The running example will go back to chasing geese in a moment, but it is worth naming what this chapter demonstrated about the system the book has built: the coverage generator, the GSD arithmetic, the detect-then-investigate mission structure, and the discipline of asking what was actually measured all transferred to a sensing problem the running example never posed — which is what it means for engineering machinery to be general. What did not transfer is the part this Part is circling: a crop scout’s drone answers to the farmer whose field it flies, but a system that autonomously pursues wild animals answers to parties who never signed the work order. The account the previous chapter said no telemetry stream records is still owed, and the next chapter renders it.

text:
28.1 Learning Objectives
The account falls due here. Two chapters ago, the post-flight diagnostics chapter conceded that its entire apparatus — the ULog, the replay, the evidence-first culture — answers every question about a flight except whether the flight should have happened; the previous chapter, returning from the crop fields, closed by renewing the debt: a system that autonomously pursues wild animals answers to parties who never signed the work order. And the debt is older than Part V. The Harassment Pattern Generation chapter built the deterrent patterns and then said plainly that bounding a harm is not the same as justifying it, deferring the justification — when deterrence is warranted, what repeated disturbance costs, who decides, by what standard — to this chapter. The Real-Time Inference chapter flagged its own version before the system ever flew — responsible AI as a set of design requirements that bind earliest — and promised the full treatment here. This chapter pays all three notes, and it does so the way the rest of the book has tried to do everything: with the real literature, the real numbers, and the real system — including one number in the running example’s own shipped code that this chapter will spend a great deal of time looking at, because it is the most instructive engineering-ethics artifact the book has.
The subject deserves a plain statement before any framework dresses it up. The Goose Management System exists to frighten wild animals on purpose. Every other chapter could treat that fact as a mission parameter; this one treats it as a question. The review this book has leaned on for wildlife–drone interactions throughout — a systematic screening of over 1,600 publications down to 74 quantified studies of how drones disturb animals — ends its abstract by posing the problem to this book’s exact audience: can we design drones that minimize disturbance to animals while still complying with the legislation that governs transparent drone operation (Afridi et al. 2025)? The authors pose it as an open engineering question, not a solved one, and that is the honest register for this chapter too. It will not end in a clean verdict. It will end with the tension named accurately, a structured way to reason about it, and a short list of design principles that a reader building such a system can actually apply.

title: 28  The Ethics and Ecology of Autonomous Wildlife Management
text:
Summarize the systematic-review evidence on how drone altitude, horizontal proximity, approach angle, speed, and repeated exposure drive wildlife stress responses — and explain why a literature written to avoid disturbance can neither validate nor simply indict a mission whose purpose is to cause it.
Apply that evidence, together with measured Canada-goose flight-initiation distances, to critique the running example’s shipped harassment parameters — the 3 m orbit default against the same project’s own 8–15 m design band and its own flagged 3–4 m danger zone — and argue why the gap is an ethics finding, not merely a tuning bug.
Evaluate a deterrence mission with the Five Domains animal-welfare model instead of ad hoc judgment, and explain why the laboratory-research “Three Rs” framework fits a deterrence mission poorly.
Distinguish what is legal from what is right for this system specifically: why non-contact goose hazing is broadly permit-free under U.S. wildlife law, how the Endangered Species Act’s definition of “harass” describes the mission almost verbatim, and what the dual-permission regulatory model adds that Part 107 cannot.
Explain the habituation–escalation dynamic — why a deterrent engineered to stay effective is under structural pressure to become more aggressive over time — and summarize the published argument that continuing to escalate a partially failing non-lethal deterrent can be the more harmful choice.
Extend the responsibility analysis to the humans in the frame, delivering the privacy-by-design and bias-auditing obligations flagged in Part III, including why a species-confusion audit of the detector is simultaneously a welfare audit and a legal-exposure audit.
State, and ground in cited evidence, concrete design principles for an autonomous deterrence system: an FID-anchored minimum approach distance, a tiered descent protocol, behavioral monitoring that overrides fixed timers, escape-route preservation, and per-flock exposure caps.

title: 28  The Ethics and Ecology of Autonomous Wildlife Management
text:
28.2 Key Vocabulary

Wildlife disturbance — any change a drone induces in an animal’s behavior or physiology — vigilance, alarm calling, interrupted feeding, flight, elevated heart rate — whether or not the operator observes it; the quantity the drone-impact literature measures, and the quantity a deterrence mission deliberately produces within bounds.
Stress response — the behavioral and physiological cascade a perceived threat triggers, from head-up vigilance through alarm to panicked flight; critically, the physiological component can be large while the behavioral component is invisible — animals have shown significant cardiac responses to drones without moving at all (Afridi et al. 2025).
Alert distance — the separation at which an animal first shows detectable vigilance toward an approaching threat; always larger than the flight-initiation distance, and the earliest externally observable sign that a stress response has begun.
Flight-initiation distance (FID) — the Harassment Pattern Generation chapter’s behavioral threshold, reappearing here as a welfare boundary: the separation at which the animal abandons what it was doing and flees. Operating far inside FID does not make a deterrent more effective; it converts controlled movement into panic.
Minimum approach distance — the hard floor on separation between aircraft and animal, held outside the collision-and-panic envelope and enforced by the trajectory generator as a constraint; its value must be anchored to measured species-specific response data, not to convenience.
Escape-route preservation — the design rule, taught with the herding corridor in Part IV, that a deterrent must always leave the animals one open, unpressured direction; pressure with no exit produces scatter and injury risk rather than dispersal.
Cumulative stress — stress that accumulates across repeated exposures rather than resetting between them; the review evidence indicates repeated drone exposure carries cumulative physiological cost, while the long-term consequences remain the field’s largest acknowledged unknown (Afridi et al. 2025).
Habituation (behavioral) — the Part IV term, now carrying its ethical edge: as a flock learns a stimulus is harmless, the system’s effectiveness decays, and the cheapest engineering responses — closer, longer, more aggressive — all spend the animal’s welfare to buy the metric back.
Five Domains model — a structured animal-welfare assessment framework spanning nutrition, physical environment, health, and behavior, all feeding a fifth, integrative domain of mental state; developed to replace checklist-style welfare thinking with an account of what the animal actually experiences (Mellor 2016).
Tiered descent protocol — the review literature’s recommended engagement pattern: begin at a distance the animal tolerates and close only as observed behavior permits, rather than committing to a single fixed close-range geometry (Afridi et al. 2025).
Dual-permission model — a regulatory structure, used in several conservation jurisdictions, requiring two separate approvals before a drone flies near wildlife: an aviation authority’s operational permit and a wildlife-management agency’s conservation-specific approval; the aviation permit alone — the Part 107 layer — says nothing about the animals.
Escalation pressure — the structural pull on any deterrence program to intensify its stimulus as effectiveness fades; not a character flaw of the operators but a predictable system dynamic, and one the wildlife-management literature treats as an ethically live decision point rather than a routine tuning step.

title: 28  The Ethics and Ecology of Autonomous Wildlife Management
section: 28.3 What the Disturbance Literature Actually Says
text:
28.3 What the Disturbance Literature Actually Says
The book’s anchor source on wildlife–drone interaction deserves to be read closely here, because its findings are the measuring stick everything else in this chapter is held against. The review synthesizes 74 quantified studies across aquatic, avian, and terrestrial species — seals, elephants, penguins, kangaroos, dolphins, and, importantly for the running example, geese — and its operational findings organize cleanly along the axes an engineer can actually control (Afridi et al. 2025).
Altitude is a primary factor. The review’s headline operational recommendation is that maintaining altitudes of 40–80 m reduces stress, particularly for large mammals and birds. The pattern beneath the number is consistent across its studies: stationary birds showed minimal reaction to drones staying above 40 m; Adélie penguins reacted at 50 m and gentoo penguins at 30 m, with vigilance most pronounced at 10–20 m; most seabird species in one multi-species study showed significant stress at 10 m but little at 50 m. Responses intensify sharply as the last few tens of metres close.
Horizontal proximity matters at least as much. The review treats approach distance as its own axis, distinct from altitude, and its numbers are of the same order: roughly 30–50 m to minimize avoidance behavior in large mammals, and 50–80 m for birds, especially near nesting or breeding sites. These figures echo what Part IV already reported from the primary studies: no observable disturbance to waterfowl only above roughly 40 m (McEvoy, Hall, and McDonald 2016), 75 m or more over nesting snow geese (Barnas et al. 2018), and about 100 m survey altitude for non-disturbing goose observation (Bech-Hansen et al. 2019). A more recent, larger empirical study — 561 birds across 22 species — went so far as to recommend a round-number code of practice: no approach within about 100 m (Weston et al. 2020).
Geometry matters independently of distance. Animals cannot look directly above themselves, and the review finds direct or overhead approaches provoke stronger responses than lateral or oblique ones — a drone descending from above, or banking sharply over a flock, reads as a stooping raptor. This is the same finding Part IV built the pattern taxonomy on (Vas et al. 2015; Mulero-Pázmány et al. 2017), and the review sharpens it with a striking data point: drones could approach waterfowl within 4 m without significant disturbance — provided the approach was a careful lateral pass, never from overhead. Distance and geometry trade against each other; the gentlest documented close approaches are single, slow, oblique passes, not sustained presence.
Speed and duration bound the dose. Speeds below 5 m/s are recommended near groups or juveniles. And on repeated exposure the review is direct: the evidence indicates that repeated drone exposure causes cumulative stress, that sessions should be limited to necessary time — flight sessions of no more than 10–15 minutes are the typical recommendation — and that brief exposures let animals return to normal behavior sooner. It is equally direct about what is not known: the long-term consequences of chronic, repeated exposure are the field’s biggest open gap. Nobody has measured what a season of automated daily harassment does to a resident flock, because no one has run that experiment.
Then comes the sentence a chapter like this one cannot walk past. In its ethics section, the review states its normative position without hedging: responsible drone use must abide by rules that optimize wildlife welfare, and disturbance beyond some point, and any physical harm caused to animals, are totally unacceptable regardless of the perceived conservation value or data-collection aim of the study (Afridi et al. 2025). Note the sentence’s full reach — it does not stop at physical harm; it draws the unacceptability line somewhere inside disturbance itself. Read strictly, that sentence and the Goose Management System cannot both be comfortable. The review is written for research and monitoring drones, where disturbance is an unwanted side effect of data collection and the entire engineering problem is suppressing it. The running example inverts the premise: disturbance is not its side effect but its product. Every recommendation above was derived to answer “how do we fly without the animals reacting?” — and a deterrence mission must operate inside the reaction envelope, because being reacted to is the point. Part IV made this inversion argument once already, to explain why the survey literature’s standoff numbers could neither validate nor indict a close-range deterrent design. This chapter has to hold both halves of that argument honestly. The inversion means the 40–100 m figures are not a rulebook the running example is guilty of breaking. It does not mean the literature has nothing to say. The physiological findings — what proximity, geometry, and repetition do to an animal’s stress state — describe the animal, not the mission, and they transfer entirely. A deterrence system is exempt from the survey literature’s objectives. It is not exempt from its biology.

title: 28  The Ethics and Ecology of Autonomous Wildlife Management
section: 28.4 The Case of the Three-Metre Orbit
text:
28.4 The Case of the Three-Metre Orbit
Now the number. The Harassment Pattern Generation chapter taught the orbit pattern with a design band of 8–15 m radius, and disclosed, candidly but as a simulation-versus-field sizing note, that the shipped harassment_node.py defaults to orbit_radius_m = 3.0. This chapter re-opens that disclosure, because the full record is worse than a mismatch between a default and a recommendation, and it deserves to be laid out plainly, item by item, from the running example’s own artifacts.
The running example’s design documentation — the same document that specified the 8–15 m orbit band Part IV taught — does not merely prefer larger radii. Discussing how closely the navigation behavior should ever approach the birds, it prescribes a horizontal keep-out buffer of roughly 5–8 m, and then flags the region inside it in as many words: “If you get closer than 3–4 meters, you risk a bird-strike (which damages the drone and harms the wildlife) or causes the geese to scatter in panic instead of moving controllably.” Two pages later, specifying the harasser behavior itself, the same document recommends starting “outside the goose’s likely flush distance… a common practical starting point for hazing drones is roughly 8–15 m radius,” explicitly noting that a bigger radius is safer and the parameter should be field-tuned. The shipped code defaults to exactly 3.0 m: inside the document’s own flagged bird-strike-and-panic zone, three to five times tighter than the same document’s own recommendation, with no recorded rationale for the override.
And the radius is not the only discrepancy — it is one of three, and every one of them points the same direction. The design documentation says to hold the drone slightly above the goose’s cruising altitude, not level with it — a deliberate vertical offset, consistent with the approach-angle literature’s finding that geometry modulates threat. The shipped orbit_altitude_m is a fixed 3.0 m above ground, derived from nothing about the target’s actual height; the “slightly above, not level” intent simply is not implemented. The documentation specifies that the harasser’s termination criterion is behavioral — the engagement ends when the goose has left, with time and attempt limits as backstops (its own suggested caps: ten revolutions or five minutes). The shipped node implements only the backstop: elapsed >= orbit_duration_s, fifteen seconds, with the goose’s actual response read nowhere in the file. The one termination mode the design document called out as what makes a harasser a harasser — did the animal actually move? — is the one that did not ship. Three specified safety-relevant behaviors; three shipped simplifications; all three spending margin the design had explicitly reserved.
How bad is 3 m, concretely? The design document’s 3–4 m threshold is, it must be said, the project’s own engineering judgment — no source in the published literature supplies a validated “bird-strike distance,” and this book will not launder an internal estimate into an empirical fact. But independent data brackets the number from both sides, and none of it is comforting. On the collision side: a Canada goose spans up to about 1.85 m of open wing, so a 3 m orbit radius is less than two wingspans from the bird’s center — a bird that flares, lunges, or startles into flight can close a metre in a fraction of a second, the flock-center estimate carries the half-metre-scale uncertainty priced in the Coordinate Frames chapter, and the aircraft tracks its setpoints imperfectly in wind. Three error sources, each a large fraction of a metre, sharing roughly a metre of true clearance. On the stress side, the most directly on-species data available comes from a controlled study of Canada geese responding to an approaching vehicle: geese showed alert responses at mean distances of roughly 88–120 m and took flight at measured flight-initiation distances of 38.6 m (tangential approach) to 70.9 m (direct approach), with 80 % of directly approached geese choosing flight over walking (Blackwell et al. 2019). A ground vehicle is not a drone, and the study’s absolute numbers should not be quoted as drone FIDs — but as a same-species baseline for where a Canada goose decides an approaching object is a threat worth fleeing, the comparison is stark: even the lowest measured FID, under the least alarming geometry tested, is thirteen times the shipped orbit radius. The closest documented drone approach that did not disturb birds — 4 m, in the study the review cites — was a single, careful, slow lateral pass under favorable conditions (Vas et al. 2015; Afridi et al. 2025); the shipped configuration holds station at 3 m continuously, circling, for the full engagement. And the tight radius degrades the geometry too: at 3 m radius and 3 m altitude the drone sits at an elevation angle of
\[
\beta = \arctan\!\left(\frac{h}{R}\right) = \arctan\!\left(\frac{3.0}{3.0}\right) = 45^{\circ}
\]
above the bird’s horizon — halfway to the overhead position the approach-angle literature identifies as maximally threatening — where the design band’s geometry (\(R = 12\) m, \(h = 6\) m) puts it at a distinctly lateral \(27^{\circ}\). The tight orbit is not just closer; it is closer and steeper, the two aggravating factors compounding. Figure 28.1 puts every number in this section on one linear scale, and the picture makes the argument faster than the paragraph does: the shipped radius is not near the bottom of the debated range. It is an order of magnitude below the entire conversation.






Figure 28.1: Every distance in this chapter’s argument, drawn to one linear scale: the shipped 3 m orbit radius sits inside the design documentation’s own flagged danger zone, an order of magnitude below measured Canada-goose flight-initiation distances and the disturbance-avoidance literature’s recommendations. The inset magnifies the first 16 m, where the entire shipped-versus-designed discrepancy lives.



Part IV offered the standard defense, and it should be weighed rather than repeated: the defaults are sized for the simulation world the node was validated in, where the goose is a scripted asset and nothing has a heartbeat, and a field deployment would set the parameters into the design band through the ROS 2 parameter system built for exactly that purpose. Every word of that is true, and it is not enough. Defaults are what ship. Decades of deployed-systems experience — and this book’s own Part II — say that the path of least resistance becomes the fielded configuration, which is precisely why the fail-safe doctrine puts systems in their safe state by default and requires deliberate action to leave it. The harassment node inverts that doctrine: its default is the configuration its own design documentation flags as dangerous, and reaching the safe configuration requires someone to remember, understand, and act. A parameter file is not a safety argument. And there is a subtler cost: because the node reads the goose’s behavior nowhere, the system cannot even notice the consequences its design document predicted. If a 3 m orbit produces exactly the panic scatter the documentation warned of, the node completes its fifteen seconds, publishes done, and logs a success. The discrepancy is not only that the system may cause the failure mode its designers named — it is that the system, as shipped, is structurally incapable of finding out.
One more honest note, because this chapter’s credibility depends on it: no published study measures flight-initiation or injury outcomes for an orbiting multirotor at single-digit ranges from geese, and the harassment-pattern literature’s central gap — no validated minimum approach distance exists for a deliberate deterrence mission — cuts in every direction. The literature’s silence does not convict the 3 m default. But silence is not a defense either, and this is the crux: when the external literature is silent, the only anchor a project has is its own documented engineering judgment — and here the project’s own judgment did supply an answer, twice, in the same document, and the shipped code overrode it without explanation. That, precisely, is the ethics finding. Not that an engineer chose a number the literature cannot check, but that the system’s single most welfare-relevant parameter ended up inside its own project’s flagged danger zone through what the artifacts suggest was nothing more deliberate than a default nobody revisited.

title: 28  The Ethics and Ecology of Autonomous Wildlife Management
section: 28.5 A Rubric Instead of a Shrug: The Five Domains
text:
28.5 A Rubric Instead of a Shrug: The Five Domains
The instinctive vocabulary for what the previous section found — “too close,” “risky,” “not great for the goose” — is not analysis, and a chapter that stopped there would be doing the ad hoc hand-wringing it promised to avoid. Animal-welfare science has a structured instrument for exactly this evaluation. The Five Domains model, developed and refined since the 1990s as the successor to the older “Five Freedoms” checklist, assesses an animal’s welfare across four physical domains — (1) nutrition, (2) physical environment, (3) health, (4) behavior — whose states feed a fifth, integrative domain: (5) the animal’s mental state, the affective experience that is welfare’s actual currency (Mellor 2016). The model’s design insight is that the first four domains are what an engineer can observe and influence, while the fifth is what ethically matters; running a design through the domains one at a time turns “is this cruel?” into five smaller, answerable questions. Run the harassment mission through it.
Nutrition. Every engagement interrupts foraging, and geese manage tight daily energy budgets — the review’s discussion of threat-sensitive foraging notes that disturbance costs compound for animals already near energy deficit (Afridi et al. 2025). A fifteen-second orbit costs little; the relevant dose is the season’s interruptions, which is why per-flock engagement counting (an aggregate no current node computes) belongs in the system’s telemetry, not just its ethics chapter.
Physical environment. Displacement from chosen ground is not a side effect of this mission; it is the mission. The Five Domains lens does not forbid that — wildlife management displaces animals routinely — but it insists the displacement be to somewhere: the herding corridor’s open exit, toward viable habitat, is what separates relocation from mere eviction. Part IV’s escape-route preservation rule is, in this framework, a Domain 2 obligation.
Health. This is where the 3 m default fails outright: collision risk on the order of a wingspan, panicked flight into structures or each other, and the physiological load that does not announce itself — the review documents significant cardiac stress responses in animals that showed no visible behavioral change at all (Afridi et al. 2025). An operator watching a calm-looking flock through the running example’s own camera has no evidence the geese are experiencing the encounter calmly.
Behavior. The model asks whether the animal can express its normal behavioral repertoire — here, whether it can execute a controlled, oriented escape. And this is the domain where the design documentation’s own language turns out to be welfare science without the citation: geese that “scatter in panic instead of moving controllably” are geese denied exactly this domain. Controlled pressure and panic are not rhetorical opposites; they are adjacent regions on Domain 4’s spectrum, and the orbit radius is the parameter that selects between them.
Mental state. The integration: is the cumulative experience a brief, tolerable “moved along,” or a repeated fear experience from a threat that returns daily and cannot be predicted or appeased? The honest answer is that the field does not know — chronic-exposure effects are the review’s declared biggest gap — and a system designed today should therefore log what a future answer will need: engagement counts, response intensities, return times, per flock, per season.
Two framework notes complete the toolkit. First, the review itself reaches for the Three Rs — replacement, reduction, refinement — the ethical framework governing laboratory animal research (Fenwick, Griffin, and Gauthier 2009; Afridi et al. 2025). For research drones the mapping works: replace a live approach with a pre-recorded cue, reduce flights, refine procedures to minimize stress. For a deterrence mission it fails structurally, and the chapter should say so rather than force it: a harassment mission cannot be “refined” toward not disturbing the animal, because non-disturbance is mission failure, not welfare success. The Three Rs assume the animal’s distress is orthogonal to the objective; here it is the objective. Second, for the decision this framework cannot make — whether to run the mission at all — wildlife management has its own purpose-built process: a practical ethics-assessment framework developed specifically to let wildlife managers weigh ethical considerations alongside biological and social evidence in a concrete management decision (Smith et al. 2024). The Five Domains model evaluates the animal’s side of a design; the management framework structures the institutional decision. A serious deployment of the Goose Management System would run through both — and the Try It at the end of this chapter has the reader do exactly that in miniature.

title: 28  The Ethics and Ecology of Autonomous Wildlife Management
section: 28.6 Legal Is Not the Same as Right
text:
28.6 Legal Is Not the Same as Right
The Airspace Law chapter drew this book’s regulatory floor: Part 107, the compliance chain, the principle that an organization’s own rules must exceed the FAA minimum because the FAA manages airspace hazards, not your hazards. This section extends that principle to its sharpest case, because for wildlife the gap between the legal floor and the ethical question is not a margin — it is a chasm, and the running example sits in the middle of it.
Start with the striking fact: the harassment mission, as designed and even as shipped, is very probably entirely legal. The Migratory Bird Treaty Act — the century-old federal statute protecting Canada geese among a thousand other species — prohibits “take”: killing, capturing, hunting, selling, transporting. Non-contact harassment that stresses a bird, or even nearly collides with it, is not take so long as no bird is actually injured. And below the federal layer, state wildlife agencies consistently advise that scaring, repelling, or herding Canada geese — with dogs, noise, visual deterrents, and by extension drones — requires no permit at all, provided the birds are not touched, injured, or killed. A drone orbiting a goose at three metres, inside its own design team’s flagged bird-strike zone, is breaking no wildlife law on the available evidence. Whatever is wrong with the 3 m default, a regulator is not coming to fix it. Part 107 governs the aircraft; nothing in the running example’s compliance chain so much as mentions the animal.
Now the comparison that gives the distinction teeth. U.S. wildlife law does contain a precise legal definition of harassment — in the Endangered Species Act’s implementing regulations. Under 50 CFR § 17.3, to “harass” a protected animal is to commit “an intentional or negligent act or omission which creates the likelihood of injury to wildlife by annoying it to such an extent as to significantly disrupt normal behavioral patterns which include, but are not limited to, breeding, feeding, or sheltering.” Read that against the running example. An intentional act: the mission state machine literally has a state named HARASS_TARGET. Likelihood of injury: a 3 m orbit inside a flagged bird-strike zone. Significant disruption of feeding and sheltering: that is the mission’s success criterion. The Goose Management System’s core behavior is, nearly word for word, the thing this regulation defines as a federal wildlife crime — with one decisive difference: the definition applies only to species listed as threatened or endangered, and the Canada goose, abundant to the point of nuisance, is not listed. Fly the identical harassment_node.py profile, at the identical radius, against a whooping crane or a piping plover, and the same fifteen seconds of flight plausibly becomes a federal offense. Against a goose it is a Tuesday.
Sit with what that asymmetry means. Nothing about the act changes between those two flights — the same aircraft, the same orbit, the same stress inflicted on a bird of roughly the same neurology. What changes is a listing status, a decision made on population-conservation grounds: there are too few whooping cranes for any to be expendable, and more than enough geese. The law is tracking species scarcity, which is a perfectly rational thing for conservation law to track — and is simply not the same quantity as the humaneness of the act, which does not vary with the population count of the animal experiencing it. “It’s legal” therefore answers a question this chapter is not asking. The legal system has deliberately declined to regulate the welfare of individual non-listed wild animals against non-contact harassment; the ethics of doing it are exactly as open as they were before the statute book was consulted.
Other jurisdictions have built regulatory structure closer to the ethical question, and the review documents the pattern: a dual-permission model, in which flying a drone near wildlife requires both the aviation authority’s operational permit and a separate, conservation-specific approval from the wildlife agency responsible for the area and species — the review’s worked example, a Kenyan conservancy, requires national aviation clearance plus approvals from three separate wildlife and research bodies before any conservation drone flies (Afridi et al. 2025). The structural insight travels even where the requirement does not: the aviation gate and the wildlife gate ask different questions, and passing the first says nothing about the second. An organization deploying the Goose Management System under U.S. law faces only the aviation gate — which is an argument for building the second gate institutionally, exactly as the Airspace Law chapter argued organizations must build rules stricter than the FAA’s: a written wildlife-impact review, run through a framework like the previous section’s, signed by someone accountable for the animals the way the RPIC is accountable for the aircraft. The law supplies no such person. The design review must.
